LAW302 Conflict of Laws

Every J and C lesson put to work on made-up facts: the rule, a hypothetical, then the application, hidden until you have tried it yourself. 325 hypotheticals, 44 flowcharts and 80 test questions. The rules are taught in the LAW302 lessons.

Question 1 · Jurisdiction, injunctions and foreign judgments

J1HYPOS · Q1 · J1
Clause triage: what the jurisdiction clause promises, and the CCAA
Read the jurisdiction clause first and ask what it promises. That tells you who, if anyone, is in breach, and breach decides the test later (strong cause or Spiliada). If the Hague Convention applies through the CCAA, it overrides everything: the chosen court must hear the case and other courts must step aside.
57 hypotheticals · 7 flowcharts · 8 questions
J2HYPOS · Q1 · J2
Existence when the defendant is in Singapore: service in and submission
The court has jurisdiction as of right over a defendant served in Singapore or who submits. For every route, name two things together: the founding provision (which part of s 16 SCJA) and the mode of service (which rule). Only a never-registered foreign company needs the Adams v Cape presence test.
38 hypotheticals · 5 flowcharts · 8 questions
J3HYPOS · Q1 · J3
Existence when the defendant is abroad: service out
A defendant outside Singapore can be brought in only through O 8: without approval if the contract allows service out, otherwise with approval on the "appropriate court" ground, where the claimant must show (a) a good arguable case of nexus through a para 63(3) factor, (b) Singapore is forum conveniens, and (c) a serious question to be tried.
46 hypotheticals · 6 flowcharts · 8 questions
J4HYPOS · Q1 · J4
Exercise: Spiliada, forum conveniens and strong cause
Once the court has jurisdiction, ask whether it should use it. If someone broke a jurisdiction clause, the party in breach must show strong cause. If no one did, run Spiliada: is another forum clearly more appropriate (stage 1), and would the claimant be denied substantial justice there (stage 2)? Who bears the burden depends on service in or out, and stay or set-aside.
29 hypotheticals · 5 flowcharts · 8 questions
J5HYPOS · Q1 · J5
The SICC: written agreements, transfer and joinder
The SICC is a division of the High Court for international commercial cases. A case gets there in three ways: a written jurisdiction agreement (primary jurisdiction), transfer from the General Division ("more appropriate"), or joinder. Once there under a written agreement, Spiliada and strong cause disappear: the SICC declines only if hearing the case is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of process.
17 hypotheticals · 6 flowcharts · 8 questions
J6HYPOS · Q1 · J6
Anti-suit injunctions: stopping a party suing abroad
An ASI is an order against a person, not a foreign court, telling it to stop suing abroad. Name your basis first, because the elements differ. Contractual: amenability, breach of the clause, no strong reasons. Vexation: amenability, sufficient interest (usually natural forum), vexation, no undue injustice. Abuse of process: amenability and Singapore's self-evident interest in protecting its own process.
28 hypotheticals · 7 flowcharts · 8 questions
J7HYPOS · Q1 · J7
Foreign judgments: enforcement, recognition and AEIs
First ask whether the party wants to enforce the foreign judgment (a sword, to recover money) or have it recognised (a shield, or an estoppel). Then pick the regime: CCAA if the foreign court was the chosen court in a Hague case; REFJA is not examinable; otherwise the common law, where the judgment must be on the merits, from a court with international jurisdiction (presence or submission), final and conclusive, and for a definite sum, with no defence such as fraud, natural justice or public policy.
33 hypotheticals · 8 flowcharts · 8 questions

Question 2 · Choice of law

C1HYPOS · Q2 · C1
Choice of law methodology: characterise, connect, apply
Choice of law is a three-step machine: characterise the issue (contract? tort? property? procedure?), pick the connecting factor for that category, and apply the law it points to. Procedure always stays with Singapore law. Foreign law must be pleaded and proved like a fact; if no one pleads it, Singapore law applies. Two overlays can override the chosen law: Singapore's mandatory rules and its fundamental public policy.
24 hypotheticals · 8 questions
C2HYPOS · Q2 · C2
Contract choice of law: the proper law and illegality
A contract is governed by its proper law, found in three stages: an express choice (virtually conclusive if bona fide, legal and not against public policy), else an implied choice, else the law of closest and most real connection. Formation, form and capacity have their own rules. Illegality can enter by seven routes: the proper law, forum public policy, Foster v Driscoll, Lemenda, Ralli Brothers, tainting, and reliance as a defence.
27 hypotheticals · 8 questions
C3HYPOS · Q2 · C3
Tort choice of law: double actionability and the flexible exception
A tort claim must be actionable under BOTH Singapore law (as if everything happened here) AND the law of the place where the tort was in substance committed. The claimant proves the first limb; the defendant must plead and prove that the foreign law gives no liability. A strictly applied flexible exception can displace either law, or both, where it is purely fortuitous.
26 hypotheticals · 8 questions

LAW301 Legal Theory and Philosophy

Rules seem clear until you have to apply them. Each hypo lesson takes one section of your sheet and puts every block to work on made-up facts: the rule as the sheet states it, a hypothetical, then the application, which stays hidden until you have tried it yourself. 286 hypotheticals in all, covering all 155 numbered blocks of the Core and Theorist versions, with 256 quick-check questions.

1HYPOS · SECTION 1
Engine (map, menus, distinctions, self-critique, ledger)
The engine is technique, not theory: a map to find your blocks, menus to open and frame, distinctions to cut a statement, and a ledger to finish.
14 min · 8 questions
2HYPOS · ARCHETYPE 2
LP v NLT, and why theory matters
Naming something "law" is an evaluation, so the choice between LP and NLT is a live one. Hard cases such as Riggs turn on a theory of law's grounds.
48 min · 20 questions
3HYPOS · ARCHETYPE 3
Rule of law and Fuller
The rule of law is a real but thin morality. It binds rulers and comes in degrees, but it cannot guarantee just laws.
29 min · 19 questions
4HYPOS · ARCHETYPE 4
Moral objectivity and scepticism
The sceptic's case is inconclusive, and its own demands presuppose moral truth. So the sceptic's conclusion fails. Fallibility calls for deliberation and provisional judgement, not for tolerance as dogma, or silence.
22 min · 14 questions
5HYPOS · ARCHETYPE 5
Finnis for law-makers
Finnis gives legislators real limits on the issue, and leaves much to prudence.
27 min · 15 questions
6HYPOS · ARCHETYPE 6
Pluralist legislation, Rawls v Finnis
No law on the issue is neutral. Its reasons must be accessible to every citizen, sound on the merits and fitted to circumstances.
33 min · 20 questions
7HYPOS · ARCHETYPE 7
Enforcement of morals
Every answer to whether law should enforce morality, repeal included, takes a moral stand. The real question is which reasons justify which degree of coercion.
32 min · 20 questions
8HYPOS · ARCHETYPE 8
Unjust laws, Radbruch and retroactivity
An unjust law stays law unless it is intolerably unjust. But validity never settles whether the judge or citizen should obey it.
32 min · 16 questions
9HYPOS · ARCHETYPE 9
Adjudication (Dworkin, ALR, CLS)
The statement overstates. Judges justify by fit and political morality, and rules leave some cases open, not all.
28 min · 16 questions
10HYPOS · ARCHETYPE 10
Lawyering (Pepper, Thunder, Kennedy)
The statement fails. The lawyer's role is moral. Law sets a floor, and prudence, dialogue and rare objection decide the hard cases above it.
28 min · 17 questions
11HYPOS · ARCHETYPE 11
Constitution and judicial role
The statement is overstated. The Constitution relocates, rather than settles, the NLT v LP debate. Courts should presume a law valid, save at intolerable injustice.
29 min · 16 questions
12HYPOS · ARCHETYPE 12
Roles, who decides
The statement is right as a presumption. Roles have limits, but where they lie is contested, and abdication is a vice too.

LAW302 · HYPO LESSON J1 · 57 HYPOTHETICALS · 7 FLOWCHARTS · 8 QUESTIONS

J1 hypotheticals: Clause triage: what the jurisdiction clause promises, and the CCAA

The rules behind these hypotheticals are taught in Lesson J1, where the word-for-word pre-write is too. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

Applications:
ℹ HOW TO USE THESE HYPOTHETICALS

Each concept is set out as Rule, then Hypothetical, then Application. "Variation" lines flip one fact so you can see how the answer moves. Section numbers follow the J1 notes. (+) helps the party relying on the clause; (−) helps the party resisting it.

The flowcharts redraw the hypotheticals in this site's chart style: the chip on each arrow names the hypothetical (or version) that takes that path. The hypo test at the end checks you can run the facts yourself.

1J1.0 The regime router

Rule: There are three regimes: (1) the General Division at common law (J2 to J4), (2) the CCAA (J1.2 to J1.4), and (3) the SICC (J5). Within its scope the CCAA displaces both of the others. The SICC displaces Spiliada for cases heard there. "Not every Convention case will be an SICC case, and not every SICC case will be a Convention case" (Yeo). Run the CCAA first, then the SICC, and fall back on the common law. At common law, ask two questions: is anyone in breach, and who bears the burden?

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Lionfish's Three Contracts

Lionfish Trading Pte Ltd, a Singapore company, signs three contracts in 2022:

  • (a) A supply contract with Bergmann GmbH (Germany): "The Singapore High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction."
  • (b) A loan from Kestrel Bank plc (England): "The Borrower submits to the exclusive jurisdiction of the English courts; the Lender may sue the Borrower in any other competent court."
  • (c) A mining offtake with Ruritania Ore SA: "The parties submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the SICC."

Disputes arise under all three, and Lionfish sues in Singapore on each.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) is a CCAA case. The clause is exclusive, designates one Contracting State, was concluded after 1 October 2016, and the case is international and commercial. Singapore must hear it (s 11; J1.3), so Spiliada and strong cause drop out (C&Y). A post-2016 "Singapore High Court" clause includes the SICC (s 2(2)–(3) CCAA; O 2 r 2(1) SICC Rules). The CCAA decides whether Singapore hears the case; the SICC Rules decide where internally, subject to s 11(5) and O 2 r 4(4) (J5.4). If it stays in the General Division, it is a Convention case that is not an SICC case.
  • (b) is not a CCAA case, because an asymmetric clause is not exclusive (CHLOE V; J1.2.1). There is no SICC agreement, so the common law applies. Breach: Lionfish (the restricted party) sues outside England, so it breaches its England-only promise and bears strong cause (J4.3).
  • (c) is an SICC case by written jurisdiction agreement (J5.2). It is not a Convention case, because the clause is expressly non-exclusive, which displaces both s 3(2) and the s 18F presumption. This is Yeo's point in reverse.

2J1.1 Characterising the clause

J1.1(a) The Three Promises

Rule: A choice of court agreement may contain:

  • (1A) a promise to submit to the chosen court;
  • (1B) a promise not to object to its exercise of jurisdiction (e.g., on FNC grounds); and
  • (2) a promise not to sue anywhere else.

(1A) and (1B) are prorogation; (2) is derogation. An EJC contains all three. Per Bambang Sutrisno (in Shanghai Turbo (CA)), a NEJC contains (1A) but not (2). Whether a NEJC contains (1B) is a matter of construction under its proper law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Durian Export Deal

Musang Fruits Sdn Bhd (Malaysia) sells durians to Orchard Gourmet Pte Ltd (Singapore). The contract says: "All disputes shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Malaysia." A shipment arrives rotten. Orchard Gourmet sues in Singapore. Separately, Musang sues Orchard Gourmet in Kuala Lumpur for the price, and Orchard Gourmet applies in KL for a stay on the basis that Singapore is the more convenient forum.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This is an EJC, so it contains all three promises. By suing in Singapore, Orchard Gourmet breaches promise (2) (not to sue elsewhere). By objecting in KL on FNC grounds, it also breaches promise (1B) (not to object to the chosen court). Breach is what moves the burden: in Singapore, Orchard Gourmet will have to show strong cause (J4.3).

  • Variation: If the clause read "non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Malaysia", suing in Singapore would breach nothing, because a NEJC has no promise (2) (Bambang Sutrisno). Whether objecting in KL breaches (1B) would depend on the clause's proper law (J1.1.2).

J1.1(b) How Exclusivity Is Decided

Rule: Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), the clause is construed under its governing law, but its effect on Singapore's jurisdiction is for the lex fori. Per C&Y, "exclusive" is the conclusion, not the starting point. Labels get their ordinary meaning, but many clauses are unlabelled, paired with an FNC waiver, or asymmetric.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Jakarta Warehouse Lease

A lease governed by Indonesian law between a Singapore tenant and an Indonesian landlord says: "The District Court of South Jakarta shall have jurisdiction." It has no "exclusive" label. The tenant sues in Singapore. The landlord says the clause is exclusive.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Singapore asks what the clause means under Indonesian law, which is its proper law. If an expert shows Indonesian law reads "shall have jurisdiction" as mandatory and exclusive, the clause is an EJC. Whatever the meaning, Singapore law (the lex fori) decides the consequence: the tenant, having breached, must show strong cause. The missing label does not decide the case either way, because exclusivity is a conclusion of construction. If Indonesian law is not proved, the presumption of similarity applies and Singapore construction governs.

J1.1(c) Wording Indicators

Rule: "Exclusively" → EJC. "Shall be heard by" → mandatory, so likely exclusive under the proper law. "May be referred to" or "submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of" → NEJC.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Draft Clauses

A trainee shows you three drafts for a Thai hotel contract:

  1. "Disputes shall be heard by the courts of Bangkok."
  2. "Disputes may be referred to the courts of Bangkok."
  3. "Disputes shall be submitted exclusively to the courts of Bangkok."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(3) is plainly an EJC. (1) is mandatory ("shall be heard"), so it is likely exclusive under its proper law, and a claimant who sues in Singapore probably faces strong cause. (2) is permissive ("may"), so it is a NEJC: suing in Singapore is no breach, and Spiliada applies.

J1.1(d) SICC Clauses and s 18F

Rule: If the clause names the SICC, s 18F SCJA presumes it exclusive unless there are express contrary words. Whether s 18F applies where foreign law governs a non-CCAA clause is debated (J5.2.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Quiet SICC Clause

A Singapore company and a Malaysian contractor sign a construction contract in March 2016, governed by English law: "Disputes shall be resolved by the Singapore International Commercial Court." Because the clause predates 1 October 2016, the CCAA does not apply (J1.2.2). One party sues in the General Division.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

On its face, s 18F presumes the SICC clause exclusive because there are no express contrary words. Suing in the General Division would then breach the clause, and the internal allocation is handled under J5. (±) The other side argues that English law governs the clause and the CCAA does not apply, so it is debated whether s 18F (a Singapore statute) should decide exclusivity at all instead of English-law construction (J5.2.2).

J1.1.1 Singapore NEJC: The Contractual Approach (must write)

Rule: Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), adopting Noble Power, Singapore takes the contractual approach (left open in Orchard Capital). It does not take the general approach, under which a NEJC is merely a Spiliada factor. Under Singapore law, "submit" means consenting to the named court's jurisdiction and waiving any objection to its exercise (Yeo's "narrow waiver of objection"). Otherwise the clause would be "devoid of purpose" (Briggs, adopted in Shanghai Turbo (CA)), and this holds even if Singapore had no jurisdiction without the clause. Consequence: any challenge by the defendant (setting aside service or a stay, even in favour of another named court) is an attempt to escape the clause, so the defendant must show strong cause. High Court cases that treated a Singapore NEJC as a mere Spiliada factor were wrongly decided. The CA went "one step further" than Bambang Sutrisno, whose clause had an express FNC waiver. Open: whether the same applies to standard-form or non-negotiated contracts; by analogy with Vinmar, probably yes.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Shenzhen Joint Venture

Merlion Capital Pte Ltd and Dragon Gate Ltd (PRC) sign a Singapore-law joint venture agreement: "Each party irrevocably submits to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore." Dragon Gate has no presence in Singapore, and every asset and witness is in Shenzhen. Merlion sues in Singapore and serves Dragon Gate in China. Dragon Gate applies to set aside service, arguing that China is clearly the more appropriate forum, and points to older High Court decisions that treated a Singapore NEJC as just one Spiliada factor.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Under Singapore law, by agreeing to "submit", Dragon Gate waived any objection to Singapore's exercise of jurisdiction. That is the narrow waiver. Its set-aside application is therefore an attempt to escape the clause, so Dragon Gate must show strong cause (J4.3); Merlion does not have to prove Singapore is forum conveniens. It does not matter that Singapore would have had no jurisdiction over Dragon Gate without the clause: the waiver is what gives the clause its purpose (Briggs). The older High Court cases were wrongly decided (Shanghai Turbo (CA)). Note that this clause had no express FNC waiver, unlike Bambang Sutrisno, yet the result is the same. That is the "one step further".

  • Variation (Open): If the NEJC were buried in Merlion's online standard terms, accepted by click-through, Shanghai Turbo (CA) left the point open. By analogy with Vinmar (strong cause applies to non-negotiated EJCs), the answer is probably still strong cause.
  • Variation (Several named courts): If the clause read "non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of the PRC or Singapore", Dragon Gate's application for a stay in favour of the PRC would still be an attempt to escape the Singapore limb, so strong cause still applies (J1.1.3).

J1.1.2 Proper Law and Foreign NEJCs

Rule (Proper Law of the NEJC, ±): Whether a NEJC contains promise (1B) is for its proper law. If foreign law is unproved, the presumption of similarity reads in the Singapore waiver. If foreign law is proved and implies no waiver, the clause contains only (1A), so the defendant's FNC objection is no breach and Spiliada applies (J4.1; J4.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ruritanian Rice Contract

A rice contract is governed by Ruritanian law and says: "The Buyer submits to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore." The Seller sues in Singapore. The Buyer seeks a stay in favour of Ruritania.

  • Version 1: Neither party adduces evidence of Ruritanian law.
  • Version 2: The Buyer's expert proves that, under Ruritanian law, "submit" means bare consent and implies no waiver of FNC objections.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Version 1: By the presumption of similarity, Ruritanian law is treated as identical to Singapore law, so the narrow waiver is read in. The Buyer's stay is a breach of (1B), and it bears strong cause.
  • Version 2: Under its proper law the clause contains only (1A). The Buyer's objection breaches nothing, so ordinary Spiliada applies. Because the Buyer was served in Singapore and seeks a stay, it bears the burden at stage 1 (J4.1). The two versions show how proof of foreign law can change who bears the burden.

Rule (Foreign NEJC: no breach either way): Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), the "wide waiver of objection" is rejected. Suing in Singapore despite a foreign NEJC is no breach. The defendant's objection is no breach either, as Singapore is not named. Plain Spiliada applies (J4.1). Weight: a foreign NEJC shows only that the foreign court is an appropriate forum, not clearly more appropriate, so it carries little weight. How much depends on whether it was closely negotiated or chosen for neutrality.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Phuket Villa Fit-Out

A Singapore contractor and a Thai developer agree: "Each party submits to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Thailand." The contractor sues in Singapore for unpaid fees; the developer seeks a stay, arguing that by agreeing to Thailand the contractor waived the right to sue elsewhere.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The developer's "wide waiver" argument is rejected (Shanghai Turbo (CA)). The contractor's suit is no breach (there is no promise (2)), and the developer's stay application is no breach (Singapore is not named). So plain Spiliada applies. The clause shows only that Thailand is an appropriate forum, so it carries little weight on the question whether Thailand is clearly more appropriate.

  • Variation: If the parties had haggled over the clause for weeks and picked Thailand as neutral ground, it would carry more weight, but it is still a factor, not a trump.

Rule (Drafting around the defaults, practice): For a Singapore NEJC without the waiver, add "without prejudice to each party's right to object on FNC grounds". To make a foreign NEJC bind, add a promise not to sue elsewhere.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Cautious Client

Your client wants Singapore available as a forum but wants to keep the right to argue FNC if it is sued there. A second client wants a Hong Kong NEJC that actually stops the counterparty suing in Singapore.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

For the first client, draft "The parties submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore, without prejudice to each party's right to object on grounds of forum non conveniens." This rebuts the Shanghai Turbo waiver, so a challenge goes to Spiliada. For the second client, add "and neither party shall commence proceedings in any court other than Hong Kong". This inserts promise (2), so the clause becomes exclusive in effect.

Rule (FNC Waiver, Bunge): Where a Singapore EJC carries an FNC waiver (e.g., "no Party will argue to the contrary"), grounds founded on convenience cannot amount to strong cause.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Palm Oil Witnesses

A Singapore EJC adds: "Each party agrees that the Singapore courts are the most appropriate forum and no Party will argue to the contrary." The defendant seeks a stay because all its witnesses and documents are in Indonesia.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Bunge, convenience-based grounds (witnesses, documents) cannot be strong cause where the defendant has expressly waived them. The stay fails. Only a non-convenience ground (e.g., an unforeseeable denial of justice) could even be argued.

J1.1.3 Floating and Multi-Forum Clauses

Rule: Per Shanghai Turbo (CA) and C&Y, a floating jurisdiction clause is valid at common law if it is not too uncertain. A floating choice of law clause is void (C2). A floating jurisdiction clause needs an election mechanism (e.g., one party's option, or a prescribed event).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Owner's Option

A charterparty says: "Disputes shall be referred to the courts of Singapore or England, as the Owner may elect by written notice within 30 days after a dispute arises."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The election mechanism (the Owner's notice) makes the clause sufficiently certain, so it is valid at common law. Once the Owner elects Singapore, the clause operates as a choice of Singapore.

Rule (Severance): Where a floating choice of law is coupled with a jurisdiction choice, the void law part is severable if the two are joined only by "and" and the contract has a severance clause (Shanghai Turbo (CA)). Contrast The Iran Vojdan, where the forum choice was parasitic on the law choice.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Two-Headed Clause
  • Clause A: "This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of Singapore or the PRC, and the courts of Singapore shall have jurisdiction." The contract also contains a severance clause.
  • Clause B: "Disputes shall be decided by the courts of whichever country's law the Owner selects as the governing law."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In Clause A, the floating law choice is void, but the jurisdiction choice stands on its own (joined by "and", with a severance clause), so it is severed and survives (Shanghai Turbo (CA)). In Clause B, the forum is defined by reference to the void law choice, so it is parasitic and falls with it (The Iran Vojdan).

Rule (No mechanism → both courts): Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), "Singapore/or PRC" with no election mechanism is a NEJC to both Singapore and the PRC, each party submitting to whichever court is seised. Letting the claimant elect at the moment of suit was rejected because it would encourage a race to sue. Several named fora: the waiver applies to each named forum, so a defendant's objection in either court is a breach.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Slash Clause

A JV agreement says: "Disputes shall be resolved by the courts of Singapore/or PRC." There is no election machinery. The claimant sues in Singapore. The defendant seeks a stay in favour of the PRC courts.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The clause is a NEJC to both Singapore and the PRC. The defendant submitted to Singapore once Singapore was seised, and the narrow waiver applies to each named forum. Its stay application is a breach, so it must show strong cause. It cannot argue that the claimant should not have been free to choose: the CA preferred the "both courts" reading precisely to avoid a race to sue that a "claimant elects" reading would encourage.

J1.1.4 Clause Bank Drill (handout exercise)

Rule summary:

  • Foreign EJC ("exclusively to the courts of X"; "exclusively to the courts of X or Y", i.e. two fora with all others excluded; "shall be heard by the courts of X"): a claimant suing in Singapore breaches, so the claimant bears strong cause, whether it served in (and the defendant seeks a stay) or served out.
  • Foreign NEJC ("may be heard by…"; "non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of X"): no breach, so Spiliada, with the burden set by service in or out and set-aside or stay.
  • Singapore NEJC ("non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore"; "of the courts of X or Singapore"): a defendant objecting breaches, so the defendant bears strong cause.
  • Asymmetric, with submission ("A may sue B in any court, B submitting to it; B may sue A only in Y"): if A sues in Singapore, B agreed to submit, so B bears strong cause to stay; if B sues in Singapore, B breaches its Y-only promise, so B bears strong cause.
  • Asymmetric, without submission (±): if A may merely sue B anywhere, without B submitting, A suing in Singapore is permitted, but B never agreed to submit, so B's stay goes to Spiliada (Week 10 handout). If B sues in Singapore, it still breaches the EJC for Y, so strong cause is on B.
  • Protective promise ("all submit to X; under no circumstances shall B be subjected to any other court"): A suing B in Singapore breaches the second limb, so strong cause is on A; B suing A in Singapore breaches nothing, so Spiliada.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Six Clauses, One Exam Morning

In each case, Claimant sues Defendant in Singapore and Defendant applies for a stay.

  1. "Exclusively to the courts of Hong Kong or Tokyo."
  2. "May be heard by the courts of Hong Kong."
  3. "Non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Hong Kong or Singapore."
  4. A loan: "Lender may sue Borrower in any court, and Borrower submits to the jurisdiction of any such court; Borrower may sue Lender only in Hong Kong." Lender is the Claimant.
  5. Same loan, but it says only "Lender may sue Borrower in any court" (no submission). Lender is the Claimant.
  6. "All parties submit to the courts of Hong Kong; under no circumstances shall the Guarantor be subjected to any other court." The Bank sues the Guarantor in Singapore.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Two fora are named and all others are excluded, so this is a foreign EJC. Claimant breaches and bears strong cause.
  2. Foreign NEJC, so no one is in breach. Spiliada; Defendant bears the stage 1 burden on a stay of a served-in action.
  3. A Singapore NEJC (the Shanghai Turbo pattern). Defendant objecting breaches the waiver and bears strong cause, even though it seeks a stay in favour of Hong Kong, another named court.
  4. Asymmetric with submission. Lender is permitted to sue anywhere, and Borrower agreed to submit, so Borrower's stay is an attempt to escape the clause and Borrower bears strong cause.
  5. Asymmetric without submission. Lender is permitted to sue in Singapore, but Borrower never promised to submit, so Borrower's stay is decided under Spiliada. (±) Lender argues that a submission is implied; Borrower replies that the clause omits one.
  6. Protective promise. The Bank's suit breaches the "under no circumstances" limb, so the Bank bears strong cause. Had the Guarantor sued the Bank in Singapore, no limb would be breached, so Spiliada would apply.

3J1.2 Does the CCAA apply? (s 8)

(Three principles: the chosen court must hear; a non-chosen court must decline; its judgment must be recognised (J7.5). Gateways: exclusive; one Contracting State; concluded after entry into force; international; civil or commercial. Write only the ones in issue.)

J1.2.1 Exclusive Choice of Court Agreement (s 3)

Rule (Express EJC, +): Per s 3(1), a clause is exclusive if, concluded in writing or by accessible electronic means, it designates the courts of one State for disputes in connection with the contract, to the exclusion of any other court.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The DocuSign Distribution Deal

A Singapore distributor and a Mexican manufacturer sign by DocuSign in 2021: "The courts of Mexico City shall have exclusive jurisdiction over any dispute in connection with this Agreement."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

It was concluded by electronic means that are accessible for later reference, it designates the courts of one Contracting State, and it excludes all others. This is an express exclusive agreement under s 3(1). Go on to check the remaining gateways (date, international, civil or commercial).

Rule (Deemed exclusive, +): Per s 3(2), a clause such as "the parties submit to the jurisdiction of the [State] courts" is deemed exclusive unless the parties expressly provide otherwise. At common law, the same unlabelled clause could go either way under its proper law (J1.1). Rebuttal (−): if the clause says "non-exclusive" or allows suit "in any other competent court", s 3(2) is displaced. Trap (Chong): where the facts call the clause non-exclusive, do not invoke s 3(2). The CCAA does not apply, and this is a recurring exam error.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Unlabelled Clause
  • Version 1: "The parties submit to the jurisdiction of the courts of England." (2020, Singapore buyer v English seller)
  • Version 2: "The parties submit to the jurisdiction of the courts of England, without prejudice to either party's right to sue in any other competent court."
  • Version 3: The exam question says: "The contract contains a non-exclusive English jurisdiction clause."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Version 1: Deemed exclusive under s 3(2), so the CCAA may apply, and Singapore must stay under s 12 unless an exception applies. Note the contrast: at common law, whether this clause is exclusive would be a question of English-law construction.
  • Version 2: The express "any other competent court" words displace s 3(2). The CCAA does not apply, so go to the common law (a foreign NEJC → Spiliada).
  • Version 3: The facts have already characterised the clause as non-exclusive. Do not argue s 3(2); state that the CCAA does not apply and move to the common law.

Rule (Asymmetric clause, −): Per CHLOE V, following the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (VCLT art 32), an asymmetric clause is not exclusive under the CCAA, so s 12 cannot be engaged, even on the court's own motion and even though a party conceded the point. Support: Etihad (EWCA) (obiter): the Convention probably excludes asymmetric clauses, as the Diplomatic Session rejected a Swiss proposal to cover clauses exclusive "for some or all of the parties". Counter (+): earlier first-instance dicta (Commerzbank v Liquimar; Etihad (EWHC)) read the wording as wide enough, but reliance on them is weak after CHLOE V. Consequence: at common law the clause stays exclusive against the restricted party (C&Y), so J1.1 applies.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Syndicated Loan Squeeze

Pelican Shipping Pte Ltd borrows from a syndicate led by Albion Bank. The facility agreement (2019) says: "The English courts have exclusive jurisdiction. This clause is for the benefit of the Lenders only; the Lenders may take proceedings in any other court with jurisdiction." Pelican sues Albion in Singapore for wrongful acceleration. Albion asks for a stay. At the hearing a concession is made on the CCAA point, and the judge considers whether to apply s 12 of her own motion.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The clause is asymmetric: exclusive for Pelican, open for the Lenders. Per CHLOE V, it is not an "exclusive choice of court agreement" under the CCAA, so s 12 is not engaged. The court cannot engage it of its own motion, and a party's concession does not change that. Albion's reliance on Commerzbank v Liquimar and Etihad (EWHC) is weak; Etihad (EWCA) and the rejected Swiss proposal point the other way. But Albion is not left without a remedy: at common law the clause is still exclusive against Pelican, the restricted party. Pelican is in breach, so it must show strong cause (J4.3).

Rule (Floating clause, ±): Where a clause lets a party choose between Court A and Court B, CCAA coverage is unclear (C&Y). (−) Before election there is no chosen court, so arguably no s 3(1) agreement exists. (+) Once notice of election is served, the clause crystallises into a mutually exclusive choice of Court A and is probably within the CCAA. Unilateral election (±): s 3 requires agreement between the parties, but arguably one party's election suffices where all parties agreed it could elect, or where the other party received written notice and did not object.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Charterer's Notice

A 2020 charterparty says: "Disputes shall be heard exclusively by the courts of Singapore or the courts of England, as the Charterer shall elect by notice." On 3 March 2024 the Charterer serves written notice electing Singapore. The Owner does not reply. On 1 April the Owner sues in England. In a mirror dispute, the Charterer sues in Singapore and the Owner seeks a stay in favour of England.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(+) The Charterer argues that after the 3 March notice the clause crystallised into an exclusive choice of Singapore, so the CCAA applies and Singapore must hear the case (s 11). The unilateral election suffices because both parties agreed in advance that the Charterer could elect, and the Owner received written notice and did not object. (−) The Owner argues that s 3 requires an agreement designating one court. At the time of contracting there was none, only a menu, so the clause is outside the CCAA and the common law applies. Either way, at common law the clause is valid (J1.1.3), and after the election the Owner's stay application would face strong cause.

Rule (More than one State, −): A clause designating "Singapore or England" is not a designation of the courts "of one Contracting State" (s 3(1)), so it is outside the CCAA, though it may be exclusive at common law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Two-Country Clause

"Disputes shall be submitted exclusively to the courts of Singapore or England." The claimant sues in Singapore; the defendant wants a mandatory s 11 / s 12 analysis.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Two States are named, so the clause is outside the CCAA. At common law it is an EJC for two fora with all others excluded (J1.1.4): suing in Singapore breaches nothing, and if the defendant objects to Singapore, it breaches the waiver attached to each named forum, so it bears strong cause.

Rule (Separability, +): Per s 5, the clause is independent of the contract, so its validity cannot be challenged solely because the contract is said to be void for misrepresentation or terminated.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Terminated Agency

A German principal terminates a Singapore agent and argues that the whole agency agreement (with its exclusive Singapore clause) was void for misrepresentation, so the clause falls with it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Under s 5 the clause is treated as an independent agreement. An attack on the main contract does not by itself touch the clause, so the principal must attack the clause directly.

J1.2.2 Contracting State and Date

Rule: The chosen court's State must be a Contracting State, and the clause must have been concluded after the HCCCA entered into force for it (Singapore: 1 October 2016). Check the HCCH status table. UK clauses (±): the HCCCA applied to the UK via the EU from 1 October 2015 and in its own right from 1 January 2021. Continuity across Brexit is contested, so an English clause concluded between those dates is arguable either way.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Old Clause and the Brexit Clause
  • Clause 1: An exclusive "Singapore High Court" clause in a contract signed on 15 June 2015.
  • Clause 2: An exclusive English courts clause signed on 1 March 2018 between a Singapore company and an English company. The Singapore company sues in Singapore in 2024.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Clause 1: It was concluded before 1 October 2016, so the CCAA does not apply to it as a Singapore choice. Singapore's jurisdiction rests on the common law: the claimant serves in or out, and the defendant's objection meets strong cause.
  • Clause 2 (±): (+) The defendant argues the HCCCA bound the UK via the EU from 2015, and the UK's 2021 accession continued that, so the clause is covered and Singapore must stay under s 12. (−) The claimant argues that the UK's own entry into force was 1 January 2021, so a 2018 clause predates it and is outside the CCAA, which leaves common law strong cause. Flag the contest; the practical result may be similar either way because both routes favour a stay, but the tests differ (s 12 exceptions versus strong cause).

J1.2.3 International Case (s 4)

Rule: Per s 4(1), a case is international unless the parties reside in the same Contracting State and everything else, apart from the chosen court's location, is connected only with that State. Per s 6, a company resides at its statutory seat, place of incorporation, central administration or principal place of business. Wholly domestic (−): if both parties reside in Singapore and the contract was negotiated and performed wholly in Singapore, choosing a foreign court does not make the case international (C&Y).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Dutch Defendant and the Domestic Deal
  • Case A: Tembusu Logistics Pte Ltd sues Van Dijk BV (incorporated in the Netherlands) in Singapore on a contract with an exclusive Singapore clause.
  • Case B: Two Singapore companies sign, negotiate and perform an office-cleaning contract entirely in Singapore, but choose "the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of England". One sues in Singapore.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Case A: Under s 6, Van Dijk resides in the Netherlands (its place of incorporation). The parties do not reside in the same State, so the s 4(1) exception fails and the case is international.
  • Case B: Both parties reside in Singapore and every element is Singaporean. The only foreign element is the chosen court, which s 4(1) tells you to ignore. The case is not international, so the CCAA does not apply. The English clause still operates at common law: the claimant breached by suing in Singapore and faces strong cause.

J1.2.4 Civil or Commercial Matter (ss 9–10)

Rule: "Civil or commercial" has an autonomous meaning that mainly excludes public and criminal law (C&Y). Insurance is not excluded merely because of its subject matter (s 9(6)). Excluded: s 9(1) excludes consumer agreements and employment or collective agreements. s 9(2) excludes matters such as insolvency, carriage of goods, competition, personal injury, non-contractual property damage, rights in rem in land and IP validity. s 9(3) excludes arbitration. IP (±): non-contractual infringement of a patent or trade mark (not copyright) is excluded unless it could have been brought as a breach of contract between the parties. Preliminary question (+): per s 9(5), IP validity raised only as a preliminary question or defence does not exclude the case; per s 9(7), a State being a party does not exclude it either. Interim measures (+): per s 10, these are outside the CCAA, so Singapore may grant a Mareva or interim ASI whatever the chosen court.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Medtech Licensing Mess

Helix Devices Pte Ltd (Singapore) licenses a patented stent design from Sonora Labs SA de CV (Mexico) under a 2021 licence with an exclusive Mexico City courts clause. The licence includes a product liability insurance clause. The following claims arise in Singapore:

  1. Sonora sues Helix for unpaid royalties. Helix's defence is that the patent is invalid.
  2. Sonora sues Helix for patent infringement after the licence was terminated, for sales made outside the licence's scope.
  3. A Singapore patient sues Helix for personal injury caused by a defective stent.
  4. Helix's insurer, Lion City Insurance, sues Sonora under an indemnity in the licence.
  5. Sonora, before suing in Mexico, applies in Singapore for a Mareva over Helix's Singapore bank accounts.
  6. The Ministry of Health, as a party, sues Sonora under a government procurement side agreement containing the same clause.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Within the CCAA. It is a commercial royalty claim. Patent validity is raised only as a defence or preliminary question, which does not exclude the case (s 9(5)). Singapore must stay under s 12.
  2. (±) Non-contractual patent infringement is excluded (s 9(2)), unless it could have been brought as a breach of the licence between the parties. Sonora argues that sales outside the licence's scope are a breach of the licence's field-of-use term, so the claim could have been framed in contract and is within the CCAA. Helix argues that post-termination sales are pure infringement, so the claim is excluded and goes to the common law.
  3. Excluded. Personal injury falls under s 9(2), and the patient is not a party to the clause anyway.
  4. Within the CCAA. Suing in Helix's shoes by subrogation, the insurer takes the benefit of the licence subject to the burden of its clause (Hai Jiang 1401; J1.5), and a claim under the licence indemnity is commercial. Section 9(6) (insurance is not excluded merely by its subject matter) is not the reason: this claim is under the licence, not an insurance contract.
  5. Outside the CCAA. Interim measures are excluded by s 10, so Singapore may grant the Mareva even though Mexico is the chosen court (J6.5.3).
  6. Not excluded merely because a State is a party (s 9(7)), as long as the matter itself is civil or commercial and not an exercise of public power.

J1.2.5 Validity, Existence and Capacity

Rule (Validity): Per ss 11(1) and 12(1)(a) and the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, validity is for the law of the chosen court's State, including its choice of law rules. This single reference point deters forum shopping. Example: if Singapore is chosen and the contract is governed by French law, Singapore's choice of law rules point to French law, and per s 5 the clause survives unless it is attacked directly. Existence (consent): the CCAA is silent, but per Hartley–Dogauchi (and C&Y), whether a party consented is also for the law of the chosen court, which avoids a split between validity and existence. Capacity: if the chosen court's law treats capacity as a matter of validity or existence, that law governs. As a non-chosen court, Singapore may also refuse a stay if the party lacked capacity under Singapore law (s 12(1)(b)). This is also a ground to refuse recognition (s 15(1)(b); J7.5).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The French Wine Distributor

Château Lavigne SARL and Grand Cru Pte Ltd sign a French-law distribution agreement with an exclusive Singapore High Court clause. Lavigne is sued in Singapore and argues: (1) the clause was signed under duress; (2) its signatory never consented to the jurisdiction clause because it was in a separate rider; (3) separately, in a Paris action, Grand Cru argues that its own signatory lacked capacity.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Validity: Singapore is the chosen court, so Singapore law including its choice of law rules decides. Those rules point to French law as the governing law. Duress in procuring the contract does not void the clause unless the duress is aimed at the clause itself (s 5).
  2. Existence: By Hartley–Dogauchi, consent to the rider is also tested under Singapore law including its choice of law rules, so the same reference point applies. Validity and existence are not split.
  3. Capacity: In Singapore, the chosen court, Grand Cru's capacity is tested under Singapore law including its choice of law rules, as part of validity or existence if that law treats it so. In the Paris action, France (an EU Contracting State) is a non-chosen court, so it applies its own version of s 12(1)(b): it may refuse to dismiss if Grand Cru lacked capacity under French law, including its choice of law rules. Reversed, Singapore as a non-chosen court would apply s 12(1)(b), and the same lack of capacity could defeat recognition of the chosen court's judgment (s 15(1)(b); J7.5).

4J1.3 Singapore is the chosen court (s 11)

Rule (Must hear, must write): Where the clause designates the Singapore High Court or the SICC and the CCAA applies, Singapore must not decline unless the clause is null and void under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules (s 11(1)). No FNC, no lis pendens: per s 11(2), Singapore cannot decline in favour of another State, so neither Spiliada nor strong cause applies, and per C&Y no other s 11(3) ground has been prescribed. Witnesses abroad, the governing law, or proceedings pending abroad are irrelevant.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Monterrey Witnesses

Jade Circuits Pte Ltd sues Monterrey Components SA (Mexico) in Singapore under a 2022 contract with an exclusive Singapore High Court clause. Monterrey seeks a stay: all 12 witnesses are in Mexico, the contract is governed by Mexican law, and Monterrey has already sued Jade in Monterrey for a negative declaration.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The CCAA applies (the clause is exclusive, Singapore and Mexico are both Contracting States, the clause post-dates entry into force, and the case is international and commercial). Under s 11(1)–(2) Singapore must hear the case. Spiliada, strong cause and lis pendens are all unavailable, and no s 11(3) ground has been prescribed, so the stay is dismissed. Monterrey's witnesses, the governing law and the Monterrey action are all irrelevant.

Rule (Null and void, −): A defendant may argue the clause is null and void (e.g., procured by fraud, or the defendant's agent lacked authority). That is for Singapore law including its choice of law rules (s 11(1)), and per s 5 the alleged invalidity of the contract does not by itself affect the clause.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Rogue Sales Manager

Monterrey (above) now argues that its sales manager had no authority to agree to a Singapore clause, so the clause is null and void. It also says the whole contract was induced by Jade's fraud about chip specifications.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Authority goes to the clause itself, so it is a proper s 11(1) argument, decided by Singapore law including its choice of law rules (e.g., the law governing the agent's authority). The fraud about specifications attacks the contract, not the clause. Under s 5 that does not affect the clause, so Singapore still must hear the case.

Rule (Internal allocation, ±): Per s 11(4), Singapore's rules on subject-matter, value and internal allocation are unaffected. But per s 11(5), on a discretionary transfer to another Singapore court, the court must take the parties' choice into account. Otherwise, per art 8(5) HCCCA, a foreign court may refuse recognition against a party that objected in time (J5.4.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Unwanted Transfer

The clause says "the Singapore International Commercial Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction." The claimant files in the General Division. The General Division considers transferring the case to the SICC, or vice versa, and the defendant objects in time.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Singapore may allocate internally (s 11(4)). On a discretionary transfer, though, it must give due weight to the parties' choice of the SICC (s 11(5)). If it ignores that choice over a timely objection, a judgment could be refused recognition in another Contracting State under art 8(5). Recognition abroad is the practical risk.

Rule (Serving abroad): General Division (+): the claimant seeks approval on the "has the jurisdiction" ground (O 8 r 1(1) ROC 2021), created partly for CCAA cases, so no nexus or forum conveniens inquiry arises (C&Y; J3.1.1). If the contract permits service out, no approval is needed (O 8 r 1(3); J3.1.5). Open (±): whether the defendant may still argue the claim is outside the CCAA, and so resist "has the jurisdiction", should be raised inter partes. SICC (+): no permission is needed to serve a party to the written jurisdiction agreement (O 5 r 6(2)(a) SICC Rules; J5.2.4).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Serving the Mexican Supplier

Jade must serve Monterrey in Mexico.

  • Route 1: The General Division, where the contract says nothing about service.
  • Route 2: The General Division, where the contract says "each party consents to service of process outside Singapore".
  • Route 3: The SICC under an SICC jurisdiction agreement.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Route 1: Jade applies for approval on the "Singapore has the jurisdiction" ground. Because the CCAA obliges Singapore to hear the case, there is no nexus gateway or forum conveniens inquiry. (±) Monterrey may argue inter partes that its claim is outside the CCAA (e.g., it is really a non-contractual patent claim), so the ground is not made out.
  • Route 2: Under O 8 r 1(3), no approval is needed at all.
  • Route 3: Under O 5 r 6(2)(a) SICC Rules, no permission is needed because Monterrey is a party to the written jurisdiction agreement.

5J1.4 Singapore is not the chosen court (s 12)

Rule (Must stay or dismiss, must write): Per s 12(1), "despite any other written law or rule of law", Singapore must stay or dismiss unless exception (a)–(e) applies. Per s 12(2), a stay on other grounds remains possible. Two stages (6DM): (1) Is there an exclusive agreement that does not designate a Singapore court for these proceedings? (2) Does an s 12(1) exception apply? Standard (6DM): at stage 1 the defendant must show a good arguable case, not the arbitration prima facie standard. This is because the CCAA has no kompetenz-kompetenz equivalent and no supervisory appeal structure, and a good arguable case matches the robust common law stay analysis.

J1.4.1 Stage 1: An EJC That Does Not Designate Singapore

Rule (Ambiguous clause, +): Similar to 6DM, where "the local courts" in an English-law distribution agreement meant England because the agreement renewed an earlier English-clause agreement on a related party's template, an ambiguous clause may be resolved by prior dealings, the template used or the governing law. (−) If the clause designates Singapore, is asymmetric or is non-exclusive, s 12 is not engaged (CHLOE V), and the stay is decided at common law: strong cause for an EJC, Spiliada for a foreign NEJC (J4).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"The Seller's Country"

Kopi King Pte Ltd (Singapore) has bought coffee machines from Brera Macchine Srl (Italy) for six years. Each year's contract is on Brera's template and has said "the courts of Milan shall have exclusive jurisdiction." The 2023 renewal, on the same template, was redrafted by a junior employee to say "the courts of the Seller's country shall have exclusive jurisdiction; this Agreement is governed by Italian law." Kopi King sues in Singapore, and Brera invokes s 12.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Stage 1: Brera must show a good arguable case (not merely prima facie) that there is an exclusive agreement for a court other than Singapore. Similar to 6DM ("the local courts" = England), the renewal context, Brera's template and the Italian governing law all point to "the Seller's country" meaning Italy. Brera has the better of the argument, so stage 1 is satisfied and the analysis moves to the exceptions.

  • Variation (−): If the clause said "the courts of the Seller's country or any other competent court", it would be non-exclusive. s 12 would not be engaged, and Kopi King's suit would be tested under Spiliada (J4).

J1.4.2 Stage 2: The Exceptions (s 12(1)(a)–(e))

Rule (Starter): Per Hartley–Dogauchi (and C&Y), exceptions (c) and (d) apply "only in the most exceptional circumstances" and are read narrowly. If an exception applies, Singapore may exercise jurisdiction under its own law, and the defendant's stay falls to be decided at common law (J4).

Rule ((a) Null and void, ±): The clause must be null and void under the chosen State's law, including its choice of law rules, not Singapore law. The claimant must prove that law as fact, or the presumption of similarity applies (C1.6.3). By analogy, the s 12(1)(c) argument in 6DM failed for want of evidence of English law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Unproved Italian Law

Kopi King argues the Milan clause is void because Italian law requires jurisdiction clauses in standard terms to be specifically approved in writing, and Kopi King never separately signed the clause. It files no expert evidence of Italian law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Exception (a) is tested under Italian law (the chosen court's State), including Italian choice of law rules. Kopi King must prove the Italian rule as a fact. Without expert evidence, the presumption of similarity applies and Singapore law is treated as the same as Italian law. Singapore law has no such signature formality, so the argument fails, as the unproved English-law point did in 6DM.

Rule ((b) Incapacity, +): A party lacked capacity to conclude the clause under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules (e.g., minority, or a statutory bar under its foreign law of incorporation, C2.8; per ss 23, 25 and 25B CA, a Singapore company rarely lacks capacity).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Municipality's Clause

Aurland Kommune, a Norwegian municipality, signs a 2022 supply contract with a German vendor containing an EJC for the courts of Frankfurt. A Norwegian statute bars municipalities from submitting disputes to foreign courts. The municipality later sues in Singapore.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Germany is a Contracting State, so s 12 is engaged. Under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules, a corporation needs capacity under both its law of incorporation and the proper law (C2.8.2). Per Haugesund Kommune, a statutory bar can remove capacity even where the foreign law has no ultra vires doctrine, so the municipality arguably lacked capacity to agree to the clause. Exception (b) applies, so Singapore may hear the case, and any stay is decided at common law. Had a Singapore company signed, ss 23, 25 and 25B CA would stop the clause failing only for lack of capacity.

Rule ((c) Manifest injustice): Per 6DM, adopting Hartley–Dogauchi, manifest injustice covers, for example, no fair trial in the chosen State because of bias or corruption, party-specific reasons that preclude suit there, or an agreement procured by fraud. Per Brand & Herrup (in 6DM), it must be clear, extremely serious and highly probable, not speculative. Public policy: this means basic norms, not the chosen court's technical departure from a forum mandatory rule, and a clause is not disregarded merely because it would not bind under Singapore domestic law. Fragmentation (−): similar to 6DM, where the risk that a related individual could not be joined in England failed s 12(1)(c), the test is "very different" from, and far higher than, fragmentation as strong cause at common law (Vinmar), and the claimant there led no evidence of English law. Domestic policy (−): similar to Motacus (in 6DM), where England's policy of fast construction adjudication did not justify ignoring a Paris EJC absent evidence that enforcement could not proceed in Paris; Parliament could have made an art 21 declaration. Exceptional case (+): cogent evidence that the chosen State's courts are not independent, that the claimant faces arrest there, or that the clause was procured by fraud.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Reasons Not to Go to Ruritania

Ruritania is a Contracting State (fictional). Banyan Builders Pte Ltd sues Ruritania Steel Co in Singapore despite an exclusive Ruritanian courts clause, and resists a s 12 stay on four grounds:

  1. Fragmentation: Banyan's claim against Ruritania Steel's Singapore-based director (not a party to the clause) must be heard in Singapore, so splitting the case would cause inconsistent findings. Banyan files no evidence of whether Ruritanian courts could join the director.
  2. Domestic policy: Singapore's Security of Payment Act policy favours fast payment for construction work.
  3. Public policy: Ruritanian law caps damages in a way that a Singapore statute would not allow.
  4. Bias: Banyan files affidavits from two former Ruritanian judges, a UN Special Rapporteur report and a published anti-corruption court finding showing that Ruritania Steel's chairman (the President's brother) has a record of directing outcomes in commercial cases against foreigners. Banyan's managing director has also been placed on a Ruritanian arrest list after criticising the government.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Fails. As in 6DM, a risk that a related individual cannot be joined in the chosen forum is not manifest injustice. The s 12(1)(c) standard is "very different" from, and far higher than, fragmentation as strong cause at common law (Vinmar), and Banyan has led no evidence of Ruritanian joinder law.
  2. Fails. As in Motacus, a forum's procedural policy does not justify ignoring an EJC where there is no evidence that the claim cannot be enforced in the chosen forum. Singapore could have made an art 21 declaration and did not.
  3. Fails. Public policy means basic norms, not a technical departure from a forum mandatory rule, and the clause is not disregarded merely because Singapore domestic law would treat it differently.
  4. Likely succeeds. This is the exceptional case Hartley–Dogauchi contemplates: cogent evidence (not speculation) that there would be no fair trial, plus a party-specific reason (the risk of arrest) that precludes Banyan from suing there. It is clear, extremely serious and highly probable (Brand & Herrup). Exception (c) applies, and Ruritania Steel's stay is then decided at common law (J4.3, strong cause on Banyan, where the same evidence may well also amount to strong cause).

Rule ((d) Cannot reasonably be performed, ±): This needs exceptional reasons beyond the parties' control, arguably akin to frustration. (+) War in the chosen State, or its courts ceasing to function. (−) Mere delay or expense is not enough.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Closed Courthouse
  • Version 1: Civil war breaks out in the chosen State and its commercial courts have been shut for nine months with no reopening date.
  • Version 2: The chosen State's courts have a three-year backlog, and litigating there would cost twice as much as in Singapore.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Version 1: The clause cannot reasonably be performed for exceptional reasons beyond the parties' control, much like frustration. Exception (d) applies.
  • Version 2: Delay and expense are not enough. Exception (d) fails, and the stay is mandatory.

Rule ((e) Chosen court declined, +): If the chosen court has declined jurisdiction (e.g., dismissed the claim on jurisdictional grounds), Singapore may hear the case under its own rules without breaching the Convention.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Sent Back from London

A Singapore claimant first sues in London under an English EJC. The English court dismisses the claim, holding that the clause does not cover tort claims. The claimant re-sues in Singapore, and the defendant invokes s 12.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The chosen court has declined jurisdiction, so exception (e) applies. Singapore may take jurisdiction under its own rules without breaching the Convention.

Rule (Case management, −): Per 6DM, any risk of inconsistent outcomes with related proceedings can be met by a limited case-management stay of those related proceedings, especially at an early stage (J4.5).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Parallel Director Claim

Suppose Banyan had relied only on fragmentation (reason 1 above, which fails), so its claim against Ruritania Steel is stayed under s 12. Banyan's claim against the Singapore director remains in Singapore.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The court need not keep the contract claim in Singapore to avoid inconsistency. It may instead impose a limited case-management stay on the director claim pending the Ruritanian proceedings, especially as the case is at an early stage (6DM; J4.5).

Conclusion template: "No exception applies, so the action is [stayed / dismissed] under s 12(1)." Or: "Exception [(x)] applies, so the defendant's stay is decided at common law (J4.1)."

6J1.5 Scope of the agreement

(Write this before strong cause: if the claim or party is outside the clause, ordinary Spiliada applies instead.)

Rule (Governing law): Per C&Y, subject-matter scope and party scope are for the proper law of the clause, not the lex fori. If that law is unproved, Singapore construction applies by the presumption of similarity, with contra proferentem as a fallback where the governing law recognises it.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ambiguous "Arising Under"

A clause governed by New York law covers disputes "arising under this Agreement". The claimant argues it covers only contract claims, not tort claims. Neither party proves New York law. The clause was drafted by the defendant.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Scope is for New York law. Since it is unproved, Singapore construction applies by the presumption of similarity (Fiona Trust: broad construction, below). If ambiguity remains, contra proferentem may be used against the defendant as drafter, but only where the governing law recognises it, and with New York law unproved, Singapore law does.

J1.5.1 Subject-Matter Scope

Rule (Broad construction, +): Per Fiona Trust, applied to jurisdiction clauses in Trisuryo and Bunge, rational businessmen are presumed to want all disputes arising out of their relationship decided in one forum unless the words clearly exclude them. Reframing rarely escapes (+): per The Jian He (and Rickshaw), a claimant may frame its claim in tort or equity, but reframing a contractual dispute rarely escapes a widely drafted clause.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Negligent Misstatement Detour

A Hong Kong EJC covers "all disputes arising out of or in connection with this Agreement." The buyer, unhappy with a software system, sues the seller in Singapore for negligent misstatement and in equity for breach of confidence, but not for breach of contract.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Fiona Trust (applied in Trisuryo and Bunge), rational businesspeople want all disputes from their relationship in one forum, and nothing in the wording clearly excludes tort or equity. Per The Jian He and Rickshaw, relabelling a contractual dispute as tort or equity rarely escapes a widely drafted clause. The claims fall within the clause, so the buyer is in breach and bears strong cause.

Rule (Separate agreement within scope, +): Similar to Trisuryo, where a trust claim resting on a separate oral agreement fell within the Indonesian EJC because it contradicted the deeds' warranty that the shares were free of others' rights, a claim under a side agreement falls within the clause if it contradicts or turns on a term of the main contract.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Oral Nominee Arrangement

Under a share sale deed with an exclusive Jakarta clause, the seller warrants that the shares are "free from any third-party rights". Later, the seller's brother sues in Singapore, claiming that under an oral arrangement he is the beneficial owner of half the shares, held on trust by the seller.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

As in Trisuryo, the claim rests on a separate oral agreement, but it directly contradicts the deed's warranty that the shares are free of others' rights, so it turns on a term of the deed and falls within the Jakarta clause. (Whether the clause binds the brother, as a party, is a separate question: J1.5.3.)

Rule (No presumption at the outset, −): Per COSCO (CA), the inquiry does not start from a presumption that all competing claims go to one forum; it depends on the nature of the claims and the clause's express words, "forum fragmentation [being] a fact of life". Where the claim falls outside, fragmentation is accepted (Asiana). Tests are tools (±): per COSCO (CA), the causative-connection, closely-knitted and parallel-claims tests are tools, not formulae. A tort claim that can be recast in contract plainly falls within the clause, and so may one met by contractual cross-claims from the same incident (The Angelic Grace), e.g., an allision during cargo loading. Jurisdiction clauses too: though COSCO (CA) concerned an arbitration clause, scope is construed the same way for an EJC (Fiona Trust; C&Y).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Jetty Allision

During cargo loading at a Singapore terminal, the vessel Sea Lotus allides with the terminal operator's jetty. The charterparty between the shipowner and the charterer (who also operates the terminal through a division) has an exclusive Hong Kong clause for "disputes arising under this Charter". The terminal sues the owner in Singapore in tort for jetty damage. The owner counterclaims in Hong Kong under the charter for delay caused by the charterer's unsafe berth.

  • Variation: the terminal is a separate company with no contract with the owner, and its claim is for damage to a crane during an unrelated maintenance visit.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(+) The owner argues the claim falls within the clause. The tort claim arises from the same incident as contractual cross-claims (unsafe berth, delay), and like The Angelic Grace it is closely knitted to the charter and could be recast as a breach of the safe-berth warranty. The tests (causative connection, closely knitted, parallel claims) are tools pointing the same way, and though COSCO (CA) was an arbitration case, the same construction applies to an EJC. (−) The terminal argues COSCO (CA): there is no presumption at the outset that everything goes to one forum. "Arising under" is narrower than "in connection with", and fragmentation is a fact of life.

  • In the variation, the crane claim is unconnected to the charter and the claimant is a stranger, so it is outside the clause. Fragmentation is accepted (Asiana), and the claim is tested under Spiliada.

Rule (Global Partners, +, persuasive): Per Global Partners (NSWCA), "in connection with" cannot be read down, and an EJC is construed as liberally as an arbitration clause, securing one coherent forum for all disputes from the relationship. A globally operating contract invites multiplicity, so there is no basis for a narrow reading.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Global Fund Mandate

An investment management agreement for a fund operating in 14 countries has an exclusive English clause for disputes "arising out of or in connection with" it. The investor sues in Singapore, claiming the clause should be read narrowly to cover only fee disputes, because the fund's global scale makes multiple proceedings inevitable anyway.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Global Partners, "in connection with" cannot be read down, and an EJC gets the same liberal construction as an arbitration clause. The global scale of the relationship is a reason for one coherent forum, not against it, so all the investor's claims fall within the clause.

J1.5.2 Multiple Contracts and Competing Clauses

Rule (Extended Fiona Trust, ±): Where the clause is in Contract A and the dispute arises under Contract B (which has no clause), per Allianz v Goh Andress, adopting Terre Neuve: (a) the clause's words must be fairly capable of covering Contract B disputes; and (b) the clause is presumed to apply where the parties are the same and the contracts are interdependent, concluded together as one package, and/or cover the same subject matter. This is construction of the clause, not incorporation or variation, and the factors are guides. The ultimate question is whether the outcome is one the parties, as rational businesspeople, sensibly envisaged. Trisuryo is an earlier multi-contract example.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Equipment Package

On the same day, Delta Rig Pte Ltd and Oceanic Drilling Ltd sign (A) a sale agreement for a drilling rig with an exclusive Singapore clause covering "any dispute in connection with this Agreement or the transactions contemplated by it", and (B) a maintenance agreement for the same rig with no jurisdiction clause. Oceanic sues Delta in Norway under the maintenance agreement.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(a) The words "transactions contemplated by it" are fairly capable of covering maintenance disputes. (b) The parties are the same, the contracts were concluded together as one package, and they concern the same rig. The extended Fiona Trust presumption applies (Allianz, adopting Terre Neuve): rational businesspeople would have envisaged one forum. This is construction of clause A, not incorporation of it into B, so B's silence does not matter.

Rule (Competing clauses, ±): Where Contract A and Contract B contain competing clauses, there is no extended Fiona Trust presumption (Allianz). Per Bunge, adopting Oei Hong Leong, apply the clause the parties objectively intended, i.e. the one with which the dispute has the closest connection in its "pith and substance", presuming commercial parties do not intend similar claims to fall under inconsistent clauses. Application example: similar to Bunge, where the Singapore EJCs in the only contracts between the two disputants governed their negative declaration claim.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Shareholders' Agreement v the Loan

X and Y sign (A) a shareholders' agreement with an exclusive Singapore clause and (B) a shareholder loan agreement with an exclusive Hong Kong clause. Y sues X in Hong Kong for repayment of the loan, and X says the loan was really equity under the shareholders' agreement.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

There are competing clauses, so there is no extended Fiona Trust presumption. Ask which clause the dispute is most closely connected with in its "pith and substance" (Bunge, adopting Oei Hong Leong). The core of the dispute is whether money advanced under the loan agreement must be repaid, which points to the Hong Kong clause, even though X's defence invokes the shareholders' agreement.

  • Variation (the Bunge pattern): If Y's claim were against X alone and the only contract between those two parties contained the Singapore clause, that clause would govern.

Rule (Court clause plus arbitration clause, ±): Where a contract contains both an arbitration clause and a Singapore court clause, per the slides they may be reconciled: disputes go to arbitration, and the court clause confers supervisory jurisdiction over the arbitration.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Belt and Braces

A contract says in clause 20: "Disputes shall be referred to SIAC arbitration seated in Singapore", and in clause 21: "The courts of Singapore shall have exclusive jurisdiction." One party sues in court, relying on clause 21.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The clauses are read together: merits disputes go to arbitration, and clause 21 gives the Singapore courts supervisory jurisdiction over the arbitration (e.g., setting aside, interim relief). The court action on the merits is in breach of clause 20.

J1.5.3 Party Scope (argue privity first)

Rule (Privity first, −): Per Asiana, adopting Team Y&R, whether a clause avails claims against third parties is construction, and in keeping with privity it usually will not, absent "a quite clear indication otherwise".

Rule (Third party relying: proper law): Per C&Y, a third party may rely on the clause if its governing law permits. Per VKC v VJZ, CRTPA s 2(1)(b) ("purports to confer a benefit") does not apply to an EJC, because an EJC confers a procedural, not substantive, right, and the Act expressly deals only with arbitration clauses (s 9). Critique (+, Chong): the "procedural" label is wrong, because if an EJC were merely procedural its breach could not found an ASI or damages (J1.7). Routes left: per VKC v VJZ, the third party might "arguably" rely on s 2(1)(a) (the clause expressly provides that it may enforce) or s 2(3) (it is identified by name, class or description); the equitable route (Hai Jiang 1401) was left open. So draft an express third-party right if protection is wanted.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Subcontractor's Shield

A main contract between Owner and Main Contractor has an exclusive Singapore clause. The Owner sues the Main Contractor's subcontractor, Precision Welding, in Indonesia in tort. Precision wants to rely on the Singapore clause to get an ASI, and argues the clause "purports to confer a benefit" on it under CRTPA s 2(1)(b).

  • Variation: the clause adds "This clause may be enforced by any subcontractor of the Contractor."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(−) By privity, a clause in the Owner and Main Contractor contract usually does not reach claims against strangers without a "quite clear indication" (Asiana, Team Y&R). Precision's s 2(1)(b) argument fails because, per VKC v VJZ, an EJC confers only a procedural right and the CRTPA expressly covers only arbitration clauses (s 9). (+) Chong's critique: if the clause were truly procedural, its breach could not ground an ASI or damages, yet it does. Make that point, but recognise that VKC v VJZ binds.

  • In the variation, Precision can argue s 2(1)(a) (the clause expressly provides that subcontractors may enforce it) and s 2(3) (identified by class), routes that VKC v VJZ left "arguably" open, alongside the equitable route (Hai Jiang 1401). The drafting lesson is to include express third-party wording.

Rule (Third party bound, −): Generally no, by privity, unless the third party takes by assignment, subrogation or agency, or otherwise claims under the contract, taking the benefit subject to the burden (Hai Jiang 1401; J6.5.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Subrogated Insurer

A cargo owner's contract with a carrier has an exclusive Singapore clause. After a loss, the cargo insurer pays the cargo owner and, by subrogation, sues the carrier in Shanghai.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The insurer is not a party, but it claims under the contract by subrogation, so it takes the benefit subject to the burden (Hai Jiang 1401) and is bound by the clause. Suing in Shanghai is a breach, which may support a contractual ASI (J6.5.2).

Rule (Closely connected non-parties, +, persuasive): Similar to Global Partners, where group companies named as "Indemnified Persons" who took part in the very decisions complained of were "not strangers" ("there are non parties and non parties"), so the EJC bound the claimant in its claims against them. Counter (−): per Hive Marketing (NSWCA), a stay of related claims against non-parties is not automatic or presumptive merely because of a risk of multiplicity. After Asiana and COSCO (CA), Global Partners is an example of the "quite clear indication", not the default, so it fails where the affiliates are strangers linked only by common ownership.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Fund Manager's Affiliates
  • Version 1: An investor signs an English EJC with FundCo. The agreement names FundCo's affiliates as "Indemnified Persons", and two affiliates made the investment decisions the investor complains of. The investor sues the affiliates in Singapore.
  • Version 2: Same, but the affiliates are not named anywhere in the agreement and had no role in the decisions; they merely share a parent with FundCo.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Version 1 (+): Like Global Partners, the affiliates are "not strangers": they are named as Indemnified Persons and took part in the very decisions complained of. That is the "quite clear indication" that Asiana requires, so the clause binds the investor in its claims against them.
  • Version 2 (−): Per Hive Marketing, the risk of multiplicity does not automatically extend the clause. After Asiana and COSCO (CA), common ownership alone is not a clear indication, so the claim is outside the clause and Spiliada applies.

Rule (Bypass manoeuvre): Where a claimant sues only the non-party abroad to sidestep the clause, though the contracting party is the obvious defendant, the suit may be restrained as vexatious even if the clause does not bind the non-party (Clearlake, in Asiana; J6.5.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Suing the Parent Instead
