LAW302 · HYPO LESSON J4 · 29 HYPOTHETICALS · 5 FLOWCHARTS · 8 QUESTIONS

J4 hypotheticals: Exercise: Spiliada, forum conveniens and strong cause

The rules behind these hypotheticals are taught in Lesson J4, where the word-for-word pre-write is too. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

Applications:
ℹ HOW TO USE THESE HYPOTHETICALS

Each concept is set out as Rule, then Hypothetical, then Application. (+) helps the claimant keep Singapore; (−) helps the defendant's stay or set-aside. Existence is in J2/J3; clauses are characterised in J1.

The flowcharts redraw the hypotheticals in this site's chart style: the chip on each arrow names the hypothetical (or version) that takes that path. The hypo test at the end checks you can run the facts yourself.

1J4.0 Burden map (must write)

Rule:

  • General rule: per C&Y and Shanghai Turbo, the burden lies on the party seeking release from its promise about where to sue, whether in a stay or a set-aside.
  • No breach (Spiliada): for no clause, a foreign NEJC, or a claim outside the clause (J1.5): if the defendant was served in, it bears stage 1; if served out, the claimant bears it on a set-aside and the defendant on a stay (Zoom).
  • Singapore EJC or NEJC: the defendant's stay or set-aside objects to the agreed forum, so strong cause is on the defendant, with the NEJC waiver implied under Singapore law or the presumption of similarity (Shanghai Turbo; J1.1).
  • Singapore clause, served out: per Chong's answer scheme and C&Y, in practice the claimant need only show the clause is valid, binds the defendant and covers the dispute, plus a serious question; strong cause then shifts to the defendant (J3.2).
  • Foreign EJC: the claimant breaches by suing here, so strong cause is on the claimant, even though the defendant brings the stay or set-aside, whether served in or out.
  • Existence not disputable: where service needed no approval (O 8 r 1(3); NW Corp) or rests on "has the jurisdiction" outside the CCAA, the defendant may attack only exercise, and it bears that burden (C&Y).
  • (CCAA: no discretion (J1.3/J1.4). SICC with a written jurisdiction agreement: O 2 r 3 replaces both tests (J5.3).)
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Six Defendants, Six Burdens

In each case, Claimant (Singapore) sues Defendant (Indonesia).

  1. No clause; Defendant was served in Singapore and seeks a stay.
  2. No clause; Defendant was served in Jakarta and applies to set aside.
  3. No clause; Defendant was served in Jakarta and applies only for a stay.
  4. "Non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Singapore courts" (Singapore law); Defendant was served in Jakarta and applies to set aside on forum grounds.
  5. "Exclusive jurisdiction of the Jakarta courts"; Defendant was served in Singapore and seeks a stay.
  6. The contract says "process may be served by courier to the addresses in Schedule 1" and names Singapore courts non-exclusively; Defendant was served by courier in Jakarta and argues there is "no gateway".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Spiliada; Defendant bears stage 1, and Claimant bears stage 2.
  2. Forum conveniens; Claimant bears the burden of showing Singapore is clearly more appropriate (Zoom).
  3. Spiliada; Defendant bears stage 1 because it chose a stay (Zoom). Tactically this is a mistake: Defendant should have applied to set aside.
  4. Singapore NEJC: Defendant's objection breaches the waiver, so strong cause on Defendant (Shanghai Turbo). Claimant need only show a good arguable case that the clause is valid, binding and covers the dispute, plus a serious question.
  5. Foreign EJC: Claimant breached by suing here, so strong cause on Claimant, even though Defendant made the application.
  6. Service under O 8 r 1(3) needed no approval, so existence cannot be disputed and the "no gateway" argument fails (NW Corp). Defendant can only attack exercise, and because the clause names Singapore, its forum objection is a breach, so strong cause is on Defendant.

2J4.1 Stay under Spiliada

J4.1.1 Starter and Framework

Rule (Starter, must write): As the defendant was served in Singapore or has submitted, jurisdiction exists as of right, so it may only seek a stay (O 6 r 7(5)(b) / r 12(4)(b)). Per Spiliada, the foreign forum must be available and clearly or distinctly more appropriate "for the interests of all the parties and the ends of justice". Two stages: (1) does the foreign forum have the most real and substantial connection with the dispute? (2) would the claimant be denied substantial justice there? Which test: Spiliada applies absent agreement; a breached foreign EJC engages strong cause (J4.3); an international arbitration clause engages a mandatory stay (IAA s 6), not FNC. Procedure and power: the defendant states the ground in its defence or affidavit (O 6 r 7(4); r 12(3)), and it is heard first (O 9 r 7). The power is SCJA Sch 1 para 9, with O 9 r 16(1)(b) and O 3 r 2(2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Bali Resort Collapse

Tropika Resorts Pte Ltd (Singapore) hires Bali Bangun PT (Indonesia) to build a resort in Bali. The roof collapses. Bali Bangun's director is served in Singapore while Bali Bangun has a permanent project office here, so service is valid as of right. Bali Bangun wants the case heard in Denpasar.

  • Variation A: the contract has an SIAC arbitration clause.
  • Variation B: the contract has an exclusive Denpasar courts clause.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Jurisdiction exists as of right, so Bali Bangun can only seek a stay. It must state the ground in its defence or affidavit (O 6 r 12(3)), and the stay is heard first (O 9 r 7). The court's power is Sch 1 para 9 SCJA. With no clause, Spiliada applies: Bali Bangun must show at stage 1 that Indonesia is available and clearly more appropriate; Tropika may then show at stage 2 that it would be denied substantial justice there.

  • Variation A: a mandatory IAA s 6 stay, not FNC.
  • Variation B: Tropika breached the EJC, so strong cause on Tropika (J4.3), not Spiliada.

Rule (Waiver by delay, +): Per Sun Jin and C&Y, the defendant's delay is relevant but not decisive, read with the steps it has taken. The test is "the competing interests of the parties and the justice of the case as a whole".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Late Stay Application

Bali Bangun files a defence on 1 March stating that Singapore should not exercise jurisdiction (O 6 r 12(3)), but does not apply for a stay until 1 November. In the meantime the parties exchange documents and attend two case conferences.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The eight-month delay is relevant but not decisive (Sun Jin). The court considers it together with the steps taken (document exchange, case conferences), and asks whether a stay now serves "the competing interests of the parties and the justice of the case as a whole". (+) Tropika argues that eight months of progress here makes a stay wasteful. (−) Bali Bangun signalled its challenge from day one and took only procedural steps.

Rule (Meaning): Per Spiliada, forum non conveniens means "not the appropriate forum" for the dispute, not mere practical convenience such as the cost of flying witnesses in. Comparative, not abstract: per JIO and C&Y, the defendant must show the foreign forum clearly more appropriate; Singapore having few links is not enough. If the factors are scattered across several countries or finely balanced, there is no stay. Two foreign fora: per C&Y, a stay may still be granted if two foreign fora are each clearly more appropriate, though the court does not say which is the natural forum. Relativity: per JIO, the comparison is Singapore against the foreign forum, so the fact that a third country's law governs does not help the claimant, and a third forum's equal claim does not make Singapore the natural forum.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Scattered Shipping Dispute
  • Version 1: A Singapore shipowner sues a Greek charterer in Singapore. The vessel was built in Korea, damaged in Brazil, repaired in Rotterdam, and the charter is governed by English law. The charterer's only argument is that "Singapore has hardly any connection".
  • Version 2: Same, but the charterer argues for a stay in favour of either Greece or England, each of which it says is clearly more appropriate than Singapore.
  • Version 3: The charterer seeks a stay in favour of Greece. The shipowner argues that because English law governs, Greece is no better than Singapore.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Version 1: No stay. Showing that Singapore is weakly connected is not enough; the charterer must point to a forum that is clearly more appropriate (JIO). The factors are scattered across Korea, Brazil, the Netherlands and England.
  • Version 2: Per C&Y, a stay can be granted if each of Greece and England is clearly more appropriate than Singapore, without the court having to pick between them.
  • Version 3: Per JIO, the comparison is Singapore against Greece. That English law governs is neutral between them (both would have to apply foreign law), so it does not make Singapore the natural forum. The question is whether the other factors make Greece clearly more appropriate.

Rule (Each claim its own forum): Per C&Y, the contract claim and the tort claim each have a natural forum, but overlapping claims arising from the same facts tilt towards one forum to avoid inconsistent findings. Burden, legal v evidential: per Spiliada and JIO, the defendant bears the stage 1 legal burden and the claimant stage 2; evidential burdens shift as each proves what it asserts. Some weight goes to jurisdiction founded as of right (C&Y). Appellate review: per Spiliada and C&Y, precedents help little, and the judge's evaluation stands unless there is a misdirection in principle, wrong factors were weighed or ignored, or the decision was plainly wrong; so frame an error on governing law as one of principle (Rotary). Forum shopping (±): per Spiliada, the claimant's advantage is the defendant's disadvantage. Per C&Y, only abusive shopping (oppressive, risking inconsistent judgments) offends, and it is policed by FNC, ASIs and choice of law (Goh Suan Hee).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Appeal on Governing Law

A Singapore judge refuses to stay a claim in favour of Saudi Arabia, treating Saudi governing law as "neutral because foreign law can be proved by experts". The defendant appeals. The claimant had sued in Singapore because Singapore awards higher damages and wider disclosure than Saudi Arabia; the defendant calls this forum shopping.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Appellate review: discretionary evaluations are rarely overturned, so the defendant should frame the error as one of principle. Treating a materially different, weighty foreign governing law as neutral is a misdirection (cf Rotary, where Saudi law governing the JVA was "a weighty factor"). Forum shopping: wanting higher damages and wider disclosure is ordinary; the claimant's advantage is simply the defendant's disadvantage (Spiliada). It is not abusive unless it is oppressive or risks inconsistent judgments (C&Y; Goh Suan Hee). Burden: the defendant carries the legal burden at stage 1. Once it shows Saudi Arabia is clearly more appropriate, the claimant carries stage 2, with the evidential burden on each side for what it asserts.

Availability of the Foreign Forum

Rule: Legal availability: per C&Y, the foreign forum is available if its courts have jurisdiction over the defendant and will exercise it, assessed at the date of the stay application. If no forum is available, Singapore is the natural forum by default. Leave needed abroad (+): per Hindocha, the forum is unavailable if jurisdiction there needs permission to serve out; this is cured by the defendant's undertaking to submit or evidence that permission was or would be granted. Foreign court declines (+): if the foreign court stays its own proceedings, the forum is unavailable. Singapore may stay pending the foreign jurisdiction ruling, with the claimant able to apply to lift the stay if the foreign court declines (Rappo; C&Y). Practical availability → stage 2: per C&Y (following the SGCA), fair trial, time bar or missing remedy points go to stage 2, not availability. Non-court forum (−): per The Rainbow Joy, a labour tribunal abroad suffices if competent over the dispute, even with narrower remedies, comity being between nations, not courts.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Is Hong Kong Even Open?
  1. A Singapore claimant sues a Hong Kong-incorporated defendant whose sole director lives in London. The defendant seeks a stay in favour of Hong Kong, but the Hong Kong court would need leave to serve the London-based co-defendant.
  2. The claimant has also sued in Hong Kong, where the defendant's challenge to the Hong Kong court's jurisdiction is still pending.
  3. A Filipino seafarer sues a Singapore shipowner here for unpaid wages. The owner seeks a stay in favour of the Philippine National Labor Relations Commission, which can award wages but not aggravated damages.
  4. The claimant's claim is time-barred in Hong Kong.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Hong Kong is unavailable against any defendant that would need leave to be served there (Hindocha), unless that defendant undertakes to submit to Hong Kong or there is evidence that leave was or would be granted.
  2. Until Hong Kong rules, its availability is uncertain. Singapore may grant a limited stay pending Hong Kong's jurisdiction ruling, the claimant applying to lift it if Hong Kong declines (Rappo; C&Y). Had the Hong Kong court already stayed its own proceedings, Hong Kong would be unavailable.
  3. As in The Rainbow Joy, a competent labour tribunal is an available forum even though its remedies are narrower. Comity is between nations, not between courts.
  4. The time bar does not make Hong Kong unavailable. It is a stage 2 argument (C&Y).

J4.1.2 Stage 1: Connecting Factors

Rule (Quality over quantity): Per Rappo and JIO, the court draws no "balance sheet" of tenuous contacts; only links relevant to the dispute count, so a Singapore bank account or directorships here are disregarded. Parties: per C&Y, connections are judged at the time of the events and at the time of the suit. Domicile carries little weight in commerce, and less for highly mobile or multi-jurisdiction parties (Mulacek). A claimant in Singapore and a defendant abroad cancel out; residence in neither forum is neutral. A company is where it actually does business, e.g., its Jakarta office (JIO). Internal management (±): per Oro Negro, the place of incorporation is prima facie the forum for corporate governance disputes.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Jakarta Business Run Through Singapore Shells

An Indonesian conglomerate's two founding families fall out. The claimant family sues the defendant family's patriarch, Mr Wijaya, in Singapore. Mr Wijaya holds Singapore directorships in five holding companies and has a Singapore bank account, but he runs the business from the Jakarta head office. He is a jet-setter with homes in four countries. One claim concerns misrepresentations made in Jakarta about an Indonesian coal mine; another concerns the conduct of board meetings of a Singapore-incorporated holding company.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Quality over quantity: the Singapore directorships and bank account are tenuous and irrelevant to the dispute, so they are disregarded; no balance sheet is drawn (Rappo; JIO). Parties: Mr Wijaya's domicile carries little weight given his mobility (Mulacek). The business is done from Jakarta, which is where the company "is" (JIO). Corporate governance: the board-meeting claim concerns the internal management of a Singapore-incorporated company, so Singapore is prima facie the forum for that claim (Oro Negro), even if the misrepresentation claim points to Jakarta.

Rule (Clauses at stage 1): Foreign NEJC (no breach): per Shanghai Turbo, the clause shows only that the foreign forum is an appropriate forum, so it carries little weight; a breached clause engages strong cause instead (J4.3). Singapore clause without a promise (+): per Chong's answer scheme, where a clause naming Singapore contains no promise under its proper law, Spiliada applies, but the clause still points to Singapore at stage 1.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Weak Clauses
  1. "The parties submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Vietnam"; the claimant sues in Singapore.
  2. "Submit to the jurisdiction of the Singapore courts", governed by Ruritanian law, which (as proved) reads it as bare consent with no waiver.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(1) No breach, so it is a Spiliada factor of little weight in Vietnam's favour (Shanghai Turbo). (2) No breach by the defendant's objection, so Spiliada applies, but the Singapore clause still counts at stage 1 in Singapore's favour (Chong).

Rule (Witnesses): Convenience (+): per JIO, location carries little weight given video-link, and less still where the foreign forum is nearby, like Malaysia or Indonesia (Chan Chin Cheung). Compellability (−): per JIO, non-party witnesses abroad who are not compellable here point to the foreign forum, if the defendant shows their evidence is "at least arguably relevant" to its defence. Reduced (+): the weight falls if the witnesses will attend or testify by video (Raffles Education), or are the defendant's own employees, not third parties (Chong's feedback); it is neutral if the problem arises in both fora (C&Y). Defence not pre-judged: per C&Y, the court must not be claimant-centric and may infer the defendant's likely defence from the statement of claim, but a reticent defendant cannot complain.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Johor Factory Fire

A Singapore insurer, subrogated to a Singapore manufacturer, sues a Malaysian electrical contractor in Singapore over a fire at a Johor factory. The contractor's defence (not yet filed) is likely to be that the fire was caused by the factory's own maintenance staff. The witnesses are:

  • (a) 10 of the contractor's own electricians in Johor Bahru;
  • (b) 3 independent fire investigators employed by the Johor fire department, who will not voluntarily come to Singapore;
  • (c) 2 maintenance workers formerly employed by the manufacturer, now living in Kuala Lumpur, who say they are happy to testify by video.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(a) The contractor's own employees can be made available, so there is no real compellability problem (Chong). Johor is a short drive from Singapore, and video-link is available, so convenience carries little weight (JIO; Chan Chin Cheung). (b) Non-compellable non-party witnesses favour Malaysia, if the contractor shows their evidence is at least arguably relevant to its defence (JIO). The court may infer that defence (staff negligence) from the statement of claim and must not be claimant-centric. (c) Willing video witnesses carry reduced weight (Raffles Education). Net: (b) is the only weighty witness factor favouring Malaysia.

Rule (Documents): Per C&Y, location is neutral, but language, translation, admissibility, and disclosure available only abroad may tip it. Events, contract: per C&Y and Rotary, the place of contracting or performance is neutral unless formation or performance is disputed, and fortuitous links get little weight. Events, tort (−): per JIO and The Albaforth, the place of the tort, located by the substance test (C3), is prima facie the natural forum unless fortuitous. Tort as starting point only: per The Peng Yan, the place of the tort is only a starting point; per Oro Negro and Chen v BHNV, a tort parasitic on or intimately connected with the contract claim follows that claim's forum.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Misrepresentation Received in Jakarta

A Singapore seller's sales director, on a call from Singapore, made misrepresentations to an Indonesian buyer's CEO in Jakarta, who relied on them there and signed a sale contract governed by Singapore law. The buyer sues the seller in Singapore for (a) misrepresentation in tort and (b) breach of contract. The documents are in Bahasa Indonesia.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Tort: by the substance test (C3), a misrepresentation is committed where it is received and relied on, i.e. Jakarta, so Indonesia is prima facie the natural forum for that claim (JIO; The Albaforth). But the place of the tort is only a starting point (The Peng Yan). If the tort claim is intimately connected with the contract claim (the same deal, the same facts), it follows the contract claim's forum (Oro Negro; Chen v BHNV). Contract: the place of contracting is neutral unless formation is disputed (Rotary), and Singapore governing law points to Singapore (below). Documents: location is neutral, but Bahasa documents needing translation tilt slightly towards Indonesia (C&Y).

Rule (Governing law):

  • When weighty: per Rickshaw and JIO, a prima facie view of the governing law suffices. It weighs where the dispute turns on law, not on fact (e.g., what was said). Characterise first: the contract and the tort follow their own rules (C2; C3).
  • Not the OPL test: per Chong's feedback, do not conflate the two. Connections to the contract overlap, but witness compellability and where a patent is registered go to Spiliada only.
  • More weight (−): per Rotary, Saudi law governing the JVA was "a weighty factor". Weight rises with an express choice of law (Rappo) or a trust (C&Y), and with very different systems, e.g., Swiss law, which has no trust doctrine (Ivanishvili v Credit Suisse).
  • Less weight (+): weight falls where the foreign law is similar to Singapore's, unpleaded (though the court may notice that it likely differs: Rickshaw; JIO), referable to a foreign court (ROC O 29 / O 29A), or transferable to the SICC (J4.4).
  • Split or different choice: per C&Y, where the claims are governed by different laws, or the foreign court would apply a different law, the factor is reduced or neutral.
  • Framing the claim (+): per Rickshaw, absent bad faith a claimant may plead tort to sidestep a German choice of law clause, shaping the litigation (C&Y).
  • Singapore statute: per JIO, the Misrepresentation Act points to Singapore only if Singapore law governs the contract.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Governing Laws
  1. Swiss trust: a Singapore beneficiary sues a Swiss bank, alleging it held assets on trust; the account terms are expressly governed by Swiss law.
  2. Australian contract: a contract is expressly governed by Australian (NSW) law, and the dispute turns on what was said at a meeting.
  3. Mixed claims: a contract governed by German law (with a German choice of law clause), and a tort claim for negligent misstatement, which the claimant pleads to sidestep the German clause.
  4. Misrepresentation Act: the claimant relies on s 2(1) of the Misrepresentation Act, but the contract is governed by Indonesian law.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Heavy weight towards Switzerland: an express choice of a very different system (Swiss law has no trust doctrine) on the central legal issue (Ivanishvili; Rappo; C&Y on trusts).
  2. Light weight: NSW law is similar to Singapore's, and the dispute turns on fact (what was said), not law (Rickshaw; JIO).
  3. Split laws, reduced weight (C&Y). Absent bad faith, the claimant may frame the claim in tort to avoid the German clause (Rickshaw), which shapes the litigation, though the German contract still counts for Germany.
  4. No pull towards Singapore: the Misrepresentation Act applies only if Singapore law governs the contract (JIO). Here Indonesian law governs, so the statute adds nothing.
  • Not the OPL test (Chong): in (1), do not reason "the account was opened in Zurich, so Swiss law governs, so Switzerland". At stage 1, ask which forum is more appropriate, which includes non-OPL factors like witness compellability.

Rule (Related proceedings): Weight: per Lakshmi and C&Y, overlapping proceedings abroad matter for the risk of inconsistent judgments (and then duplication), weighed by progress, parties and issues, not by who sued first (cf the EU first-seised rule). Disregarded: proceedings that are unrelated, or infected by the same breach, are irrelevant (Oro Negro). Parallelism the claimant created by suing in both forums is disregarded (IM Skaugen (CA)), as is a tactically manufactured link (C&Y). Undertaking to discontinue (+): per C&Y, a claimant that has sued in both Singapore and abroad may undertake to discontinue abroad to neutralise the factor. Shape of the litigation (±): per C&Y and Mulacek, staying the claim may fragment or consolidate the dispute with co-defendants, with the risk greatest in multi-party cases. Cambridgeshire factor (−): per Spiliada, expertise built up abroad through related litigation over the same casualty favours that forum, but only in complex technical cases and not on mere assertion (C&Y). SICC factor (±): relevant only if the claimant names the SICC feature suiting the dispute and transfer is prima facie available (Rappo); never decisive alone (IM Skaugen) (J4.4).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Oil Rig Litigation

A jack-up rig owned by a Singapore company collapses off Mexico. Proceedings follow:

  • (a) The rig's Mexican insurers have sued the Norwegian designer in Oslo, and that case is at trial, with expert evidence on the rig's legs already heard.
  • (b) The Singapore owner sues the designer in Singapore, and also (to protect its position) in Mexico.
  • (c) The designer seeks a stay in favour of Norway.
  • (d) Separately, the designer points to an unrelated Norwegian lawsuit between the owner's parent and a bank.
  • (e) The owner's Singapore claim joins three other defendants (a Singapore yard, a Korean steel supplier and a Mexican operator) who cannot all be sued in Norway.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) Weighs towards Norway: the Oslo case overlaps on the same issues and is well advanced, creating a real risk of inconsistent judgments (Lakshmi). The Cambridgeshire factor also applies: the Norwegian court has built up expertise in a complex technical casualty (Spiliada), though the designer must evidence this, not just assert it (C&Y).
  • (b) Disregarded: the owner's own Mexican suit is self-created parallelism (IM Skaugen (CA)). The owner can neutralise it by undertaking to discontinue in Mexico (C&Y).
  • (d) Irrelevant: unrelated proceedings (Oro Negro).
  • (e) Shape of the litigation (+): staying the claim against the designer would fragment a multi-party dispute in which the other defendants can only be sued together in Singapore (Mulacek; C&Y). That weighs against a stay.
  • SICC: if the owner says the SICC's international panel and technical case-management features suit this case, and transfer is prima facie available, that is relevant but never decisive (Rappo; IM Skaugen).

J4.1.3 Stage 2: Substantial Justice

Rule (Threshold, −): Per Rotary, once the foreign forum is clearly more appropriate, refusing a stay is "at least unusual"; the claimant needs cogent evidence of a real and material risk of injustice there. Real risk, cumulatively (+): per AK Investment, a real risk in this case suffices, not proof that justice "will not" be done, and several irregularities may add up even though none suffices alone (C&Y). Comity (must write, −): per The Hung Vuong-2 and C&Y, the court is slow to impugn foreign courts, especially a well-established system (Shen Sophie: US / China), so generalised complaints fail.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Kyrgyz Telecom Case

A Singapore investor sues Kyrgyz defendants. Kyrgyzstan is clearly the more appropriate forum. The investor's evidence: (i) the Kyrgyz defendants' associates were appointed to the regulator; (ii) the investor's local manager was arrested on a pretext; (iii) the Kyrgyz court refused the investor time to translate documents; (iv) a lawyer acting for the investor was disbarred mid-case. No single item proves corruption.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Refusing a stay after stage 1 is "at least unusual" (Rotary), so the investor needs cogent evidence. Per AK Investment (itself a Kyrgyz case), the investor need not show that justice will not be done, only a real risk in this case, and items (i)–(iv) may be considered cumulatively even if none suffices alone. Comity counsels caution about impugning a foreign system (The Hung Vuong-2), but this evidence is specific to the case, not a generalised complaint. A stay is likely refused.

  • Contrast (Shen Sophie): a bare assertion that "the US (or Chinese) courts are slow and expensive" impugns a well-established system without cogent evidence, and fails.

Rule (Ordinary differences, −): Per C&Y, ordinary differences in procedure and remedies are disregarded. Per Spiliada and Trendtex, higher damages or discovery here do not defeat a stay if substantial justice is available abroad. Higher damages (−): per Chong's feedback, a legitimate juridical advantage alone is not conclusive; per Goh Suan Hee, a likely higher award here was neutral, the governing law of quantum being open. Relief unavailable (−): per Rappo, the absence of a constructive trust or tracing abroad is no injustice where the foreign law governs, as the relief would be unavailable here too; per The Rainbow Joy, narrower remedies are not decisive. Foreign public policy (±): per Trisuryo, a foreign public policy barring the claim is relevant but not determinative, rejecting the view that it is "a strong factor in favour of a stay". Security here (+): per Spiliada, the claimant keeps its security under a conditional stay.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Lower Damages Complaint

A Singapore claimant injured when the defendant's ferry ran aground in Thai waters would recover about one third as much in Thailand as in Singapore. Thai procedure has no document discovery. The claimant also arrested the defendant's vessel in Singapore as security.

  • Variation: the claim is for a constructive trust over Swiss assets, and Swiss law (which governs) does not recognise constructive trusts.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Lower damages and no discovery are ordinary differences (Spiliada; Trendtex). A legitimate juridical advantage in Singapore is not conclusive (Chong). In Goh Suan Hee, a likely higher award was treated as neutral because the governing law of quantum was itself open, and the same may apply here. A stay is likely granted. Security: the stay can be conditional, so the claimant keeps the vessel arrest as security (Spiliada).

  • In the variation, there is no injustice: if Swiss law governs, a Singapore court would not award a constructive trust either (Rappo).

Rule (Delay, −): Delay is disregarded unless egregious (C&Y); per Grains and Industrial (and Chong's feedback), even alleged delays of over 10 years in India failed. Funding and legal aid (±): per Connelly v RTZ, the claimant takes the foreign forum as it finds it, so the absence of legal aid alone fails, unless the dispute cannot be justly tried without lawyers and experts the claimant cannot fund (Lubbe v Cape). Illustration (+): per Chong (seminar), lack of funding counts only if the claimant cannot pursue the claim abroad at all (Singapore being less generous on legal aid). Similar to Limbu v Dyson (EWCA), where migrant workers at Malaysian factories, unable to fund suit there, sued the parent in England.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Factory Workers' Claim

Nepalese migrant workers at a Malaysian electronics factory sue the factory's Singapore parent company in Singapore for forced labour and injuries. Malaysia is the natural forum. The workers have been deported to Nepal, cannot afford Malaysian lawyers, Malaysia offers no legal aid or conditional fees for such claims, and the case needs expert medical and supply-chain evidence. A Singapore law firm acts pro bono. The parent also points out that the Malaysian courts are slow.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Delay: the slowness of the Malaysian courts is not egregious and is disregarded (Grains and Industrial: even 10+ years failed). Funding: ordinarily, the workers take Malaysia as they find it (Connelly v RTZ). But where a complex claim needing lawyers and experts cannot be pursued abroad at all for want of funding, that is substantial injustice (Lubbe v Cape; Chong). The facts mirror Limbu v Dyson. Singapore is not generous on legal aid either, so the point is not whether Singapore is cheaper but whether the claim can be brought in Malaysia at all. A stay is likely refused.

Rule (Time bar, ±): Per Spiliada, if the claimant reasonably sued here and did not unreasonably let time run abroad, the stay is conditional on the defendant waiving the bar. Limits (−): per Chong's feedback, assert that the claimant is out of time abroad only if the facts say so; parties often file protective writs in several fora. If only some claims are barred, the court is less willing to keep the case (C&Y; FLPA: J4.2.4).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Missed Deadline
  • Version 1: A claimant sued in Singapore in good faith (it had a Singapore office and a plausible case for Singapore), and while the stay application was pending the two-year limitation period in Vietnam expired.
  • Version 2: The claimant's lawyers advised it to file a protective writ in Vietnam, but it chose not to and let time run.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Version 1: the claimant acted reasonably and did not unreasonably let time run, so per Spiliada the stay is granted on condition that the defendant waives the Vietnamese time bar. Version 2: the claimant knowingly let time run, so the stay is unconditional and the bar is its own fault. (Note: under the FLPA, if Vietnamese law governs, Singapore would apply the Vietnamese period too, so the bar may follow the claimant here anyway: J4.2.4.)

Rule (Unfair rules of evidence, ±): Per Rotary, system-wide rules (e.g., discounting the evidence of non-Muslim or female witnesses) can in principle ground injustice, but only if they prejudice the claimant on the facts; cogent evidence is needed (Best Soar). Instability (−): per Shafeeg, political unrest abroad is insufficient while the courts still function to try the dispute. Unfair trial or danger (+): cumulative irregularities (AK Investment) or risks of assassination or trumped-up charges (Deripaska) suffice on cogent evidence, as does a system that "flies in the face of all accepted principles of justice" (Q & M v Poh Kiat). No trial anywhere (+): per AK Investment (applying Connelly v RTZ), where trial abroad "never could" occur, justice favours Singapore; investing in a country does not bind the claimant to its courts. Stay is suspensory (±): per Rotary, where the evidence of arrest or danger is thin, a stay is granted, but the claimant may lift it on fresh cogent evidence of exceptional circumstances striking at its basis, not as "a standing invitation". Defendant's stage 2 (±): if stage 1 fails, the defendant may in principle show injustice in Singapore (IM Skaugen (HC)), e.g., no legal aid or contingency funding for a foreign defendant, but it rarely succeeds (C&Y).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Five Stage 2 Pleas
  1. A Singapore Hindu businessman resists a stay to a forum whose courts give a non-Muslim witness's evidence half the weight of a Muslim's. His case turns on documents, and the only witness of fact on his side is Muslim.
  2. A claimant cites street protests in the foreign capital; the courts are open and hearing commercial cases.
  3. A Russian oligarch's former business partner says he faces trumped-up charges and threats if he returns to Russia, with cogent evidence (prior arrests of associates, an Interpol red-notice attempt).
  4. A Singapore company stayed in favour of a foreign forum later finds that the local prosecutor has issued an arrest warrant for its director on the eve of trial.
  5. The defendant loses stage 1 (Singapore is the natural forum) and argues that, as a foreign defendant, it cannot get legal aid or conditional fees in Singapore.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. The discriminatory evidence rule can ground injustice in principle (Rotary), but only if it prejudices this claimant on the facts. His case turns on documents and his only witness is Muslim, so there is no prejudice and the plea fails (Best Soar: cogent evidence needed).
  2. Political unrest while the courts still function is insufficient (Shafeeg).
  3. Cogent evidence of risks to personal safety and trumped-up charges suffices (Deripaska). Singapore keeps the case.
  4. Rotary: a stay is suspensory, so the company may apply to lift it on fresh, cogent evidence of exceptional circumstances that strike at the basis of the stay (an arrest warrant on the eve of trial plausibly does). It is not a "standing invitation" to relitigate.
  5. In principle a defendant can run stage 2 (IM Skaugen (HC)), but this plea rarely succeeds (C&Y); lack of funding for a foreign defendant is unlikely to be substantial injustice.
  • Bonus: if the foreign system "flies in the face of all accepted principles of justice" (Q & M v Poh Kiat), or trial there "never could" occur (AK Investment, applying Connelly), justice favours Singapore. Investing in that country does not bind the claimant to its courts.

J4.1.4 Evaluation: Spiliada v the Australian "Clearly Inappropriate Forum" Test

Rule: Per Voth, an Australian court stays only if it is "a clearly inappropriate forum", asking whether local trial is oppressive or vexatious rather than whether the foreign forum is more appropriate; reaffirmed in Puttick v Tenon. Singapore's rejection: per JIO and Eng Liat Kiang, the defendant must show the foreign forum is clearly more appropriate, a test that stays cases more readily even where Singapore could try them. Comity: per C&Y, Spiliada respects the foreign forum as the natural forum and is more consonant with comity at stage 1, but its stage 2 judges foreign courts, which Voth avoids, so a defendant should confine comity arguments to stage 1. Outcome-determinative? The tests diverge only where the foreign forum is more appropriate but Singapore is not clearly inappropriate.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Claimant Who Prefers Australian Law

A Singapore claimant sues a Malaysian defendant in Singapore. Malaysia is clearly more appropriate (most witnesses, events and law), but Singapore has real connections too (the claimant's residence and some meetings). The claimant argues that Singapore should adopt Voth, under which a stay would be refused because Singapore is not clearly inappropriate.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Singapore has rejected Voth (JIO; Eng Liat Kiang); the defendant need only show Malaysia is clearly more appropriate. This is exactly the case where the tests diverge (Malaysia is more appropriate, but Singapore is not clearly inappropriate), so the choice is outcome-determinative: under Spiliada, a stay is granted. Evaluation: Spiliada is more respectful of comity at stage 1 (it defers to the natural forum), but at stage 2 it invites a Singapore judge to criticise Malaysian courts, which Voth avoids. So the defendant should keep its arguments at stage 1 and avoid inviting a stage 2 contest.

3J4.2 Forum conveniens on service out (burden on the claimant)

J4.2.1 Burden and Standard

Rule: Mirror image (must write): per Zoom, forum conveniens (service out) and forum non conveniens (stay) are one Spiliada test with the burden reversed: the claimant shows Singapore is more appropriate; on a stay, the defendant shows the foreign forum is. It goes only to PD para 63(2)(b), not a free-standing discretion. Burden stays on the claimant: per Spiliada, Oriental Insurance and Zoom, the claimant bears it without notice and still when the defendant applies to set aside, jurisdiction over a foreign defendant being "an imposition" on it (Li Shengwu). Not merely equal (−): per Sudarga, the claimant must show Singapore is the more appropriate forum, with the most real and substantial connection (Oro Negro). How much more (±): per Spiliada, AK Investment and Zoom, "clearly" more appropriate; per Oro Negro (adopting Siemens), "on balance" suffices, "by a hair or by a mile". Cite "clearly", flag Oro Negro, and argue both. Asymmetry is deliberate: on a stay, the defendant must show the foreign forum is clearly or distinctly more appropriate (JIO; CIMB), protecting jurisdiction as of right. JIO's relativity answers the defendant's better-forum point; it does not let the claimant rest on parity. Quality, not quantity: per Oro Negro (following JIO and Rappo), the claimant cannot win by counting connecting factors.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Singapore v Dubai, Neck and Neck

A Singapore trader serves a Dubai trader out. The contract was negotiated in both cities, performed in both, and has no governing law clause. The claimant lists 14 Singapore connections (bank accounts, meetings, emails sent from Singapore); the defendant lists 6 Dubai connections, but those 6 concern the key disputed delivery.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The claimant bears the burden throughout, both without notice and inter partes (Zoom; Oriental Insurance), because service out is "an imposition" on the defendant (Li Shengwu). Showing that Singapore is as appropriate as Dubai fails (Sudarga). Counting 14 contacts does not help; quality matters, and the 6 Dubai connections go to the heart of the dispute (Oro Negro; JIO; Rappo). On "clearly more appropriate", the claimant fails. On Oro Negro's "on balance" standard ("by a hair") it might scrape through if the governing law tips towards Singapore. Argue both.

J4.2.2 Stage 1: Centre of Gravity (burden on the claimant)

Rule: Choice of law does double duty: the governing law found under C2/C3 for gateways (e) and (f) is also a stage 1 factor. Whether double actionability applies at service out is open (J3.1.2), but per Shen Sophie the place of the tort must be located anyway, being prima facie the natural forum. Putative proper law: for a formation dispute, take the putative proper law, the law most closely connected to the negotiations (Lew v Nargolwala). Governing law across both courts: per C&Y, if Singapore would apply Singapore law and the foreign court would apply its own law, the factor is neutral; it favours a forum only where both courts would apply that forum's law. Witnesses: compellability matters more than convenience; employee witnesses raise no real compellability problem. Personal connections: a claimant in Singapore and a defendant abroad is neutral. A defendant's state links are irrelevant at stage 1 (a civil claim against a company raises no immunity), though they may matter at stage 2.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The State-Owned Shipbuilder

A Singapore owner serves a Vietnamese state-owned shipyard in Hanoi, claiming a declaration that no shipbuilding contract was concluded. The negotiations took place mostly in Singapore. Singapore choice of law would apply Singapore law (as the putative proper law); a Vietnamese court would apply Vietnamese law. The yard's witnesses are all its own employees.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Putative proper law: for a formation dispute, the law most closely connected with the negotiations, arguably Singapore law (Lew v Nargolwala). But a Vietnamese court would apply Vietnamese law, so per C&Y the governing law factor is neutral (each court applies its own law). Witnesses: the yard's employees raise no compellability problem. Personal connections: neutral (one party in each country). The yard's state ownership is irrelevant at stage 1 (no immunity in a civil commercial claim), though it may matter at stage 2 if there is cogent evidence that Vietnamese courts favour state-linked parties (J4.2.3).

J4.2.3 Stage 2 After Service Out

Rule: Claimant wins stage 1 (±): per IM Skaugen (HC), the defendant may still show it would suffer injustice here; confine this to procedural differences (e.g., broader disclosure abroad), not aspersions on Singapore's courts. Merits no answer (+): that the defendant would win abroad but lose here goes to the merits; per Vinmar and Chong, the court does not engage with the merits at the jurisdictional stage. Claimant fails stage 1: second bite? (must write): per Oro Negro and IM Skaugen (CA), this is open. For: Lewis v King, Metall. Against: Konamaneni and Fentiman. Against (−): per Konamaneni, failing stage 1 "is the end of the matter"; per Allenger, running stage 2 would confer jurisdiction where none was established. For: Spiliada itself (+): Spiliada was a service-out case: England was not the natural forum, yet leave was granted because the claim was time-barred in Canada, and Lord Goff also weighed the defendant's residence and the gateway invoked. For: principle (+): per Shen Sophie (adopting Yeo) and C&Y, access to justice and even-handed treatment apply both ways, both bases rest on statute, and O 8 was meant to expand extraterritorial jurisdiction. Konamaneni's fallback (+): even on the narrow view, injustice abroad may make the forum not "available" at stage 1, though the SGCA prefers fair-trial points at stage 2; on Spiliada's framing, "appropriate forum" is the conclusion reached after stage 2. Substance (±): run J4.1.3; e.g., an allegation that foreign courts favour state-linked parties needs cogent evidence (AK Investment) and is risky, because if it fails the case goes abroad with the allegation on record.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Shipyard Again

Continuing the shipyard case: (a) the court finds Vietnam is the natural forum (stage 1 fails for the owner); (b) the owner has an affidavit from a former Vietnamese judge saying commercial courts there routinely favour state-owned enterprises; (c) the yard, alternatively, says it would be unfairly prejudiced in Singapore because Vietnamese procedure would let it obtain broader disclosure; (d) the owner adds that it would lose in Vietnam because Vietnamese law requires formal approval for SOE contracts.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Second bite (must write): (−) Konamaneni and Allenger say failure at stage 1 is the end. (+) Spiliada itself granted leave despite stage 1 because of the Canadian time bar; Shen Sophie (adopting Yeo) and C&Y stress even-handedness and O 8's expansionary purpose; the point is open after Oro Negro and IM Skaugen (CA). Fallback: even on Konamaneni, cogent evidence of bias may make Vietnam not "available".
  • Substance: one affidavit alleging general SOE bias must be cogent and case-specific (AK Investment). It is risky: if it fails, the case goes to Vietnam with that allegation on the record.
  • (c) Defendant's stage 2: if the owner had won stage 1, the yard could in principle argue injustice in Singapore (IM Skaugen (HC)), but should confine itself to procedural points like disclosure, not aspersions on Singapore's courts.
  • (d) Merits: that the owner would lose in Vietnam is a merits point, and the court does not engage with the merits at this stage (Vinmar; Chong).

J4.2.4 Time Bars and the FLPA

Rule: Common law: per C&Y, a foreign rule extinguishing the right was substantive and one barring the remedy procedural, so a claimant could be out of time abroad but in time here, which was a classic stage 2 argument. FLPA: per FLPA s 3(1), where foreign law governs, its limitation law applies and Singapore's does not; per s 3(2), in tort the lex loci delicti's period applies, or that of the single law chosen under the flexible exception (C3). Public policy: per FLPA s 4(2) and Recovery Vehicle 1, the foreign period is disapplied only for "undue hardship" caused by the bar itself, weighing its reasonableness, the claim's complexity and the claimant's reason for letting time run. Effect: if every court applies the lex causae's period, the bar follows the claimant everywhere, so time bars recede at stage 2, surviving only where the two courts' choice of law rules differ (C&Y).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The One-Year Bar

A Singapore company sues a Philippine company in Singapore under a contract governed by Philippine law. The Philippine limitation period (assume 1 year) has expired; Singapore's 6-year period has not. The Philippine defendant seeks a stay, and the claimant argues at stage 2 that it would be time-barred in Manila.

  • Variation A: the claim is in tort for an accident in Manila.
  • Variation B: the claimant let time run because the defendant's misleading assurances persuaded it that settlement was imminent.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Under FLPA s 3(1), a Singapore court applies the Philippine period because Philippine law governs, so the claim is also time-barred in Singapore. The bar follows the claimant everywhere, and the stage 2 argument evaporates (C&Y).

  • Variation A: s 3(2) applies the lex loci delicti's period (Philippine) for the tort, unless the flexible exception selects Singapore law as the single applicable law (C3).
  • Variation B: the claimant invokes s 4(2) public policy for undue hardship caused by the bar itself (Recovery Vehicle 1), weighing the bar's short length, the claim's complexity and its good reason for letting time run (the defendant's assurances).

J4.2.5 Parallel Proceedings and Strategy

Rule: No first-seised rule: unlike Brussels (the "Italian torpedo"), each court decides for itself, so both may keep the case, risking duplication and conflicting judgments. No estoppel from the foreign ruling (±): per Lakshmi, a foreign ruling that the foreign court is the natural forum does not estop Singapore, though it may bear on comity. Use: the foreign proceedings are a stage 1 factor weighed by progress and overlap (J4.1.2), and may support a limited stay or forum election (J4.5). No separate stay application: per Zoom, the defendant should argue forum within its set-aside, where the claimant bears the burden (the "obvious advantage": C&Y); a separate stay on the same material is "wholly unnecessary and likely counter-productive". Fall-back stay not submission: per Zoom and O 6 rr 7(6), 12(5), a fall-back stay is not submission, but running it takes on the stage 1 burden that the defendant could have left with the claimant. Practice tip: advise the claimant to serve in where possible.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Race to Two Courts

A Hong Kong buyer sues a Singapore seller in Hong Kong, and the Hong Kong court rules that it is the natural forum. The Singapore seller then sues the buyer in Singapore for the price, serving out. The buyer applies to set aside, arguing that (a) Hong Kong was first seised, (b) Singapore is bound by the Hong Kong ruling, and, separately, (c) it files a stay application repeating its forum arguments.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(a) There is no first-seised rule at common law; the Hong Kong action is a stage 1 factor weighed by its progress and overlap. (b) The Hong Kong ruling does not estop Singapore (Lakshmi), though comity gives it some weight. (c) The buyer should argue forum within the set-aside, where the seller bears the burden. A separate stay on the same material is "wholly unnecessary and likely counter-productive" (Zoom) and volunteers for the stage 1 burden. If Singapore keeps the case, the risk of conflicting judgments remains, and the buyer may consider an ASI (J6) or ask for a limited stay (J4.5).

4J4.3 Strong cause

J4.3.0–J4.3.1 Starter and Nature of the Test

Rule (Starter, must write): Where the claimant sues here in breach of a foreign EJC, or the defendant seeks a stay or set-aside in breach of a Singapore EJC or NEJC, per Vinmar (restating The Eleftheria) the court holds the parties to their bargain unless the party in breach shows strong cause, whether on a stay or a set-aside (Shanghai Turbo).

  • Not Spiliada (must write): strong cause applies where a party breaches the clause; Spiliada where no one does. Never call Spiliada "the strong cause test".
  • Higher hurdle: per Vinmar, the test rests on party autonomy and commercial certainty, so "it should take more" to keep the case from the chosen court than on FNC, the court being asked to sanction a breach.
  • Foreseeable factors: per Vinmar, witnesses abroad or foreign law foreseeable at contracting carry little weight, and parties are deemed to know the chosen court's procedure and delays (Shanghai Turbo).
  • FNC waiver: per Bunge, with an express FNC waiver, grounds founded on convenience cannot amount to strong cause.
  • Singapore NEJC: per Shanghai Turbo, strong cause means the same for a Singapore NEJC, the defendant equally reneging on its promise; witnesses, documents and residence in China, with related Chinese proceedings, were insufficient there.
  • Two grounds: per Vinmar, where only the clause's parties are involved, strong cause is generally abuse of process or denial of justice; with non-parties, fragmentation may suffice (J4.3.4). The list is not closed.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Thai Chemicals EJC

Vinyl Asia Pte Ltd (Singapore) buys chemicals from Siam Petro PCL (Thailand) under a contract with an exclusive Singapore courts clause. Vinyl Asia sues in Singapore for non-delivery. Siam Petro applies for a stay, arguing: (1) all its witnesses and documents are in Bangkok; (2) the contract is governed by Thai law; (3) Singapore litigation is slower and more expensive than Bangkok; (4) related proceedings between Siam Petro and its supplier are pending in Bangkok.

  • Variation: the clause adds "and no party will argue that any other forum is more convenient".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Siam Petro, by objecting, breaches the EJC, so it must show strong cause (Vinmar; Shanghai Turbo), not merely that Bangkok is more appropriate. This is a higher hurdle: the court is asked to sanction a breach. (1)–(3) were all foreseeable when Siam Petro agreed to Singapore, so they carry little weight; parties are deemed to know the chosen court's procedure and costs. (4) Related proceedings with different parties (its supplier) are not strong cause (Shanghai Turbo: Chinese proceedings were insufficient there). Absent abuse or denial of justice, the stay is refused.

  • In the variation, the express FNC waiver means convenience-based grounds cannot be strong cause at all (Bunge).

J4.3.2 The Eleftheria Factors (as restated in Vinmar)

Rule: (a)–(c) connections: where the evidence is and the relative cost of trial; whether a foreign law applies and differs materially; how closely each party is connected with the foreign forum. These are usually foreseeable, so rarely enough alone. (d) abuse; (e) prejudice: (d) whether the applicant is acting abusively; (e) whether the claimant would be prejudiced abroad by losing security, being unable to enforce, facing a time bar, or getting no fair trial for political, racial or religious reasons. Flip for a Singapore clause: the factors are framed for a suit here in breach of a foreign EJC. Where the defendant objects to a Singapore EJC or NEJC, keep (a)–(c) but flip (d) and (e): the claimant's seising is abusive, or the defendant would be prejudiced defending here (Shanghai Turbo; Vinmar). Caution on flipped (e): like a defendant's Spiliada stage 2, this tells a Singapore judge Singapore is unjust, so confine it to concrete, cogently evidenced prejudice. Foreseeable prejudice: per Chong's mid-term comments, that the claim is time-barred abroad but alive under Singapore's longer period is arguably no prejudice to a defendant that agreed to Singapore's jurisdiction and so foresaw its time limits. Enforcing a Singapore judgment: per C&Y, that a Singapore judgment may not be enforced where the defendant's assets are was foreseeable, so it weighs little; (e)(ii) concerns the claimant's inability to enforce the foreign judgment.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Running the Factors Both Ways
  • Scenario A (foreign EJC): a Singapore buyer sues in Singapore despite an exclusive Hong Kong clause. It arrested the seller's vessel in Singapore as security, and argues (e) it would lose that security in Hong Kong.
  • Scenario B (Singapore EJC): a Thai defendant objects to a Singapore EJC, arguing (flipped (e)) that it would be prejudiced in Singapore because (i) the claim is time-barred under Thai law but not under Singapore's 6-year period, (ii) a Singapore judgment would not be enforceable in Thailand, where its assets are, and (iii) it cannot get Thai-language interpretation for key witnesses in Singapore.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Scenario A: loss of security is a classic (e) prejudice factor. But Singapore can protect it, e.g., by a stay conditional on the security remaining in place, so it is unlikely to amount to strong cause by itself.
  • Scenario B: flipped (e) must be concrete and cogently evidenced (it invites a Singapore judge to call Singapore unjust). (i) The defendant agreed to Singapore and so foresaw Singapore's limitation periods, so this is arguably no prejudice (Chong). (ii) Non-enforceability of the Singapore judgment in Thailand was foreseeable when it agreed to Singapore, so it weighs little; (e)(ii) is really about the claimant's ability to enforce a foreign judgment (C&Y). (iii) Interpretation is readily arranged and is not cogent prejudice. Strong cause is not shown.

J4.3.3 Abuse of Process and Denial of Justice

Rule: Merits irrelevant (must write): per Vinmar, overruling The Jian He, an argument that the defendant has no genuine defence is not entertained: parties choose a forum to "win or lose" there, whatever the merits. Why: a merits inquiry breeds uncertainty, cost and delay; the merits are irrelevant to FNC, IAA stays and ASIs; and seeking the agreed forum's procedural advantages (e.g., its interest or costs rules) is legitimate. Abuse reformulated: (d) asks whether the applicant is acting abusively, a very high threshold, e.g., the defendant admits liability and quantum but cannot pay, or runs a media campaign abroad to taint the trial. Euromark (treating (d) as irrelevant) was not followed. Chosen court unavailable: strong cause exists where the chosen court is dissolved or unavailable through war, or trial there would be so overwhelmingly difficult as to deny justice, if unforeseeable; notorious delay is foreseeable and insufficient. No remedy at all: per Trisuryo, strong cause was shown because Indonesian law would not recognise the trust over Indonesian shares, so the claimant could get no remedy abroad; it was exceptional, and foreign illegality goes to the merits, not the stay. Time bar: per Vinmar, a bar abroad counts only if the claimant shows "very good reasons" for not filing a protective writ there; otherwise it is self-induced.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"They Have No Defence Anyway"

A Singapore seller sues an Indian buyer in Singapore for US$2m despite an exclusive Mumbai courts clause. The seller argues strong cause because:

  1. The buyer has no defence: it signed an acknowledgment of the debt.
  2. Mumbai commercial courts are notoriously slow (five years to trial).
  3. The buyer is running a press campaign in India accusing the seller of fraud to prejudice the Mumbai judges.
  4. The Mumbai limitation period has now expired; the seller had considered filing a protective claim in Mumbai but decided it was too expensive.
  5. (Variation) A natural disaster has destroyed the Mumbai commercial court building and records, and the court has suspended all commercial cases indefinitely.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Irrelevant. Vinmar overruled The Jian He: the court does not inquire into the merits, because parties chose Mumbai to "win or lose" there. A merits inquiry would breed uncertainty, cost and delay.
  2. Insufficient. Notorious delay was foreseeable at contracting.
  3. Arguable abuse under (d). Per Vinmar, abuse is a very high threshold, but a media campaign in the chosen forum designed to taint the trial is one of Vinmar's own examples. (Equally, a buyer that admits liability and quantum but simply cannot pay may be acting abusively by insisting on Mumbai.) Euromark's view that (d) is irrelevant was not followed.
  4. Self-induced. The seller needs "very good reasons" for not filing a protective writ, and cost is not one (Vinmar).
  5. Strong cause. The chosen court is unavailable for unforeseeable reasons, akin to war or dissolution (Vinmar).
  • Trisuryo contrast: had Indian law refused to recognise the very right claimed (as Indonesian law refused to recognise the trust over Indonesian shares in Trisuryo), so that the seller could get no remedy at all in Mumbai, that exceptional situation could be strong cause. But an argument that the claim is illegal under Indian law goes to the merits, not the stay.

J4.3.4 Fragmentation and Standard Forms

Rule: Fragmentation (±): per Vinmar (citing Donohue), where non-parties are involved, splitting the dispute across Singapore and abroad risks duplication, inconsistent findings and a race to judgment, and may be strong cause, unless foreseeable at contracting. Limited overlap: per Shanghai Turbo, related foreign proceedings with different parties, causes of action or remedies are not strong cause. Counterweight: per Hive Marketing, a stay of the related claims is discretionary, not presumptive, merely because multiplicity or inconsistent decisions may follow; otherwise the court paints with "too broad and indiscriminate a brush" (CSFB v MLC). Use both ways: plead it against the party in breach invoking fragmentation (the foreseeable price of the clause), and against the party resisting a stay on multiplicity alone. The one-stop rationale belongs to scope (J1.5), fragmentation being "a fact of life" (COSCO (CA)). CCAA contrast: per 6DM, the risk that a related party cannot be joined abroad might be strong cause at common law but falls far short of s 12(1)(c) manifest injustice under an HCCCA clause. Standard form contracts (±): per Vinmar (tentatively; ZI Pompey), strong cause still applies for consistency, though autonomy is weaker; consumers and employees are better protected by forum mandatory rules. Shanghai Turbo left this open for NEJCs.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Fraud With Five Defendants

A Singapore bank lends to a Chinese borrower under a facility with an exclusive Hong Kong clause. It later discovers a fraud involving the borrower and four non-parties (two Singapore directors, a BVI shell and a Singapore auditor). The bank sues all five in Singapore. The borrower seeks a stay of the claim against it in favour of Hong Kong.

  • Variation A: when the facility was signed, the bank already knew the borrower's guarantors and directors were Singapore-based and would have to be sued here.
  • Variation B: the clause was in the borrower's standard-form terms, not negotiated.
  • Variation C: the clause instead chooses the English courts and was concluded in 2022, so it is a CCAA clause (Hong Kong is not a Contracting State).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The bank is in breach (it sued in Singapore despite the Hong Kong EJC), so it must show strong cause. Fragmentation (+): with four non-parties who can only be sued together in Singapore, splitting the case risks duplication, inconsistent findings and a race to judgment, which may be strong cause (Vinmar, citing Donohue). Counter (−): a stay is not presumptive merely because of multiplicity (Hive Marketing; CSFB v MLC: not "too broad and indiscriminate a brush"). Fragmentation is "a fact of life" (COSCO (CA)).

  • Variation A: the fragmentation was foreseeable when the bank agreed to Hong Kong, so it is the price of the clause and not strong cause.
  • Variation B: per Vinmar (tentatively, citing ZI Pompey), strong cause still applies to standard forms for consistency, though autonomy is weaker; the bank is not a consumer needing forum mandatory protection. (For a Singapore NEJC in a standard form, Shanghai Turbo left the point open.)
  • Variation C: under the CCAA there is no strong cause test at all. The risk that related parties cannot be joined in England falls far short of s 12(1)(c) manifest injustice (6DM), so the stay is mandatory (J1.4).

5J4.4 The SICC factor in the General Division's Spiliada analysis

Rule: Relevant (+): per Rappo, the court must not "shut its eyes" to the possibility of transfer to the SICC (foreign law on submissions under s 18L; international judges). Internal allocation: per Rappo (citing Yeo) and C&Y, transfer is a later question of internal allocation (J5.4), and there must be no "unprincipled jurisdictional grab". Burden on the claimant (−): per Rappo, the SICC is not "a free pass": the claimant must name the particular SICC feature and show the dispute suits it, with the transfer requirements prima facie met; absent a prima facie international and commercial case, it gets no weight. Never decisive (−): per IM Skaugen, the judge erred in letting the SICC factor tip a German-law, German-tort fraud claim to Singapore; alone it cannot displace the foreign forum, which "would virtually always" be the forum. At most a discount (±): per IM Skaugen, it discounts the weight of the foreign governing law, depending on its similarity to Singapore law and the complexity of the issues.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"But the SICC Can Hear Indian Law"

A Singapore investor sues an Indian promoter in the General Division over an Indian-law shareholders' agreement. The promoter seeks a stay to India, relying on Indian governing law. The investor replies: "The case can be transferred to the SICC, where Indian law can be argued by submission (s 18L) and an Indian-trained international judge can sit."

  • Variation A: the investor just says "the SICC is a world-class court" without more.
  • Variation B: the claim is a German-law fraud committed in Germany between German parties, and the SICC is the investor's only Singapore link.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The SICC factor is relevant; the court must not "shut its eyes" to it (Rappo). The investor has named the specific features (s 18L foreign-law submissions, an international judge) and shown that the dispute suits them, and the case is prima facie international and commercial, so transfer requirements look met. Indian law is a common law system similar to Singapore's, so the discount on the governing law factor is significant (IM Skaugen). But transfer is a later question of internal allocation (no "jurisdictional grab"), and the SICC factor alone is not decisive.

  • Variation A: no weight. The SICC is not "a free pass" (Rappo).
  • Variation B: as in IM Skaugen, the SICC factor cannot tip a German-law, German-tort case to Singapore; Germany "would virtually always" be the forum. And for a civil-law system with complex issues, the discount is slight.

6J4.5 Overlays: lis alibi pendens, limited stay and forum election

Rule: Three routes: where the dispute is also pending abroad, the defendant may rely on it at stage 1, seek a limited stay, or make a common claimant elect; it is no bar here, unlike the EU first-seised rule. Limited stay: per Rappo and 6DM, the court may stay the Singapore action (or part of it) pending the foreign jurisdiction ruling or related proceedings, managing the fragmentation risk at an early stage. Forum election, common claimant: per Koh Kay Yew and Virsagi, where the claimant sues the defendant here and abroad on the same issues, it must elect unless it justifies the multiplicity, to "prevent the inherent abuse" of using different judicial systems. Case management only: per Rappo, election never fixes the trial forum: if the claimant elects Singapore, the defendant may still seek an FNC stay; if it elects the foreign forum, the action here is stayed and the defendant may seek an ASI (Koh Kay Yew; J6). Exception: unless the defendant accepts the claimant's choice or made a representation that the claimant relied on (Rappo). FNC first: per Rappo, where the defendant runs both, FNC is decided first, and election follows only if the foreign forum is not clearly more appropriate (C&Y). Different parties or issues: election does not apply to related proceedings with different parties or issues, or where the defendant sues abroad (reversed parties); these go to FNC or an ASI.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Suing Twice

Mr Tan (Singapore) sues his former business partner, Mr Rappaport (Switzerland), for an account of profits both in Singapore and in Geneva, on the same issues. Mr Rappaport applies in Singapore for (i) an FNC stay in favour of Switzerland and, alternatively, (ii) an order that Mr Tan elect between the two fora.

  • Variation A: Mr Rappaport had earlier written, "I am content for this to be resolved in Singapore," and Mr Tan dropped plans to sue in Hong Kong in reliance.
  • Variation B: the Geneva proceedings were brought by Mr Rappaport against Mr Tan for a negative declaration.
  • Variation C: Mr Rappaport says the Geneva court is about to rule on its own jurisdiction.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

FNC first (Rappo): if Switzerland is clearly more appropriate, the Singapore action is stayed and election is moot. If FNC fails, election follows. Mr Tan is a common claimant suing on the same issues in two systems, so he must elect unless he justifies the multiplicity (Koh Kay Yew; Virsagi). Election is case management only (Rappo): if he elects Singapore, Mr Rappaport can still seek an FNC stay later (e.g., if circumstances change); if he elects Geneva, the Singapore action is stayed, and Mr Rappaport may seek an ASI against any revival (Koh Kay Yew).

  • Variation A: Mr Rappaport's representation, relied on by Mr Tan, triggers the Rappo exception, so election fixes Singapore and he cannot later seek a stay.
  • Variation B: reversed parties, so election does not apply. The Geneva action is a stage 1 factor (related proceedings) or a ground for an ASI (J6).
  • Variation C: a limited stay of the Singapore action pending the Geneva court's jurisdiction ruling manages the risk of fragmentation at an early stage (Rappo; 6DM).
