LAW302 · HYPO LESSON J5 · 17 HYPOTHETICALS · 6 FLOWCHARTS · 8 QUESTIONS

J5 hypotheticals: The SICC: written agreements, transfer and joinder

The rules behind these hypotheticals are taught in Lesson J5, where the word-for-word pre-write is too. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

Applications:
ℹ HOW TO USE THESE HYPOTHETICALS

Each concept is set out as Rule, then Hypothetical, then Application. (+) helps the party wanting the SICC; (−) helps the party resisting it. Regime routing is in J1.0.2; the SICC factor in General Division Spiliada is in J4.4.

The flowcharts redraw the hypotheticals in this site's chart style: the chip on each arrow names the hypothetical (or version) that takes that path. The hypo test at the end checks you can run the facts yourself.

1J5.0 Roadmap in one hypothetical

Rule (order): (1) Nature and subject matter (s 18A; s 18D; O 2 r 1(3), (8)). (2) Route 1: written jurisdiction agreement (O 2 r 1(1), (7); s 18F; O 2 r 2; service under O 5 r 6(2)). (3) Exercise under O 2 r 3(2)–(3) only. (4) Route 2: transfer from the General Division (O 2 r 4(1); HCCCA consent under O 2 r 4(4), (7); O 2 r 5(1); no relitigation under O 2 r 4(8)). (5) SICC → General Division (O 2 r 4(5); O 2 r 5(2)). (6) Route 3: joinder (s 18D(3); O 10 rr 5–7; service on C abroad; C's stay under O 2 r 3(2)).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Andean Copper Dispute

Condor Mining SA (Chile) and Strait Metals Pte Ltd (Singapore) sign a 2021 copper offtake agreement governed by English law: "The parties submit to the jurisdiction of the Singapore International Commercial Court." Strait Metals sues Condor in the SICC for short delivery and wants to join Condor's Peruvian parent, Inca Holdings, which guaranteed performance but did not sign the jurisdiction clause.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Subject matter: the claim is international (Condor's place of business is in Chile) and commercial (it arises from an offtake relationship), the General Division could hear it, and no prerogative relief is sought (s 18D(1); O 2 r 1(1)). Being under a written jurisdiction agreement, it is presumed international and commercial (O 2 r 1(8)).
  2. Route 1: the clause is a written jurisdiction agreement (O 2 r 1(7)), so the SICC has primary jurisdiction over the claim against Condor, and transfer need not be discussed (Chong). Exclusive? The CCAA applies (Singapore is a Contracting State, the clause post-dates 2016, and the case is international and commercial). s 3(2) CCAA deems the unlabelled clause exclusive, so s 18F need not be argued.
  3. Service: Condor is served in Chile without permission (O 5 r 6(2)(a)).
  4. Exercise: no Spiliada and no strong cause. Condor can only argue that the case is contrary to the SICC's international and commercial character, or an abuse of process (O 2 r 3(2)); its Chilean connections are irrelevant (O 2 r 3(3)).
  5. Joinder of Inca (Route 3): s 18D(3) and O 10 rr 5–7, with permission, and Inca served in Peru with permission under O 5 r 6(1) (it is not a party to the written jurisdiction agreement). Inca may resist under O 2 r 3(2), and its foreign connections can be weighed, because O 2 r 3(3) protects only parties to the agreement.

2J5.1 Nature and subject-matter jurisdiction

Rule (Nature): Per s 18A SCJA, the SICC (launched 5 January 2015) is a division of the General Division, so it is a national court: its judgment is a Singapore High Court judgment, enforceable abroad as such (including under the HCCCA); appeals lie to the Court of Appeal; and jurisdiction over the defendant still rests on s 16 SCJA. Court, not tribunal: unlike an arbitral tribunal, the SICC can coerce a third party into the proceedings (J5.6). Per Parliament, though influenced by arbitration, it is "a new way of thinking about international dispute resolution".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"Isn't the SICC Just Arbitration?"

Condor's general counsel argues that the SICC is "essentially arbitration in a courtroom", so (i) an SICC judgment should be enforced under the New York Convention, (ii) appeals are excluded, (iii) the SICC needs no in personam jurisdiction under s 16 SCJA, and (iv) it cannot bring in Inca, a non-signatory, any more than a tribunal could.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

All four points are wrong. The SICC is a division of the General Division (s 18A). (i) Its judgments are Singapore High Court judgments, enforced abroad as court judgments (e.g., under the HCCCA in another Contracting State, that State's reciprocal enforcement statute, or its common law), not as arbitral awards. (ii) Appeals lie to the Court of Appeal. (iii) Jurisdiction over Condor still rests on s 16 SCJA (here, service under the SICC Rules founding s 16(1)(a)). (iv) As a court, it can coerce Inca into the proceedings by joinder. That is the key advantage over arbitration.

Rule (Special features): The SICC has international judges, may disapply Singapore evidence rules, including on privilege (s 18K SCJA), and may decide foreign law on submissions instead of proof (s 18L). Confidentiality and counsel: the SICC may allow confidentiality or registered foreign counsel (O 16 r 9; s 18M), more readily in "offshore" cases with no substantial connection to Singapore. Standalone rules: where the SICC Rules are silent, the SICC may do what is necessary, applying the ROC with modifications or looking to foreign law or international practice (O 1 r 11(3)). Per C&Y, the standalone SICC Rules 2021 (in force from 1 April 2022) stress its independence and international character, including procedural flexibility responsive to international commerce (O 1 r 3).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Offshore Arbitration-Style Case

A Korean shipyard and a Greek owner (neither with any Singapore connection) chose the SICC. They want (a) their English QCs and Korean lawyers to argue the case; (b) the hearing to be confidential; (c) Korean law on liquidated damages decided on lawyers' submissions rather than expert evidence; (d) civil-law style document production instead of Singapore's discovery rules; (e) a procedure for an issue the SICC Rules do not address.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(a) Registered foreign counsel may appear (s 18M), especially in an offshore case with no substantial Singapore connection. (b) Confidentiality may be ordered (O 16 r 9), more readily in an offshore case. (c) Foreign law may be determined on submissions (s 18L). (d) The SICC may apply other rules of evidence (s 18K). (e) Where the Rules are silent, it may do what is necessary, applying the ROC with modifications or looking to international practice (O 1 r 11(3)), consistent with the 2021 Rules' emphasis on flexibility (O 1 r 3).

Rule (Subject matter, s 18D): The SICC hears (1) international and commercial actions the General Division could hear in its original civil jurisdiction (s 18D(1)); (2) IAA proceedings on international commercial arbitration (s 18D(2)); (3) pre-action applications for documents, injunctions or search orders, and committal; and (4) international and commercial corporate insolvency, restructuring and dissolution. IAA proceedings (±): permission is needed to serve out (O 5 r 6), and the SICC may decline under O 2 r 3(2) (C&Y). Per C&Y, "international" follows IAA s 5(2), "commercial" the Model Law art 1(1) note, and investment or State arbitrations may be included.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
What Can Go to the SICC?
  1. A Hong Kong lender's claim against a Malaysian borrower for loan repayment.
  2. An application to set aside an SIAC award between Indian and Japanese parties.
  3. A pre-action application for disclosure to identify which of a Dutch company's subsidiaries received misappropriated funds.
  4. A scheme of arrangement for a Singapore-listed group with creditors in eight countries.
  5. A challenge to a bilateral investment treaty award against a State, seated in Singapore.
  6. Judicial review of a Singapore ministry's decision.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(1) Within s 18D(1). (2) Within s 18D(2) (IAA proceedings), but serving the Japanese party abroad needs permission (O 5 r 6), and the SICC may decline under O 2 r 3(2). (3) A pre-action application, within scope. (4) International and commercial corporate restructuring, within scope. (5) Arguably within scope: per C&Y, "commercial" follows the Model Law note, and investment or State arbitrations may be included (±). (6) Outside scope: prerogative relief is excluded.

J5.1.1 International and Commercial (O 2 r 1(3))

Rule: International (+): per O 2 r 1(3)(a), the action is international if one party's place of business, or the place where a substantial part of the obligations is to be performed, or the subject matter's closest connection, is outside Singapore, or if all parties named on filing expressly agreed that it relates to more than one State. Place of business: per O 2 r 1(4)–(6), a party's place of business is where it carries on business; if it has several, the one most closely connected to the written jurisdiction agreement; if none, its habitual residence. It is fixed when the agreement was concluded (or, on transfer, when the case began or as the General Division decides). Commercial (+): per O 2 r 1(3)(b), the action is commercial if its subject matter arises from a commercial relationship, contractual or not, or it is an in personam IP dispute, or all parties expressly agreed so; the parties themselves need not be in a commercial relationship (O 2 r 1(5)). Presumption (+): per O 2 r 1(8), where each party submitted under the clause, the action is presumed international and commercial, subject to review under O 2 r 3 (C&Y). Per Chong, where the facts are objectively international and commercial, say so briefly and move on. Rebuttal (−): the defendant shows, e.g., that both parties trade only in Singapore, all obligations were performed here, or the dispute is a residential tenancy or an individual's guarantee. Even where the parties agreed the case into scope (O 2 r 1(3)(a)(ii), (b)(iii)), per C&Y the SICC may decline it as contrary to its character (O 2 r 3(2)).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four "International" Disputes
  1. Strait Metals v Condor (above): Condor's place of business is Chile.
  2. A Singapore company and a Singapore subsidiary of a German group, both trading only in Singapore, sign an SICC clause for an office fit-out in Raffles Place. The German parent has offices in 30 countries.
  3. Two Singapore residents with an SICC clause in a residential tenancy, who add: "The parties agree this dispute relates to more than one State and is commercial."
  4. A Singapore inventor sues a Singapore licensee in the SICC for infringing her Singapore patent; the licensee manufactures in Vietnam, where a substantial part of the licence obligations is performed.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Objectively international and commercial, so say so briefly and move on (Chong).
  2. (−) Rebuttal: both contracting parties' places of business are in Singapore (the German parent is not a party; place of business is fixed at contracting), and all obligations are performed here. The O 2 r 1(8) presumption is rebutted, so the action is not international.
  3. They agreed the case into scope (O 2 r 1(3)(a)(ii), (b)(iii)), so it is technically within O 2 r 1(3). But per C&Y the SICC may still decline it under O 2 r 3(2), because a residential tenancy between two Singapore residents is contrary to its international and commercial character.
  4. International, because a substantial part of the obligations is performed in Vietnam (O 2 r 1(3)(a)). Commercial, as an in personam IP dispute (O 2 r 1(3)(b)).

3J5.2 Route 1: written jurisdiction agreement

J5.2.1 Starter and Conditions (O 2 r 1(1))

Rule: Starter (must write): per O 2 r 1(1) and s 18D(1), the SICC has jurisdiction if, when first filed, (a) the action is international and commercial and one the General Division could hear; (b) each named party submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement; and (c) no prerogative relief is sought. In personam basis: jurisdiction over the defendant is founded by service under s 16(1)(a) SCJA. The clause is a promise; s 16(1)(b) submission is a separate basis needing conduct such as filing a defence on the merits (J2.2). Written jurisdiction agreement (+): per O 2 r 1(7), an agreement to submit to the exclusive or non-exclusive jurisdiction of the SICC, in writing or in an accessible form usable for later reference. Per C&Y, both EJCs and NEJCs qualify. Primary jurisdiction ends the inquiry: per Chong, if the clause gives the SICC primary jurisdiction, transfer need not be discussed; transfer matters only for a party or claim outside the clause.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Email Clause and the Three Defendants

A Singapore fintech, PayLah Pte Ltd, enters into a software licence with Bytewise Ltd (India) through an online portal. The portal terms, saved as a downloadable PDF, say: "The parties submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the SICC." PayLah sues in the SICC, naming (1) Bytewise, (2) Bytewise's US parent, which did not accept the portal terms, and (3) seeks, among other things, an order quashing a Singapore regulator's decision.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Written agreement: the portal terms are in an accessible form usable for later reference, so they qualify (O 2 r 1(7)), and a NEJC qualifies as much as an EJC (C&Y). (b) Each named party submitted: the US parent did not, so O 2 r 1(1)(b) fails as filed. PayLah should sue Bytewise alone under Route 1 and bring in the parent by joinder (J5.6), or sue in the General Division and seek a transfer. (c) No prerogative relief: the quashing order is prerogative relief, so it must be dropped. In personam basis: the clause is a promise; jurisdiction over Bytewise is founded by service (s 16(1)(a)), not by the clause itself, and not s 16(1)(b) unless Bytewise takes a step such as filing a merits defence. Primary jurisdiction: against Bytewise, the SICC has primary jurisdiction, so there is no need to discuss transfer for that claim (Chong).

J5.2.2 Exclusive or Not? (s 18F SCJA)

Rule: Presumption of exclusivity (+): per s 18F(1), absent express contrary words (s 18F(2)), the parties are taken to have agreed (a) to submit exclusively to the SICC; (b) to carry out its judgment without undue delay; and (c) to waive recourse to foreign courts against the judgment or its enforcement, so far as validly waivable. When does s 18F apply (route by facts): per C&Y, CCAA case: s 3(2) CCAA deems the clause exclusive whatever its governing law, so s 18F need not be argued. Singapore law governs the clause: s 18F applies, so the clause is exclusive absent express non-exclusive wording. Non-CCAA case, foreign law governing: debated; s 18F governs only if it is a forum mandatory rule. C&Y take no side, noting that Yip and Chong differ.

  • s 18F is a forum mandatory rule (+, Chong): per the Chong & Yip 2019 article, s 18F applies whatever the governing law: (i) the presumption against extraterritoriality is rebutted for a court set up to hear international disputes; (ii) s 18F(1)(a) is inspired by art 3(b) HCCCA (now s 3(2) CCAA); (iii) it keeps non-CCAA SICC clauses consistent with CCAA SICC clauses.
  • s 18F is not mandatory (−, Yip): it applies only where Singapore law governs the clause (in a CCAA case, s 3(2) CCAA deems exclusivity). Party autonomy is an important value of the SICC (C&Y), and a presumption rebuttable by contrary words is not an overriding mandatory rule. So the clause is construed under the foreign law. Reply (+): per C&Y, the SICC balances party autonomy against expedience, as O 2 r 2(1) shows.
  • Why it matters: little for exercise, since O 2 r 3 treats EJCs and NEJCs alike. It matters for breach: per C&Y, suing in a foreign court breaches only an exclusive SICC clause, which founds an ASI or damages.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Silent SICC Clause and the Texas Lawsuit

A licence between Lone Star Energy Inc (Texas) and Merlion Solar Pte Ltd says: "The parties submit to the jurisdiction of the SICC." Merlion sues in the SICC. Lone Star sues Merlion in Houston. Merlion wants an ASI and damages in Singapore, arguing that the SICC clause is exclusive, so Lone Star's Houston suit is a breach.

  • Version 1: the licence is governed by Singapore law and was concluded in 2015 (pre-CCAA).
  • Version 2: governed by Texas law, concluded in 2015. Under Texas law (proved), "submit to the jurisdiction" is permissive.
  • Version 3: governed by Texas law, concluded in 2020 (CCAA applies: Singapore is the chosen Contracting State, and the case is international and commercial).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Version 1: Singapore law governs the clause, so s 18F applies. With no express contrary words, the clause is exclusive, Lone Star's Houston suit breaches it, and that founds an ASI and damages (J6; J1.7). Lone Star is also taken to have agreed to carry out the SICC judgment and to waive recourse to foreign courts against it, so far as validly waivable.
  • Version 2 (±): non-CCAA, foreign law. (+) Merlion argues with Chong that s 18F is a forum mandatory rule: the presumption against extraterritoriality is rebutted for an international court, the section mirrors art 3(b) HCCCA, and consistency with CCAA clauses requires it. (−) Lone Star argues with Yip that s 18F applies only where Singapore law governs; party autonomy is central to the SICC, and a rebuttable presumption is not an overriding mandatory rule. So Texas law governs, and the clause is permissive. Reply: the SICC balances autonomy against expedience (cf O 2 r 2(1)). Stakes: the SICC's exercise of jurisdiction does not depend on this (O 2 r 3 treats EJCs and NEJCs alike), but Merlion's ASI and damages depend on there being a breach, which needs exclusivity.
  • Version 3: s 3(2) CCAA deems the clause exclusive regardless of Texas law, so there is no need to argue s 18F.

J5.2.3 Clauses Naming the High Court or General Division (O 2 r 2)

Rule: Post-2016 High Court clause includes the SICC (+): per O 2 r 2(1) and s 2(2)–(3) CCAA, a clause concluded on or after 1 October 2016 naming the Singapore High Court or General Division includes the SICC unless a contrary intention appears, so the claimant may file directly in the SICC.

  • Critique (−): per C&Y, O 2 r 2(1) seems to bar evidence that the parties never contemplated the SICC, contrary to Singapore's contextual interpretation and party autonomy.
  • Reply (+): per C&Y, the lost autonomy buys HCCCA enforceability of the SICC judgment and fits the SICC's international template; per Hartley–Dogauchi, "the courts of France" lets French law allocate internally.
  • Specific reference needed? (−): per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), arguably the clause needs a more specific reference to the SICC to qualify as a written jurisdiction agreement for it.

Pre-2016 clause (−): per O 2 r 2(2), a clause concluded before 1 October 2016 "does not of itself" submit to the SICC; per Chong, there is no primary jurisdiction, so the claimant sues in the General Division and seeks a transfer (J5.4). SICC-only clause (−): per O 2 r 2(3), a clause naming the SICC alone is not "of itself" submission to the General Division (C&Y). Foreign law governs the clause: is O 2 r 2(1) procedural or substantive? (±): (+) it is a forum rule on internal allocation and on the scope of submission to a Singapore court, so the lex fori applies; (−) construing the clause is substance for its proper law, as party autonomy requires. Likely outcome (Chong): the foreign law probably has no rule on construing "the General Division of Singapore", so it falls back on O 2 r 2(1). If Singapore law governs: the question does not arise: O 2 r 2(1) applies, and absent express contrary words s 18F makes the clause exclusive (C&Y).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four High Court Clauses
  1. A 2019 contract (Singapore law): "The Singapore High Court shall have jurisdiction." The claimant files in the SICC. The defendant leads evidence that neither party had heard of the SICC when contracting.
  2. A 2014 contract: "The Singapore High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction." The claimant files in the SICC.
  3. A 2020 contract: "The SICC shall have exclusive jurisdiction." The claimant files in the General Division.
  4. A 2021 contract governed by French law: "The General Division of the High Court of Singapore shall have jurisdiction." The defendant argues that French law governs construction and that, as a matter of French construction, a named court means only that court.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. (+) Under O 2 r 2(1), a post-2016 High Court clause includes the SICC unless a contrary intention appears, so the claimant may file directly in the SICC. (−) The defendant's evidence that the parties never contemplated the SICC seems barred by O 2 r 2(1), which C&Y criticise as contrary to contextual interpretation and autonomy. The defendant may also argue (Chong) that a more specific reference to the SICC is needed for a written jurisdiction agreement. Reply: the loss of autonomy buys HCCCA enforceability and mirrors Hartley–Dogauchi's "courts of France" (internal allocation by the forum). Because Singapore law governs, s 18F also makes the clause exclusive, absent contrary words.
  2. A pre-2016 clause does not of itself submit to the SICC (O 2 r 2(2)). There is no primary jurisdiction, so the claimant should sue in the General Division and apply for a transfer (J5.4).
  3. An SICC-only clause is not of itself submission to the General Division (O 2 r 2(3)), so the claimant cannot rely on it alone there.
  4. (±) The claimant argues that O 2 r 2(1) is a procedural forum rule on internal allocation, so it applies regardless of French law. The defendant argues that construction is substance for the proper law (French law). Likely outcome (Chong): French law has no rule on construing "the General Division of Singapore", so it falls back on O 2 r 2(1), and the clause includes the SICC.

J5.2.4 Serving the Defendant Out of Singapore (O 5 r 6)

Rule: No permission needed (+): per O 5 r 6(2), a defendant abroad may be served out without permission if it is a party to the written jurisdiction agreement (r 6(2)(a)), or bound by a contract allowing service out (r 6(2)(b)), whether or not the clause mentions service. Per O 5 r 6(5), the SICC may still review jurisdiction under O 2 r 3. Permission needed (±): otherwise, per O 5 r 6(1), permission is granted if the SICC "has the jurisdiction to hear the action and it is appropriate for the case to be heard in the Court". Per C&Y, FNC does not apply, so the defendant's Spiliada factors are irrelevant; appropriateness turns on the SICC's international and commercial character.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Serving Condor and Inca

Strait Metals serves Condor (party to the SICC clause) in Santiago, and wants to serve Inca Holdings (guarantor, not party to the clause) in Lima. Inca argues that Peru is clearly the more appropriate forum.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Condor: no permission needed (O 5 r 6(2)(a)), even though the clause says nothing about service, though the SICC may still review jurisdiction under O 2 r 3 (O 5 r 6(5)). Inca: permission is needed (O 5 r 6(1)): the SICC must "have the jurisdiction" (via joinder, s 18D(3)) and it must be "appropriate". Per C&Y, FNC does not apply, so Inca's Spiliada argument that Peru is clearly more appropriate is beside the point; appropriateness asks about the SICC's international and commercial character.

J5.2.5 Challenging the Existence of Jurisdiction

Rule: Apply within 14 days after serving the Defendant's Statement (O 2 r 7); a defendant disputing service may apply to set it aside (O 2 r 6). Attack the clause (−): e.g., void or never agreed for mistake, misrepresentation, duress or lack of authority. Reply (+): per s 5 CCAA (CCAA cases) and the common law (J1.6), the clause is separable. Attack the nature of the dispute (−): rebut the O 2 r 1(8) presumption. Consequence of success: per O 2 r 3(5), if the SICC lacks jurisdiction, it must transfer the case to the General Division if that court has jurisdiction and all parties consent; otherwise it may dismiss, stay or make any order. Deemed consent to transfer: per O 2 r 3(6), a "High Court" or "General Division" clause counts as each party's consent to the General Division hearing the case (C&Y). Finality: per O 2 r 3(7), a decision that the SICC has and will exercise jurisdiction, or a transfer to the General Division, is final unless permission to appeal is granted.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Condor's Counterattack

Condor applies, 10 days after serving its Defendant's Statement, to dispute the SICC's jurisdiction on three grounds: (1) the offtake agreement was induced by Strait Metals' misrepresentation about smelter capacity, so the clause falls with it; (2) the dispute is really domestic because both parties' traders are based in Singapore; (3) alternatively, its signatory lacked authority to sign any jurisdiction clause.

  • Variation: the clause had read "the Singapore High Court shall have jurisdiction" (2019), and the SICC upholds ground (2).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The application is in time (within 14 days of the Defendant's Statement, O 2 r 7). (1) The clause is separable (s 5 CCAA, since this is a CCAA case; and J1.6 at common law). Misrepresentation inducing the contract does not touch consent to the clause, so the ground fails. (2) Condor tries to rebut the international and commercial presumption (O 2 r 1(8)), but its place of business is in Chile (place of business is fixed at contracting, O 2 r 1(4)–(6)), so the ground fails. (3) This goes to the clause itself, so it is a proper attack (decided under the CCAA validity rules: J1.2.5). If any ground succeeded, the SICC would transfer to the General Division only if that court has jurisdiction and all parties consent; otherwise dismiss or stay (O 2 r 3(5)). A decision upholding jurisdiction is final unless permission to appeal is granted (O 2 r 3(7)).

  • In the variation, a "High Court" clause counts as each party's consent to the General Division hearing the case (O 2 r 3(6)), so the SICC must transfer it to the General Division rather than dismiss.

4J5.3 Exercise of jurisdiction in the SICC (O 2 r 3)

Rule: The test (must write): per O 2 r 3(2), the SICC may decline only if exercising jurisdiction is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of its process, on its own motion or on application (O 2 r 3(4)). Foreign connections irrelevant (+): per O 2 r 3(3), where there is a written jurisdiction agreement, the SICC must not decline "solely on the ground that the action … is connected to a jurisdiction other than Singapore". Per C&Y and Chong, there is no Spiliada balancing, Australian test or strong cause. Same test for EJCs and NEJCs (+): per C&Y, the old O 110 r 8 "appropriateness" wording left room to treat a NEJC differently; the 2021 Rules close that gap, as the SICC Committee intended. Justification (evaluation): per the SICC User Guide (Note 1), connections are ignored because the parties agreed in writing to "an international court"; per C&Y this is circular, the SICC not being a true international court. C&Y prefer party autonomy: commercial parties may choose a neutral, specialist forum and must accept the consequences. Contrary to international and commercial character (−): a dispute that is in substance local, or consumer-type, brought in only by agreement under O 2 r 1(3)(a)(ii) or (b)(iii). Objectively international and commercial (+): there is then little ground to decline (Chong). Abuse of process (−): e.g., filing in the SICC only to delay well-advanced foreign proceedings or to relitigate an issue decided abroad (cf tactical "wait and see" conduct, J6.3.1.3). Consequence: per O 2 r 3(5)–(6), if the SICC declines, it must transfer the case to the General Division where that court has jurisdiction and all parties consent (deemed for a "High Court" clause); otherwise it may dismiss or stay.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Requests to Decline
  1. Condor (Chile) asks the SICC to decline: all witnesses, documents and the mine are in Chile; the governing law is English; Chile is "clearly more appropriate". The SICC clause is non-exclusive.
  2. Two Singapore residents used an SICC clause (agreeing the case "relates to more than one State") for a dispute over a condominium renovation.
  3. A Thai company lost in the Bangkok courts after a five-year trial on a supply contract with an SICC NEJC. It now files in the SICC on the same issues, hoping for a different result.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Refused. O 2 r 3(3) bars declining solely because the case is connected to Chile, and there is no Spiliada, no Australian test and no strong cause (C&Y; Chong). That the clause is non-exclusive does not matter: the 2021 Rules apply the same test to EJCs and NEJCs (closing the gap left by old O 110 r 8). The case is objectively international and commercial, so there is little ground to decline (Chong). Evaluation: the User Guide's justification (the parties agreed to an "international court") is circular (C&Y), and party autonomy is the better justification: Condor chose a neutral forum and must accept the consequences.
  2. May decline. A local renovation dispute brought in only by the parties' agreement under O 2 r 1(3)(a)(ii) is contrary to the SICC's international and commercial character (C&Y). If declined, transfer to the General Division needs all parties' consent; otherwise dismiss or stay (O 2 r 3(5)).
  3. May decline for abuse of process. Relitigating an issue already decided abroad abuses the SICC's process (O 2 r 3(2)), as would filing just to delay advanced foreign proceedings.

5J5.4 Route 2: transfer from the General Division to the SICC (s 18J(2) SCJA; O 2 r 4)

(Per C&Y, this has been the main source of SICC cases so far. Apply within 28 days, with evidence of the transfer conditions and any consent (O 2 r 7). Existence was founded under General Division rules: service in (J2) or service out under O 8 (J3).)

J5.4.1 Non-CCAA Case (O 2 r 4(1))

Rule: Requirements (must write): a party applies, or the court acts on its own motion after hearing the parties (O 2 r 4(3)). Per O 2 r 4(1), the court may transfer if (a) the action is international and commercial when the order is made; (b) no prerogative relief is sought; and (c) the SICC is more appropriate. Only route: per Chong, where the clause predates 1 October 2016 or does not cover the claim against a non-party, transfer under O 2 r 4(1)(c) is the only way into the SICC. More appropriate (+): per C&Y (the Rules give no factors): the international elements and their relevance; the SICC's capability to handle them; the parties' level of consent; and connections to Singapore. Not complexity: per Chong, the test turns on how international and commercial the dispute is, not on its complexity, which a General Division judge can also handle. International judge: an International Judge with expertise in the relevant foreign law favours the SICC (Chong). Weak Singapore link: per C&Y, a case poorly connected to Singapore is arguably more suited to the SICC. Consent: per C&Y, since the General Division may transfer without every party's consent, it should lean towards transfer where all or most parties consent. Overlap with Spiliada: per C&Y, where the defendant seeks a stay at the jurisdictional stage, most factors other than consent are weighed at Spiliada stage 1, where the SICC factor alone cannot displace the foreign forum (IM Skaugen). Not more appropriate (−): a straightforward Singapore-law debt claim, or a largely domestic dispute, that a General Division judge can resolve expeditiously.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Pre-2016 Distribution Agreement

In 2014, Tropical Spice Pte Ltd and Kerala Exports Ltd (India) signed a distribution agreement governed by Indian law: "The Singapore High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction." In 2024 Tropical Spice sues Kerala in the General Division for termination damages, serving out under O 8. The dispute turns on difficult questions of Indian contract and competition law. An International Judge of the SICC is a former Indian Supreme Court judge. Kerala consents to transfer; Tropical Spice opposes, saying the case is "simple".

  • Variation: the dispute is a straightforward Singapore-law claim for S$80,000 in unpaid invoices between two Singapore-based trading companies.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The 2014 clause predates 1 October 2016, so it does not of itself submit to the SICC (O 2 r 2(2)). There is no primary jurisdiction, and transfer under O 2 r 4(1) is the only route (Chong). (a) The action is international (Kerala's place of business is in India) and commercial; (b) no prerogative relief is sought; (c) more appropriate: the international elements (Indian law, Indian party) are central; the SICC can handle them (s 18L submissions on Indian law; an Indian International Judge, which Chong flags as favouring the SICC); and one party consents, which leans towards transfer (C&Y). Tropical Spice's "simple case" point misses the test: it turns on how international and commercial the dispute is, not on its complexity (Chong). Transfer is likely. The application must be made within 28 days with supporting evidence (O 2 r 7), or the court may act on its own motion (O 2 r 4(3)).

  • In the variation, a domestic Singapore-law debt claim that a General Division judge can resolve quickly is not more appropriately heard in the SICC.
  • Spiliada overlap: had Kerala sought a stay to India, most of these factors would be weighed at Spiliada stage 1, where the SICC factor alone cannot displace India (IM Skaugen; J4.4).

J5.4.2 CCAA Case With a "High Court" or "General Division" EJC (O 2 rr 4(4), 4(7), 5(1))

Rule: Every party's consent (must write): where the CCAA applies and the clause names the Singapore High Court or General Division, per O 2 r 4(4) transfer also needs every party's consent. Per C&Y, this goes beyond s 11(5) CCAA ("take into account") in order to protect HCCCA recognition: art 8(5) lets a foreign court refuse recognition against a party that objected in time. Deemed consent (+): per O 2 r 4(7), where the clause names the receiving court, each party is treated as consenting. With O 2 r 2(1) (a post-2016 High Court clause includes the SICC), consent is doubly deemed (C&Y). Counter (−): per C&Y, it is unclear whether deemed consent meets the CCAA threshold; if a party objected in time, the SICC judgment risks refusal under art 8(5); arguably the General Division should insist on actual consent. Discretion only: per s 15(4)(b) CCAA (the art 8(5) equivalent), the risk arises only where the transfer was discretionary, not mandated by internal allocation rules. SICC expressly excluded (±): where the clause names the High Court "excluding the SICC", per O 2 r 5(1) transfer may be conditional on every party varying the clause to name the SICC. Per C&Y, the rule is strictly unnecessary (there is no transfer without consent anyway) but nudges the parties to vary, securing clean HCCCA enforcement. Handout question: can a "High Court" EJC case started in the General Division be transferred without breaching the HCCCA? Yes, per O 2 r 4(4) and (7), if every party consents, actually or by deemed consent, subject to the art 8(5) risk where a party objected in time.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Objecting Mexican Defendant

A 2021 supply contract between a Singapore buyer and Aztec Steel SA (Mexico) says: "The Singapore High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction." The buyer sues in the General Division. The court, on the buyer's application, considers transferring the case to the SICC. Aztec objects in writing at once. Aztec's assets are all in Mexico (a Contracting State).

  • Variation: the clause reads "the Singapore High Court (excluding the SICC)".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This is a CCAA case, so transfer needs every party's consent (O 2 r 4(4)), which goes further than s 11(5) CCAA in order to protect recognition. Deemed consent (+): the clause names the High Court, which under O 2 r 2(1) includes the SICC, so per O 2 r 4(7) Aztec is treated as consenting, doubly deemed (C&Y). Counter (−): Aztec objected in time. If the transfer is discretionary, a Mexican court may refuse to recognise the SICC judgment under art 8(5) HCCCA (s 15(4)(b) CCAA is Singapore's equivalent), and all of Aztec's assets are in Mexico. C&Y doubt that deemed consent meets the Convention's threshold, so arguably the General Division should insist on actual consent here. Answer to the handout question: yes, a transfer is possible without breaching the HCCCA if every party consents, actually or by deeming, but with an art 8(5) recognition risk where a party has objected in time.

  • In the variation, the express exclusion of the SICC means there is no deemed consent. Per O 2 r 5(1), the court may make the transfer conditional on all parties varying the clause to name the SICC. That is strictly unnecessary (consent is needed anyway), but it gives a clean basis for HCCCA enforcement.

J5.4.3 After Transfer: No Relitigation of Jurisdiction

Rule: Existence (−): per O 2 r 4(8)(b)(i), the SICC "must not reconsider whether it has jurisdiction unless there has been a material change in circumstances such that the court may cease to have jurisdiction" (e.g., a new party, or no valid service on the defendant). Exercise (−): O 2 r 3(2) (and arguably (3)) applies in principle, but the General Division will usually have decided any stay already. Arguably the defendant's consent to the transfer also waives objection.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Second Thoughts After Transfer

After Tropical Spice's case (J5.4.1) is transferred to the SICC with Kerala's consent, Kerala (i) argues the SICC lacks jurisdiction because the General Division wrongly found a gateway, and (ii) asks the SICC to decline because India is more appropriate. Later, Tropical Spice joins a new defendant whom it has not validly served.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(i) The SICC must not reconsider its jurisdiction absent a material change in circumstances (O 2 r 4(8)(b)(i)), and the General Division's gateway finding is not a change, so Kerala cannot reopen it. (ii) O 2 r 3(2) applies in principle, but the General Division will already have dealt with any stay, and Kerala's consent to the transfer arguably waives its objection. The new, unserved defendant is a material change in circumstances, so jurisdiction over that party can be examined.

6J5.5 Transfer from the SICC to the General Division (O 2 rr 4(5), 5(2))

Rule: Requirements (+): outside O 2 r 3(5), per O 2 r 4(5), a party may apply with all parties' consent if the General Division has jurisdiction (it does: s 18A) and is more appropriate (C&Y). More appropriate, low threshold (+): per C&Y, since all parties consent, the threshold is low; the relevant questions are whether the international elements are germane to the dispute and whether a Singapore judge can resolve it expeditiously. Not more appropriate (−): per Chong, where the action is objectively international and commercial (e.g., the defendant is abroad), it is hard to see why the General Division is more appropriate. CCAA SICC-only clause (±): per O 2 r 5(2), where the CCAA applies and the clause names only the SICC, transfer may be conditional on every party varying the clause to name the General Division (C&Y). Deemed consent applies where the clause names the receiving court (O 2 r 4(7)).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Trimming the Case Back
  1. Two parties sued in the SICC over a S$200,000 dispute about a Singapore warehouse lease between a Singapore company and the Singapore branch of a Hong Kong company. The only foreign element (the Hong Kong parent) is irrelevant to the issues. Both now want to move to the General Division to save costs.
  2. Same as Strait Metals v Condor, but both want to move to the General Division.
  3. A 2022 CCAA clause names "the SICC" only; both parties want to move to the General Division.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. With all parties' consent, the threshold is low. The international element is not germane, and a General Division judge can decide quickly, so transfer is appropriate (O 2 r 4(5); C&Y).
  2. (−) The action is objectively international and commercial (a Chilean defendant), so it is hard to see why the General Division is more appropriate (Chong), even with consent.
  3. Per O 2 r 5(2), the transfer may be conditional on every party varying the clause to name the General Division, to keep CCAA/HCCCA enforceability clean. Without a variation there is no deemed consent, because the clause does not name the receiving court (O 2 r 4(7)).

7J5.6 Route 3: joinder of additional parties (s 18D(3) SCJA; O 10)

Rule: Starter (must write): per s 18D(3)–(4), once the SICC has jurisdiction over an international and commercial action, it may hear claims by or against additional parties (joinder, counterclaims, third- and subsequent-party proceedings) if the action as a whole remains international and commercial; the additional party's own claims need not be (C&Y). Key advantage (+): per C&Y (citing the SICC Committee Report), coercive joinder is a key advantage over arbitration: a non-signatory can be bound in one proceeding. Requirements (+): per O 10 r 5(1), the party may be joined if the O 10 joinder requirements are met and the claims by or against it seek no prerogative relief and are appropriate for the SICC, which considers its international and commercial character (O 10 r 5(3)). Connected issues (+): per O 10 r 6(1), joinder is appropriate "so that the Court can resolve all the matters in dispute in the proceedings or any issues that are connected to those matters". No common questions (−): per Chong, joinder fails where the claim against the new party shares no common question of law or fact with the claim against the defendant (e.g., a pre-contractual tort against a post-contractual breach). No written agreement needed (+): per O 10 r 5(2), the new party need not have submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement, unless it is a State or sovereign, which must have (C&Y). Permission (±): per O 10 r 7(1), SICC permission is generally required, on application by an existing party or the new party itself (O 10 r 7(3)), but not where the new party submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement and the originating application is not yet served (O 10 r 7(2)(a)). Service in Singapore: per O 5 r 2, personal service founds jurisdiction under s 16 SCJA (apply J2.1). Service abroad (±): per O 5 r 6(2), without permission if the party is bound by a written jurisdiction agreement or an agreement allowing service out; otherwise, per O 5 r 6(1), with permission if the SICC "has the jurisdiction" and "it is appropriate"; per C&Y, FNC does not apply. Resisting joinder (−): the new party may seek a stay under O 2 r 3(2). O 2 r 3(3) (the foreign-connections bar) protects only parties to a written jurisdiction agreement: the User Guide ignores connections because the parties agreed in writing, and the new party did not, so the SICC may weigh its foreign links. Burden: arguably the party seeking joinder bears it, as it must show the claims are "appropriate" for the SICC (O 10 r 5(1)(b)(ii)).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Bringing in Inca, the Bank and the Ministry

In Strait Metals v Condor (SICC, Route 1), Strait Metals wants to join:

  • (A) Inca Holdings (Peru), Condor's parent, which guaranteed Condor's delivery obligations. It never signed the SICC clause.
  • (B) Andes Bank (Chile), which issued a letter of credit. Strait Metals' claim against it is that, two years before the offtake agreement, its relationship manager made a negligent misstatement about Condor's creditworthiness.
  • (C) The Chilean Ministry of Mining, which Strait Metals alleges colluded in Condor's export restrictions.
  • (D) Lim, a Singapore-resident trader who brokered the deal and allegedly took secret commissions from Condor. His claim against Strait Metals is a purely domestic claim for unpaid brokerage fees.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (A) Inca: Joinder is appropriate. The guarantee claim is bound up with the main delivery dispute, so the court "can resolve all the matters in dispute" (O 10 r 6(1)). Inca need not have signed a written jurisdiction agreement (O 10 r 5(2)), but permission is needed (O 10 r 7(1)), and service in Lima needs permission under O 5 r 6(1) ("has the jurisdiction" and "appropriate", with no FNC). If Inca seeks a stay under O 2 r 3(2), the O 2 r 3(3) bar does not protect Strait Metals, because Inca did not agree in writing; the SICC may weigh Inca's Peruvian connections. Strait Metals arguably bears the burden of showing the claims against Inca are appropriate for the SICC (O 10 r 5(1)(b)(ii)). This coercive joinder is the SICC's key advantage over arbitration (C&Y).
  • (B) Andes Bank: Joinder likely fails. A pre-contractual negligent misstatement shares no common question of law or fact with Condor's post-contractual short delivery (Chong).
  • (C) The Ministry: As a State party, it can only be joined if it submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement (O 10 r 5(2); C&Y). It did not, so joinder fails. (State immunity issues aside.)
  • (D) Lim: His own claim need not be international or commercial, as long as the action as a whole stays international and commercial (s 18D(3)–(4); C&Y). Lim is in Singapore, so he is personally served under O 5 r 2, founding jurisdiction under s 16 SCJA (J2.1).

8J5.7 Links to other files (applied)

Rule: ASIs: per C&Y, an SICC written jurisdiction agreement supplies sufficient interest unless the claim is not international and commercial or abuses process (J6.2.1). Breach of an exclusive SICC clause may need no strong reasons test, or a modified one; for a NEJC, the SICC should refrain if the foreign proceedings came first (J6.3.1.3). ASI sought from the SICC: per Chong, if the SICC has primary jurisdiction under the clause, the O 2 r 3(2) test arguably governs the ASI application. For HCCCA cases see J6.5.3; s 10 CCAA leaves interim measures outside the Act. Spiliada in the General Division: per Rappo, a possible SICC transfer is relevant if the claimant articulates a suitable SICC feature; per IM Skaugen, it cannot alone displace the natural forum (J4.4). Damages for breach: suing abroad in breach of an exclusive SICC or CCAA clause breaches the contract (J1.7). Recognition: the chosen court's judgment is recognised under CCAA Part 3 (J7.5); art 8(5) non-recognition after a contested transfer is why the transfer rules insist on consent (J5.4.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Lone Star's Houston Suit, Revisited

Back in Lone Star v Merlion (J5.2.2): (1) in Version 1 (Singapore law, s 18F exclusive), Merlion asks the SICC for an ASI against the Houston suit; (2) in a variation, the SICC clause is expressly non-exclusive, and Lone Star had sued in Houston before Merlion filed in the SICC; (3) Merlion also claims damages for its Houston defence costs.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. The SICC written jurisdiction agreement supplies sufficient interest for an ASI (unless the claim is not international and commercial or is abusive). Breach of the exclusive clause gives a contractual basis; C&Y suggest the strong reasons test may be unnecessary or modified (J6.3.1.3). Per Chong, because the SICC has primary jurisdiction, the O 2 r 3(2) lens arguably governs whether it should act.
  2. With a NEJC and the Houston proceedings first in time, C&Y suggest the SICC should refrain from granting an ASI (J6.3.1.3), since suing in Houston is no breach of a non-exclusive clause.
  3. Suing in Houston in breach of an exclusive SICC clause is a breach of contract, so damages are available in principle (J1.7; subject to Tradewaves: "can", not "must"). And if Lone Star ever needs to enforce a Houston judgment in Singapore, the breach may support a recognition defence (J7).
