For a local judgment, TT International would ask whether the ruling directly affects future rights (yes: 30 years of rent), is clearly wrong (arguably, after the CA ruling), turns on a point not reasonably arguable before the Hong Kong court (doubtful), involves no claw-back of accrued rights (only future rent), and causes great injustice (likely). For a foreign judgment it is open (Merck). C&Y prefer option (iv): ask whether, under Hong Kong law, the ruling is conclusive for future rent periods, consistent with how finality is tested (J7.1.3).

6J7.4 REFJA (outline only, for comparison)

(Not examinable as a regime (Chong): if X is gazetted, say one line, then run the common law, citing REFJA only as an analogue under Merck's convergence aim.)

Rule: One-line router: per ss 3, 4(7)(a), a judgment of a gazetted court may be registered and then has local force; per s 7(1), the creditor cannot then sue on it at common law. Analogues: non-money relief (±): registrable if "just and convenient" (s 4(4)), unlike at common law. Excess damages (±): only the compensatory part of treble or punitive damages is registered (s 4(5)); compare Licea. Excluded (−): taxes, fines, penalties and judgments on judgments (ss 2(1), 3(4)). Residence, not presence (−): the debtor must have been resident (or a company with its principal place of business) in X (s 5(3)(a)(iv)). Protest is not submission (+): appearing only to contest jurisdiction, invite the court not to exercise it, or protect seized property is not submission (s 5(3)(a)(i)), matching IGCF against Henry v Geoprosco. Breach of agreement (−): the X court is not deemed to have jurisdiction where its proceedings breached the clause and the debtor did not submit (s 5(4)(b)). Fraud and public policy (±): registration is set aside for fraud or where enforcement offends public policy (s 5(1)(a)(iv)–(v)); per Chong, as REFJA words public policy like the common law, Venetian Macau is authoritative for the common law too.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Hong Kong Comparison

A Hong Kong judgment (Hong Kong is gazetted) awards (i) HK$10m compensatory damages, (ii) HK$5m punitive damages and (iii) an injunction. The debtor was in Hong Kong on a two-day trip when served and lives in Singapore. It applied in Hong Kong only to set aside service on FNC grounds, and lost.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

One line: Hong Kong is gazetted, so the creditor could register under REFJA (and if it does, cannot sue at common law, s 7(1)). For comparison: under REFJA, mere presence on a two-day trip is not enough (residence is required, s 5(3)(a)(iv)), whereas at common law temporary presence suffices (Adams v Cape). The FNC set-aside is a protest, not submission (s 5(3)(a)(i)), which matches IGCF. The injunction is registrable if just and convenient (s 4(4)), unlike at common law, and only the compensatory part of the damages would be registered (s 4(5)), mirroring Licea severance. Then run the common law fully.

7J7.5 CCAA (Hague choice of court agreements)

Rule (Starter): Where the X court, in an HCCCA Contracting State, is the court chosen in an exclusive COCA, the creditor applies under the CCAA rather than suing afresh. Per s 13(4), the court must recognise or enforce unless a ground in ss 14–16 applies, and the list is exhaustive. (REFJA is ousted, s 2A; the common law remains open, s 21.)

J7.5.1 Scope

Rule: Chosen court (±): per s 2(1), only judgments of the chosen court, or of a court to which it transferred the case under internal allocation rules, qualify; per Hartley–Dogauchi, the basis on which the X court took jurisdiction is irrelevant. Scope conditions: exclusive COCA, civil or commercial, international, concluded after the HCCCA entered into force for X and Singapore (Singapore: 1 Oct 2016); whether an asymmetric clause qualifies is for J1. Judgment (+): a final decision on the merits, a consent order or judgment, a default judgment, or a costs determination relating to one, including non-money judgments; interim relief is excluded (s 10; Motacus), though Singapore may grant interim relief in support (s 10(2)). Judicial settlement (+): per ss 2(1) and 20, a settlement approved by or concluded before the chosen court, ending the proceedings and officially recorded, is enforced (not "recognised") like a judgment if enforceable in X; a consent order is a "judgment" instead. Remedy unknown in Singapore (±): per Hartley–Dogauchi, give it as much effect as possible (e.g., the nearest equivalent order).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Paris Commercial Court Orders

A 2020 exclusive clause chose the Paris Commercial Court for a distribution contract between a Singapore distributor and a French brand. The Paris court made: (i) a final damages judgment of €5m; (ii) an interim order freezing the distributor's stock; (iii) a costs order; (iv) a judicially recorded settlement on a separate claim; (v) an astreinte (a periodic penalty payment for non-compliance with an order to return stock), a remedy unknown in Singapore. Separately, (vi) the Paris court transferred one claim to the Paris Commercial Court's international chamber under French internal allocation rules, which gave judgment.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(i) A final judgment of the chosen court, so within the CCAA. The basis on which Paris took jurisdiction is irrelevant (Hartley–Dogauchi). (ii) Interim relief is excluded (s 10; Motacus), though Singapore may grant its own interim relief in support (s 10(2)). (iii) A costs determination relating to a judgment is included. (iv) A judicial settlement is enforced like a judgment (not "recognised") if enforceable in France (ss 2(1), 20). (v) Unknown remedy: give it as much effect as possible, e.g., the nearest equivalent order (Hartley–Dogauchi), though the debtor may argue that its penal character engages public policy or excess damages (s 16). (vi) A transferee court under internal allocation rules counts (s 2(1)), subject to the s 15(4) objected-transfer ground (J7.5.4).

J7.5.2 Procedure and Effect

Rule: Application and service (+): per s 13(1) and O 37 ROC 2021, the creditor applies to the General Division without a fresh action; per O 37 r 6(4), it may serve the order on the debtor abroad without permission. Time bar (±): (+) per C&Y, no limitation period applies, since no implied debt is sued on; (−) but per s 13(2), if the judgment is no longer enforceable in X (e.g., time-barred there), Singapore cannot enforce it. Effect in the State of origin (±): recognised only if it has effect in X, and enforced only if enforceable there (e.g., an expired time-limited injunction cannot be enforced). No review of the merits (+): per s 13(3)(a), save to apply Part 3; per s 13(1), recognised as a General Division judgment would be. Jurisdictional findings bind (+): per s 13(3)(b), the court is bound by the X court's findings of fact on which it assumed jurisdiction (e.g., that the COCA was concluded, exclusive, international), unless the judgment was by default. Per C&Y, only facts bind, not their legal evaluation (e.g., "accessibility").

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Enforcing the Paris Judgment Ten Years On

The French brand applies in Singapore in 2034 to enforce the 2024 Paris judgment. The distributor, now based in Vietnam, says: (a) more than six years have passed; (b) French law gives judgments a ten-year enforcement life, which has just expired; (c) the Paris court was wrong on the merits; (d) the Paris court found that the clause was "accessible for subsequent reference" and that the parties concluded it in 2020, but the distributor disputes both points; (e) the Paris order included a two-year injunction that has expired.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The brand applies by O 37 application (no fresh action) and serves the order in Vietnam without permission (O 37 r 6(4)). (a) No Singapore limitation period applies (C&Y), but (b) under s 13(2), if the judgment is no longer enforceable in France, Singapore cannot enforce it, which makes the French ten-year life decisive. (c) No review of the merits (s 13(3)(a)). (d) The Paris court's findings of fact that the clause was concluded in 2020 bind (s 13(3)(b)), unless the judgment was by default; its legal evaluation that the clause was "accessible" does not (C&Y). (e) An expired injunction has no effect in France, so it cannot be enforced (s 13(2)).

J7.5.3 Mandatory Refusal (s 14)

Rule: No timely notice (±): (−) refusal is mandatory if the debtor was not notified of the originating document in time to arrange its defence (s 14(a)); (+) not where X law allowed notification to be contested and the debtor appeared and argued the case without contesting it. Procedural fraud (−): mandatory if the judgment was obtained by fraud in connection with procedure (e.g., deliberately serving a wrong address, misleading the debtor about the hearing, bribing a judge or witness, concealing key evidence) (s 14(b)); per C&Y, roughly extrinsic fraud. Public policy (−): mandatory if recognition would be manifestly incompatible with Singapore public policy, including a breach of fundamental procedural fairness (s 14(c)); per C&Y, intrinsic fraud (e.g., perjury at trial) may fall here.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Problems With the Mexico City Judgment

A Mexico City court (chosen under a 2021 exclusive clause) gave judgment against a Singapore distributor.

  1. The claim was served on the distributor's old address, which the claimant knew it had left; the distributor learned of the case after judgment.
  2. The distributor was served late but appeared and argued the merits fully without objecting to the late service, even though Mexican law allowed such an objection.
  3. The claimant's CEO gave perjured evidence at trial.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Mandatory refusal under s 14(a) (no timely notice), and probably also s 14(b): deliberately serving a known wrong address is procedural fraud, roughly extrinsic fraud (C&Y).
  2. No refusal under s 14(a): Mexican law allowed the notification to be contested, and the distributor appeared and argued without contesting it.
  3. Perjury is intrinsic, not procedural, so s 14(b) does not apply. Per C&Y it may fall within s 14(c), but "manifestly incompatible" sets a high bar. So the distributor's intrinsic fraud plea fares worse than at common law (J7.5.4, "narrower").

J7.5.4 Discretionary Refusal (ss 15–16) and Severance (s 19)

Rule:

  • COCA null and void (±): (−) under X law, including its choice of law rules (s 15(1)(a)); (+) not if the X court held it valid, and per C&Y that ruling binds even in a default judgment, on law and fact.
  • Incapacity (−): a party lacked capacity under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules (s 15(1)(b)); capacity is thus tested under both X law (via (a)) and Singapore law.
  • Service contrary to Singapore fundamentals (±): (−) s 15(1)(c); (+) per C&Y, it caters for States treating foreign service as a sovereign act, which Singapore does not, so it rarely applies to service here.
  • Inconsistent Singapore judgment (−): s 15(1)(d), earlier or later, not necessarily on the same cause of action; e.g., Singapore took jurisdiction under s 12 because the clause was void.
  • Inconsistent earlier foreign judgment (±): s 15(1)(e); the other judgment must be earlier, between the same parties, on the same cause of action, and recognisable here.
  • Pending review or appeal (±): s 15(2)–(3): the court may refuse, set aside or postpone, but the creditor may apply again once the appeal is decided.
  • Objected transfer (−): s 15(4): where the chosen court exercised a discretion to transfer over the debtor's timely objection, the court may refuse the transferee court's judgment against the debtor; not if the transfer was mandated. Who objected (±): per C&Y (Hartley–Dogauchi), s 15(4) protects only a timely objector against whom judgment went, so the judgment is enforceable against a party who requested or did not oppose the transfer. If the clause names "the courts of X", the transferee is itself chosen.
  • Excess damages (±): s 16: refusal insofar as damages exceed compensation for actual loss, considering whether the award covers costs and expenses of the X proceedings.
  • Severance (+): s 19: the court must enforce a severable part if applied for.
  • Narrower than common law (±): per C&Y, the CCAA grounds are generally narrower (exhaustive; "manifestly"; procedural fraud only; binding findings), but add COCA-specific grounds (s 15(1)(a)–(b), (4), s 16).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The London Commercial Court Judgment

A 2022 exclusive clause chose "the courts of England and Wales". Judgment was given against a Singapore company, Orchid Ltd, for £10m compensatory and £5m exemplary damages.

  1. Orchid argues the clause was void under English law for misrepresentation. The English court, in a default judgment, held it valid.
  2. Orchid argues that its signatory lacked capacity under Singapore law (Orchid's constitution forbade foreign submissions).
  3. Orchid was served under the Hague Service Convention by post.
  4. Earlier, Orchid had sued in Singapore, and the Singapore court refused a s 12 stay, holding the clause null and void, then gave judgment for Orchid.
  5. A Mexican judgment between the same parties on the same cause of action, given earlier, went the other way.
  6. Orchid's appeal is pending in the English Court of Appeal.
  7. The High Court transferred the case, over Orchid's timely objection, from the Commercial Court to the Business and Property Courts in Manchester, which gave the judgment.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. s 15(1)(a): validity is tested under English law, including its choice of law rules. But the English court held the clause valid, and per C&Y that ruling binds even in a default judgment. Fails.
  2. s 15(1)(b): capacity is tested under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules (here, corporate capacity under the law of incorporation, Singapore). Capacity is thus checked under both laws, but this ground likely fails: per ss 23, 25 and 25B CA, no act of a Singapore company is invalid only for lack of capacity, so a restriction in Orchid's constitution does not remove it (C2.8.2).
  3. s 15(1)(c): caters for States that treat service as a sovereign act, which Singapore does not, so it rarely applies. Fails.
  4. s 15(1)(d): an inconsistent Singapore judgment (here, after Singapore took jurisdiction under s 12 because the clause was void). Strong ground for refusal.
  5. s 15(1)(e): an earlier inconsistent foreign judgment between the same parties on the same cause of action, if recognisable in Singapore. Possible ground.
  6. s 15(2)–(3): the court may postpone or refuse, and the creditor may reapply after the appeal.
  7. s 15(4) (±): a discretionary transfer over Orchid's timely objection allows refusal against Orchid. But the clause names "the courts of England and Wales", so Manchester is itself a chosen court, and s 15(4) does not bite (C&Y).
  • Damages: the £5m exemplary portion may be refused under s 16 (exceeding compensation for actual loss, allowing for whether part of it reflects costs). The creditor applies under s 19 to sever and enforce the £10m.
  • Overall: the CCAA is generally narrower than the common law (exhaustive, "manifestly", binding findings), so Orchid's best grounds are the COCA-specific and conflicting-judgment grounds.

J7.5.5 Judgment of a Non-Chosen Court in Breach of an Exclusive COCA

Rule: The gap (±): where the COCA chose X court 1 but the creditor sued in Y court in breach, (+) per C&Y the Y judgment is outside the CCAA, which does not bar its enforcement under REFJA or the common law; (−) submitted that the common law should recognise a defence (J7.2.6); if Y is gazetted, s 5(4)(b) REFJA already applies.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Clause Chose Paris, the Creditor Went to Bangalore

A 2021 exclusive clause chose the Paris Commercial Court. The French brand instead sued the Singapore distributor in Bangalore and obtained judgment, the distributor having appeared only to contest jurisdiction. It seeks to enforce in Singapore.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The Bangalore judgment is not a chosen-court judgment, so it is outside the CCAA, and the CCAA does not itself bar its enforcement under other regimes (C&Y). India is gazetted under REFJA, so (if REFJA were run) s 5(4)(b) denies jurisdiction because the proceedings breached the agreement and the distributor did not submit. At common law, the distributor argues the J7.2.6 breach defence, using REFJA s 5(4)(b) as an analogue and Merck's convergence aim, and in any event Bangalore lacks international jurisdiction (no presence, and a jurisdiction protest is not submission).

8J7.6 Anti-enforcement injunctions (AEIs)

Rule (Starter): Per Sun Travels and C&Y, beyond the usual ASI requirements (J6), the debtor must show exceptional circumstances tied to unconscionability; breach of an AEI is contempt. Why caution (−): an AEI implies the debtor delayed in not seeking an ASI earlier, wastes the X court's time and costs, stops other courts deciding recognition for themselves, and interferes with execution in X; it is akin to nullifying the judgment. Breach or vexation not enough (−): per Sun Travels, neither the creditor's breach of an EJC or arbitration clause nor vexatious conduct suffices alone, and party autonomy is no separate basis (Arkhangelsky creates no "agreement" category). Fraud (+): the creditor's fraud in obtaining the judgment (perjury, forged evidence) is an exceptional circumstance, as in Ellerman Lines v Read (reliance on a Turkish judgment procured by the salvor's perjury was restrained). No knowledge (+): per Sun Travels (citing Ecobank), the debtor did not know the judgment was being sought until it was delivered (obtained secretly or too quickly), so its delay is not unconscionable. Delay (±): mere passage of time is not enough; delay counts against the debtor only when coupled with knowledge and/or prejudice to the creditor or third parties (such as the X court); simply limiting the relief to reflect the delay, as the judge did, is not the answer. Applicant's silence (−): both sides' conduct matters; if the debtor knew of the fraud before judgment but stayed silent, the equities may tilt against it. No closed list (±): a new category needs the equities to favour relief: either a response to the creditor's unconscionable conduct, or the debtor has not lost equity through unconscionable delay; as in Sun Travels (Hilton delayed until after the Maldivian judgment). Alternatives (+): AEIs "should generally be refused", so the debtor should instead resist recognition in Singapore (J7.2), claim damages for breach (J1.7), or resist enforcement in Y.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Maldivian Resort Judgment

A Singapore hotel operator, Lotus Hotels, managed a Maldives resort under an agreement with a Singapore-seated arbitration clause. The resort owner sued Lotus in the Maldives for US$30m. Lotus knew of the suit, contested jurisdiction there for two years, lost, and only after the Maldivian judgment sought an AEI in Singapore to stop the owner enforcing worldwide.

  • Variation A: the owner obtained the Maldivian judgment in a hearing Lotus was never told of, two weeks after filing.
  • Variation B: the judgment rests on forged management accounts presented by the owner.
  • Variation C: as in B, but Lotus knew of the forgery before judgment and said nothing in the Maldives, planning to use it later.
  • Variation D: the owner's suit was merely vexatious (a duplicative claim), with no fraud.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Lotus must meet the ASI requirements (amenability, interest, breach of the arbitration agreement) plus exceptional circumstances (Sun Travels). Breach of the arbitration clause alone is not enough, and party autonomy is no separate category (Arkhangelsky). On the main facts, Lotus knew of the proceedings and waited until after judgment, exactly like Hilton in Sun Travels. An AEI would waste the Maldivian court's resources, pre-empt other courts' recognition decisions and effectively nullify the judgment. Refused. Lotus should instead resist recognition wherever the owner enforces, including in Singapore (J7.2.6 breach defence; fraud and natural justice if available), and claim damages for breach (J1.7).

  • A: no knowledge until delivery, a judgment obtained secretly and quickly, so Lotus's "delay" is not unconscionable (Sun Travels, citing Ecobank). Exceptional circumstances exist.
  • B: fraud in obtaining the judgment is an exceptional circumstance (Ellerman Lines v Read: perjury-based Turkish judgment).
  • C: both sides' conduct matters. Lotus's silence while knowing of the fraud tilts the equities against it (Sun Travels).
  • D: vexation alone is not enough (Sun Travels).
  • Delay generally: mere passage of time is not decisive; it counts only with knowledge and/or prejudice to the owner or the Maldivian court. And the answer is not simply to "trim" the AEI to reflect delay, as the first-instance judge in Sun Travels did.
← J6 hyposC1 hypos →
LAW302 · HYPO LESSON C1 · 24 HYPOTHETICALS · 8 QUESTIONS

C1 hypotheticals: Choice of law methodology: characterise, connect, apply

The rules behind these hypotheticals are taught in Lesson C1, where the word-for-word pre-write is too. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

Applications:
ℹ HOW TO USE THESE HYPOTHETICALS

Each concept is set out as Rule, then Hypothetical, then Application. "Variation" lines flip one fact. Contract choice of law is in C2; tort in C3.

The hypo test at the end checks you can run the facts yourself.

1C1.0 Roadmap in one hypothetical

Rule (order): (1) Characterise the issue (Macmillan; Raiffeisen; Re Cohn; Rickshaw). (2) Substance or procedure (Star City; Goh Suan Hee). (3) Battlegrounds: remedies, damages, limitation (FLPA), evidence. (4) Proof of foreign law: not pleaded v pleaded but unproved (Brownlie), experts, references, SICC submissions. (5) Overlays: forum mandatory rules (JIO Minerals), fundamental public policy, renvoi.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Phuket Jet-Ski Crash

Wei Ling, a Singapore resident, rents a jet-ski in Phuket from Andaman Watersports Co (Thai) under a written rental form. She is injured when the jet-ski's throttle sticks. She sues Andaman in Singapore (Andaman's director was served here). Issues: (a) is Andaman liable? (b) the rental form's clause excluding liability for personal injury; (c) Thai law caps general damages at a low figure, while Singapore's awards are higher; (d) Thailand's limitation period is one year, and she sued after 18 months; (e) neither party has pleaded Thai law on the exclusion clause.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Characterise: liability for the injury is tort (C3); the exclusion clause is a contract issue under the rental form's proper law (C2), though the court looks at the true issue, not the label (Macmillan).
  2. Substance v procedure: liability is substantive. On Star City and the traditional split, quantum is procedural, so Singapore figures apply, but Goh Suan Hee (obiter) doubts the split (C1.4).
  3. Damages: heads of damage follow the lex causae; quantum may follow Singapore law (traditional view) or Thai law (if substantive, per Goh Suan Hee).
  4. Limitation: FLPA s 3(2) applies the Thai period (the lex loci delicti, "for the purpose of actionability"), unless the flexible exception selects Singapore law. She may plead undue hardship under s 4(2).
  5. Proof: Thai law on the exclusion clause is not pleaded, so Singapore law applies in its own right (Brownlie).
  6. Overlays: UCTA may apply as a forum mandatory rule if s 27(2) is triggered (C1.7); fundamental public policy is unlikely to be engaged.

2C1.1 Characterisation

C1.1.1 The Three Stages; Which Law Characterises

Rule: Per Macmillan (endorsed in Philippines v Maler), the court (1) characterises the issue (e.g., contractual validity, liability for an accident, title to shares) as a category, (2) selects the conflict rule's connecting factor, and (3) applies the law it points to. Stages 2 and 3 are plainly for the lex fori, so disputes turn on stage 1.

  • Lex fori: per HMRC v Shahdadpuri, the lex fori characterises the issue. Using the potential leges causae is circular (they are found only after characterising) and invites cumulation or gaps.
  • Enlightened lex fori: per Raiffeisen, it characterises in a "broad internationalist spirit", and per Auld LJ in Macmillan, unconstrained by domestic distinctions, so an agreement without consideration is still contractual (Re Bonacina). Foreign law may inform the category (cf Red Sea).
  • Issue, not cause of action: per Murakami Takako and JIO Minerals, the court looks "beyond the formulation of the claim" to the true issue, so framing a claim as restitution or constructive trust cannot steer the governing law. In Macmillan, the restitution claim was really about priority over the shares, which is for the lex situs.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Gratuitous Italian Promise

Rossi, in Milan, promised in a signed letter to transfer his shares in a Singapore company to his nephew in Singapore, with no consideration. Under Italian law, which the parties chose, a written gratuitous promise of this kind is binding. Under Singapore domestic law, a promise without consideration (not under seal) is not a contract. The nephew sues for specific performance. Rossi's estate argues: (a) the court should use Italian categories to characterise; (b) since there is no consideration, this is not a "contract" at all, so the contract choice of law rule cannot apply; (c) the nephew's alternative claim, framed as a constructive trust over the shares, should be decided by Singapore law because it is "equitable".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(a) The lex fori characterises (HMRC v Shahdadpuri). Using Italian law would be circular, because we do not yet know that Italian law governs until we characterise. (b) But the lex fori is enlightened: it characterises in a broad internationalist spirit (Raiffeisen), unconstrained by domestic rules like consideration (Auld LJ, Macmillan). An agreement without consideration can still be "contractual" for choice of law purposes (Re Bonacina), so Italian law, as the chosen proper law, governs whether the promise binds. (c) The court looks to the true issue, not the claim's label (Murakami Takako; JIO Minerals). If the real question is whether Rossi or a third party has priority to the shares, as in Macmillan, it may be a question of title for the lex situs (Singapore, where the company is incorporated). If the real question is whether Rossi is bound by his promise, it is contractual.

C1.1.1(b) Categories Are Man-Made; Stages Interact

Rule: Per Raiffeisen, categories are "man-made, not natural" and may be redefined or extended, and the stages are not taken "in turn and in isolation", so a characterisation is tested against the law it selects. Use (+): a party argues that category A yields an inappropriate law (e.g., the lex situs of a fortuitously located debt), favouring category B, as Raiffeisen preferred the insurance contract's law over the French lex situs. Use (−): the other side calls this result-driven, so the established category applies.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Assigned Insurance Proceeds

A Singapore shipowner insured its vessel with a Japanese insurer under an English-law policy, then assigned the policy proceeds to Bank A (Singapore). The proceeds, a debt owed by the insurer, are treated as situated in France because the insurer's paying branch is in Paris. Bank B claims the same proceeds under a later French-law charge. Bank A argues that whether the assignment binds the insurer is a contract question for the policy's English law. Bank B argues it is a property question for the lex situs, French law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(+) Bank A, following Raiffeisen: categories are man-made and the stages interact, so test the characterisation against the law it selects. A "property" characterisation would select French law only because the paying branch happens to be in Paris, a fortuitous location for a debt. A contractual characterisation selects the policy's own law, which is more appropriate, just as Raiffeisen preferred the insurance contract's law over the French lex situs. (−) Bank B says this is result-driven reasoning: priority between competing assignees is a classic property issue, so the established category (lex situs) should apply.

C1.1.1(c) Why Foreign Law at All; Jurisdiction-Selecting Rules

Rule: Per Goh Suan Hee, applying foreign law deters forum shopping for a higher award here, and "he who travels to X must accept its law", protecting expectations and uniform outcomes. Jurisdiction-selecting, not rule-selecting: Singapore's rules pick the governing law through the connecting factor whatever its content (contrast US interest analysis in Babcock v Jackson), so a party escapes that law only by re-characterisation, the tort flexible exception, a mandatory rule, or public policy.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"But Malaysian Law Is Unfair to Me"

Ahmad, a Singapore resident, is injured in a road accident in Johor caused by a Malaysian driver. Malaysian damages are lower. Ahmad's counsel argues the court should apply Singapore law because Singapore's law is "better" and Singapore has a strong interest in compensating its residents, as an American court would reason under Babcock v Jackson.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Singapore's choice of law rules are jurisdiction-selecting: they pick the governing law by the connecting factor (here, the place of the tort for double actionability), not by comparing the content of the rules or the forum's interest in applying them (contrast Babcock v Jackson). Per Goh Suan Hee, applying the law of the place where Ahmad chose to travel deters forum shopping and respects expectations: he who travels to Malaysia accepts its law. Ahmad can escape Malaysian law only through re-characterisation, the flexible exception (C3.6), a forum mandatory rule (C1.7) or fundamental public policy (C1.8), not because Singapore law is more generous.

C1.1.2 Framing the Cause of Action

Rule: Freedom to frame (+): per Rickshaw, absent bad faith, a claimant may frame its claim most advantageously, tort liability being concurrent (Henderson v Merrett), so a tort claim is characterised as tort despite a contractual relationship or a foreign choice of law clause. Limit, equity follows its foundation (−): an equitable claim rooted in the contract is usually characterised as contractual (C1.1.5), and per Macmillan the court looks to the true issues, so the sub-issue may still follow the contract's law. Why re-framing usually fails: tort is no safe harbour: per Ong Ghee Soon, whether a contractual choice of law can govern the tort is unresolved (C3.6.5); issue, not cause of action: sub-issues (limitation, capacity, formalities) may follow other laws; choice of court clauses: per The "Jian He", the jurisdiction clause is construed generously as to subject matter, catching tortious or equitable claims (J1).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The German Employment Contract

Klaus, a German engineer employed by a German company under a German-law employment contract (with a German jurisdiction clause), worked at the company's Singapore subsidiary. He allegedly diverted business secrets to a competitor. The company sues him in Singapore (a) in tort for conspiracy, and (b) in equity for breach of fiduciary duty and confidence, hoping to escape German law, which is more lenient to employees.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(a) (+) Absent bad faith, the company may frame its claim in tort (Rickshaw), and tort liability is concurrent with contract (Henderson v Merrett), so the conspiracy claim is characterised as tort, despite the German-law contract. (−) But re-framing rarely escapes the clause entirely. Whether the contractual choice of German law can also govern the tort through the flexible exception is unresolved (Ong Ghee Soon; C3.6.5). Particular sub-issues (e.g., limitation) may follow other laws. And the German jurisdiction clause, construed generously (The "Jian He"), may catch the tort claim, so the company may face strong cause (J1). (b) (−) As in Rickshaw itself, the fiduciary and confidence claims are rooted in the employment relationship, so they are characterised as contractual and governed by German law (C1.1.5).

C1.1.3 Menu of Categories

Rule: Contract: validity, construction, discharge; express, implied or objective choice; the proper law (C2). Tort: liability for negligence, defamation, etc.; the forum and the place of the tort; the lex fori and lex loci delicti (double actionability) (C3). Title to property: the situs; the lex situs. Succession: immovables by situs (lex situs); movables by domicile (lex domicilii). Marriage: formal validity by place of celebration (lex loci celebrationis); capacity by domicile (lex domicilii). Unjust enrichment / equity: restitution by the proper law of the obligation (C3.11); a fiduciary claim by its legal foundation (C1.1.5).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Late Mr Lim's Estate

Mr Lim died domiciled in Singapore, leaving (i) a villa in Bali, (ii) shares in a Hong Kong company, and (iii) a bank account in London. He had married his second wife in Las Vegas when he was 17 (he was domiciled in Singapore then). The estate also has (iv) a claim against a London art dealer who sold Mr Lim a forged painting under an English-law contract, and (v) a claim to recover money paid by mistake to a Jakarta supplier.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (i) Villa (immovable): succession by the lex situs (Indonesian law).
  • (ii) and (iii) Shares and account (movables): succession by the lex domicilii (Singapore law). Title to the shares, as distinct from succession, is for the lex situs (likely Hong Kong, where the company is incorporated and the register is kept).
  • (iv) Forged painting: a contract claim under its proper law (English), or a tort claim for misrepresentation under double actionability.
  • (v) Mistaken payment: unjust enrichment, governed by the proper law of the obligation (C3.11).
  • Marriage: formal validity is for the lex loci celebrationis (Nevada); his capacity to marry at 17 is for his lex domicilii (Singapore).

C1.1.4 Rule Characterisation, Cumulation and Gap

Rule: Cause of action / rule characterisation: per C&Y, the tort and unjust enrichment categories are framed as causes of action, so issues within the claim usually follow them; pure rule characterisation of competing rules worsens cumulation and gap. Parallel exercise: per Auld LJ in Macmillan, issue characterisation needs a parallel classification of the rule, as in Haugesund Kommune, where the capacity issue led to Norwegian law and the court then asked whether the Norwegian provision was a capacity rule. Application: per Re Cohn, a forum rule is substantive or procedural according to whether it goes to the existence of the right or merely regulates proof, and likewise the foreign rule. In Re Cohn both survivorship presumptions were substantive, so only the German lex causae's applied. Cumulation: if the foreign rule is substantive and the forum rule procedural, both apply and clash, so a party urges re-characterising the forum rule. Gap: if the foreign rule is procedural and the forum rule substantive, neither applies, so a party urges re-characterising in a broad internationalist spirit (Raiffeisen).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Tsunami Survivorship Puzzle

A German-domiciled mother and her daughter die together in a tsunami in Sri Lanka; no one knows who died first. The mother's movables are in Singapore. Succession is governed by German law (her domicile). Germany has a rule that persons dying together are presumed to have died simultaneously. Singapore has a statutory presumption that the younger survived the elder.

  • Version 1: both rules are characterised as substantive (going to who inherits).
  • Version 2: the German rule is substantive; the Singapore rule is characterised as procedural (an evidential presumption).
  • Version 3: the German rule is characterised (by German law itself) as procedural; the Singapore rule as substantive.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Characterise the rules in parallel with the issue (Macmillan, Auld LJ; Haugesund Kommune). Ask whether each rule goes to the existence of the right or merely regulates proof (Re Cohn).

  • Version 1: both are substantive, so only the lex causae's (German) rule applies, as in Re Cohn. Simultaneous death means the daughter does not inherit from the mother.
  • Version 2: cumulation. The German substantive rule applies (lex causae) and the Singapore procedural rule applies (lex fori). They clash: simultaneous death versus the daughter surviving. The party who benefits from German law urges re-characterising the Singapore rule as substantive, so only the German rule remains.
  • Version 3: gap. The German rule is procedural (so not applied in Singapore) and the Singapore rule is substantive (but Singapore law is not the lex causae), so neither applies. A party urges re-characterising in a broad internationalist spirit (Raiffeisen) so that one rule fills the gap.
  • C&Y's point: framing categories as causes of action (succession, tort) and keeping issues within them reduces these problems. Pure rule-by-rule characterisation makes cumulation and gaps worse.

C1.1.5 Novel Issue: No Established Category

Rule: Legal foundation: per Rickshaw, rejecting the Australian lex fori approach, choice of law for breach of fiduciary duty, confidence or trust centres on its legal foundation (contract or tort) by its "nature and origins" in the factual matrix, as Rickshaw applied the employment contract's German law. Rappo / Perry: fiduciary or trust claims founded on an oral agreement, or on asset management agreements (AMAs), are contractual, so Swiss law governed; per Perry, the quality, not quantity, of connecting factors makes the contract outweigh the situs of the money or the place of incorporation. Caveats: Rickshaw left open a separate equitable category for novel claims, and per Raiffeisen a new category may be recognised.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Geneva Wealth Manager

A Singapore tycoon, Mr Rappaport-Tan, orally agreed with a Geneva wealth manager that the manager would hold and invest US$200m for him. The money was held in accounts in Singapore and in a BVI company. The relationship was later documented in Swiss-law asset management agreements. The tycoon sues in Singapore for breach of fiduciary duty, breach of trust and a constructive trust over the Singapore accounts, arguing that Singapore law (situs of the money) or BVI law (place of incorporation) governs.

  • Variation: the manager, a stranger with no contract, took the tycoon's confidential data from a hacked server.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Fiduciary and trust claims have no established category, so look to their legal foundation, their "nature and origins" in the factual matrix (Rickshaw). Here the claims arise from the oral agreement and the AMAs, so they are contractual (Rappo; Perry), and the AMAs' Swiss law governs. Per Perry, the quality of the contractual connection outweighs the number of other factors (the situs of the money in Singapore, the BVI incorporation). Note the consequence (C1.3): Swiss law may not recognise trusts or constructive trusts, so those remedies may be unavailable even in Singapore (Rappo; Perry).

  • In the variation, there is no contract, so the foundation is closer to tort (a wrong by a stranger). Rickshaw also left open a separate equitable category, and per Raiffeisen a new category may be recognised.

3C1.2 Substance v procedure

Rule: Starter: per CIFG v Polimet, substance follows the lex causae and procedure the lex fori, so if a matter is procedural Singapore law applies without choice of law analysis. Test: per Star City, by the provision's effect and purpose: a rule on the existence of the right is substantive; one that regulates proceedings to enforce it is procedural. Scenario A (+): "no obligation exists to pay sums won on a wager" negates the right, so it is substantive. Scenario B (−): "no action shall be brought" bars only enforcement, so it is procedural. Functional critique: per C&Y, the wide procedural category reflects old judicial parochialism, now tempered by FNC, so the losing party argues procedure covers only the "mode or conduct of court proceedings" (Goh Suan Hee), as in Australia (Pfeiffer), Canada (Tolofson) and Hong Kong (First Laser). Consequence: quantum, remedies or a writing requirement would then follow the lex causae, curbing forum shopping, though a party must plead and prove more foreign law. Status: per CIFG v Polimet, Star City remains law because Goh Suan Hee left this open; apply Star City first and the functional view in the alternative.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Sydney Casino Debt

A Sydney casino extends credit to a Singapore businessman, governed by NSW law, under which the debt is valid. He gambles and loses A$2m, and the casino sues him in Singapore. s 5(2) Civil Law Act provides that "no action shall be brought or maintained in any court for recovering any sum of money ... alleged to be won upon any wager".

  • Variation: the statute instead read "no contract by way of gaming or wagering shall create any obligation to pay".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Apply Star City first: look at effect and purpose. s 5(2)'s "no action shall be brought" wording bars enforcement in a Singapore court, so it is procedural and applies as part of the lex fori, regardless of NSW law. The casino loses (this was Star City itself). (±) The casino runs the functional critique in the alternative: procedure should cover only the "mode or conduct of court proceedings" (Goh Suan Hee; Pfeiffer; Tolofson; First Laser), so a rule denying recovery is substantive and governed by NSW law. But Star City remains law (CIFG v Polimet), as Goh Suan Hee left the point open. (s 5(2) is also an overriding forum mandatory rule: C1.7.)

  • In the variation, "shall not create any obligation" negates the right, so it is substantive. As a Singapore rule it would then apply only if Singapore law were the lex causae (or as an overriding mandatory rule).

4C1.3 Remedies

C1.3.1 Final Remedies

Rule: Traditional, procedural: per Phrantzes v Argenti and Shanghai Electric, the court grants only its own remedies, so a constructive trust, tracing or specific performance is available or not according to whether Singapore law recognises it. Modern, lex causae decides entitlement: per Goh Suan Hee, it is "untenable in principle to separate remedy from rights", so the lex causae decides whether, and what kind of, remedy lies. Rappo / Perry: per Rappo, a constructive trust or tracing was unavailable even in Singapore under Swiss law, remedies being "a function of the law that governs the relevant relationship"; per Perry, the trust claim failed as Swiss law does not recognise trusts. FNC link: per Rappo, the remedy's absence abroad is then no substantial injustice at Spiliada stage 2. Synthesis, functional equivalent: per C&Y, the lex causae decides entitlement, but the court grants only remedies known to the lex fori, so for a foreign remedy unknown here it grants the functional equivalent, if any.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Remedies, Three Laws
  1. Under a Swiss-law asset management agreement (as in C1.1.5), the tycoon seeks a constructive trust and tracing in Singapore.
  2. Under a Greek-law dowry arrangement, a daughter sues her father in Singapore for the Greek remedy of an order to "constitute a dowry", unknown to Singapore law.
  3. Under a French-law sale of a unique antique car, the buyer seeks specific performance; French law readily orders performance in kind.
  4. In the tycoon's case (1), the manager seeks a stay to Switzerland, and the tycoon argues that he would suffer injustice there because Swiss courts will not order a constructive trust.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Modern view (Goh Suan Hee; Rappo; Perry): Swiss law, governing the relationship, decides entitlement, and it does not recognise trusts or constructive trusts, so those remedies are unavailable even in Singapore.
  2. Traditional view (Phrantzes v Argenti): Singapore grants only its own remedies, so it refuses an unknown Greek remedy. Synthesis (C&Y): Greek law decides the entitlement, and Singapore grants the closest functional equivalent known to Singapore law (e.g., a money judgment for the amount Greek law would require), if any.
  3. French law decides entitlement to performance in kind. Singapore grants specific performance, a remedy known to it, if French law entitles the buyer to it.
  4. Per Rappo, the absence of the remedy in Switzerland is no substantial injustice, because it would be unavailable in Singapore too (J4.1.3).

C1.3.2 Interim Remedies

Rule: General, procedural: per C&Y, a Mareva or interlocutory ASI protects the court's own processes, so the lex fori governs. Exception, substantive injunction: per Shanghai Electric, restraining a call on an on-demand bond is substantive, as it deprives the beneficiary of immediate payment, so the bond's governing law decides, subject to the remedy being known to the lex fori. Carve-out, comity: interim relief raising comity, such as an ASI against foreign proceedings, stays solely with the lex fori, whatever the lex causae says.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Freezing, Restraining and Stopping a Bond Call

A PRC contractor and an Indonesian employer have a construction contract governed by PRC law. The contractor's Singapore bank issued an on-demand performance bond governed by English law. The employer wants to call the bond. The contractor seeks in Singapore: (a) a Mareva over the employer's Singapore assets; (b) an injunction restraining the employer from calling the bond, arguing that PRC law (the underlying contract's law) allows such injunctions on a lower "unconscionability" threshold; (c) an ASI against the employer's Jakarta proceedings, arguing that English law (the bond's law) would grant it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(a) A Mareva protects the court's own processes, so it is procedural and governed by Singapore law (C&Y). (b) Restraining a bond call is substantive, because it deprives the beneficiary of immediate payment (Shanghai Electric). So the bond's governing law (English law, not PRC law) decides whether the call can be restrained, subject to the remedy being known to Singapore law. (c) An ASI raises comity, so it is governed solely by the lex fori, Singapore law, whatever English law says (C&Y; J6).

5C1.4 Damages

Rule: Traditional split: per Boys v Chaplin and Harding v Wealands, heads of damage (pain and suffering, loss of profits, dependency) are substantive, so the head must exist under the lex causae, but quantum is procedural, so the Singapore amount applies. Critique: per Goh Suan Hee (obiter), the split is "wholly artificial", so if quantum is substantive the lex causae amount applies (cf The "Reecon Wolf"). Reasons: it encourages forum shopping for a higher award, making outcomes a matter of chance, and he who travels to a country accepts its law, including quantum. Support: Art 15(c) Rome II and Pfeiffer v Rogerson apply the lex loci delicti to quantum. C&Y: foreign legislatures link liability to quantum (e.g., a cap tied to insurance costs), so severing them distorts the lex causae, and quantifying a head unknown here is hard. Status: left open; the CA cautioned claimants against suing here for a larger award, and in Goh Suan Hee the damages gap was a neutral FNC factor. Law v fact: if quantum is substantive, per Goh Suan Hee, the lex causae's rules of law (a statutory cap, a case-law scale) apply, but facts (local social and economic conditions) remain for the forum. Remoteness and mitigation: per D'Almeida Araujo v Becker, remoteness is substantive even though it affects quantum, as (per C&Y) is mitigation. Contributory negligence: open; it goes to the extent of liability, so a defendant argues it is substantive on a functional view, applying the lex causae's apportionment rule.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Langkawi Boat Accident

Mr Goh, a Singapore resident, is injured in a boat accident in Langkawi caused by a Malaysian tour operator's negligence. He sues in Singapore. Malaysian law (the lex loci delicti) (i) recognises damages for pain and suffering, but (ii) has a statutory cap on general damages and a lower conventional scale; (iii) does not recognise damages for loss of "amenity of holiday"; (iv) treats his loss of a planned business deal as too remote; (v) reduces his damages by 50% for not wearing a life jacket (Singapore might reduce by 25%); and (vi) living costs in Langkawi are lower than in Singapore.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (i) Head: pain and suffering is a head recognised by Malaysian law, so it is recoverable (heads are substantive: Boys v Chaplin; Harding v Wealands).
  • (iii) Head unknown: loss of holiday amenity is not a head under Malaysian law, so it is not recoverable even if Singapore law recognises it.
  • (ii) Quantum: on the traditional view, quantum is procedural, so Singapore scales apply and Mr Goh gets more. On the Goh Suan Hee critique (obiter), the split is "wholly artificial": it encourages forum shopping, and Mr Goh, who travelled to Malaysia, should accept Malaysian quantum, including the cap (supported by Rome II art 15(c) and Pfeiffer; and C&Y's point that the cap is tied to the liability regime). The CA left this open and cautioned against suing here for a bigger award.
  • Law v fact: if quantum is substantive, the Malaysian rules (the cap, the scale) apply, but the facts of Mr Goh's loss (e.g., his Singapore earnings) are still assessed by the forum (Goh Suan Hee).
  • (iv) Remoteness: substantive (D'Almeida Araujo v Becker), so the Malaysian rule applies.
  • (v) Contributory negligence (±): open. The operator argues it goes to the extent of liability and so is substantive (like remoteness), applying Malaysia's 50% reduction. Mr Goh argues it concerns the assessment of damages and so is procedural.
  • FNC link: in Goh Suan Hee, the damages gap was treated as neutral at the FNC stage (J4).

6C1.5 Limitation periods

C1.5.1 Common Law Position (context only)

Rule: Per BBA v BAZ, a statute extinguishing the right was substantive (following the lex causae), but one barring the remedy was procedural, so Singapore's limitation period applied. Substantive wording (+): "D shall be absolved from liability unless suit is brought within 3 years". Procedural wording (−): "all actions shall be commenced within 3 years". Counter: the split breeds gaps and cumulation, prompting the FLPA.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Before the FLPA

A contract governed by Ruritanian law. Ruritania's statute says "all actions on contracts shall be commenced within 2 years". The claimant sued in Singapore after 3 years (inside Singapore's 6 years).

  • Variation: the statute said "the debtor shall be absolved from liability after 2 years".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Under the old common law, "all actions shall be commenced" bars the remedy, so it was procedural. The Singapore 6-year period applied, and the claim survived. In the variation, "absolved from liability" extinguishes the right, so it was substantive: the Ruritanian period applied, and the claim was barred. (If the Ruritanian rule were procedural and Singapore's substantive, there would be a gap, with no period applying; if the reverse, cumulation. These problems prompted the FLPA.)

C1.5.2–C1.5.3 FLPA: General Rule and Tort

Rule: s 3(1) + s 6(2): only the lex causae's limitation law applies, not Singapore's, and its procedural or substantive label is irrelevant (s 6(2)). Renvoi is excluded (ss 3(5), 6(2)), so only the lex causae's domestic period applies. The rule applies equally to equitable claims. Tort, s 3(2): a foreign law considered "for the purpose of actionability" is deemed to apply under s 3(1), a "clear reference" to double actionability (IM Skaugen), so the lex loci delicti's period applies. Flexible exception: if it selects a single lex causae, that law's period applies (the Limitation Act if Singapore law governs). Contrast England: per Metall, s 1(2) UK FLPA 1984 applies both the English and the foreign periods to double actionability matters, whereas Singapore's s 3(2) applies only the lex loci delicti's period.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Two Claims After the FLPA

Same Ruritanian contract (2-year period). And a separate tort claim for an accident in Ruritania (Ruritania: 1 year; Singapore: 3 years for personal injury). The claimant sued in Singapore after 18 months. Ruritanian conflict rules would refer limitation to the law of the forum.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Contract: under s 3(1), only Ruritania's limitation law applies, whatever its label (s 6(2)). 18 months is within 2 years, so the claim is in time. Ruritania's conflict rule referring to the forum is ignored, because renvoi is excluded (ss 3(5), 6(2)). Tort: under s 3(2), Ruritanian law, considered for actionability under double actionability, supplies the period: 1 year, so the claim is barred. Singapore's 3 years is not applied cumulatively, unlike England, where s 1(2) UK FLPA applies both (Metall). Flexible exception: if the court applies Singapore law alone under the flexible exception (C3.6), the Limitation Act's period applies instead, and the claim survives.

C1.5.4 Public Policy: s 4(2) Undue Hardship

Rule: Per s 4(2) FLPA, a foreign period is contrary to public policy if it causes a party undue hardship. Per Recovery Vehicle 1 (adopting The Pegasus), that is "greater hardship than the circumstances warrant", even for a claimant at fault where the consequences are disproportionate to its fault. Factors: the objective reasonableness of the foreign bar (being shorter than Singapore's is not enough), the complexity of the claim, and the claimant's justification for letting time run. Causation: the hardship must flow from the foreign period itself, not from, e.g., the assignor's directors' refusal to sue. Self-induced hardship (−): an assignee that bought the debts knowing they might be time-barred suffers no undue hardship.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Late Claimants
  1. A Singapore company's claim under an Indonesian-law contract is barred by a 1-year Indonesian period. The claim is complex (forensic accounting), the company was misled by the defendant's assurances of settlement, and it filed two weeks late.
  2. The same, but the company simply did not notice the deadline.
  3. A distressed-debt fund bought, at a steep discount, claims from a liquidator, knowing that some were probably time-barred under the governing Thai law. The claims had become barred because the assignor's former directors had refused to sue.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Undue hardship likely: a short bar, a complex claim, and a good justification (the defendant's assurances). The consequences (total loss of the claim for a two-week delay) are disproportionate to any fault (Recovery Vehicle 1; The Pegasus). That the Indonesian period is shorter than Singapore's is not enough by itself.
  2. Weaker: there is no good justification. But even a claimant at fault may succeed if the consequences are disproportionate (The Pegasus), so it is arguable either way.
  3. No undue hardship: the hardship flows from the directors' refusal to sue, not from the Thai period itself (causation), and the fund bought knowing of the risk, so its hardship is self-induced (Recovery Vehicle 1).

C1.5.5 Equitable Claims and Laches

Rule: Unlike s 4(3) UK FLPA 1984, the FLPA has no laches carve-out, consistent with choice of law for equity (Rickshaw), so the lex causae's time bar applies to the equitable claim. Backstop: per C&Y, if the claimant's delay is unacceptably long though within the foreign period, the foreign statute may be disapplied on Singapore public policy.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Long-Delayed Trust Claim

A beneficiary's claim for breach of fiduciary duty is governed by Swiss law (contractual foundation: C1.1.5), which has a 10-year limitation period. The beneficiary waited 9 years, during which the fiduciary changed position, witnesses died and documents were destroyed. Under Singapore law, laches would bar the claim.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Under the FLPA, the lex causae (Swiss) period applies to equitable claims too, and there is no carve-out preserving Singapore's laches doctrine (unlike UK FLPA s 4(3)). The claim is within 10 years, so it is not time-barred. Backstop (C&Y): if the delay is unacceptably long and prejudicial, the Swiss period may be disapplied on public policy (cf s 4(2)), though using public policy to shorten a foreign period is unusual and needs strong facts.

7C1.6 Evidence and proof of foreign law

C1.6.1 Characterisation of Evidential Matters

Rule: What / how divide: per C&Y, what must be proved is substantive (lex causae), and how is procedural, so admissibility of an Indonesian notarised deed is for the lex fori (Banque Indosuez). Burden of proof: per Re Fuld's Estate (No 3), generally procedural, so Singapore's allocation applies. Writing requirements: s 6 CLA 1909 bars any "action" on a guarantee or disposition of immovables without signed writing, so per Leroux v Brown it is procedural and binds even a foreign-law contract here. Counter: on a functional view, the writing rule may be substantive and follow the proper law (C2.7). Parol evidence discrepancy: per Korner v Witkowitzer, evidence to vary the contract is procedural, but per St Pierre, evidence to interpret it is substantive, a split C&Y find hard to justify. SICC carve-out: per s 18K SCJA (SICC O 13 r 15), the SICC may disapply Singapore evidence rules and apply foreign rules, including on privilege and the taking of evidence.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Oral French Guarantee

A French parent orally guaranteed its Singapore subsidiary's debts to a Singapore bank, in a French-law arrangement. French law (assume) enforces oral commercial guarantees. The bank sues in Singapore. Issues: (a) s 6 CLA (no action on a guarantee without signed writing); (b) the bank wants to admit an Indonesian notarised deed as evidence of the subsidiary's debts; (c) who bears the burden of proving payment; (d) the parent wants to adduce pre-contract emails, first to vary the guarantee's cap and second to interpret an ambiguous term; (e) if in the SICC, the parent wants French rules on privilege applied.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) s 6 CLA says no "action" shall be brought, so per Leroux v Brown it is procedural and bars the claim in Singapore even though French law governs and would enforce the guarantee. (±) On the functional view (C1.2.3), the writing rule goes to the substance of the obligation and should follow French law (C2.7), but Leroux reflects the current law.
  • (b) How a fact is proved is procedural, so admissibility of the Indonesian deed is for Singapore law (Banque Indosuez).
  • (c) The burden of proof is procedural, so Singapore law allocates it (Re Fuld's Estate (No 3)).
  • (d) Using the emails to vary the guarantee is a procedural (parol evidence) question for Singapore law (Korner v Witkowitzer); using them to interpret is substantive, for French law (St Pierre). C&Y find the split hard to justify, and the parent can exploit it by framing its evidence as going to interpretation.
  • (e) In the SICC, s 18K allows disapplying Singapore evidence rules and applying French rules on privilege (SICC O 13 r 15).

C1.6.2 Pleading and Proving Foreign Law

Rule: Pleading: per Brownlie and The "Chem Orchid", a party relying on foreign law must plead and prove it; there is no judicial notice. Per Goh Chok Tong v Tang Liang Hong, pleading is not obligatory (save for immovables, registered interests and incorporation), so a party pleads only where foreign law is more advantageous. Fact of a peculiar kind: per Parkasho v Singh (in C&Y), foreign law is fact "of a peculiar kind"; per EFT Holdings, it is more open to appellate review, so where it resembles Singapore law an appellate court may form its own view. Two modes of proof: per Pacific Recreation, official statute books or law reports under s 40 EA, or expert opinion on content and effect, including how the foreign court reads the statute, under s 47 EA. Raw sources: admissible here, unlike the traditional English expert-only rule (but see Brownlie), though per AQCEL Synergies the court need not give weight to raw Hong Kong sources where the provision's reach is unclear. Construing a foreign contract: the expert proves the foreign rules of construction without pushing personal views, and the court construes the contract (Pacific Recreation). Expert preferable: where the foreign law is from a different tradition, has no Singapore equivalent, or the issue is complex or controversial. Similar laws: per TMT v RBS, it is "odd" to prove English law as foreign law, so parties may submit directly on construction, flagging only "real and relevant" differences. Foreign-language statute: per Byers v Saudi National Bank (C&Y), an expert is crucial for a foreign-language statute on unfamiliar concepts, but not for an English-language statute on similar concepts. Criticism of experts: per Wu Yang, partisan experts are "singularly unhelpful", hence a common expert (O 12 r 3(1) ROC 2021; SICC O 14 r 2(4)(a)) or, rarely, a court expert (O 12 r 3(3)).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Proving Four Foreign Laws

A multi-jurisdictional dispute involves:

  1. A Hong Kong statute. The claimant tenders the Hong Kong ordinance and two Hong Kong cases, without an expert.
  2. Saudi law on agency (in Arabic, based on Sharia principles with no Singapore equivalent).
  3. English law on the construction of a charterparty.
  4. Japanese company law on directors' duties, where each side's expert says the opposite.
  5. On appeal, the losing party argues that the trial judge misunderstood the (common law) Australian law, which the experts said was materially similar to Singapore law.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Raw sources are admissible under s 40 EA (Pacific Recreation), unlike the traditional English rule. But per AQCEL Synergies, where the provision's reach is unclear, the court may give them little weight without expert evidence.
  2. An expert is essential: a different legal tradition, a foreign-language source, unfamiliar concepts (Pacific Recreation; Byers v Saudi National Bank). The expert proves content and effect, including how Saudi courts read the rules (s 47 EA).
  3. Per TMT v RBS, it is "odd" to prove English law as foreign law; parties may simply make submissions on construction and flag only "real and relevant" differences.
  4. Partisan experts are "singularly unhelpful" (Wu Yang), so the court should order a common expert (O 12 r 3(1) ROC 2021) or, rarely, appoint its own (O 12 r 3(3)).
  5. Foreign law is fact "of a peculiar kind" (Parkasho v Singh, in C&Y), more open to appellate review than ordinary facts (EFT Holdings), especially where it resembles Singapore law, so the appellate court may form its own view.
  • Pleading tactics: a party need plead foreign law only where it is more advantageous (Goh Chok Tong v Tang Liang Hong); otherwise it may leave Singapore law to apply by default (C1.6.3). The exceptions are immovables, registered interests and incorporation, where foreign law must be pleaded.

C1.6.3 Default Rule and Presumption of Similarity

Rule: Not pleaded, default rule: per Brownlie, if neither party pleads foreign law, Singapore law applies in its own right (adversarial procedure, arguably tacit agreement), not by presumption; per EFT Holdings, no conflicts issue arises. Pleaded but unproved: per Brownlie, once foreign law is pleaded the court must apply it, so a party failing to prove its case under it may simply lose (EFT Holdings), unless the foreign law is presumed similar to Singapore law (The "Chem Orchid"). Nature of the presumption: per Brownlie, a rule of evidence on content, applied only where it is fair and reasonable to expect the foreign law to be materially similar; per D'Oz, a "rule of convenience", refused where holding the defendant liable under unproved foreign law is unjust. When (in)appropriate: per Brownlie, it suits a common law system, "great and broad" principles, and interlocutory stages (service out, stay) more than trial, and is less apt for a statutory rule, though the question is whether the foreign law has a materially similar rule (rejecting Shaker v Al-Bedrawi). Limits: tactical reliance: a burdened party that pleads foreign law then rests on the presumption cannot improve its position, and this may be an abuse (Tamil Nadu); gaps: not a bar, since where a foreign statute is proved but not its interpretation, similar interpretive principles are presumed (Brownlie); foreign public policy: per PT Jaya Putra v Guthrie, Indonesian public policy is best decided by the Indonesian court, so it is not presumed; different traditions: not for tax law or a civil law system lacking universal principles (C&Y), and per AQCEL Synergies refused where evidence showed Hong Kong law differs; intrusive relief: per EFT Holdings explaining OMG Holdings, no injunction against conduct abroad on a bare presumption, though per C&Y presumably damages may be had. FNC overlay: per Rickshaw and JIO Minerals, likely differences in unproved foreign law still carry weight at the FNC stage.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Egyptian Bus Crash and the Others
  1. Brownlie-style: a Singapore tourist is injured on an Egyptian hotel excursion. Neither party pleads Egyptian law. The hotel later argues that Singapore law cannot apply because "the tort was in Egypt".
  2. The tourist pleads Egyptian law (hoping for higher damages) but adduces no evidence of it.
  3. The hotel pleads Egyptian law as a defence (a statutory exclusion of liability for tour operators) but proves nothing; the tourist says the presumption of similarity should apply.
  4. A party proves the text of an Indonesian statute but not how Indonesian courts interpret it.
  5. A party argues that a contract is contrary to Indonesian public policy, without proving Indonesian law.
  6. A party seeks an injunction restraining the defendant's conduct in Hong Kong, based on unproved Hong Kong law. The other side has led evidence that Hong Kong law differs on the point.
  7. A party, having the burden of proof, pleads Thai law and then relies on the presumption of similarity because Singapore law is more favourable to it.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Neither party pleaded Egyptian law, so Singapore law applies in its own right (Brownlie). No conflicts issue arises (EFT Holdings), and the hotel's argument fails.
  2. Once pleaded, the court must apply Egyptian law. If the tourist proves nothing, the court may presume similarity if fair and reasonable (Brownlie). Egyptian law is a civil law system, and the presumption is less apt for civil law systems lacking universal principles (C&Y). If it does not apply, the tourist may simply lose (EFT Holdings).
  3. The presumption is a rule of convenience (D'Oz) and less apt for a statutory rule (Brownlie). The question is whether Egyptian law has a materially similar rule (not, as in Shaker v Al-Bedrawi, a blanket refusal). Singapore law has no general statutory exclusion for tour operators, so if similarity is presumed, the defence fails.
  4. A gap in proof of interpretation is no bar: similar interpretive principles are presumed (Brownlie).
  5. Indonesian public policy is best determined by Indonesian courts and is not presumed similar (PT Jaya Putra v Guthrie).
  6. There is evidence of difference, so the presumption is refused (AQCEL Synergies). And no injunction against foreign conduct will be granted on a bare presumption (EFT Holdings, explaining OMG Holdings), though damages may be possible (C&Y).
  7. Tactical reliance cannot improve the party's position and may be an abuse (Tamil Nadu).
  • FNC overlay: even if foreign law is unproved, its likely differences still count at the FNC stage (Rickshaw; JIO Minerals).
  • Stage: the presumption is more readily applied at interlocutory stages (service out, stay) than at trial (Brownlie).

C1.6.4 References to Foreign Courts (O 29 / O 29A ROC 2021)

Rule: O 29, specified courts: per O 29 ROC 2021 (SICC O 15), on a party's application the court may order that a question of foreign law be determined in proceedings in a "specified court" (e.g., NSW, Bermuda, DIFC), or of its own motion in a non-specified court, backed by MOUs (also New York). O 29A, China: per O 29A ROC 2021 (SICC O 15A, from 3 April 2022), a question of PRC law goes court-to-court to the Supreme People's Court, though who bears the costs is unclear. Westacre origin: in Westacre v Yugoimport, as the experts diametrically disagreed on whether the English judgment was enforceable in England (a RECJA precondition), the CA adjourned for an English ruling, which Tomlinson J gave. Limits: per C&Y, foreign courts may refuse an advisory role, and the parties bear foreign costs on top, so few start it voluntarily (in Ng Teck Sim, both parties appealed against a Thai-law referral order).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Unresolvable Expert Conflict

In a Singapore trial, two experts flatly contradict each other on a novel point of NSW trust law, and two other experts disagree on PRC company law. A third issue turns on Thai land law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

NSW: NSW is a "specified court", so on a party's application the court can order that the question be determined in NSW proceedings (O 29), as in Westacre (where the CA adjourned for an English ruling on whether the English judgment was enforceable, and Tomlinson J gave it). PRC: under O 29A, the question can go court-to-court to the Supreme People's Court, though who bears the costs is unclear. Thai law: Thailand is not specified, so the court could act of its own motion (O 29). But the parties may resist, as in Ng Teck Sim (both appealed a Thai-law referral), because of the added foreign costs, and the Thai court may decline an advisory role (C&Y).

C1.6.5 SICC: Foreign Law on Submissions

Rule: Per s 18L SCJA (SICC O 16 r 8), the SICC may decide foreign law on submissions instead of proof, by counsel, a restricted-registration foreign lawyer or a registered law expert. Advantages: cost-efficient (as in arbitration), avoids an artificial fact/law split, and suits an international bench familiar with the foreign law. Extending it generally: weigh accuracy and cost savings against the fact-based tradition and the judge's unfamiliarity with the foreign law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Indian Law in the SICC

In an SICC dispute governed by Indian law, the parties propose that their Indian senior advocates make legal submissions on Indian contract law, with an International Judge who is a former Indian Supreme Court judge on the bench. A General Division judge in a related case wonders whether to adopt the same approach.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Under s 18L (SICC O 16 r 8), the SICC may determine Indian law on submissions by counsel or restricted-registration foreign lawyers instead of proof by experts. This is cost-efficient, avoids treating law as fact, and suits a bench with Indian expertise. The General Division has no equivalent power. Extending it would trade the fact-based tradition (and the judge's possible unfamiliarity with Indian law) for accuracy and cost savings, a policy choice for reform.

8C1.7 Forum mandatory rules

Rule: Starter: per C&Y, overriding mandatory rules are so crucial to Singapore's political, social or economic interests that parties cannot contract out by choosing foreign law (cf Art 11(1) Hague Principles). Per Skilling, a contract breaching a Singapore licensing statute is unenforceable to the extent of the conflict, whatever the proper law. Effect: the rule is superimposed, with the proper law governing the rest, though it may sink the whole contract (e.g., a foreign gambling contract under s 5(2) CLA). Tiers: only the international tier overrides a foreign proper law; a domestic mandatory rule binds only if Singapore law governs. Which laws count: per Sim See Kee, illegality at the place of contracting, residence or incorporation is irrelevant, and the place of performance enters only via Foster / Ralli / Lemenda (C2.10). Express scope first: the statute may spell out its reach (e.g., s 27(2) UCTA); otherwise, whether it overrides foreign law is statutory construction (JIO Minerals). Parliamentary intention: per JIO Minerals, a statute overrides foreign law if Parliament clearly intended so; choice of law rules are "useful tools" to ascertain its geographical scope. Two aspects of the presumption against extraterritoriality (overlapping; both yield to clear intention): choice of law aspect: the statute applies only if Singapore law governs the issue, so as UAE law (contract) or Indonesian law (tort) governed in JIO, the Misrepresentation Act did not apply; territorial aspect: the statute reaches only conduct within Singapore, unless displaced by clear, possibly implied, intention (Parno), as for the TCM Practitioners Act (Huang Danmin). Gauging intention: a conduct-regulating or protective statute (e.g., s 37 PCA, the TCM Practitioners Act) more readily applies extraterritorially, unlike one merely supplementing common law remedies (e.g., the MA). Types: overriding (applies irrespective of the proper law, e.g., export or import controls, s 5(2) CLA); conditional (s 27(2) UCTA applies despite a foreign choice if (a) the term was imposed wholly or mainly to evade it, or (b) a party dealt as consumer while habitually resident here and the essential steps for contracting were taken here, by him or on his behalf). Contrast bona fide (C2.2.2): "wholly or mainly" is wider than "sole purpose", and the chosen law survives subject to the Act, whereas a non-bona fide choice is struck out. Flip side: per s 27(1) UCTA, if Singapore law governs only by the parties' choice, ss 2–7 do not apply. Examples: s 5(2) CLA (overriding, so a foreign casino's claim fails whatever its proper law: Star City; its "no action" wording also makes it procedural; for judgments, Poh Soon Kiat); the Misrepresentation Act (per JIO Minerals, it reaches misrepresentations abroad only if the contract has a Singapore proper law); s 18F SCJA (debated whether it applies as a forum mandatory rule to a non-CCAA SICC agreement governed by foreign law: J5).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Five Statutes Against Foreign Law
  1. Unlicensed financial adviser: a Hong Kong-law advisory contract under which a Hong Kong firm, unlicensed in Singapore, advised Singapore clients in Singapore, contrary to the Singapore Financial Advisers Act. The firm sues for fees.
  2. Misrepresentation Act: a misrepresentation made in Jakarta induced a UAE-law contract; the claimant seeks damages under s 2(1) MA.
  3. Prevention of Corruption Act: a Singapore citizen bribed an official in Vietnam; the question is whether s 37 PCA reaches the conduct.
  4. UCTA: (a) a Singapore consumer, habitually resident here, buys a car online from a German dealer, contracting from her Singapore home, under German-law terms that exclude all liability; (b) a Singapore company and a Singapore supplier choose New York law "to avoid UCTA" for a purely Singapore deal; (c) two Hong Kong companies choose Singapore law for a contract with no Singapore connection, and one invokes UCTA ss 2–7.
  5. Gambling: a UK online casino sues a Singapore resident on an English-law gambling debt.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Skilling: a contract breaching a Singapore licensing statute is unenforceable to the extent of the conflict, whatever the Hong Kong proper law. The rule is superimposed, and Hong Kong law governs the rest of the contract. Only the international tier of mandatory rules overrides a foreign proper law; a licensing regime protecting the Singapore market is of that kind. Illegality under the place of contracting or incorporation would be irrelevant (Sim See Kee).
  2. JIO Minerals: the MA merely supplements common law remedies, and by the choice of law aspect of the presumption it applies only if Singapore law governs the contract. UAE law governs, so the MA does not apply.
  3. PCA s 37: a conduct-regulating statute aimed at corruption, so it more readily applies extraterritorially (JIO Minerals). The territorial aspect of the presumption is displaced by clear, here express, intention (cf the TCM Practitioners Act in Huang Danmin, where intention was implied: Parno).
  4. UCTA: (a) s 27(2)(b) applies: she dealt as consumer, was habitually resident here, and the essential steps were taken here, so UCTA applies despite the German choice. (b) s 27(2)(a): the term was imposed "wholly or mainly" to evade UCTA, so UCTA applies. This is wider than the "sole purpose" test for bona fide choices (C2.2.2), and New York law survives subject to UCTA, whereas a non-bona fide choice would be struck out entirely. (c) s 27(1): where Singapore law governs only because the parties chose it, ss 2–7 do not apply.
  5. s 5(2) CLA: an overriding mandatory rule, so the claim fails whatever the English proper law (Star City). Its "no action" wording also makes it procedural (C1.2). For enforcement of foreign gambling judgments, see Poh Soon Kiat and Venetian Macau (J7).

9C1.8 Fundamental public policy of the forum

Rule: Per C&Y, the court refuses an offending foreign rule or contract only if it infringes Singapore's fundamental (international) public policy, which is narrower than domestic policy, so being void or objectionable domestically is not enough (cf Art 11(3) Hague Principles: "manifestly incompatible"). Examples: per Royal Boskalis, a contract procured by extreme duress (a human-shield threat); per Foster v Driscoll, a contract to break a friendly State's law; whereas economic duress stays with the proper law (Dimskal) (C2.10). Proper law's own rule: per Kahler, a contract illegal under the proper law is unenforceable, unless that illegality rule itself offends Singapore public policy (The Playa Larga; Re Helbert Wagg). Distinguish forum mandatory rules: direction: a mandatory rule applies positively, with its own scope, while public policy negatively filters the offending foreign rule; trigger: a mandatory rule turns on statutory construction (JIO Minerals), public policy on the result offending fundamental principles. Statutory instance: s 4(2) FLPA (undue hardship). Hierarchy (judgments context): per Poh Soon Kiat, statutory policy outranks higher international policy, which outranks domestic policy, but per C&Y only statutory policy of equally high, extraterritorial intent should rank first (J7). Cross-refer: illegality (Foster; Ralli Brothers; Lemenda; Royal Boskalis) in C2.10; foreign judgments in J7.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Contracts Under Scrutiny
