  1. A Kuwaiti-law contract was signed by a dredging company's managers while Iraqi forces held them hostage as human shields.
  2. An English-law contract to smuggle whisky into a country where alcohol is prohibited (a friendly State).
  3. A Greek-law charter renegotiated under threat of the shipowner withholding the vessel (economic duress), valid under Greek law.
  4. A German-law contract is illegal under German law because it was concluded with a Jewish-owned company (a Nazi-era racial law). Separately, a Cuban-law contract is void under a Cuban confiscation decree aimed at the counterparty's nationality.
  5. A New York-law contract for a pre-nuptial agreement of a kind Singapore domestic law treats with suspicion.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Royal Boskalis: extreme duress of this kind offends Singapore's fundamental public policy, so the contract is refused enforcement whatever Kuwaiti law says.
  2. Foster v Driscoll: a contract to break a friendly State's law offends public policy (C2.10).
  3. Dimskal: economic duress stays with the proper law. Greek law upholds the contract, so it is enforced; this is not a fundamental-policy case.
  4. Kahler: illegality under the proper law normally makes the contract unenforceable, unless the illegality rule itself offends Singapore public policy (The Playa Larga; Re Helbert Wagg). A racially discriminatory law, or a confiscatory decree aimed at nationality, offends fundamental public policy, so the court disregards it and enforces the contract.
  5. A rule that is merely contrary to domestic policy is not enough. Only fundamental (international) public policy, "manifestly incompatible" (cf Hague Principles art 11(3)), justifies refusal.
  • Contrast with C1.7: in (1)–(4), public policy works negatively (filtering foreign law, triggered by an offensive result). A forum mandatory rule (e.g., UCTA) works positively, applying by its own terms as a matter of statutory construction.

10C1.9 Renvoi (operation non-examinable; deploy only if the reference to foreign law is challenged)

Rule: Single v total renvoi: a party argues that the reference to law R includes its conflict rules, pointing back to Singapore (remission) or on to law T (transmission). Single renvoi applies R's conflict rules; total renvoi decides as the R court would, for uniform outcomes. Approaches: per Ong Ghee Soon Kevin (obiter), renvoi may be taken by blanket rule, by category (Iran v Berend), or case by case (The WD Fairway (No 3)), the last rightly rejected as too uncertain (Blue Sky One). Against renvoi: per Credit Suisse Life v Ivanishvili (PC), renvoi is complex, circular (total renvoi on both sides) and subordinates the forum's choice of law policy to R's; and per ss 3(5), 6(2) FLPA it is excluded for limitation. Contract, excluded: per Ong Ghee Soon and Amin Rasheed, the proper law means the foreign law's domestic law (cf Art 20 Rome I). Tort, rejected by the PC: per Credit Suisse, renvoi has never applied in tort or obligations, so the lex loci delicti means its domestic law; Neilson (HCA) is unpersuasive because FNC curbs forum shopping. Formally open in Singapore (C3.9.3).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Paris Painting and the Malaysian Contract
  1. Movables: title to a painting stolen in Singapore and sold in France is governed by the lex situs, French law. French conflict rules would refer the question to the law of the place where the painting was stolen (Singapore).
  2. Contract: a contract is governed by Malaysian law. Malaysian conflict rules would apply Singapore law to the particular issue.
  3. Tort: the lex loci delicti is Thai law. Thai conflict rules would apply the law of the parties' common residence (Singapore).
  4. Limitation: the lex causae (Indonesian law) would, under Indonesian conflict rules, apply Singapore's limitation period.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Title to movables (±): if renvoi applies by category (Iran v Berend), a party may argue that "French law" includes French conflict rules, which remit to Singapore law (single renvoi), or that Singapore should decide as a French court would (total renvoi). A case-by-case approach (The WD Fairway (No 3)) was rightly rejected as too uncertain (Blue Sky One). Per Credit Suisse Life v Ivanishvili (PC), renvoi is circular and subordinates the forum's policy, so it should be resisted.
  2. Contract: renvoi is excluded; the proper law means Malaysian domestic law (Ong Ghee Soon; Amin Rasheed; cf Rome I art 20).
  3. Tort: per Credit Suisse (PC), renvoi has never applied in tort, so Thai domestic law applies. Neilson (HCA), which applied renvoi in tort, is unpersuasive because FNC already curbs forum shopping. Formally open in Singapore (C3.9.3).
  4. Limitation: excluded by statute (FLPA ss 3(5), 6(2)), so only Indonesia's domestic limitation period applies.

LAW302 · HYPO LESSON C2 · 27 HYPOTHETICALS · 8 QUESTIONS

C2 hypotheticals: Contract choice of law: the proper law and illegality

The rules behind these hypotheticals are taught in Lesson C2, where the word-for-word pre-write is too. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

Applications:
ℹ HOW TO USE THESE HYPOTHETICALS

Each concept is set out as Rule, then Hypothetical, then Application. "Variation" lines flip one fact. Methodology (characterisation, proof, mandatory rules) is in C1.

The hypo test at the end checks you can run the facts yourself.

1C2.0 Roadmap in one hypothetical

Rule (order): (1) Characterise each issue: interpretation, performance, discharge and material validity go to the proper law; formation to the putative proper law; form to the proper law or the lex loci contractus; capacity to its own rules. (2) Stage 1, express choice (Vita Food; Peh Teck Quee), with its attacks; a failed choice skips Stage 2. (3) Stage 2, implied choice. (4) Stage 3, objective proper law. (5) Overlays: a promissory clause, forum mandatory rules, illegality routes A–G. (6) Technique: EPL → IPL → OPL with reasons; flag an unclear threshold and assume it met.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Rice Shipment From Yangon

Golden Grain Pte Ltd (Singapore) agreed with Irrawaddy Rice Co (Myanmar) to buy 10,000 tonnes of rice CIF Singapore, payment in USD by letter of credit opened in Singapore. Clause 20: "This contract is governed by English law." Irrawaddy's 17-year-old managing director signed; there was no witness. Myanmar later banned rice exports. Golden Grain sues for non-delivery. Irrawaddy argues (a) the English-law clause is invalid because Golden Grain misrepresented its creditworthiness; (b) the contract was never formed because Irrawaddy never accepted the final price; (c) it is formally invalid for lack of a witness; (d) its MD lacked capacity; (e) performance is illegal under the Myanmar export ban.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Stage 1: clause 20's choice of English law is virtually conclusive (Peh Teck Quee) unless it is not bona fide, not legal, or contrary to public policy. English law needs no connection with the contract.
  2. (a) Material validity: misrepresentation about creditworthiness affects the contract, not consensus on the clause (CIMB), so English law governs whether the contract is voidable.
  3. (b) Formation: governed by the putative proper law (English law via clause 20, with the double bootstrap) (Lew v Nargolwala).
  4. (c) Form: valid if it complies with either the proper law (English) or the lex loci contractus (AQCEL).
  5. (d) Capacity: for a company, the law of incorporation and the proper law (Dicey r 162). The MD's personal minority goes to the company's authority or capacity under Myanmar corporate law.
  6. (e) Illegality: route E (Ralli Brothers) asks whether performance is illegal at the contractual place of performance. Under CIF, shipment from Myanmar is arguably part of the performance, so the ban may bite. Alternatively, frustration under English law (Peh Teck Quee reading).

2C2.1 The governing framework

Rule (Global starter): Per Amin Rasheed, the proper law governs validity, construction, effect and discharge. Per Pacific Recreation (approving OUI v Turegum), it is found by (1) express choice, (2) implied choice, or (3) the closest and most real connection (Bonython). Characterisation: per Re Bonacina, an agreement without consideration is still contractual for conflicts purposes (Raiffeisen). Scope: per C&Y, the proper law governs interpretation, incorporation of terms, performance, discharge, material validity (duress, misrepresentation: CIMB), and illegality under it, and per s 3(1) FLPA its limitation period applies. Not covered: formation, form, capacity, and procedure (burden of proof; arguably quantum), unlike Art 9 Hague Principles. No renvoi: per Amin Rasheed and Ong Ghee Soon, the proper law means its domestic rules (cf Art 8 Hague Principles).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
What Does the Proper Law Govern?

In Golden Grain v Irrawaddy (English proper law), list which law governs each issue: (i) the meaning of "fair average quality"; (ii) whether a later email added a demurrage term; (iii) whether delivery in two lots was adequate performance; (iv) whether the contract was discharged by Irrawaddy's repudiation; (v) whether Golden Grain's misrepresentation makes it voidable; (vi) the limitation period; (vii) who bears the burden of proving that the rice was defective; (viii) whether English conflict rules would refer any issue to Myanmar law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(i)–(v) are governed by English law as the proper law: interpretation, incorporation of terms, performance, discharge and material validity (Amin Rasheed; C&Y; CIMB). (vi) English limitation law applies under s 3(1) FLPA (C1.5). (vii) The burden of proof is procedural, so Singapore law applies (C1.6.1); unlike Hague Principles art 9, the proper law does not cover it. (viii) No renvoi: "English law" means English domestic law (Amin Rasheed; Ong Ghee Soon).

Rule (Preliminary rules): Subsequent conduct: per Las Vegas Hilton, the proper law is fixed at contracting, so later conduct invoking a law is irrelevant, though per James Miller it may found an estoppel. Non-national law: per Musawi and C&Y, only a country's law (including a state within a federation) qualifies, so a choice of Sharia law or the lex mercatoria fails as the proper law, leaving the IPL or OPL. Contrast: arbitrators may apply chosen "rules of law" (Model Law art 28(1)), and Hague Principles art 3 allows UNIDROIT-type rules unless forum law bars them, as Singapore's common law does. Fallback: incorporate the rules as terms of a contract governed by a national law (C2.2.9).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Islamic Finance Facility and the Later Letters
  1. A Singapore bank's murabaha facility with a Malaysian borrower says: "This Agreement shall be governed by the principles of the Glorious Sharia."
  2. Another facility says: "Governed by the law of New South Wales" (a state within a federation).
  3. A third contract says nothing about law, but after a dispute arose, both parties' lawyers wrote letters referring to "the applicable Thai law", and the claimant spent heavily preparing a Thai-law case.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Sharia law is not the law of a country, so it cannot be the proper law (Musawi; C&Y). Go to the IPL or OPL. An arbitral tribunal could apply it as "rules of law" (Model Law art 28(1)), and Hague Principles art 3 would allow non-State rules, but Singapore's common law does not. The parties' fallback is to incorporate Sharia principles as terms of a contract governed by, say, Singapore law (as in Beximco, C2.2.9).
  2. A state within a federation counts as a "country's" law, so it is valid.
  3. The proper law is fixed at contracting, so the later letters are irrelevant (Las Vegas Hilton). But the party who led the other to rely on Thai law may be estopped from denying it (James Miller).

3C2.2 Stage 1: express choice

C2.2.1 Starter

Rule: Per Peh Teck Quee, applying Vita Food, an express choice is virtually conclusive unless it is not (a) bona fide, (b) legal, or (c) consistent with public policy, each tested by the lex fori on objective intention, so a party's claim not to have seen the standard terms is irrelevant. Unrelated law permitted: the chosen law needs no connection (cf Art 2(4) Hague Principles), as parties may want a neutral law or one well developed on the subject (Amin Rasheed). Limbs (b) and (c): "legal" is of unclear meaning, and the public policy limb duplicates the general reservation, so an attacking party leads with bona fides (C&Y).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Neutral Law

A Korean shipbuilder and a Brazilian owner sign a shipbuilding contract on the builder's standard form choosing English law. Neither party has any English connection. The owner says (a) it never read the standard terms, and (b) English law has nothing to do with the contract.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(a) Intention is objective, so the owner's failure to read the terms is irrelevant (Peh Teck Quee). (b) The chosen law needs no connection: parties often choose a neutral law, or one with well-developed shipping law (Amin Rasheed; cf Hague Principles art 2(4)). The choice stands unless it is not bona fide (C2.2.2). Attacks on "legality" or public policy are weak and largely duplicative (C&Y).

C2.2.2 Attack: Not Bona Fide

Rule: Per Peh Teck Quee, choosing a law to evade the moneylending, exchange control or consumer laws of another country defeats the clause only if evasion was the sole purpose. "Another law": usually the OPL, but possibly a forum mandatory rule (Golden Acres), whose evasion fails twice: the rule applies anyway and the clause is struck out. Scenario A (bona fide, +): as in Peh Teck Quee (the bank operated, the facility was booked, accounts kept and tax paid in Singapore), a genuine connection with the chosen law means the clause stands. Scenario B (not bona fide, −): no or negligible connection, plus the timing of insertion or the sole beneficiary of the evasion, show that evading the OPL was the sole purpose, so the clause is struck out completely, unlike under s 27(2) UCTA.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Malaysian Borrower's Singapore Loan
  • Version 1: A Malaysian borrower takes a loan from a Singapore bank's Singapore branch. The facility is booked in Singapore, the accounts are kept there and tax is paid there. The contract chooses Singapore law. Malaysian exchange control law would have restricted the loan. The borrower says the clause was chosen to evade Malaysian law.
  • Version 2: A Malaysian moneylender lends to Malaysian borrowers in Johor, all dealings being in Malaysia, but inserts, at the last minute and only in its high-interest loans, a clause choosing the law of Vanuatu, where there is no moneylending regulation.
  • Version 3: A Singapore retailer's consumer terms choose Utopian law for Singapore consumers, solely to avoid UCTA.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Version 1: As in Peh Teck Quee, Singapore law has a genuine connection (booking, accounts, tax), so the choice is bona fide. Even if it also helped avoid Malaysian exchange control, evasion was not the sole purpose.
  • Version 2: There is no connection with Vanuatu; the clause was inserted at the last minute, only in the high-interest loans, and benefits only the lender. Evasion of Malaysian moneylending law (the OPL) was the sole purpose, so the clause is struck out completely, and the OPL (Malaysian law) governs.
  • Version 3: Evading a forum mandatory rule (Golden Acres) fails twice: UCTA applies anyway (s 27(2): imposed "wholly or mainly" to evade it, which is a wider test than "sole purpose"), and, if the sole purpose was evasion, the clause is struck out. Contrast s 27(2) alone, under which Utopian law would survive subject to UCTA (C2.2.7).

C2.2.3 Attack: Vitiating Factor Infecting the Clause

Rule: Separability: per Maldives Airports (cf Art 7 Hague Principles), the choice of law clause belongs to the separable dispute resolution framework, so per CIMB misrepresentation, duress or mistake vitiating the contract does not necessarily infect it. Test (C&Y): whether the vitiating factor leaves no consensus on the clause itself, not whether the contract is void or voidable; if it is infected, the OPL governs material validity. Disputed v agreed: per CIMB, a merely disputed fraud or misrepresentation leaves the chosen law applying "as if the contract were valid", lest a bare allegation neutralise the clause, unlike an agreed absence of any agreement. Scenario A (clause survives, +): fraud as to the subject matter, or a common fundamental mistake about the goods, affects the contract but not consensus on the law. Scenario B (clause falls, −): non est factum infects everything (CIMB), and arguably no matching offer and acceptance does too (left open in Maldives Airports). Overlap, duress: per Royal Boskalis, extreme duress (a human-shield threat) engages forum public policy, whereas per Dimskal economic duress stays with the proper law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Forged Bonds and the Blindfolded Signatory

A Swiss-law bond purchase between a Singapore fund and a Panamanian seller:

  1. The fund alleges that the seller fraudulently misdescribed the bonds' credit rating; the seller denies it.
  2. Both parties were mistaken about which bond series was being sold.
  3. The fund's elderly director signed believing the document was a non-binding letter of intent (non est factum).
  4. The parties' signed versions had different prices, so there was arguably no matching offer and acceptance.
  5. The seller's agents threatened to kill the director's family unless he signed.
  6. The seller threatened to withhold another unrelated delivery unless the fund signed (economic duress).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. A disputed misrepresentation does not neutralise the clause, so Swiss law applies "as if the contract were valid" (CIMB). Fraud as to the subject matter does not touch consensus on the choice of law.
  2. A common mistake about the goods affects the contract, not the clause (CIMB), so Swiss law governs.
  3. Non est factum infects everything, including the clause (CIMB), so material validity goes to the OPL.
  4. Arguably no consensus at all, so the clause falls too (C&Y; left open in Maldives Airports). Go to the OPL, or treat it as a formation issue under the putative proper law (C2.6).
  5. Extreme duress engages forum public policy (Royal Boskalis; C2.10.2), whatever Swiss law says.
  6. Economic duress stays with the proper law (Dimskal), so Swiss law decides.

C2.2.4 Attack: Unclear Expression of Choice

Rule: Per Enka v Chubb and Compagnie Tunisienne, the lex fori's ordinary interpretation rules construe an ambiguous choice, the proper law being a connecting factor; as there, "the law of the flag" with several flags meant the flag of the vessels primarily used.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"The Law of the Seller's Place of Business"

A contract says: "This contract is governed by the law of the Seller's place of business." The seller has offices in Hong Kong (head office) and Singapore (the office that negotiated and performed this contract).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Singapore law, as the lex fori, construes the ambiguous clause using ordinary interpretation rules (Enka v Chubb). As in Compagnie Tunisienne (several flags, so the flag of the vessels primarily used), the court reads the clause in context: "the Seller's place of business" most naturally means the place of business primarily involved in this contract, Singapore.

C2.2.5 Attack: Floating Proper Law

Rule: Floating clause void: as contracts cannot exist "in a legal vacuum" (Amin Rasheed), a clause applying law A or law B on one party's election or a future event is "meaningless" and of no legal effect (Shanghai Turbo), so skip Stage 2. No election mechanism: as in Shanghai Turbo (cl 17: "laws of Singapore/or People's Republic of China"), the missing mechanism adds to the uncertainty. Which law tests validity? (argue both): per C&Y, the Shanghai Turbo HC on balance used the lex fori (also testing both candidate laws), whereas The Iran Vojdan used the OPL (German law: void as small print, though it permits floating clauses; Iranian law, presumed English: void as floating). Lex fori (−): per Prof Chong, under Singapore law the clause is invalid even with an election mechanism, so the OPL governs. OPL (+): if the OPL permits floating clauses, the clause is valid, and law A governs once a party elects or sues first. Paired jurisdiction clause: per The Iran Vojdan, jurisdiction options "intimately connected" with the law choice fall with it, as the Shanghai Turbo HC held of the "and … /or" pairing (contrast separate sub-clauses in The Frank Pais). Rebuttal: the Shanghai Turbo CA severed the jurisdiction part as not interdependent, backed by the severance clause, reading it as submission to whichever named court is seised, so the resisting party must show strong cause (J4). Contract survives: striking out the clause leaves the contract under the OPL, though per C&Y, if no law at all was intended, "a contract without a law is no contract at all". Distinguish a change of proper law: in theory a floating clause has no law until crystallisation (void), while a change varies an existing law (valid), but the line is fine, since the OPL operates meanwhile in both.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Owner's Option Clause

A charterparty says: "This charter shall be governed by English law or Singapore law, as the Owner may elect at the time of any dispute, and disputes shall be referred to the courts of London or Singapore accordingly." There is a severance clause. When a dispute arises, the Owner elects Singapore law and sues in Singapore. The OPL, absent the clause, is Panamanian law (which, assume, permits floating clauses).

  • Variation: the clause reads "laws of Singapore/or England" with no mechanism.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Validity of the floating clause (±): (−) On the lex fori approach (Shanghai Turbo HC; Chong), Singapore law treats a floating choice as void even with an election mechanism, because the contract cannot exist in a legal vacuum (Amin Rasheed). So skip Stage 2 (C2.2.8) and go straight to the OPL, Panamanian law. (+) On the OPL approach (The Iran Vojdan), test validity by Panamanian law. If Panamanian law permits floating clauses, the clause is valid, and Singapore law governs from the Owner's election. Argue both. Jurisdiction part: (−) The Iran Vojdan: the jurisdiction option is "intimately connected" with the law choice ("accordingly"), so it falls with it. (+) The Shanghai Turbo CA: sever the jurisdiction part, as it is not interdependent and there is a severance clause, and read it as submission to whichever named court is seised. The charterer resisting Singapore must then show strong cause (J4.3). Contract survives under the OPL. Change v float: the Owner might argue that the clause is really a valid change of proper law on election (C2.2.6), but per C&Y the line is fine, since Panamanian law operates in the meantime either way.

  • In the variation, the lack of an election mechanism makes the clause even more uncertain (as with Shanghai Turbo's cl 17), so it is void, and the OPL governs.

C2.2.6 Change of Proper Law; Split Proper Law

Rule: Change: per Kredietbank v Sinotani (and James Miller), parties may change the proper law, though whether the lex fori or the original proper law decides if the change is allowed is open. Limits: per the SAL Report, Singapore should adopt Art 2(3) Hague Principles: no prejudice to formal validity or third-party rights, which suggests a lex fori conflicts question. Split / dépeçage: per Libyan Arab Foreign Bank, law A may govern one part and law B the rest (cf Art 2(2) Hague Principles), but per Kahler a split is not inferred "readily or without good reason", parties expecting one law (Enka). Coherence: the split must be internally coherent, so not different laws on repudiation depending on which party is innocent.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Variation and the Split
  1. A 2019 distribution agreement governed by Indonesian law was varied in 2023, by a signed amendment, to be governed by Singapore law. A guarantor who guaranteed the distributor's obligations in 2020 says the change cannot prejudice it. A 2021 mortgage of the distributor's stock registered in Indonesia under Indonesian formal requirements is also challenged.
  2. A loan agreement says: "Payment obligations are governed by New York law; all other matters by Singapore law."
  3. A sale contract says: "If the Buyer repudiates, English law governs; if the Seller repudiates, Thai law governs."
  4. A contract has a general choice of Singapore law, but one schedule refers to "warranties under the Indonesian Civil Code".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. The parties may change the proper law (Kredietbank v Sinotani; James Miller). Whether the change is permitted is decided by the lex fori or the original proper law (open). Following the SAL Report's suggestion (Hague Principles art 2(3)), the change cannot prejudice formal validity (the 2021 mortgage stays valid) or third-party rights (the guarantor is not bound to worse terms).
  2. A valid split (Libyan Arab Foreign Bank; cf Hague Principles art 2(2)), and internally coherent.
  3. Incoherent: the law applicable to repudiation depends on which party is innocent, so this split is not permitted.
  4. A split is not inferred "readily or without good reason" (Kahler; Enka). The reference is more likely an incorporation of Indonesian warranties as terms (C2.2.9) within a Singapore-law contract.

C2.2.7 Overlay: Forum Mandatory Rule Superimposed

Rule: Per s 27(2) UCTA, the Act applies despite a foreign choice if the clause was imposed wholly or mainly to evade it, or a consumer habitually resident here dealt and the essential steps were taken here; the chosen law then applies subject to UCTA. Flip side: per s 27(1), if Singapore law governs only by the parties' choice, ss 2–7 do not apply.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Online Furniture Purchase

A Singapore consumer, from home, buys a sofa online from a Danish retailer whose terms choose Danish law and exclude all liability for defects. The sofa collapses.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The consumer dealt as consumer, is habitually resident here, and the essential steps for contracting (browsing, ordering, paying) were taken in Singapore, so s 27(2)(b) applies UCTA despite the Danish choice. Danish law still governs the contract, but subject to UCTA, so the exclusion must pass UCTA's reasonableness test (or is void, if s 6 applies). This is superimposition, not striking out (contrast a non-bona fide choice: C2.2.2). (Full analysis: C1.7.)

C2.2.8 Effect of an Ineffective Express Choice

Rule: Per Shanghai Turbo and The Iran Vojdan, as the parties turned their minds to the governing law and failed (not bona fide, floating, infected), inferring a choice is "artificial", so go straight to Stage 3. Low stakes: per Pacific Recreation, skipping Stage 2 is "not as significant a step as it seems", as the same factors recur at Stage 3.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
After the Floating Clause Fails

In the charterparty (C2.2.5, lex fori approach), the clause is void. The Owner wants the court to infer Singapore law from the Singapore jurisdiction option at Stage 2.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Shanghai Turbo and The Iran Vojdan, the parties turned their minds to the governing law and failed, so inferring a choice is artificial; go straight to Stage 3. Little is lost, because the jurisdiction option (if severed and valid) is still a factor in the closest-connection analysis (Pacific Recreation).

C2.2.9 Choice v Incorporation of Foreign Law

Rule: Per C&Y, a choice of law X applies it as living law (later amendments apply), whereas incorporating UCP 600 or Sharia principles makes them terms, which crystallise at formation unless agreed otherwise. Validity and interpretation: per Beximco, non-State rules may be incorporated if the proper law permits and they are sufficiently certain, being construed by the proper law with regard to their home system.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Sharia-Compliant Lease and the Amended Statute
  1. A Singapore-law ijara (lease) says: "Subject to the principles of the Glorious Sharia, this Agreement is governed by Singapore law."
  2. A contract says: "This contract incorporates the provisions of the Thai Civil and Commercial Code on sale, as at the date of this contract." Thailand amends those provisions two years later.
  3. Another contract says: "This contract is governed by Thai law." Thailand amends its sale provisions two years later.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. As in Beximco, the Sharia reference cannot be a choice of law (not a country's law), and incorporation fails unless the principles are sufficiently certain to be terms. Broad references to Sharia "principles" are not, so Singapore law governs without them. More specific incorporated rules could work as terms, construed by Singapore law with regard to their Sharia home system.
  2. Incorporation makes the Code provisions terms that crystallise at formation, so the pre-amendment version applies.
  3. A choice applies Thai law as living law, so the amendments apply (subject to Thai transitional rules).

4C2.3 Stage 2: implied choice of law

Rule (Starter): Per Pacific Recreation, absent an express clause, a choice may be inferred from the terms and circumstances, weighing the Las Vegas Hilton factors, which carry differing weight. Per Enka v Chubb, an implied choice is as effective as an express one, and the Vita Food limits apply. Factors (weightiest first):

  • Jurisdiction or arbitration clause (heavy): submitting to the courts of, or arbitration in, country Y implies law Y, the chosen forum being presumed to apply its own law (Pacific Recreation). Contrast: per Art 4 Hague Principles, such a clause is "not in itself equivalent to a choice of law".
  • Standard form or terms of art (strong): per Lord Diplock in Amin Rasheed, a Lloyd's SG form scheduled to the MIA 1906, or terms of art peculiar to a law, imply that law. Caveat: per Lord Wilberforce, a universally used form shows nothing, reaching English law only at Stage 3.
  • Related contract (can be decisive): per JIO Minerals, contract A, so closely related to contract B under law X (sent to the buyer, cited three times, essential), takes law X, even between different parties.
  • Language and currency (little): English (the lingua franca) and USD carry little weight, unlike an esoteric language or currency (Pacific Recreation); per Lupofresh, universal terms like "cif UK port" are neutral.
  • Residence, business, purpose: these count (Las Vegas Hilton), but the place of contracting matters little unless performance is also there (Pacific Recreation).
  • Form pointing away: a deed or indemnity unknown to law X points away from it: "why would parties intentionally use forms and terms inapposite to the governing law?" (Pacific Recreation).

Limits on inference: Pointing away is not pointing towards: per Pacific Recreation, factors negating Chinese law did not imply Singapore law (deeds being known to all common law systems), so the court moved to Stage 3. Principle of validation: per C&Y (cf Pacific Recreation), parties are presumed to intend a valid contract (ut res magis valeat), so they chose the law under which the contract and each term are valid. Limits: not where formation or a vitiating factor is disputed, and arguably irrelevant at Stage 3 (Coast Lines v Hudig, Megaw LJ; contra Lord Denning), which seeks connection, not intention.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Kuwaiti Insurance Policy and the Chinese Deed
  1. A Kuwaiti company insures a vessel with a Kuwaiti insurer using the Lloyd's SG form scheduled to the Marine Insurance Act 1906 (an English statute). There is no choice of law clause. Kuwait had no marine insurance law at the time.
  2. A shareholder dispute: a Singapore investor and a Chinese promoter sign (in Shanghai, in English, with prices in USD) a "Deed of Indemnity" (a deed, unknown to PRC law), with an SIAC arbitration clause seated in Singapore.
  3. The same, but with no arbitration clause; the only clue is the deed form.
  4. A share sale between A and B, with no choice of law, is expressly "conditional on and to be read with" a UAE-law shareholders' agreement between B and C, which the sale document refers to three times.
  5. A contract between an Indian seller and a Thai buyer, in Hindi, priced in Indian rupees, with no choice of law clause.
  6. A contract that would be void for illegality under law A but valid under law B, with no choice of law clause.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. (Lord Diplock, Amin Rasheed): the SG form and its MIA 1906 terms of art imply English law; Kuwaiti law could not even give them meaning. (Lord Wilberforce): a universally used form shows nothing, so English law is reached only at Stage 3. Argue the stage according to the client.
  2. The SIAC clause is heavy: the chosen seat is presumed to apply its own law, so Singapore law is implied (Pacific Recreation), though Hague Principles art 4 says such a clause is not itself a choice. The deed form points away from PRC law, since parties would not use forms inapposite to the governing law (Pacific Recreation). English and USD carry little weight. The place of contracting (Shanghai) matters little unless performance is also there.
  3. Pointing away is not pointing towards: the deed form negates PRC law but does not imply Singapore law, because deeds are known to all common law systems. Go to Stage 3 (Pacific Recreation).
  4. Related contract: like JIO Minerals, so closely related to the UAE-law shareholders' agreement (essential, cited three times) that it takes UAE law, even though the parties differ.
  5. An esoteric (non-lingua-franca) language and the local currency carry real weight towards Indian law (Pacific Recreation), together with the seller's residence.
  6. Validation (C&Y): parties are presumed to intend a valid contract (ut res magis valeat), which points towards law B. But this does not apply where formation or a vitiating factor is disputed, and it is arguably irrelevant at Stage 3, which seeks connection, not intention (Megaw LJ in Coast Lines v Hudig; contra Lord Denning).

5C2.4 Stage 3: objective proper law

Rule (Starter): Per Bonython, the contract is governed by the law with which the transaction has its closest and most real connection, being per Pacific Recreation (approving The Assunzione) what just and reasonable persons would have intended had they thought about it, weighing the same factors as at Stage 2. Rebutting objections:

  • Weak Stage 2 factor now decisive: Stage 3 imputes rather than finds a choice, so the deed being unknown to Chinese law, too weak at Stage 2, may be decisive (Pacific Recreation). Spectrum: per Amin Rasheed (Lord Wilberforce) and Lew, Stages 2 and 3 "merge".
  • Vita Food limits inapplicable: they police a choice, so a party cannot attack the OPL as not bona fide.
  • Not confined to the parties' candidates: the court may apply a third law (e.g., US or UAE law), but only after inviting the parties' submissions (natural justice) (Pacific Recreation; JIO Minerals).
  • Wrong factors: per Prof Chong, witness convenience and patent registration are Spiliada factors, irrelevant to the OPL unless connected to the contract.
  • No ties: per Lew, "courts do not in practice declare ties".

Weighting: Critique of "equal weight": per C&Y, Pacific Recreation's "equal weight" dictum is puzzling, as the place of performance carries great weight (Bonython; Enka), and later cases weigh factors differentially. Illustration: in Shanghai Turbo, performance in China was offset by the SGX-listed counterparty and references to Singapore statutes, and the CA found a good arguable case for Singapore law. Application (Chong): the strongest argument is usually the place where both parties perform, supported by the place of contracting, currency, incorporation and head office, and related transactions. Balance: as in Pacific Recreation, factors pointing away from law A may far exceed those pointing away from law B. Comparative (analogy only): Art 4 Rome I applies fixed rules, then the characteristic performer's habitual residence, subject to a manifestly closer connection.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Chinese Joint Venture With No Law Clause

A Singapore-listed company (SGX) and a Chinese businessman sign an investment agreement with no choice of law clause. Facts: (i) performance (building and operating a factory) is in China; (ii) the agreement refers to the Singapore Companies Act and SGX listing rules; (iii) it was signed in Singapore; (iv) it is in English and priced in RMB; (v) the key witnesses live in Shanghai; (vi) the Chinese party's patents are registered in China; (vii) the parties argue only for Singapore or Chinese law, but the court thinks Hong Kong law (where the escrow was held) might be closest; (viii) the Chinese party argues that the court should reject Singapore law at Stage 3 as "not a bona fide choice".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Stage 3 asks for the closest and most real connection, imputing what just and reasonable persons would have intended (Bonython; The Assunzione).

  • Weighting: the place of performance (China) carries great weight (Bonython; Enka), notwithstanding Pacific Recreation's puzzling "equal weight" dictum (C&Y). But as in Shanghai Turbo itself, performance in China can be offset by the SGX-listed counterparty and the references to Singapore statutes (ii). The signing in Singapore (iii) adds a little. English carries little weight, and the RMB pricing points to China.
  • (v) and (vi) are Spiliada factors and irrelevant to the OPL unless connected to the contract (Chong).
  • (vii) The court may apply a third law (Hong Kong) but must first invite the parties' submissions (natural justice) (Pacific Recreation; JIO Minerals).
  • (viii) The Vita Food bona fides limit polices choices, not the OPL, so it cannot be used at Stage 3 (C&Y).
  • No ties (Lew): even a slight balance decides. As in Shanghai Turbo, there is at least a good arguable case for Singapore law.
  • Rome I analogy: the characteristic performer (whoever builds and operates the factory) is habitually resident in China, which points the same way unless there is a manifestly closer connection. This is usable only by analogy.

6C2.5 Promissory choice of law clause

Rule: Default, declaratory: per Ace Insurance, a choice of law clause is declaratory, as an inferred choice cannot contain a promise and party autonomy is fettered anyway; only very clear language makes it promissory, which "governed by the law of X" is not. When breached? Per C&Y, the promise's content is construed under the proper law; it is clearly breached by seising a court whose conflict rules ignore the clause, and arguably by seising one that superimposes its own overriding mandatory rules. Consequences: if promissory: damages, an ASI on the stronger breach basis (J6), and arguably a defence to recognition or enforcement of the foreign judgment (J7). Still separable: even if declaratory, the clause belongs to the dispute resolution suite alongside the jurisdiction clause, so it is separable (C2.2.3).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"Neither Party Shall Seek the Application of Any Other Law"
  • Version 1: an Australian insurance policy says "governed by the laws of New South Wales". The insured sues in California, whose courts might apply Californian law.
  • Version 2: the policy says "governed by NSW law; and each party promises not to commence proceedings in any forum that will not apply NSW law, and not to seek the application of any other law". The insured sues in California, whose courts will apply Californian consumer statutes as overriding mandatory rules.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Version 1: as in Ace Insurance, the clause is declaratory, so there is no promise to breach and no ASI, damages or recognition defence on that basis. (Indeed, in Ace, the Californian court would have applied the chosen law anyway.)
  • Version 2: very clear language makes the clause promissory. Construed under NSW law, it is clearly breached by suing in a forum whose conflict rules ignore it, and arguably by suing in one that superimposes its own overriding mandatory rules (C&Y). The insurer may claim damages, seek an ASI on the contractual basis (J6.3.1), and arguably resist recognition of any Californian judgment (J7.2.6).

7C2.6 Formation disputes: the putative proper law

Rule: Putative proper law: because the dispute concerns existence, per Lew v Nargolwala a law agreed during negotiations governs (rare), failing which a JIO-style three-stage test applied to the negotiations or transaction finds the putative proper law, matching The Parouth and CIMB. Double bootstrap (Prof Chong): the putative law first decides whether its own choice of law clause was incorporated, then whether the contract was formed. Counter, lex fori: per Lew, applying the lex fori regardless of any connection to the forum is "illogical" and defeats uniformity, so it has no role, even residually. Counter, hybrids: Lew also rejected Yeo's lex fori fallback where the entire contract is disputed, and Briggs's lex fori test, which treats the proper law as purely subjective. Grave-injustice caveat: where the putative law binds a party by silence, Lew left open "a very small caveat, very rarely applicable", whose effect is no contract under any law, not the lex fori; per C&Y, use forum public policy instead. Cf soft law: Art 10(2) Rome I and Art 6(2) Hague Principles let a party rely on the law of its habitual residence or establishment to deny consent. Battle of forms, clashing putative laws: A's law X clause and B's law Y clause may each validate themselves, and "it makes no sense to decide which one to choose by any putative law" (Dornoch). Lex fori: The Heidberg and Dornoch applied it, but Lew now bars that fallback. Putative OPL: per Prof Chong, rejected in The Heidberg as no more correct than arbitrarily preferring one clause. Yeo (deadlock overstated): map each law's first-shot, last-shot or knock-out rule; both clauses apply only where each validates itself; where neither survives, use the putative OPL, then the lex fori. Art 6(1)(b) Hague Principles: a clause applies only if its standard terms prevail under both laws, else there is no choice. Critique, lex fori in a subsidiary role: per Prof Chong (and Teo), the negotiations alone give too few factors, and non est factum or a voiding mistake favours one side, so the lex fori should decide agreement on the putative clause and break battle-of-forms ties. Consideration, formation or validity? Per C&Y, consideration goes to validity under the proper law (Re Bonacina), but AQCEL treated it as formation for the putative law, which matters only if the two laws differ. Distinguish material validity: a contract voidable for fraud, duress or misrepresentation was formed, so its proper law governs "as if the contract were valid" (CIMB), formation and validity being distinct (contrast PT First Media).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Silent Acceptance and the Battle of the Forms
  1. Silence: a Singapore trader (Lew) and an Indian supplier negotiate by email. The supplier's last email says: "This contract is governed by Utopian law. If you do not object within 3 days, the contract is concluded." Lew stays silent. Utopian law treats silence as acceptance; Singapore law does not.
  2. Battle of forms: the Singapore buyer's purchase order says "governed by Singapore law; our terms prevail". The German seller's acknowledgment says "governed by German law; our terms prevail". Under Singapore law (a last-shot rule), the seller's terms (sent last) prevail. Under German law (a knock-out rule), conflicting terms knock each other out.
  3. Consideration: a promise under a Utopian-law clause was made without consideration; Utopian law treats consideration as irrelevant.
  4. Fraud: the buyer says the contract was induced by the seller's fraudulent misrepresentation.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Putative proper law: since formation is disputed, apply the law the contract would have had if formed (Lew v Nargolwala). The clause's own law, Utopian law, decides first whether the clause was incorporated (double bootstrap, Chong) and then whether the contract was formed: silence is acceptance, so it was. The lex fori has no role, even residually (Lew), which rejects Yeo's and Briggs's lex fori approaches. Grave injustice: Lew left open a very small caveat for being bound by silence, whose effect would be no contract at all, not Singapore law. C&Y prefer using forum public policy. Cf Rome I art 10(2) and Hague Principles art 6(2): Lew could rely on the law of his habitual residence (Singapore) to deny consent, but that is soft law only.
  2. Battle of forms: each clause validates itself under its own law, and "it makes no sense to decide which one to choose by any putative law" (Dornoch). Lex fori fallback (The Heidberg; Dornoch) is now barred by Lew. Putative OPL was rejected in The Heidberg as arbitrary (Chong). Yeo: map each law, testing each clause under its own law. Under Singapore law (last shot), the German seller's terms win, so the Singapore clause fails under its own law. Under German law (knock-out), the clashing clauses cancel out, so the German clause fails under its own law too. Neither validates itself, so use the putative OPL, then the lex fori. Hague Principles art 6(1)(b): the German clause applies only if its terms prevail under both laws. They do not under German law (knock-out), so there would be no choice, and the OPL applies. Chong/Teo critique: the lex fori should break the tie in a subsidiary role.
  3. Consideration: per C&Y it goes to validity under the proper law (Re Bonacina), so Utopian law applies and the promise binds. AQCEL treated it as formation, but that only matters if the putative law and the proper law differ.
  4. A contract voidable for fraud was formed, so this is material validity, governed by the proper law "as if the contract were valid" (CIMB). Contrast PT First Media, which blurred formation and validity.

8C2.7 Formal validity

Rule: What counts as "form": per the Giuliano-Lagarde Report, "every external manifestation required" of one expressing the will to be bound. Alternative reference rule: per AQCEL (adopting PT Jaya Putra's obiter), meeting a formal requirement under either the proper law or the lex loci contractus suffices, parties rarely thinking about formalities. Not form: per PT Jaya Putra, a government approval requirement goes to validity under the proper law. Trap, form v capacity: per AQCEL, a missing witness under s 41B CA has "no relevance" to the will to be bound, so it is form; per Integral Petroleum, a joint prokurist's missing signature has "real substance", so it is capacity (C2.8.2). Locating the place of contracting: per Transniko, the lex fori places it where acceptance is received; Art 11(2) Rome I's wider list (either party's presence or residence) is not Singapore law. Trap, "no action shall be brought": per Leroux v Brown (and Star City's right v enforceability test), s 6 CLA (no "action" on a guarantee or land sale without signed writing) is procedural, binding a foreign-law contract here. Rebuttal: per C&Y, on a functional view (Goh Suan Hee), s 6 may be substantive form (cf the criticism in Monterosso), so the proper law or lex loci contractus governs. Distinguish: form has alternative validating laws; a procedural formality binds every Singapore action; a forum mandatory rule applies because the statute overrides. Immovables: the contract to sell land follows this section, but the conveyance's formalities follow the lex situs.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Unwitnessed Deed and the Missing Second Signature
  1. A Singapore company executed a deed with a Thai counterparty, signed by one director and not witnessed, in breach of s 41B Companies Act. The deed is governed by Thai law, which requires no witness. The contract was concluded by email: the Thai counterparty made the offer from Bangkok, and the Singapore company's acceptance was received there.
  2. A Swiss company's contract was signed by only one of two joint prokurists required under Swiss commercial law.
  3. An Indonesian-law contract requires Indonesian Investment Board approval, which was never obtained.
  4. A French-law oral guarantee of a Singapore subsidiary's debts.
  5. A Singapore-law contract to sell a Bangkok condominium, and the subsequent conveyance.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Form: a missing witness has no relevance to the will to be bound, so it is form (AQCEL). Under the alternative reference rule, it is valid if it complies with either the proper law (Thai: no witness needed) or the lex loci contractus. So it is valid under Thai law anyway. Place of contracting: acceptance was received in Bangkok (Transniko), so the lex loci contractus is also Thai. Rome I's wider list does not apply.
  2. Capacity, not form: a joint prokurist's missing signature has "real substance" (Integral Petroleum), so it goes to capacity (C2.8.2), with no alternative validation.
  3. Validity, not form: government approval goes to material validity under the proper law (PT Jaya Putra).
  4. s 6 CLA: "no action shall be brought" makes it procedural (Leroux v Brown; Star City), so it binds in Singapore despite French law, and the guarantee cannot be sued on. Rebuttal: on a functional view (Goh Suan Hee; C&Y; cf Monterosso), the writing rule is substantive form, so French law (as proper law) or the lex loci contractus could validate it.
  5. The contract to sell follows the form rules here (proper law or lex loci contractus). The conveyance's formalities follow the lex situs (Thai law).

9C2.8 Capacity

C2.8.1 Natural Persons

Rule: Options: per C&Y, the rule is unsettled among the lex domicilii (unfair to an unaware counterparty), the lex loci contractus (fortuitous, or unidentifiable online) and the proper law (the modern trend: Charron; Bodley Head). Preferred, objective proper law: per C&Y, because the stronger party may impose a law under which the vulnerable party has capacity, the objective proper law should govern. Alternative rules: domicile or place of contracting (Guatemala v Nunez), or domicile or OPL (Dicey; ALRC), would validate like form, but courts have not adopted them. Immovables, Bank of Africa v Cohen: the lex situs governed capacity to contract about land, but per C&Y it should govern only capacity to convey, so a damages claim under the English proper law survives.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The 19-Year-Old Day Trader

Ravi, 19, domiciled in Ruritania (where the age of majority is 21), opens a margin trading account online from a hotel in Bali with a Singapore broker. The broker's terms choose Singapore law (majority at 18 for contracts). The objective proper law, ignoring the clause, would be Singapore law (the broker's place of business and the place of performance). Ravi incurs losses and pleads minority.

  • Variation A: the broker's terms choose Utopian law, where the age of majority is 16, though the contract has no Utopian connection.
  • Variation B: Ravi, while 19, contracts under an English-law contract to buy a flat located in Ruritania. Ruritanian law (the lex situs) says he lacks capacity to deal with land until 21. The seller sues him for damages for non-completion.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The rule is unsettled (C&Y). The lex domicilii (Ruritania) would protect Ravi but is unfair to a broker unaware of his domicile. The lex loci contractus (Bali, where he clicked) is fortuitous and hard to identify online. The proper law is the modern trend (Charron; Bodley Head). On the C&Y-preferred objective proper law (Singapore), Ravi had capacity at 19, so he is bound.

  • Variation A: the subjective (chosen) proper law, Utopian law, would give Ravi capacity, but the stronger party imposed it. That is precisely why C&Y prefer the objective proper law (Singapore), under which he also has capacity, so the result is the same here but for a sounder reason. The alternative validation rules (Guatemala v Nunez: domicile or place of contracting; Dicey/ALRC: domicile or OPL) would also validate, but courts have not adopted them.
  • Variation B: per Bank of Africa v Cohen, the lex situs (Ruritania) governed capacity to contract about land. C&Y say it should govern only capacity to convey, so a damages claim under the English-law contract survives even if Ruritanian law denies capacity to convey.

C2.8.2 Corporations

Rule: Dual test: per C&Y (Dicey r 162), a corporation needs capacity under both the law of incorporation and the proper law; a subjective proper law is acceptable here, as companies are less exploitable. Broad meaning of capacity: per the Haugesund Kommune majority, capacity is the internationalist "legal ability to exercise specific rights", so a statutory bar on swaps removed the municipality's capacity for that contract, though Norwegian law lacks ultra vires. Rule classification: per Auld LJ in Macmillan, ask whether the foreign provision is truly a capacity rule or a mere limit on power. Consequences, the proper law: per Haugesund, once the law of incorporation denies capacity, the proper law (English law) decides the consequences, so the contract is void, but the lender recovers the sums advanced in unjust enrichment, change of position failing. Counter, Etherton LJ's dissent: "capacity" should bear its domestic ultra vires meaning, especially under a chosen English law, avoiding the "bizarre result" of swaps valid under English and Norwegian domestic law yet void. Response: per C&Y, prefer the majority, consistent with Macmillan and Raiffeisen. Singapore company: per ss 23, 25 and 25B CA, a Singapore company has full capacity subject to its constitution, and no act is invalid only for lack of capacity, protecting a good-faith counterparty.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Municipal Swaps and the Singapore Subsidiary
  1. A Norwegian municipality enters English-law interest rate swaps with a Singapore bank. A Norwegian statute forbids municipalities from entering "financial transactions involving speculative risk". Norwegian law has no ultra vires doctrine. The municipality refuses to pay, and the bank sues.
  2. A Singapore company enters a guarantee in breach of its constitution, which forbids guarantees, with a Hong Kong lender who did not know of the restriction.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Dual test: the municipality needs capacity under Norwegian law (incorporation) and English law (proper law). Characterisation: is the Norwegian bar a capacity rule? Per the Haugesund majority, capacity is broadly the "legal ability to exercise specific rights", so yes, even though Norway lacks ultra vires. Check the rule's classification (Auld LJ, Macmillan). Consequences: English law, as the proper law, decides the effect: the swaps are void, but the bank recovers the sums advanced in unjust enrichment, and change of position fails. Counter: Etherton LJ would give "capacity" its domestic ultra vires meaning, avoiding the "bizarre result" that swaps valid under both domestic laws are void. C&Y prefer the majority as consistent with Macmillan and Raiffeisen.
  2. Under ss 23, 25 and 25B CA, a Singapore company has full capacity subject to its constitution, and no act is invalid only for lack of capacity, so the good-faith Hong Kong lender is protected. (The proper law must also give capacity, but a subjective proper law is fine for companies, since they are less exploitable.)

10C2.9 Forum mandatory rules (overlay; full analysis in C1.7)

Rule: Contract triggers: s 27(2) UCTA (C2.2.7); a Singapore licensing statute (Skilling); s 5(2) CLA on foreign gambling contracts; but not the Misrepresentation Act unless Singapore law governs (JIO Minerals).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Quick Triage

A Hong Kong-law contract (i) contains an exclusion clause imposed on a Singapore consumer who contracted from Singapore; (ii) was performed by a firm unlicensed under a Singapore licensing statute; (iii) is a credit line for gambling at a Macau casino; (iv) was induced by a misrepresentation in Singapore, and the claimant seeks damages under s 2(1) MA.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(i) UCTA applies via s 27(2)(b). (ii) Unenforceable to the extent of the conflict (Skilling). (iii) s 5(2) CLA overrides. (iv) The MA does not apply, because Hong Kong law, not Singapore law, governs the contract (JIO Minerals). The claimant must rely on Hong Kong misrepresentation law or a tort claim.

11C2.10 Illegality

C2.10.1 Routing Starter

Rule: Illegality may be pleaded through (A) the proper law, (B) forum international public policy, (C) Foster, (D) Lemenda, (E) Ralli, (F) tainting, or (G) reliance as a defence.

  • Court's own motion: per Fan Ren Ray (approving Edler v Auerbach), the court may refuse an ex facie illegal contract though illegality is unpleaded, but extraneous evidence of an illegal object must be pleaded.
  • Route A, proper law: per Kahler and Zivnostenka, illegality under the proper law bars enforcement, unless that illegality rule itself offends Singapore public policy (The Playa Larga; Re Helbert Wagg).
  • Irrelevant laws: per Sim See Kee (and Kleinwort), illegality at the place of contracting, or a party's residence or incorporation, is irrelevant. Conversely, per Dimskal, legality at the lex loci solutionis (LLS) cannot save a contract illegal under the proper law, a forum mandatory rule or forum international policy.
  • Framework: per C&Y, breach of foreign written law intended at formation goes to Foster, and breach in required performance to Ralli, while foreign public policy alone goes to Lemenda. Per Magdeev, "Ralli looks to action, Foster … to intention". Foster: international policy and comity; wicked intention at formation; the real intended place; bars the guilty party. Ralli: per Esben, an independent conflicts rule on the required act at the contractual LLS, intention irrelevant. Lemenda: domestic policy coinciding with the LLS's policy, at the place of contemplated performance. Wrinkle: Esben calls comity a "fundamental domestic public policy", blurring Peh Teck Quee's split between Ralli (no public policy) and Foster (forum public policy).
  • Recognition, not enforcement: per OUB v Chua, a foreign penal or revenue law is recognised as fact in routes A, C and F, not enforced, unless so objectionable that breaking it is "meritorious" (Lord Reid in Regazzoni).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Whisky, the Commission, the Freight and the Loan

Five contracts, each governed by Singapore law unless stated:

  1. A contract governed by Thai law that is illegal under Thai law (an unregistered foreign business restriction), and Singapore's rules see nothing objectionable in the Thai rule.
  2. The same Thai illegality rule, but it is a racially discriminatory decree.
  3. A contract signed in Kuala Lumpur, by parties incorporated in Malaysia, that would be illegal under Malaysian law but is legal under the Singapore proper law; performance is in Singapore.
  4. A contract that is ex facie a sale of "human organs", where illegality was not pleaded.
  5. A contract to pay a broker for introducing buyers, where the claimant argues, without pleading it, that extraneous emails show an intention to bribe officials.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Route A: illegality under the proper law (Thai) bars enforcement (Kahler; Zivnostenka).
  2. Route A with exception: an illegality rule that itself offends Singapore public policy is disregarded (The Playa Larga; Re Helbert Wagg).
  3. Illegality at the place of contracting or incorporation is irrelevant (Sim See Kee; Kleinwort). The contract is enforceable.
  4. The court may refuse an ex facie illegal contract of its own motion (Fan Ren Ray; Edler v Auerbach).
  5. Extraneous evidence of an illegal object must be pleaded (Fan Ren Ray), so the court will not act on unpleaded emails.

C2.10.2 Route B: Repugnant to Forum International Public Policy

Rule: Extreme duress: per Royal Boskalis, an Iraqi-law finalisation agreement procured by a human-shield threat was refused, as "any civilised tribunal" would refuse it; per Westacre, so is a contract for terrorism, drug trafficking, corruption or fraud under any proper law. Threshold, higher order only: per Dimskal, economic duress is for the proper law, and per C&Y Kaufman v Gerson (threats to prosecute a relative) is now doubted as an example. Undue influence: Israel Discount Bank treated it as public policy, but per C&Y it is arguably only domestic (cf Dimskal), though a party may argue that fundamental fairness makes it international.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Kinds of Pressure
  1. A Swiss-law settlement was signed by a company's executives while they were held at gunpoint.
  2. A Greek-law freight renegotiation was signed after the shipowner threatened to stop the voyage (economic duress, lawful under Greek law).
  3. A French-law guarantee was signed by a daughter after her father threatened to report her husband to the police for tax fraud unless she signed.
  4. An Israeli-law guarantee was signed by an elderly mother under her son's undue influence.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Royal Boskalis: extreme duress offends forum international policy, so the contract is refused whatever Swiss law says.
  2. Dimskal: economic duress is for the proper law (Greek), which upholds it.
  3. Kaufman v Gerson (threats to prosecute a relative) is now doubted as an example of international public policy (C&Y), so French law likely governs.
  4. (±) Israel Discount Bank treated undue influence as public policy. C&Y say it is arguably only domestic policy (cf Dimskal), so Israeli law governs. The mother argues that fundamental fairness elevates it to international policy.

C2.10.3 Route C: Intention to Break the Law of a Friendly Foreign State (Foster v Driscoll)

Rule: Comity: per Foster v Driscoll and Regazzoni (in Singapore, Patriot v Lam Hong; Esben), a contract whose real object and intention is smuggling, breaching an export ban or evading foreign customs in a friendly country is unenforceable. Wicked intention is the crux: per Magdeev (and Waugh v Morris), intention at formation decides, even if the plan was never carried out or lawful performance was possible, so a later prohibition does not suffice. Beyond the paradigm (Chong): Foster usually bites on illegality at the outset but may also apply outside it (e.g., B's smuggling in performing the contract), the thrust being the guilty party's wicked intention, so the innocent party may still sue. Territorial, not the stipulated place: per Surewin, the prohibited act must be contemplated within the foreign country, though per Foster and Regazzoni not necessarily at the stipulated place. Any written law: per Patriot and Regazzoni, penal or revenue law counts, being recognised, not enforced, without taking sides against a third State (e.g., South Africa). Proper law irrelevant: per Ang v Lyu and Surewin, Foster is forum public policy, so it applies under a Singapore or third-country proper law alike. Dominant object: per Magdeev (and Haddad v Rostamani), the illegal object must be dominant or "central to the adventure". Unilateral intention: per Royal Boskalis, it bars only its holder, so the innocent party may sue (Ang v Lyu; Surewin), though not for an order compelling the illegal performance. Mental state: per Dimplex Gems, mere knowledge does not disqualify the claimant; active participation is needed (doubting Soetanto). Failing: as in Peh Teck Quee, Foster fails where repayment is sought in Singapore and there was no contemplated adventure to break Malaysian law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Jute Smugglers and the Unaware Supplier
  1. Regazzoni-style: A agrees to sell B jute "CIF Genoa". Both know the jute will actually be sent to South Africa, where Indian law (the country of origin) bans exports to South Africa. The plan is never carried out.
  2. Later prohibition: A and B contract to ship rice to Vietnam. After contracting, Vietnam bans rice imports. There was no intention at formation to break Vietnamese law.
  3. Unilateral intention: A Singapore seller sells cigarettes to a Thai buyer. Unknown to the seller, the buyer intends to smuggle them into Thailand without paying duty. The seller sues for the price. Variation: the seller knew of the plan but took no part. Variation: the seller helped hide the cigarettes in furniture.
  4. Dominant object: a Russian employee's employment contract includes, as a small fringe benefit, a housing allowance structured to avoid Russian tax.
  5. Proper law: a contract governed by English law, litigated in Singapore, whose real object is to smuggle gold into India.
  6. Peh Teck Quee: a Malaysian borrower borrows from a Singapore bank in breach of Malaysian exchange control. The bank sues for repayment in Singapore. There was no contemplated plan to break Malaysian law in Malaysia.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Foster / Regazzoni: the real object and intention at formation was to break the law of a friendly State (India's export ban), even though the stipulated place was Genoa and the plan was never carried out (Magdeev; Waugh v Morris). Unenforceable. Indian penal law is recognised, not enforced (Patriot; Regazzoni), and Singapore takes no side on South Africa.
  2. No wicked intention at formation, so Foster does not apply; a later prohibition does not suffice. Consider Ralli (C2.10.5).
  3. Unilateral intention bars only its holder, so the innocent seller may sue for the price (Royal Boskalis; Ang v Lyu; Surewin), though not for an order compelling illegal performance. Knowledge only: mere knowledge does not disqualify the seller (Dimplex Gems, doubting Soetanto). Active participation: helping hide the goods does, so the seller is barred. Per Chong, Foster can also bite on a party's smuggling in performance, outside the paradigm of illegality at the outset.
  4. The illegal element is not dominant or central to the adventure (Magdeev; Haddad v Rostamani), so Foster does not bar the employment contract.
  5. Foster is forum public policy, so it applies whatever the proper law, English or otherwise (Ang v Lyu; Surewin). The smuggling must be contemplated within India (Surewin).
  6. As in Peh Teck Quee, Foster fails: repayment is sought in Singapore, and there was no contemplated adventure to break Malaysian law (see also Ralli, C2.10.5).

C2.10.4 Route D: Contrary to the Public Policy of the Place of Performance (Lemenda)

Rule: Double policy breach: per Lemenda, a commission for influencing Qatari officials under an English-law contract is unenforceable if contrary to both a forum policy founded on general morality and the same policy at the place where the influence is to be exerted. Domestic tier: per Phillips J, buying influence offends only domestic forum policy (it bites if performed here), hence the LLS element; international policy would make the LLS or proper law immaterial. Foreign policy alone insufficient: per Shaikh Faisal, breaching a foreign country's policy does not bar a Singapore-law contract absent a similar Singapore policy, and a government purchasing directive is government policy, not public policy in law. Rationale (contrast Foster): per C&Y, foreign policy, unlike foreign law, is intangible, and applying it risks infringing foreign sovereignty. Debate, must the proper law also be offended? Per Waller LJ in Westacre, the contract is enforceable unless it offends the domestic policy of the proper law or curial law, so per C&Y Lemenda likely bites only where the lex fori is the proper law. Advising enforcement: if the proper law does not condemn the commission, per Westacre it is payable. Advising unenforceability: Lemenda rests on the general morality of the forum and the LLS, so breaching those two suffices. Prof Chong's query: does validity under the proper law trump the coincidence of forum and LLS policy? Lemenda as a taint? Per Prof Chong, whether a Lemenda breach meets the tainting threshold, or only a breach of forum fundamental policy does, is open.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Influence Peddler
  1. A Singapore-law consultancy agreement pays a consultant a "success fee" for using his personal connections with officials of the Ruritanian Ministry of Defence to win a contract. Ruritania's public policy (not a statute) condemns buying influence; so does Singapore's general morality.
  2. The same, but governed by Utopian law, which (as proved) does not condemn such commissions, and the action is in Singapore.
  3. A Singapore-law contract breaches a Ruritanian government purchasing directive (an internal ministry guideline) requiring local partners.
  4. A Singapore-law contract offends Ruritanian public policy against foreign consultants, but Singapore has no similar policy.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Lemenda: contrary to both forum domestic policy (general morality against buying influence) and the same policy at the place where the influence is exerted (Ruritania), so unenforceable. It is only the domestic tier (it would bite if performed in Singapore), which is why the LLS's policy must coincide (Phillips J).
  2. (±) Advising enforcement: per Waller LJ in Westacre, the contract is enforceable unless it offends the domestic policy of the proper law (Utopian), which does not condemn it; per C&Y, Lemenda likely bites only where the lex fori is the proper law. Advising unenforceability: Lemenda rests on the general morality of the forum and the LLS, both of which condemn it. Chong's query: does validity under the proper law trump the coincidence of forum and LLS policy?
  3. A government purchasing directive is government policy, not public policy in law (Shaikh Faisal), so no bar.
  4. Foreign policy alone, without a similar Singapore policy, does not bar a Singapore-law contract (Shaikh Faisal). Rationale: foreign policy is intangible, and applying it risks infringing foreign sovereignty (C&Y), unlike foreign law (Foster).
  • Tainting: whether a Lemenda breach in (1) could taint a related claim is open (Chong; C2.10.6).

C2.10.5 Route E: Performance Illegal at the Place of Performance (Ralli Brothers)

Rule: Illegal performance: per Ralli Brothers, a contract (e.g., freight above the decreed rate in Barcelona, or delivery into a country after its ban) is unenforceable in so far as performance is unlawful at the contractual place of performance, whatever the proper law. Basis, three readings (results differ, so run them): per C&Y (and Day), Ralli is (1) an independent conflicts rule, (2) frustration under the proper law, or (3) comity-based abstention. (1) Independent rule (start here): per Esben, Dicey's rule rooted in comity, catching supervening and initial illegality alike; per Prof Chong arguably preferable as the later, more unequivocal SGCA ruling. (2) Frustration (alternative): Peh Teck Quee leaned to it, declining Ralli where the ban pre-dated the contract, so ask whether the proper law frustrates or permits delivery elsewhere. (3) Comity abstention: supported by dicta (Toprak; Magdeev), but per Peh Teck Quee, Ralli has "nothing to do with" public policy, unlike Foster. When it matters: per Ryder Industries, only where the proper law is not the lex fori, since Singapore domestic law frustrates the contract anyway. Haze twist (Chong): if Indonesia bans gas exports, reading (1) refuses enforcement against the Indonesian supplier, an odd result for the Singapore buyer, whereas under (2) the proper law decides whether the contract is frustrated. Place of performance, loans: per Peh Teck Quee, where the facility agreement fixes no place and permits repayment anywhere, s 8 ECA cannot make repayment demanded in Singapore illegal; Ralli bites only "in so far as" performance is unlawful. Essence only: per Magdeev, the illegal component (e.g., a sham UAE employment) must go to the essence, not be a "fringe benefit" to the loan; if it is central, severance fails. Preparatory steps excluded: per Kleinwort v Ungarische and Toprak, obtaining central bank consent or opening a letter of credit are steps to get into a position to perform, so they do not count, unlike the payment itself. Gap scenario: per Peh Teck Quee (no merger of Ralli and Foster), later illegality at a non-contractual place without illegal intention engages neither rule. Counter, critique of Esben: per C&Y, it lets the LLS intrude on the proper law's substantive obligations, leaves the consequences (whole contract or part) unclear, and makes the friendly-State requirement uncertain.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Indonesian Gas Ban (Chong's Haze Twist)

A Singapore power company (buyer) contracts with an Indonesian gas supplier for LNG delivered FOB at an Indonesian port. The contract is governed by English law.

  1. Supervening ban: after contracting, Indonesia bans LNG exports. The buyer sues the supplier for non-delivery.
  2. Initial ban: the ban already existed when the contract was signed, but both parties hoped for an exemption.
  3. Preparatory steps: the buyer must open a letter of credit and obtain Singapore central bank consent; the consent is refused.
  4. Loan variant: a Malaysian borrower's Singapore-law facility with a Singapore bank fixes no place of repayment and permits repayment anywhere; Malaysian exchange control (s 8 ECA) forbids repayment from Malaysia. The bank demands repayment in Singapore.
  5. Non-contractual place: delivery is due in Singapore, but the supplier routes the cargo through Vietnam, which later bans transit; there was no illegal intention.
  6. Fringe benefit: a Russian-law loan includes, as a minor perk, a sham UAE "employment" for the borrower's son to obtain a visa.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. (±) Reading (1), the independent rule (Esben): performance at the contractual place (the Indonesian port) is now illegal there, so the contract is unenforceable in so far as it requires performance there. That is an odd result for the Singapore buyer, who cannot sue for non-delivery (Chong's haze twist). Reading (2), frustration (Peh Teck Quee): English law, as the proper law, decides whether the ban frustrates the contract or whether delivery elsewhere is permitted. Reading (3), comity abstention (Toprak; Magdeev dicta), though Peh Teck Quee said Ralli has "nothing to do with" public policy. When it matters: only because English law, not Singapore law, is the proper law (Ryder Industries). Under Singapore domestic law, the contract would be frustrated anyway.
  2. Initial illegality: reading (1) (Esben) catches it; Peh Teck Quee declined Ralli where the ban pre-dated the contract, under the frustration reading. Chong prefers Esben as the later, unequivocal SGCA ruling.
  3. Opening a letter of credit and obtaining central bank consent are preparatory steps, not performance, so they do not engage Ralli (Kleinwort v Ungarische; Toprak). The actual payment would.
  4. As in Peh Teck Quee, no place of repayment is fixed and repayment anywhere is permitted, so repayment demanded in Singapore is not illegal. Ralli bites only "in so far as" performance is unlawful.
  5. Gap: later illegality at a non-contractual place (Vietnam) without wicked intention engages neither Ralli nor Foster (Peh Teck Quee: no merger of the two).
  6. The illegal component is a fringe benefit, not the essence, so Ralli does not bar the loan, and the perk may be severed (Magdeev).
  • Critique of Esben (C&Y): the independent rule lets the law of the place of performance intrude on the proper law's obligations, leaves the consequences (whole contract or part) unclear, and makes the friendly-State requirement uncertain.

C2.10.6 Route F: Tainting by Foreign Illegality

Rule: Starter: a party argues that contract 1, or an illegal act, taints the claim on contract 2, asking per Euro-Diam (1) is there a relevant foreign illegality, and (2) is it sufficiently connected to the claim? Where it arises: an illegal manner of performance not contractually required (Howard v Shirlstar), omitting a needed licence (Skilling), or a related illegal transaction (Euro-Diam). Singapore status: per Teng Wen-Chung, Euro-Diam cannot be accepted "unqualified", as Bowmakers reliance must be re-examined under Ochroid, and Beresford's public conscience test is not Singapore law. Theoretical basis: tainting operates via (a) the proper law (Forsyth, cited in Teng) or (b) forum international public policy, which decides Step 2. Strategy: resisting contract 1 invites tainting of contract 2, so consider conceding the smaller claim.

  • Step 1 (a lex fori conflicts question): act or transaction: Anuva excluded illegal acts, but per C&Y a transaction is made of acts (cf Howard v Shirlstar), so per Surewin ask whether the act breached foreign law, or whether Singapore would enforce contract 1. Sufficiently serious: per Ryder Industries, not every breach counts; a breach of forum international policy, a forum mandatory rule or an LLS prohibition qualifies, per Magdeev after a balancing exercise, while a Lemenda breach is unclear. Insufficient, administrative or minor: as in Ryder Industries (duty-free materials used without customs approval) and Re O'Connor (an unqualified interstate solicitor).
  • Step 2, sufficient connection: which law's principles? Unresolved, as Teng, Baker v BCS and Surewin all involved Singapore-law contracts; per Prof Chong, if tainting is part of the lex fori, Singapore's principles decide, and if part of the proper law, that law's do. Which proper law: per Chong, that of contract 2 (the claim sued on), not contract 1. Submission (C&Y; Forsyth): apply the proper law's principles unless the lex fori's rise to overriding mandatory rules or international policy, though this raises an incidental question about the related transaction's legality. If Singapore principles apply, proportionality: per Ting Siew May (applied in Surewin), refusing a contract entered into to commit an illegal act must be proportionate, weighing (a) the prohibiting rule's purpose, (b) gravity, (c) remoteness or centrality, (d) object, intent and conduct, and (e) the consequences of denial. Non-contractual claims: per Ochroid, ask whether recovery in unjust enrichment stultifies the policy, reliance being normative. Surewin application: refusing the pledge was disproportionate, as the bank was unaware, and the purpose factor "cannot apply unmodified" to foreign illegality. Caution: per Ryder Industries, the forum poorly gauges the foreign country's view of gravity, so per C&Y apply the domestic framework judiciously; if tainting runs through the lex fori, proportionality would arguably also govern Foster.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Diamond Insurance and the Gold Pledge
  1. Euro-Diam-style: a Singapore jeweller insures diamonds (Singapore-law insurance, contract 2) sent to a German buyer.
