LAW302 · HYPO LESSON C3 · 26 HYPOTHETICALS · 8 QUESTIONS

C3 hypotheticals: Tort choice of law: double actionability and the flexible exception

The rules behind these hypotheticals are taught in Lesson C3, where the word-for-word pre-write is too. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

Applications:
ℹ HOW TO USE THESE HYPOTHETICALS

Each concept is set out as Rule, then Hypothetical, then Application. "Variation" lines flip one fact. Methodology and proof of foreign law are in C1; contract in C2.

The hypo test at the end checks you can run the facts yourself.

1C3.0 Roadmap in one hypothetical

Rule (order): (1) Characterise the claim as tortious; the claimant may frame freely absent bad faith (Rickshaw). (2) General rule: double actionability, with the claimant proving the lex fori limb and the defendant the lex loci delicti limb (Boys v Chaplin; Rickshaw; EFT Holdings). (3) Locate the tort by substance (Distillers; JIO Minerals; Vibrant Group), checking s 101 OSRAA / s 6(4) THPA and local torts. (4) Foreign law unpleaded or unproved: Singapore law by default, or the presumption. (5) Flexible exception: strict and fortuity-based (Rickshaw), including party autonomy. (6) Particular torts, and contract as a tort defence (Sayers / Galaxias). (7) Overlays: damages, limitation, renvoi; evaluation; other obligations.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Batam Ferry Collision

A Singapore-registered ferry carrying Singapore day-trippers collides, in Indonesian waters off Batam, with an Indonesian fishing boat. Mr Tan, a Singapore passenger, is injured and sues the ferry operator (Singapore) and the fishing boat's Indonesian owner in Singapore for negligence. Indonesian law (assume) (i) caps general damages; (ii) has a 1-year limitation period; (iii) gives a complete defence where the victim failed to wear a life jacket. Mr Tan sues 14 months later.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Limb 1: had all the acts occurred in Singapore, negligence would be made out (duty, breach, causation, damage) (IM Skaugen counterfactual).
  • Limb 2: the tort is in substance committed in Indonesia (a single locality: the collision and injury both occurred there). The defendants must plead and prove that Indonesian law imposes no liability (EFT Holdings). If they do not, Singapore law applies by default (C3.5).
  • Defence: a defence under either law defeats the claim (C&Y), so the Indonesian life-jacket defence, if proved, is fatal unless displaced.
  • Flexible exception: Mr Tan argues that Indonesia is fortuitous for a Singapore ferry carrying Singapore passengers on a Singapore day trip (cf Boys v Chaplin, Malta). Against him: the place of a collision is rarely fortuitous (C&Y), and the exception is strictly applied (Rickshaw). As against the Indonesian fisherman, Indonesia is anything but fortuitous.
  • Limitation: s 3(2) FLPA applies the Indonesian period (1 year), so the claim is barred unless the exception selects Singapore law alone, or s 4(2) undue hardship applies.
  • Damages: heads are substantive; quantum is traditionally procedural (Singapore figures), though Goh Suan Hee doubts this (C3.9.1).

2C3.1 The governing rule

Rule: Per Rickshaw, the rule is double actionability subject to a flexible exception (Boys v Chaplin; Red Sea).

  • Two limbs: per Lord Wilberforce in Boys v Chaplin (adopted in Rickshaw), the wrong must (a) be a tort under Singapore law and (b) give civil liability between the actual parties under the lex loci delicti. Not necessarily tortious: per Ong Ghee Soon, any civil liability under the foreign law suffices (e.g., a civil-law delict, or statutory liability). Defences: per C&Y, a defence under either law defeats the claim.
  • Common denominator: absent displacement, the claimant recovers only what both laws allow (Yeo), as in McElroy v McAllister, where the widow got only funeral expenses.
  • How many leges causae? Per C&Y, the rule names no single law: two generally; one if the exception displaces the lex fori (Red Sea) or the lex loci delicti (Boys v Chaplin); a third law if both go.
  • Burden of proof: per EFT Holdings, the claimant proves limb (a), while the defendant must plead and prove non-actionability under the foreign law, limb (b) existing for the defendant's benefit. Dominance: per C&Y, this burden model and the default rule make the lex fori the dominant limb. Reversal: where the claimant invokes the exception to apply foreign law (Red Sea), the claimant must plead and prove it.
  • Characterisation: per C&Y, "tort" is not bound by domestic categories, though a domestic tort normally qualifies, and some equitable wrongs may count (Rickshaw), e.g., dishonest assistance (Grupo Torras). Foreign law may inform it: where the claimant relies solely on foreign law for a liability unknown here, the foreign law's characterisation matters (Red Sea).
  • Framing / concurrent liability: per Rickshaw, absent bad faith, the claimant may frame in tort despite a foreign choice of law clause. Contrast: equitable claims rooted in the contract follow contract choice of law, and a "parasitic" tort may follow the contract's law.
  • Rationale (evaluative): limb (b) spares a defendant not liable where it acted (EFT) and serves comity, though per Metall comity weakens where damage is caused to persons here. Limb (a), from The Halley, is "parochial" (C&Y).
  • Development (evaluative): Phillips v Eyre's "not justifiable" limb, abused in Machado v Fontes (criminal liability sufficing), became civil liability in Boys v Chaplin, the proper law of the tort being rejected (Red Sea), so a claimant cannot plead the most connected law directly.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Scottish Bus Crash (McElroy-style) and Its Variations

A Singapore resident, Mrs Lee, is killed in a bus crash in Ruritania caused by a Ruritanian driver. Her widower sues in Singapore.

  1. Singapore law gives dependency damages and funeral expenses. Ruritanian law (proved) gives only funeral expenses.
  2. Ruritanian law imposes liability under its civil code ("delictual responsibility"), not under a law of "torts".
  3. Ruritanian law makes the driver criminally liable but imposes no civil liability.
  4. The driver does not plead Ruritanian law at all.
  5. The widower wants to rely on Ruritanian law alone, which (unlike Singapore law) gives a direct claim against the driver's insurer.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Common denominator: absent displacement, the widower recovers only what both laws allow, i.e. funeral expenses, as in McElroy v McAllister. He must argue the exception (C3.6) to escape the Ruritanian limit.
  2. Any civil liability under Ruritanian law satisfies limb (b), whether or not it is called "tort" (Ong Ghee Soon).
  3. Criminal liability is not enough. That was the Machado v Fontes abuse of Phillips v Eyre's "not justifiable" limb, which Boys v Chaplin corrected to civil liability. Limb (b) fails.
  4. The driver bears the burden of pleading and proving non-actionability under Ruritanian law (EFT Holdings). Without that, Singapore law applies by default (C3.5). This makes the lex fori the dominant limb (C&Y).
  5. The widower must plead and prove Ruritanian law and invoke the exception to displace the lex fori (Red Sea). The court characterises the direct claim with regard to Ruritanian law, since he relies on it alone (Red Sea). He cannot simply plead "the proper law of the tort" (rejected in Red Sea and Boys).
  • Evaluation: limb (b) protects the defendant who was not liable where he acted (EFT), and serves comity, but per Metall comity weighs less where the harm was done to Singapore people. Limb (a), from The Halley, is parochial (C&Y). Two laws, one, or even a third may govern, depending on the exception.

3C3.2 Limb 1: actionable as a tort under the lex fori

Rule: Counterfactual test: per IM Skaugen, ask whether the acts, if all done in Singapore, would be a tort (e.g., a Spandeck duty, breach, causation, damage). Domestic bar (−): if Singapore law denies the head, supplies a complete defence, or does not allow the direct claim (Red Sea), the claimant must displace the lex fori. Statutory torts: OSRAA Parts 10–12 and s 6 THPA supply limb 1 by statute, but per JIO Minerals the Misrepresentation Act reaches a misrepresentation abroad only under a Singapore-law contract.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Would It Be a Tort Here?
  1. A Hong Kong engineer negligently certifies a crane in Hong Kong; it collapses in Shenzhen, injuring a Singapore worker.
  2. A Singapore investor sues an Indonesian adviser for "loss of chance" in a form that Singapore law does not recognise.
  3. A Japanese newspaper publishes in Japan a true but embarrassing story about a Singapore businessman; Japanese law recognises a privacy tort, Singapore law does not.
  4. A Singapore company sues an Indonesian plantation for haze damage in Singapore under s 6 THPA.
  5. A claimant relies on s 2(1) Misrepresentation Act for a misrepresentation made in Jakarta under a UAE-law contract.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Counterfactually, if the certification and the collapse had happened in Singapore, would there be negligence (a Spandeck duty, breach, causation, damage)? Very likely, so limb 1 is satisfied (IM Skaugen).
  2. If Singapore law denies the head, limb 1 fails, and the claimant must displace the lex fori under the exception (Red Sea).
  3. There is no privacy tort in Singapore, so limb 1 fails unless the claimant displaces the lex fori (Red Sea), which is hard because the Singapore connection is real.
  4. The statute supplies limb 1 (s 6 THPA), and s 6(4) also abrogates limb 2 (C3.3.4).
  5. The MA is not available (JIO Minerals), because the contract is not governed by Singapore law. Limb 1 must be met by a common law tort (deceit, negligent misstatement).

4C3.3 Limb 2: locating the tort

C3.3.1 The Substance Test

Rule: Per Distillers and Metall, look back over the events and ask where in substance the cause of action arose, finding one single place on the elements as recognised by the lex fori (C&Y). As pleaded: per Vibrant Group, the weight of act, reliance and damage depends on the tort pleaded, so reliance counts more for misrepresentation than for negligence. Single locality (+): all elements occur in one country (e.g., the place of a motor accident). Multiple locality (−): act and damage span countries, so apply the tort-specific rules. Damage not determinative: per Distillers, the place of damage "may be quite fortuitous". Policy favouring the forum (+): per Metall, the court need not "turn a blind eye" to damage caused to persons here by acts abroad. Civil, not necessarily tortious, liability: per Ong Ghee Soon, negligent misstatement was actionable under Art 41 SCO even though Swiss law has no "law of negligence" category. Same test for jurisdiction: per Metall (citing Armagas), the same locus test serves the tort gateway. Whether double actionability applies at service out is open: yes per IM Skaugen (HC), no per Nippon Catalyst, left open in Shen Sophie (J3). Divergence: the gateway needs only an act partly here, or damage here (Yeo), so it may be met even though the tort is located abroad. FNC: per JIO, the place of the tort is prima facie the natural forum unless fortuitous.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Johor Factory and the Singapore Office

A Malaysian contractor negligently installed fire sprinklers at a factory in Johor owned by a Singapore company. A fire destroyed the factory. The Singapore company's head office in Singapore suffered consequential losses (lost contracts, management time). The company sues in Singapore and serves the contractor in Malaysia under gateway (f)(ii) (damage in Singapore).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Substance test: looking back over the events, the cause of action arose in Malaysia, where the negligent installation and the physical damage occurred (Distillers; Metall). The consequential financial loss in Singapore does not relocate the tort, because the place of damage "may be quite fortuitous" (Distillers), especially for a company whose losses flow back to head office. Gateway (±): gateway (f)(ii) and choice of law can diverge (Yeo), but (f)(ii) needs damage in Singapore, not merely its effects (IM Skaugen (CA); J3). The head office's lost contracts and management time flow from the physical damage in Johor, so they are likely effects, and (f)(ii) likely fails. FNC: the place of the tort is prima facie the natural forum (JIO), so Malaysia is favoured on a stay or set-aside. At the gateway: whether the company must also show double actionability is open (IM Skaugen (HC) yes; Nippon Catalyst no; Shen Sophie left it open).

  • Metall twist: if the contractor's acts abroad had been directed at causing damage to Singapore persons, the court need not "turn a blind eye", and the substance may be in Singapore.
  • Civil liability: if Malaysian law imposed liability only under a building-safety statute rather than in negligence, that civil liability would still satisfy limb 2 (Ong Ghee Soon).

C3.3.2 Tort-Specific Rules for Multi-Locality Torts

Rule:

  • Negligence, focus on the act: per Vibrant Group, the place of the negligent act prevails, so an audit or advice performed abroad locates the tort there despite reliance and loss in Singapore. Negligent services/advice: where the services were or ought to have been rendered (Voth). Trading decisions: where the decision to speculate was made (e.g., Moscow) (Base Metal Trading). Product liability: where the product was marketed without the warning, not where it was made or where damage occurred (Distillers; Castree v Squibb). Reliance weighs less: in negligence, reliance is only one route to a duty (NTUC Foodfare; Vibrant).
  • Misrepresentation directed at the claimant (receipt + reliance): per JIO Minerals (tentatively, citing Yeo) and Ong Ghee Soon, a representation directed at the claimant and received and acted on in Singapore is a tort there, unless that place is fortuitous. Where reliance crystallises: where the claimant gave instructions via the Singapore branch, not where administrative execution occurred in Geneva (Ong Ghee Soon). Fortuitous receipt: receipt in India merely because the claimant is based there is fortuitous (JIO). Receipt and reliance split: the specific rule fails, so use the substance test, as in JIO, where negotiations and drilling made Indonesia the place. Several countries of making, receipt and reliance: where the core representations were made (e.g., Germany) may prevail, receipt being fortuitous for global operators (IM Skaugen v MAN Diesel). Receipt unclear on the pleadings: unevidenced receipt in Germany is "speculative", so Singapore law applies (Rickshaw).
  • Representation made at large: per Cordova Land (and JIO), a statement to the world at large is a tort where it is made, unlike one directed at the claimant (The Albaforth).
  • Inducing breach of contract: per Metall, the tort is where the contract was broken and the claimant injured (e.g., London), not where the inducement occurred (New York).
  • Conspiracy: per EFT Holdings, weigh the conspirators' identity and location, where they combined, the concerted acts, the claimant's location and where losses arose, as in EFT, where Taiwan prevailed. Parasitic conspiracy: one "so intimately connected" to a contract may follow its law without being located (Chen v BHNV).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Eight Cross-Border Torts
  1. Audit: a Hong Kong auditor negligently audits a Singapore-listed company's Hong Kong subsidiary, in Hong Kong. Singapore investors rely on the audited accounts and lose money in Singapore.
  2. Advice: a Sydney adviser should have rendered tax advice in Singapore (where the client's operations were) but did it from Sydney.
  3. Trading: a metals trader's employee in Moscow decides to speculate recklessly; the losses are booked in London.
  4. Product: a drug made in Germany is marketed in Singapore without a warning; the patient suffers injury in Malaysia.
  5. Directed misrepresentation: a Swiss banker phones a Singapore client in Singapore, and the client instructs the bank's Singapore branch to buy the recommended notes, while execution is done administratively in Geneva.
  6. Fortuitous receipt: an Indonesian seller emails a misrepresentation to a buyer's CEO, who happens to be based in India; the negotiations and the coal drilling are all in Indonesia.
  7. Global operator: a German engine maker's core misrepresentations about fuel consumption are made at its German HQ, received by a Norwegian shipowner's offices in Singapore, Norway and Korea, and relied on in Norway.
  8. At large: a Kenyan company issues a press release in Nairobi containing a false statement about a Singapore competitor.
  9. Inducement: a New York hedge fund induces, from New York, a London broker to break its contract with a Singapore fund; the breach occurs in London, and the Singapore fund is injured there.
  10. Conspiracy: Taiwanese directors combine in Taiwan to strip assets from a Singapore company, using concerted acts mostly in Taiwan; the losses arise in Singapore and Taiwan.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Negligence, focus on the act: the audit in Hong Kong locates the tort there, despite reliance and loss in Singapore (Vibrant Group). In negligence, reliance is only one route to a duty (NTUC Foodfare).
  2. The services ought to have been rendered in Singapore, so the tort is in Singapore (Voth).
  3. Where the decision to speculate was made: Moscow (Base Metal Trading).
  4. Where the product was marketed without the warning: Singapore, not Germany (manufacture) or Malaysia (damage) (Distillers; Castree v Squibb).
  5. Directed at the client, and received and relied on in Singapore. Reliance crystallised when the client instructed the Singapore branch, not at the Geneva execution (Ong Ghee Soon), so the tort is in Singapore.
  6. Receipt in India is fortuitous (the CEO merely happens to be based there), and receipt and reliance split. So use the substance test: negotiations and drilling make Indonesia the place (JIO Minerals).
  7. Receipt is fortuitous for a global operator, and the representations were made in Germany, so Germany may prevail (IM Skaugen v MAN Diesel). If the pleadings did not show where receipt occurred, a place of receipt would be "speculative" (Rickshaw).
  8. A statement to the world at large is a tort where it is made: Nairobi (Cordova Land; JIO). Contrast The Albaforth (a statement directed at the claimant).
  9. Where the contract was broken and the claimant injured: London, not New York (Metall).
  10. Weigh the conspirators' identity and location, where they combined, the concerted acts, the claimant's location and the losses: Taiwan prevails, as in EFT Holdings. If the conspiracy were "so intimately connected" with a contract governed by, say, Belize law, it might follow that contract's law without being located (Chen v BHNV; C3.6.5).

C3.3.3 Applying Limb 2

Rule: Limb 2 is satisfied if the foreign law gives some civil remedy for the conduct. It fails where the foreign law bars the head, provides a defence, or imposes no liability between these parties (Lord Wilberforce, Boys v Chaplin). Time bar: the foreign law's shorter period bars the claim via s 3(2) FLPA, as Georgian law did in Ivanishvili.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Tbilisi Investment

A Singapore investor sues a Georgian bank officer in Singapore for negligent misstatement made in Tbilisi. Georgian law (i) gives civil liability for negligent misstatement only against the bank, not the individual officer; (ii) has a 3-year limitation period, which has expired.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(i) There is no liability between these parties (investor and officer) under Georgian law, so limb 2 fails for the claim against the officer (Boys v Chaplin, Lord Wilberforce). The investor must displace Georgian law under the exception (C3.6.3), or sue the bank. (ii) In any event, s 3(2) FLPA applies the Georgian limitation period, which bars the claim, as Georgian law did in Ivanishvili.

C3.3.4 Statutory Deeming: Online Harms and Haze

Rule (OSRAA s 101, tort deemed in Singapore): a Part 10, 11 or 12 tort is treated as in Singapore if any element was (a) initiated in or from Singapore, (b) perceived here, or (c) caused damage here. Effect (Yeo): s 101 replaces the substance test with a statutory connecting factor, so both limbs point to Singapore law, giving the OSRAA torts the character of overriding mandatory rules. Jurisdiction (Yeo): it secures nexus and a factual presumption that Singapore is forum conveniens, leaving FNC to sieve out opportunistic foreign claims. Exception: the defendant may argue for foreign law where Singapore is so fortuitous that serious injustice results, but only exceptionally, given Parliament's intent to protect Singapore residents (Yeo). No s 101 connection (rare): the substance test applies, the tort is likely abroad, and the claimant recovers only the common denominator of the OSRAA and the foreign law (Yeo). Unilateral reading: s 101 may be a unilateral rule with no exception, but Yeo prefers the multilateral reading, as the wording only redefines the connecting factor. Critique (Yeo): if the foreign law protects the victim better, s 101 still imposes the lower OSRAA standard. Rule (OSRAA s 102, no contracting out): exclusion, jurisdiction or arbitration terms inconsistent with Parts 11 or 12 (Administrators, Platforms) are void unless fair and reasonable; Part 10 (Communicators) is not covered. Choice of law clause: a foreign choice of law clause cannot exclude OSRAA liability, party autonomy being unrecognised in tort (Yeo). Rule (THPA s 6(4), limb 2 abrogated): conduct in or outside Singapore causing haze is actionable "whether or not" actionable abroad. Standing: per s 6(3), a person suffering personal injury, property damage or economic loss in Singapore may sue, still proving the statutory tort under Singapore law. Nature: an express statutory displacement of limb 2 for haze claims, not a use of the flexible exception; per Chong, an overriding forum mandatory rule, so the THPA claim lies even though Indonesian law imposes no liability. Common law claim: per Chong, the substance test likely locates the tort in Indonesia (where the burning occurred), so if Indonesian law permits smallholder burning, limb 2 fails for a negligence or nuisance claim unless displaced.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Doxxing Post and the Haze
  1. Doxxing: a user in Thailand posts a Singapore teacher's home address with a call to harass her. The post is viewed in Singapore. The platform (incorporated in the US) has terms choosing California law and excluding liability, with a California arbitration clause.
  2. Fortuitous viewing: a dispute between two Australians about a doxxing post made and read in Australia, but also viewed once by a friend in Singapore.
  3. Foreign law more protective: a French victim of a harassing post (also perceived in Singapore) finds French law gives higher damages than the OSRAA.
  4. Haze: an Indonesian plantation company burns land in Riau. Smoke damages a Singapore resident's health and closes a Singapore restaurant for a week. Indonesian law permits controlled burning by smallholders and imposes no liability.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. s 101: an element was perceived here, and the harm was caused here, so the tort is deemed committed in Singapore, and both limbs point to Singapore law, which operates like an overriding mandatory rule (Yeo). s 102: the platform's exclusion and arbitration terms are inconsistent with Part 12 (Platforms) duties, so they are void unless fair and reasonable. The California choice of law clause cannot exclude OSRAA liability, because party autonomy is not recognised in tort (Yeo; C3.6.5). (If the defendant were only a Part 10 Communicator, s 102 would not apply.) Jurisdiction: s 101 also secures nexus and a factual presumption of forum conveniens.
  2. (±) On the multilateral reading (Yeo's preference), the defendant can argue that Singapore is so fortuitous (one view by a friend) that applying Singapore law would cause serious injustice, so Australian law applies, though only exceptionally. On the unilateral reading, s 101 has no exception. FNC would also sieve out this opportunistic claim.
  3. Critique (Yeo): s 101 still imposes the OSRAA standard even though French law protects the victim better. If there were no s 101 connection (rare), the substance test would apply, the tort would likely be in France, and the victim would recover only the common denominator of the OSRAA and French law.
  4. THPA claim: s 6(4) makes the haze conduct actionable "whether or not" actionable in Indonesia, an express statutory displacement of limb 2 (not the flexible exception). Per Chong, it is an overriding forum mandatory rule. The resident and the restaurant suffered personal injury and economic loss in Singapore, so they have standing (s 6(3)), and they still prove the statutory tort under Singapore law. Common law claim: the substance test likely locates the tort in Indonesia (where the burning occurred) (Chong). If Indonesian law permits smallholder burning, limb 2 fails for negligence or nuisance unless displaced under the exception (C3.6.3).

5C3.4 Local torts (tort committed in Singapore)

Rule: Double actionability applies to local torts: per Rickshaw, rejecting Metall's English-law-only rule as "unduly parochial" and contrary to comity, a conversion or negligence in Singapore still runs both limbs, both pointing to Singapore law. Point of difference: the exception may apply foreign law where the Singapore locus is purely fortuitous, with no stricter test, though "a liberal approach must be eschewed". Why England differs: per Yeo (cited in Rickshaw), before Red Sea the lex fori could not be displaced, so a lex fori rule for local torts made sense. Displacing Singapore law (−): Briggs's Changi transit-lounge brawl between Australians flying home. Rickshaw facts (+): the CA kept Singapore law because most connecting factors were here and the German-contract defence was "vague and unclear"; no evidence was adduced on deceit, and the German clause was conceded non-exclusive, so it did not reach the torts. Briggs's critique: the torts arose from an employment relationship under a German-law clause and were pleaded in tort to avoid German law, so the exception should have applied the contract's proper law. C&Y: fortuity should be only one ground; a test based on the significance of the connections, including the contract, gives more room, as English courts applying the contract's law show (Trafigura).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Changi Brawl and the German Employee
  1. Brawl: two Australian rugby fans, flying home from London via Changi, get into a fight in the transit lounge. One sues the other in Singapore for battery. Australian law gives a defence of consent to "sporting-style scuffles"; Singapore law does not.
  2. Rickshaw-style: Klaus, employed under a German-law contract by a German company, worked in Singapore for its Singapore subsidiary and allegedly misappropriated confidential information in Singapore. The company sues him in Singapore for conversion and breach of confidence. Klaus argues that German law, the contract's law, should govern because the contract says "German law applies to this agreement", but he gives no particulars of what German law says.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. A local tort (battery in Singapore) still runs double actionability, both limbs pointing to Singapore law (Rickshaw, rejecting Metall's lex fori-only rule). But the exception can displace Singapore law where the locus is purely fortuitous. A transit-lounge fight between two Australians flying home is Briggs's classic example, so Australian law (with its consent defence) applies. "A liberal approach must be eschewed", though, and the defendant must prove Australian law.
  2. As in Rickshaw: most connecting factors are in Singapore (the work, the acts, the subsidiary), and Klaus's German-law defence is "vague and unclear" (no particulars, no evidence). The clause was (as in Rickshaw) at most non-exclusive and did not clearly reach torts, so Singapore law applies. Briggs's critique: the claims arise out of the German employment contract and were pleaded in tort to avoid German law, so the exception should have applied the contract's law. C&Y: make fortuity one ground among others and test the significance of connections, including the contract (cf Trafigura).

6C3.5 Proof of foreign law and the presumption of similarity

Rule: Not pleaded: per EFT Holdings (applying Goh Chok Tong v Tang Liang Hong), pleading foreign law is voluntary, so if the defendant does not plead it, no conflicts issue arises and Singapore law applies without the presumption. C&Y framing: the same result is put as a presumption that foreign law equals Singapore law. Pleaded but not proved: unproved foreign law is presumed similar where fair (Brownlie), though the party bearing the burden may simply fail (EFT). Limits: FNC: the court may accept that a civil-law system probably differs without proof (Rickshaw, citing PT Jaya Putra; JIO). Intrusive relief abroad: no injunction against conduct abroad on a bare presumption (OMG Holdings), explained by the relief sought (EFT). Damages: the presumption presumably applies (C&Y). Cf Brownlie (UK): the default rule governs unpleaded law and the presumption pleaded-but-unproved law, supporting the EFT split.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Taiwanese Conspiracy Revisited

In the Taiwanese asset-stripping conspiracy (C3.3.2, item 10), the tort is located in Taiwan.

  1. The directors do not plead Taiwanese law.
  2. They plead that Taiwanese law has no tort of unlawful-means conspiracy, but adduce no evidence.
  3. At an earlier stay application, they argued only that "Taiwanese civil law probably differs".
  4. The Singapore company seeks an injunction restraining the directors from dealing with assets in Taiwan, relying on the presumption that Taiwanese law is the same as Singapore's.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. No conflicts issue arises, so Singapore law applies (EFT Holdings; Goh Chok Tong). C&Y describe this as a presumption of similarity. Brownlie calls it the default rule.
  2. Pleaded but unproved: the presumption may apply if fair (Brownlie). Taiwan is a civil-law system, so it is less apt, and the directors, who bear the burden on limb 2, may simply fail to make out non-actionability (EFT).
  3. At the FNC stage, the court may accept that a civil-law system probably differs without proof (Rickshaw, citing PT Jaya Putra; JIO).
  4. No injunction against foreign conduct on a bare presumption (OMG Holdings, as explained in EFT). Damages or an account should still be available on the presumption (C&Y), so the company should limit the relief it seeks.

7C3.6 The flexible exception

C3.6.1 Starter and Threshold

Rule: Per Rickshaw, the exception (Boys v Chaplin; Red Sea) may displace the lex fori, the lex loci delicti, or both, in favour of the law with the most significant relationship to the issue and the parties. Threshold: courts "must not be quick" to apply it unless the displaced law is purely fortuitous and applying it causes injustice, on "clear and satisfying grounds" (Lord Wilberforce), lest it become a proper law of the tort. Strictly applied: it is "imperative" that the exception be strictly applied, favouring certainty over flexibility. Fortuity and injustice, conjunctive? Unclear, but per C&Y applying a fortuitous law is the injustice, so fortuity is the real test. Stricter than Red Sea and Ang Ming Chuang (weighing contacts) and Lord Wilberforce's interest analysis. Critique (C&Y): fortuity is too restrictive and should be one way of showing an insignificant connection. Two techniques in Boys: Lord Hodson weighed contacts ("centre of gravity"); Lord Wilberforce ran an issue-specific interest analysis; Rickshaw adds fortuity. Factors: per Restatement §145 (quoted in Red Sea): the place of injury, the place of conduct, the parties' residence or incorporation, and where the relationship is centred. Burden on the invoking party: it must prove the connecting factors and the foreign law (Red Sea); a "vague and unclear" defence fails (Rickshaw).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Better Law Is Not Enough

A Singapore company sues a Singapore competitor for passing off in Singapore. The claimant points out that Ruritanian law gives far higher damages and asks the court to apply Ruritanian law under the exception "because it does better justice", since the competitor's parent is Ruritanian.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The exception requires the displaced law (Singapore) to be purely fortuitous, on clear and satisfying grounds (Rickshaw; Lord Wilberforce), and it must be strictly applied. Singapore is the centre of everything here (the parties, the conduct, the goodwill), so it is not remotely fortuitous. A more favourable foreign law is no reason to displace. The claimant bears the burden of proving both the connecting factors and Ruritanian law (Red Sea). Even on C&Y's broader "insignificant connection" approach, or Lord Hodson's centre-of-gravity test, the Restatement §145 factors all point to Singapore.

C3.6.2 Displacing the Lex Fori (Red Sea)

Rule: Exclusive lex loci delicti: per Red Sea, a claimant may rely solely on the foreign law even though the claim is unknown to the lex fori, as the insurer's direct claim was under Saudi law (Hong Kong required payment first). Whole claim: one law may govern the whole claim where "all or virtually all" factors point to it, as the Saudi contracts, works, damage and head office were "overwhelming", avoiding fragmentation (C&Y). Rickshaw test applied (+): per C&Y, Red Sea would likely survive Rickshaw, Hong Kong's only link being incorporation, so a bare Singapore incorporation may be fortuitous. Counter-factor: that the forum applies foreign law where its own gives no remedy is a factor, not a bar (Red Sea); fortuity decides under Rickshaw. Not only for deprived claimants: per Ang Ming Chuang (obiter), the law "must be just to defendants as well as plaintiffs", so Taiwanese law would have governed SIA's claim against the CAA, and a defendant may likewise invoke the foreign law. Fortuity required (−): foreign law cannot apply merely because it is more favourable where the relationship is Singapore-centred.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Saudi Hospital Construction

A Singapore-incorporated special-purpose company (SPV), whose only Singapore link is incorporation, built a hospital in Riyadh under Saudi-law contracts with a Saudi head contractor. Defects caused damage in Riyadh. The SPV's insurer, having not yet paid, wants to sue the head contractor directly in Singapore. Saudi law allows an insurer to sue before paying; Singapore law requires payment first (subrogation).

  • Variation: the defendant, a Taiwanese air traffic controller sued in Singapore over a crash in Taiwan, wants to rely on Taiwanese law (more favourable to it) rather than Singapore law.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Like Red Sea, the insurer relies solely on Saudi law, even though its direct claim is unknown to Singapore law. To do so, it must displace the lex fori: Singapore's only link is the SPV's incorporation, which is purely fortuitous, and per C&Y Red Sea would survive Rickshaw's stricter test on these facts. Because "all or virtually all" factors (contracts, works, damage, head contractor) point to Saudi Arabia, Saudi law can govern the whole claim, avoiding fragmentation. That Singapore law gives no remedy is a factor, not a bar; fortuity decides. The insurer must plead and prove Saudi law (the burden is reversed: Red Sea).

  • In the variation, the exception is not only for deprived claimants: the law "must be just to defendants as well as plaintiffs" (Ang Ming Chuang, obiter, where Taiwanese law would have governed SIA's claim against the CAA). So a defendant may invoke Taiwanese law too, if Singapore is fortuitous.

C3.6.3 Displacing the Lex Loci Delicti (Boys v Chaplin)

Rule: Issue-specific interest analysis: in Boys v Chaplin, British servicemen collided in Malta; per Lord Wilberforce, Malta had no interest in applying its special-damages-only rule to non-residents, so the foreign damages restriction yielded for parties connected with the forum. Rickshaw caveat (−): per C&Y, a road accident's place is rarely fortuitous, and soldiers stationed in Malta are less transient than transit passengers. Issue by issue: displacement may cover heads of damage only (Boys), or the whole claim where virtually all factors align (Red Sea).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Singapore Army Exercise in Brunei

Two Singapore soldiers on a three-month training exercise in Brunei are in a jeep collision; one sues the other in Singapore. Bruneian law (assume) allows only special damages (medical costs); Singapore law also allows general damages for pain and suffering.

  • Variation: the defendant is a Bruneian civilian driver.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Following Lord Wilberforce in Boys v Chaplin: Brunei has no real interest in applying its special-damages-only rule to two Singapore soldiers, so its restriction on heads of damage is displaced, and Singapore law governs that issue. Displacement can be issue-specific (heads only), with Bruneian law still governing other issues. (−) Rickshaw caveat: the place of a road accident is rarely fortuitous, and soldiers stationed in Brunei for three months are less transient than transit passengers (C&Y). Under Rickshaw's strict fortuity test the argument is harder than it was in Boys.

  • In the variation, Brunei is plainly not fortuitous as against a Bruneian driver, so Bruneian law applies.

C3.6.4 Applying the Law of a Third Country

Rule: Per Rickshaw (Red Sea "paves the way") and IM Skaugen, where the forum and the place of the tort are both purely fortuitous, a third law governs (e.g., two residents of country Z fighting in a transit lounge in country Y). Rare: it will rarely succeed, and the third law's limitation period then applies.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two New Zealanders in Dubai

Two New Zealand residents, transiting through Dubai airport on their way home from Europe, get into a fight in the transit lounge. One later visits Singapore and is served here.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Singapore (the forum) and the UAE (the place of the tort) are both purely fortuitous. As Rickshaw contemplates (with Red Sea "paving the way"), and IM Skaugen confirms, the exception may apply a third law, New Zealand law. It will rarely succeed (C&Y), and if it does, New Zealand's limitation period applies under the FLPA. (Realistically, FNC would send the case to New Zealand anyway.)

C3.6.5 Party Autonomy: Can the Contract's Law Govern the Tort?

Rule: The argument: a clause covering "all relations" or "any dispute arising out of or in connection with" applies its law to the tort, an open question (Ong Ghee Soon), though "just a small step away" (C&Y). Support: per The Rainbow Joy, the employment contract's law "should prevail" over the law of the flag for a tort on the high seas, and Rickshaw recognises an "exclusive" clause. Ong Ghee Soon (obiter) cited Yeo's hub argument, reforms abroad, Art 14 Rome II and Art 9(1)(g) Hague Principles (non-binding; pre-contractual obligations). Rainbow Joy limit: it may be confined to its facts (Ong Ghee Soon). Why allow it: per C&Y, modern tort law allocates risk (insurance, exemption clauses), narrowing the gap with contract, and autonomy brings certainty and supports Singapore's hub policy (Yeo). Exclusive v non-exclusive: per Rickshaw, whether a clause covers non-contractual claims is construction under its proper law, and the clause there was conceded non-exclusive. Ong Ghee Soon decided nothing: cl 7.29 was wide enough for torts under Swiss law, but the bank officer, a non-party, could not take its benefit absent a stipulation pour autrui (Art 112 SCO). Foreign restrictions: Art 132 Swiss PILA (post-event choice only) bites only if Swiss law includes its PIL, a renvoi question; Art 120 PILA consumer status was left aside, the claimant not being a consumer (Ong Ghee Soon). Rome II Art 14 model: a choice is valid (a) after the event, or (b) before it if all parties are pursuing a commercial activity and it is freely negotiated, with reasonable certainty, no prejudice to third parties, and no ouster of the mandatory rules of a wholly connected country. Qualifications if recognised: per C&Y, the choice must be bona fide, legal and consistent with public policy, and yields to forum mandatory rules (e.g., s 102 OSRAA). Pre- v post-tort: pre-tort choices risk weak parties contracting unwittingly, but per C&Y there should be no blanket ban, since employees and consumers are protected by targeted mandatory rules. Freely negotiated? Businesspeople routinely accept boilerplate choice of law terms, so query whether a standard form should disqualify, or whether PIL should police bargaining power at all. Route through the exception (C&Y): the chosen or proper law applies via the flexible exception as the law of the centred relationship, as in Chen v BHNV (a conspiracy "so intimately connected" to the Belize-law contract), Oro Negro and Trafigura. Caution: Chen was an FNC ruling that did not run Rickshaw's fortuity test, and Trafigura applied s 12 PIL(MP)A, so they are analogies only. Obstacle: Rickshaw's fortuity threshold and the non-exclusive concession blocked it. Application (+): where the platform or mandate was the conduit, the proper law displaces both limbs. Also an FNC factor: a choice of law clause covering torts points to that law at Spiliada stage 1 (Rainbow Joy; Rickshaw). Statutory override: a clause cannot oust Part 11 or 12 OSRAA liability; s 102 voids it unless fair and reasonable.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Swiss Private Bank Mandate

Mr Ong, a Singapore businessman (not a consumer), signed a Swiss private bank's account mandate. Clause 7.29: "All relations between the client and the Bank, and any dispute arising out of or in connection with them, are governed by Swiss law." A Singapore-based relationship manager (an employee of the bank, not a party to the mandate) made negligent misstatements to Mr Ong in Singapore, on which he relied there. Mr Ong sues (a) the bank and (b) the relationship manager in tort in Singapore. The bank and the manager both say Swiss law governs the tort under cl 7.29, under which the claim is time-barred.

  • Variation A: Mr Ong and the bank agreed on Swiss law after the misstatements, in a settlement negotiation.
  • Variation B: the claim is under OSRAA Part 12 against the bank's online platform.
  • Variation C: a separate conspiracy claim against the bank's affiliates arises out of the mandate, which was the conduit for the scheme.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Open question: whether a contractual choice of law can govern a tort is unresolved in Singapore (Ong Ghee Soon), but "just a small step away" (C&Y). For: The Rainbow Joy (the employment contract's law prevailed over the flag's for a tort at sea), Rickshaw's recognition of an "exclusive" clause, Yeo's hub argument, Rome II art 14 and Hague Principles art 9(1)(g), and C&Y's point that modern tort law allocates risk, with autonomy bringing certainty. Against: Rainbow Joy may be confined to its facts (Ong Ghee Soon), and Rickshaw's fortuity threshold remains.
  • Construction: whether cl 7.29 covers torts is a question of Swiss law (Rickshaw). It is wide ("all relations ... in connection with"), as in Ong Ghee Soon.
  • (b) The manager: even if the clause covers torts, the manager is a non-party, and cannot take its benefit absent a stipulation pour autrui under Art 112 SCO (Ong Ghee Soon). So double actionability applies to the claim against him: the tort is in Singapore (receipt and reliance), so Singapore law governs.
  • Swiss PILA restrictions: Art 132 (post-event choices only) bites only if "Swiss law" includes Swiss PIL, which is a renvoi question (C3.9.3), and renvoi should be rejected. Art 120 (consumers) does not apply, since Mr Ong is not a consumer.
  • If recognised, qualifications: the choice must be bona fide, legal and consistent with public policy, and it yields to forum mandatory rules (C&Y). On the Rome II art 14 model, a pre-tort choice binds only if all parties pursue a commercial activity and it is freely negotiated. A bank's standard-form mandate may fail "freely negotiated", though C&Y query whether boilerplate should disqualify, and argue against any blanket ban on pre-tort choices.
  • Route through the exception (C&Y): argue that Swiss law applies as the law of the relationship in which the tort is centred (cf Chen v BHNV; Oro Negro; Trafigura), but these are analogies only, and Rickshaw's strict fortuity test is a real obstacle when the tort happened in Singapore.
  • FNC: a choice of law clause covering torts points to Swiss law at Spiliada stage 1 (Rainbow Joy; Rickshaw).
  • Variation A: a post-event choice is the least controversial form of autonomy (Rome II art 14(1)(a)).
  • Variation B: s 102 OSRAA voids any term excluding Part 12 liability unless fair and reasonable, and a foreign choice of law cannot oust it (C3.3.4).
  • Variation C: the mandate was the conduit for the conspiracy, so the claim is "so intimately connected" with the contract that its (Swiss) law may displace both limbs (Chen v BHNV, by analogy).

C3.6.6 Public Policy Is Not a Ground for the Exception

Rule: In Kuwait Airways, the majority excised the Iraqi confiscatory resolution from the lex loci delicti via the exception, but Lord Scott (dissenting) said the exception is for applying the most connected law, not disapplying parts of it. Better route: Lord Steyn refused the resolution on public policy within the rule itself (C&Y), so the offending rule is excised under C1.8. Singapore position: after Rickshaw, the exception cannot do this, Iraq not being fortuitous; so the court asks whether the foreign law, without the offending rule, imposes liability.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Confiscated Aircraft

During an occupation, Ruritania's government issued a decree "transferring" a Singapore airline's aircraft at Ruritanian airports to the Ruritanian national carrier, which then used them. The Singapore airline sues the Ruritanian carrier in Singapore for conversion. Under Ruritanian law, as modified by the decree, the carrier owns the aircraft and there is no tort.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Kuwait Airways: the majority used the exception to excise the decree, but Lord Scott objected that the exception is for applying the most connected law, not for disapplying parts of it. After Rickshaw, the exception requires fortuity, and Ruritania (where the aircraft were seized and used) is not fortuitous, so it cannot be used this way. Better route: Lord Steyn's public policy approach. The confiscatory decree offends Singapore's fundamental public policy and is disregarded (C1.8). Then ask: does Ruritanian law, without the decree, impose liability for conversion? If so, limb 2 is satisfied, and the airline succeeds.

8C3.7 Particular torts

C3.7.1 Defamation

Rule: Place of publication: per Low Tuck Kwong, double actionability applies, and the tort is where the statement is published, each publication being a separate tort, so Singapore publications are local torts and the defendant must plead foreign law for foreign publications. FNC filter: the place of publication is prima facie the natural forum (C&Y). Internet publication: per Dow Jones v Gutnick and Singapore cases (Qingdao Bohai), publication is where the material is downloaded and accessed. Gutnick: the publisher's server-law rule (New Jersey) was rejected; the majority relied on practical limits, and Kirby J's global-publication rule was left to legislatures. Contrast UK: s 8 Defamation Act 2013 adopts a single publication rule. Policy choice (Mills): the law of upload favours free speech ("race to the top"), and the law of download favours reputation ("race to the bottom"), so the choice is policy, not rationality. Chan's tiered rule (habitual residence, place of reputational damage, publication) is complex and unlikely to be adopted (C&Y). Practice: few such claims reach Singapore, given the O 8 / PD para 63 nexus requirements and little reputational damage here. OSRAA: s 101 reaches only Part 10–12 harms (e.g., harassment or doxxing) (Yeo), so common law defamation stays under double actionability. Reform carve-out: the SAL LRC 2003 would keep double actionability for personal defamation (the lex fori limb filtering foreign law incompatible with Singapore's free speech values) and move business defamation to the lex loci delicti.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Indonesian Coal Magnate's Article

An article posted on a US news website (servers in New Jersey) accuses an Indonesian coal magnate of bribery. It is downloaded 5,000 times in Indonesia, 300 times in Singapore and 50 times in Hong Kong. The magnate sues the publisher in Singapore for all publications.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Per Low Tuck Kwong, double actionability applies, and each publication is a separate tort. For internet material, publication is where it is downloaded and accessed (Dow Jones v Gutnick; Qingdao Bohai), not where it was uploaded. Gutnick rejected the New Jersey server-law rule, and Kirby J's global-publication rule was left to legislatures. Singapore downloads (300): a local tort (C3.4), with both limbs pointing to Singapore law. Indonesian and Hong Kong downloads: foreign torts, for which the publisher must plead and prove Indonesian or Hong Kong law (C3.5), failing which Singapore law applies. FNC: the place of publication is prima facie the natural forum, so the Indonesian claims point to Indonesia (C&Y). Jurisdiction: the magnate must show nexus (gateway (f)) and forum; few such claims get through, given the little reputational damage in Singapore. OSRAA: s 101 does not reach common law defamation (only Part 10–12 harms), so it does not help unless there is a parallel OSRAA tort. Policy: Mills's point is that choosing the law of upload versus download is a policy choice between free speech and reputation. The UK's single publication rule (s 8 Defamation Act 2013) contrasts with the multiple-publication approach here, and Chan's tiered rule is unlikely to be adopted. Reform: under the SAL LRC 2003 proposal, personal defamation would keep double actionability (to filter foreign law incompatible with Singapore's free speech values), whereas business defamation would go to the lex loci delicti.

C3.7.2 Intellectual Property and Passing Off

Rule: Territoriality: per C&Y, statutory copyright, patent and trade mark rights are territorial: conduct abroad cannot infringe a Singapore right, nor conduct here a foreign right. Validity separate: validity follows the law of the place of creation, and the Singapore court may lack jurisdiction where infringement turns on foreign validity. Scenarios (forum Singapore; no conventions): (i) Singapore right infringed abroad: fails both limbs, and the lex fori is not fortuitous for a Singapore right. (ii) Foreign right infringed here: fails both limbs, Singapore as locus not being fortuitous for the infringing acts. (iii) Foreign right infringed there: a Malaysian copyright infringed in Malaysia may succeed via the exception displacing a fortuitous lex fori, if Singapore has jurisdiction (cf Pearce v Ove Arup). Passing off: a common law tort, so territoriality is no bar, but per OMG Holdings an injunction against passing off in Malaysia needs Malaysian law proved.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Copied Architectural Plans

A Singapore architect's designs are protected by Singapore copyright, and also by Malaysian copyright.

  1. A Malaysian developer copies the designs and builds in Kuala Lumpur. The architect sues in Singapore for infringement of her Singapore copyright.
  2. A Singapore developer copies a Thai architect's designs (protected by Thai copyright only) and builds in Singapore. The Thai architect sues in Singapore.
  3. The architect sues the Malaysian developer (who has a Singapore office, so jurisdiction exists) in Singapore for infringement of her Malaysian copyright in Malaysia.
  4. A Malaysian café chain uses the name of a famous Singapore café and trades in Johor; the Singapore café sues in Singapore for passing off and seeks an injunction covering Johor, without proving Malaysian law.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. (i) Singapore copyright is territorial and cannot be infringed by acts in Malaysia, so the claim fails both limbs. Singapore law is not fortuitous for a Singapore right, so the exception cannot help.
  2. (ii) A Thai right cannot be infringed in Singapore, so the claim fails both limbs. Singapore as locus is not fortuitous for acts done here.
  3. (iii) A Malaysian right infringed in Malaysia: the lex loci (Malaysia) gives liability, but the lex fori (Singapore) does not, since Singapore copyright is not infringed. The exception may displace the fortuitous lex fori (Pearce v Ove Arup, by analogy), so Malaysian law governs, provided Singapore has jurisdiction and the case does not turn on the validity of the Malaysian right, which may be beyond the Singapore court's jurisdiction (C&Y).
  4. Passing off is a common law tort, so territoriality is no bar, but an injunction covering Johor requires proof of Malaysian law; the presumption of similarity is not enough (OMG Holdings).

C3.7.3 Misrepresentation and Conspiracy

Rule: See C3.3.2 for the locus. Statutory misrepresentation: per JIO Minerals, the MA applies only if Singapore law governs the issue, and to a misrepresentation abroad only if the contract is governed by Singapore law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The UAE-Law Mining Contract

A Singapore investor was induced by misrepresentations made in Jakarta to sign a UAE-law contract to buy Indonesian mining concessions. It sues in Singapore in deceit and under s 2(1) MA.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Deceit: locate the tort. Receipt and reliance were split, and the negotiations and drilling were in Indonesia, so the tort is in Indonesia (JIO Minerals; C3.3.2). MA s 2(1): it reaches a misrepresentation abroad only if the contract is governed by Singapore law. Here it is governed by UAE law, so the MA does not apply (JIO Minerals; C1.7).

9C3.8 Interaction between contract and tort

C3.8.1 Contract Relied On to Negate the Tort

Rule: Two questions (C&Y, North): (i) the effect of the contract on tort liability is a tort question for double actionability; (ii) its validity is a contract question for its proper law. Galaxias: the trespass was an English tort, so English law held that a contractual right to remain negates trespass, but Greek law (the proper law) showed the crew were lawfully discharged, so the claim succeeded. In Singapore: a local tort itself runs double actionability, and for a tort abroad with a contract governed by another law, (i) follows the lex fori and the lex loci delicti, and (ii) the contract's proper law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Crew Who Would Not Leave

A Greek-law employment contract gives Filipino crew a right to remain on board a vessel until paid. The vessel is in Singapore. The owner purports to discharge them, and they stay on board. The owner sues them in Singapore for trespass. They say the contract gives them a right to remain.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Ask two questions (North; C&Y). (i) Effect: does a contractual right to remain negate trespass? That is a tort question. The tort is local, so double actionability points to Singapore law on both limbs, and Singapore law treats a contractual licence as a defence. (ii) Validity: were the crew lawfully discharged, i.e. did their contractual right end? That is a contract question for the proper law (Greek law). As in Galaxias, if Greek law says they were lawfully discharged, the defence fails and the trespass claim succeeds.

C3.8.2 Contractual Exemption or Limitation Clause as a Defence to Tort

Rule: The problem: a clause valid under its proper law excludes negligence liability that Singapore law bars or subjects to reasonableness (s 2(1) / s 2(2) UCTA). Sayers: an English worker injured on a Nigerian rig was limited by his Dutch employer's cl 8 compensation scheme, void under s 1(3) Law Reform (Personal Injuries) Act 1948 but valid in Dutch law. Majority (Salmon and Stamp LJJ), contractual characterisation: only the proper law of the contract mattered, and since it was Dutch, "this action is dead" (Salmon LJ). Critique (C&Y): treating the issue as wholly contractual is simplistic, ignoring question (i). Lord Denning, proper law of the issue: "we cannot apply two systems of law", so he applied the law closest to the issues, Dutch ("Nigeria is out"), cl 8 "turn[ing] the scale" against English law. Critique (C&Y): he never asked what effect the clause has on tort liability (North). Do not mix up the judgments: Salmon LJ found the contract Dutch, whereas Lord Denning found it English and reached Dutch law via the tort. Preferred approach (Kahn-Freund; North; cf Brodin v A/R Seljan): (1) admissibility is a tort question for double actionability, and (2) validity a contract question for the proper law, so the clause succeeds only if admissible under both Singapore law and the lex loci delicti. Incidental question: the forum's choice of law rules (simple, but they invite forum shopping) or the tort law's (Harris: coherent, avoiding "the law of no one state") pick the contract's law. Which to choose: per C&Y, it may track Singapore's views on renvoi and party autonomy in tort. Pre-existing contract: the exception may apply the contract's law to both questions, though Rickshaw declined to do so for the employment contract. OSRAA overlay: s 102 voids the clause as an admissibility rule (Yeo), or as a procedural or mandatory rule even on the Sayers view. Non-party reliance: a co-employee cannot invoke the clause unless the proper law allows it (Ong Ghee Soon).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Offshore Rig in Brunei (Sayers-style)

A Singapore engineer, employed by a Dutch company under a Dutch-law contract, is injured on an oil rig off Brunei by the company's negligence. Clause 8 limits the employer's liability for personal injury to a fixed compensation scheme. Under Dutch law cl 8 is valid. Under Singapore law, s 2(1) UCTA makes it void (death or personal injury from negligence). Under Bruneian law (the lex loci delicti), cl 8 is (assume) valid. The engineer sues the employer in tort in Singapore. A co-worker who caused the accident also tries to rely on cl 8.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the three approaches (Pathway C):

  • Sayers majority (Salmon and Stamp LJJ): the issue is contractual, so only the proper law matters. Dutch law validates cl 8, so "this action is dead". Critique (C&Y): simplistic; it ignores the separate question of what effect a contractual exclusion has on a tort claim.
  • Lord Denning: apply the law closest to the issue. Brunei is "out" (fortuitous, as Nigeria was), and the Dutch employment relationship "turns the scale", so Dutch law applies and cl 8 is valid. Critique (C&Y; North): he never asked about the clause's effect on tort liability. Don't mix up the judgments: in Sayers, Salmon LJ found the contract Dutch, whereas Lord Denning found it English and reached Dutch law via the tort.
  • Preferred (Kahn-Freund; North; cf Brodin v A/R Seljan): (1) admissibility of a contractual defence is a tort question, so the clause must be admissible under both Singapore law and Bruneian law. Singapore law (s 2(1) UCTA) forbids it, so it fails. (2) Validity is a contract question for Dutch law (valid), but it does not matter, because admissibility fails. Incidental question: which choice of law rules identify the contract's law (the forum's, simple but inviting forum shopping; or the tort law's, Harris's coherent "law of one state" view)? This tracks Singapore's views on renvoi and autonomy (C&Y). Pre-existing contract: the employer could argue under the exception that Dutch law governs both questions (C3.6.5), but Rickshaw declined to do that for an employment contract.
  • Co-worker: a non-party can rely on cl 8 only if Dutch law (the proper law) allows it (Ong Ghee Soon: no stipulation pour autrui, no benefit).
  • OSRAA variant: if the claim were a Part 11/12 OSRAA tort, s 102 would void the clause unless fair and reasonable, as an admissibility rule (Yeo), or as a mandatory rule even on the Sayers view.

10C3.9 Miscellaneous overlays

C3.9.1 Damages

Rule: Traditional: per Boys v Chaplin and Harding v Wealands, heads (pain and suffering) are substantive, so the head must exist under both laws, but quantum is procedural, so Singapore law assesses it. Remoteness and mitigation: substantive (C&Y), so double actionability governs. Goh Suan Hee critique: the split is "wholly artificial" (cf Pfeiffer v Rogerson; Art 15(c) Rome II), so if quantum is substantive, the claimant recovers only the lower figure (e.g., the foreign cap). Status: open; the lex loci delicti's rules of law on assessment would apply, but pure questions of fact stay with the forum, and the award gap was a neutral FNC factor.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Batam Ferry Damages (from C3.0)

Mr Tan (Batam ferry) claims (i) pain and suffering (recognised in both laws); (ii) "loss of a holiday" (recognised in Singapore, unknown in Indonesia); (iii) losses from a cancelled business deal (Indonesian law: too remote; Singapore law: recoverable). Indonesian law caps general damages at a level below Singapore awards.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

(i) The head exists in both laws, so it is recoverable. Quantum is traditionally procedural, so Singapore scales apply. On Goh Suan Hee (obiter), the split is wholly artificial; if quantum is substantive, the Indonesian cap applies as a rule of law, while the forum still decides the facts of Mr Tan's loss. Open. (ii) The head must exist under both laws, so it is not recoverable, absent displacement of Indonesian law. (iii) Remoteness is substantive and governed by double actionability, so a defence under either law (Indonesian: too remote) defeats it (C&Y).

C3.9.2 Limitation

Rule: Per s 3(1) and s 3(2) FLPA 2012, the lex loci delicti's domestic limitation period alone applies, renvoi being excluded (ss 3(5), 6(2)), subject to s 4(2) undue hardship. No double hurdle: unlike s 1(2) UK FLPA 1984 (Metall); and where both limbs point to Singapore law or foreign law is unpleaded, the Limitation Act applies. Tactical consequence: locating the tort in Singapore avoids the foreign shorter period. After the exception: the single lex causae's period applies: the foreign law's if the lex fori goes (Red Sea), the Limitation Act if the lex loci delicti goes (Boys), and the third law's for a third law.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Three Limitation Outcomes

A tort claim is brought after 2 years. The lex loci delicti (Ruritania) has a 1-year period; Singapore's is 6 years (3 for personal injury).

  1. The tort is in Ruritania, and both limbs apply.
  2. The defendant does not plead Ruritanian law.
  3. The exception displaces Ruritanian law (as in Boys).
  4. The exception displaces Singapore law (as in Red Sea).
  5. The claimant argues the tort was really committed in Singapore.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. s 3(2) applies the Ruritanian 1-year period, so the claim is barred, with no cumulation of Singapore's period (unlike UK FLPA s 1(2): Metall). The claimant may plead s 4(2) undue hardship.
  2. Foreign law is unpleaded, so Singapore law applies on both limbs, and the Limitation Act applies.
  3. The single lex causae is Singapore law, so the Limitation Act applies and the claim survives.
  4. The single lex causae is Ruritanian law, so the 1-year period applies and the claim is barred.
  5. Tactically, locating the tort in Singapore avoids the Ruritanian period (C3.3).

C3.9.3 Renvoi (one sentence suffices)

Rule: Per Credit Suisse Life v Ivanishvili (PC), renvoi has never applied in obligations, so the foreign law means its domestic law, applying its limitation period and excluding Art 132 Swiss PILA (raised in Ong Ghee Soon). Statutory parallels: s 9(5) PIL(MP)A and Art 24 Rome II exclude it, as ss 3(5), 6(2) FLPA do for limitation in Singapore. Singapore status: formally open in tort (C&Y; Ong Ghee Soon said nothing about tort), so treat Ivanishvili as persuasive. Reasons: complexity, circularity, subordination of forum policy, and FNC already controls forum shopping. Contrast Australia: Neilson applied Chinese conflict rules to avoid forum-dependent outcomes, a workaround for the missing exception, and was not persuasive to the Board. For renvoi (C&Y): uniformity and getting "there in one bound", but courts should be cautious before following Neilson.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Shanghai Accident

An Australian expatriate is injured in Shanghai by his Australian employer's negligence. He sues in Singapore. Chinese conflict rules would apply Australian law (the parties' common nationality), and Australian law gives him a better remedy. He argues that "Chinese law" as the lex loci delicti includes Chinese conflict rules, so Australian law applies (as in Neilson).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

One sentence: per Credit Suisse Life v Ivanishvili (PC), renvoi has never applied in tort, so "Chinese law" means Chinese domestic law. Neilson was a workaround for Australia's lack of a flexible exception and was not persuasive to the Board. The point is formally open in Singapore, but the claimant's better route is the flexible exception (C3.6.4, applying Australian law as a third law if China is fortuitous). Limitation is in any case governed by Chinese domestic law (FLPA ss 3(5), 6(2)).

11C3.10 Evaluation and alternatives

Rule (summary):

  • Critique of double actionability: the lex fori limb is "parochial" (Red Sea, quoting the Law Commission; C&Y), born of tort's criminal-law roots, with no requirement of a forum connection.
  • SAL LRC's five reasons: the lex fori limb is (1) out of step with globalisation, (2) inconsistent with other common law systems, (3) obsolete as a default that avoids proof, (4) unnecessary given FNC and public policy, and (5) a blunt instrument for forum interests.
  • Judicial signals: IM Skaugen ("an anachronism"); Ang Ming Chuang (would have departed but for precedent); Xiamen Xinjingdi ("may one day need to be reconsidered"); Lew v Nargolwala (the lex fori inappropriate even as a contract fallback).
  • Defence of the rule: limb (a) shields Singapore defendants from foreign liability unknown here, limb (b) protects defendants and comity (EFT; Metall), and the exception gives flexibility (Rickshaw).
  • Reform for Parliament: per Rickshaw, with a "wise and judicious" use of the exception meanwhile, though C&Y note the inaction on the LRC proposal and Lew's logic for judicial reform.
  • Departures from English common law: Singapore applies the rule to local torts, tests fortuity, applies only the lex loci delicti's period, and keeps the common law, England having legislated (PIL(MP)A 1995; Rome II).
  • Australia: Zhang v Renault (and Pfeiffer interstate) apply the lex loci delicti with no exception, renvoi filling the gap (Neilson).
  • Canada: Tolofson v Jensen applies the lex loci delicti, with some flexibility for international (not interprovincial) torts.
  • England and New Zealand: statute (PIL(MP)A 1995; NZ 2017) applies the lex loci delicti with a flexible exception (s 12, Trafigura), the UK keeping double actionability for defamation and Rome II governing most later torts.
  • Rome II: Art 4(1) applies the law of the place where the damage occurs (lex loci damni), sparing the substance test, with party autonomy (Art 14) and no renvoi (Art 24). Locus critique: the substance test depends on the elements as alleged under the lex fori, which favours the lex loci damni.
  • US interest analysis: Babcock v Jackson weighs the States' interests, but per C&Y it is politically sensitive, and it is doubtful whether PIL should serve foreign State interests at all.
  • Proper law of the tort (Morris): the law of the most significant relationship was rejected in Boys and Red Sea for uncertainty, the exception already importing it. Online critique (Yeo): a physical locus is increasingly out of touch, though s 101 OSRAA may entrench the place-of-tort factor against judicial development.
  • Singapore reform proposal: the SAL LRC (2003) proposed the lex loci delicti with a "significantly more substantially connected" exception, excluding personal defamation; never enacted.
  • C&Y reform package: (1) abolish the lex fori limb, and (2) give effect to tort choice of law clauses through the exception.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Essay Question, Applied to One Case

"Double actionability should be abolished in Singapore." Discuss, using this case: a Singapore resident, injured in Ruritania by a Ruritanian company's defective product, recovers nothing because Ruritanian law (the lex loci) allows the claim but Singapore law bars the particular head of damage (the lex fori limb fails). Under Rome II art 4(1), what result? Under Zhang v Renault? Under the SAL LRC proposal?

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Against the rule: the claimant loses only because Singapore law, the parochial limb from The Halley, bars the head, although the tort had nothing to do with Singapore except the claimant's residence. The SAL LRC's five reasons apply: the rule is out of step with globalisation, inconsistent with other common law systems (Australia's Zhang v Renault, Canada's Tolofson, England's PIL(MP)A s 11–12 and Trafigura, and Rome II), no longer needed as a default to avoid proving foreign law, unnecessary given FNC and public policy, and a blunt instrument. The judicial signals (IM Skaugen: "an anachronism"; Ang Ming Chuang; Xiamen Xinjingdi) point the same way. Comparative results: under Rome II art 4(1), the lex loci damni (Ruritania, where the damage occurred) applies, so the claimant recovers. Under Zhang v Renault, the lex loci delicti applies with no exception, so the claimant recovers. Under the SAL LRC proposal, the lex loci delicti applies (subject to a "significantly more substantially connected" exception), so the claimant recovers. For the rule: limb (a) protects Singapore defendants from foreign liabilities unknown here, limb (b) protects defendants and comity (EFT; Metall), and the flexible exception lets the claimant displace the lex fori when Singapore is fortuitous (Red Sea). Here, though, residence makes Singapore arguably not fortuitous, which shows how strict the Rickshaw test is. Way forward: Rickshaw says reform is for Parliament, with a "wise and judicious" use of the exception meanwhile. C&Y propose abolishing the lex fori limb and giving effect to tort choice of law clauses through the exception. Morris's proper law of the tort and US interest analysis (Babcock v Jackson) were rejected as uncertain or politically sensitive. Yeo notes that a physical locus fits online torts poorly, though s 101 OSRAA entrenches a place-based connecting factor.

12C3.11 Other obligations (outline only)

Rule: Equitable obligations: per Rickshaw, a fiduciary or confidence claim founded on a contract follows its proper law (Rappo), a separate equitable category being left open. Directors' duties: the law of the place of incorporation (Focus Energy), which party autonomy cannot vary (Base Metal Trading). Breach of confidence without a relationship: unclear: tort (Yeo), unjust enrichment, or the proper law of the obligation (Innovia Films). Knowing receipt: the place of enrichment or receipt (Thahir v Pertamina; El Ajou), though its fault element leans towards tort. Dishonest assistance: a tort, so double actionability (Grupo Torras), which is problematic if foreign law alone governs and has no accessory liability. Unjust enrichment: per Dicey Rule 230 (adopted), the proper law of the obligation: (a) the contract's (putative) proper law; (b) the lex situs for land (doubted); otherwise (c) the place of enrichment. CIMB v Dresdner: an intended but void contract goes to (a), unless the vitiating factor infects the choice of law clause; no meeting of minds goes to (c). Place of enrichment: prefer immediate over ultimate enrichment if balanced (HSBC v UOB); bribes in Singapore accounts made Singapore law apply (Thahir v Pertamina). Illegality: per Esben Finance (provisional), the Foster / Ralli comity principle extends to unjust enrichment claims, subject to stultification. Trusts: express trusts follow the settlor's chosen law or the closest connection (Trisuryo: a Singapore SPV implied Singapore law); for resulting and constructive trusts, C&Y prefer the lex situs to the law of the event (Rappo). Slide questions: promissory estoppel on contractual non-performance follows the contract's proper law; undue influence is material validity for the proper law, unless it infects the choice of law clause (CIMB).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Pertamina-Style Bribes and Other Obligations
  1. Knowing receipt / bribes: an Indonesian state oil company official received bribes from contractors, paid into Singapore bank accounts. The company sues the official's widow (who received the funds) in Singapore.
  2. Dishonest assistance: a Swiss lawyer helped a Spanish company's directors divert funds through Swiss accounts. Swiss law (the lex loci) has no accessory liability.
  3. Directors' duties: a BVI company's director, under a services agreement choosing English law, is sued for breach of fiduciary duty.
  4. Breach of confidence (no relationship): a hacker in Vietnam steals a Singapore company's trade secrets.
  5. Unjust enrichment: (a) payment under a Swiss-law contract that turns out to be void for mistake, though the mistake does not infect the choice of law clause; (b) payment where there was no meeting of minds at all; (c) a mistaken payment into the defendant's Hong Kong account, immediately transferred to his Singapore account.
  6. Trusts: (a) an express trust in a Singapore SPV structure with no express choice of law; (b) a constructive trust claimed over Swiss assets arising from a fraud in Thailand.
  7. Promissory estoppel and undue influence: under a Thai-law supply contract, the buyer relies on the seller's promise not to enforce a delivery deadline; separately, a guarantor alleges undue influence in signing a Thai-law guarantee.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Knowing receipt: the law of the place of enrichment or receipt, Singapore (Thahir v Pertamina; El Ajou). The bribes in Singapore accounts made Singapore law apply in Thahir. Its fault element leans towards tort, but receipt is the anchor.
  2. Dishonest assistance is a tort, so double actionability applies (Grupo Torras). If Swiss law alone governed and had no accessory liability, the claim would fail, which shows the problem with characterising it as tort.
  3. Directors' duties are governed by the law of the place of incorporation (BVI), which party autonomy (the English-law services agreement) cannot vary (Focus Energy; Base Metal Trading).
  4. Unclear: tort (Yeo), unjust enrichment, or the proper law of the obligation (Innovia Films). If tort, double actionability applies, with the tort likely located in Vietnam.
  5. (a) An intended but void contract goes to the contract's (putative) proper law, Swiss law, since the mistake does not infect the choice of law clause (CIMB v Dresdner; Dicey r 230(a)). (b) No meeting of minds goes to the place of enrichment (r 230(c)). (c) Prefer immediate over ultimate enrichment if balanced (Hong Kong) (HSBC v UOB). Illegality: the Foster/Ralli comity principle extends to unjust enrichment claims, subject to stultification (Esben Finance, provisional).
  6. (a) Express trust: the settlor's chosen law or the closest connection; a Singapore SPV implies Singapore law (Trisuryo). (b) Constructive trust: C&Y prefer the lex situs (Swiss law) to the law of the event (Thai law) (Rappo).
  7. Promissory estoppel on contractual non-performance follows the contract's proper law (Thai). Undue influence is material validity, so the proper law (Thai) governs it, unless it infects the choice of law clause itself (CIMB).

13C3.12 Worked pathways and exam note

Rule (pathways): A, cross-border misrepresentation: D abroad emails C in Singapore, who acts here: limb 1 is met; receipt and reliance locate the tort here unless fortuitous (JIO); D must plead foreign law; the MA may apply. B, defamation online: a post read in Singapore, X and Y is three torts (Gutnick); the Singapore one is local; s 101 reaches only a parallel OSRAA tort. C, contract clause as defence: run the Sayers majority, then Lord Denning, then admissibility under Singapore law and the lex loci, and validity under the proper law. Exam note: state the leges causae, locate the tort, check the burden (EFT), prove fortuity (Rickshaw), and keep renvoi to one sentence (Ivanishvili).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Pathway A in Full

A Hong Kong fund manager emails a Singapore retiree in Singapore, recommending a structured note with false statements about its capital protection. The retiree buys through her Singapore bank, loses S$500,000, and sues the manager in Singapore in deceit and negligent misstatement. The manager is served in Hong Kong. The note subscription agreement is governed by Singapore law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Leges causae: the lex fori (Singapore) and the lex loci delicti. Limb 1: had everything happened in Singapore, deceit and negligent misstatement would be made out (IM Skaugen counterfactual). Locate the tort: the representation was directed at the retiree and received and relied on in Singapore, so the tort is in Singapore unless that is fortuitous; it is not, since she lives and banks here (JIO Minerals; Ong Ghee Soon). So this is a local tort, and both limbs point to Singapore law (C3.4). Burden: if the manager wants Hong Kong law, he must plead and prove it (EFT). He would also need to show that Singapore is purely fortuitous to invoke the exception (Rickshaw), which it is not. MA (±): the Singapore-law subscription agreement brings in the Misrepresentation Act (JIO Minerals), but s 2(1) MA lies only against a party to the contract, and the manager is not one (the retiree bought through her bank). So against the manager she relies on deceit and negligent misstatement; s 2(1) matters only against her contracting counterparty. Renvoi: irrelevant (Ivanishvili). Limitation: the Limitation Act applies (s 3(2) FLPA with Singapore as the lex loci). Jurisdiction: gateway (f)(i) or (f)(ii), and the place of the tort is prima facie the natural forum (JIO), so Singapore is favoured (J3/J4).
