Hypos: Engine (map, menus, distinctions, self-critique, ledger)

⚡ BIG IDEA

The engine is technique, not theory: a map to find your blocks, menus to open and frame, distinctions to cut a statement, and a ledger to finish.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 1. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It is the sheet's wording, so it is what you will write in the exam.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.

11.1 The map: week → archetype → cards → tests

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The item

A table taking each topic (by slide week and lecture) to its lead archetype, its theorist cards and its tests. The Core version adds a row: Core cards 13.3–13.6 (A law-making · B judges, lawyers · C what law is · D testing a theory).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Exam Statement

"Devlin was right that a society may protect its shared morality through law. Singapore's 2007 decision on s 377A shows why. Discuss."

✔ APPLICATION · Using the mapDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Topic: enforcing morals (slide week 6; lectures 7, 9).
  • Lead archetype: 7.
  • Cards:
    • Core version: 14.12, 14.13, 14.15, 14.16;
    • Theorist version: 14.12–14.17, adding Stephen and TSH's Marriage.
  • Tests: 15.6 (Devlin's interrogatories) and 15.7 (Hart).
  • Core version: also open Core A (13.3), since this is a legislator question, at P5 (majority morality) and P6 (enforcing morality).

So, in 30 seconds you know to use 7.3 (Devlin's jury box), 7.4 (disintegration), 7.6 (2007), 14.15 (Devlin) and 15.6 (the interrogatories).

21.2 Menus

1.2.1 The six hooks

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
HookThe sheet's template
SourceThis is almost verbatim [George, as TSH reports him / Thunder's summary of the amoral view / Devlin's case for enforcement]; the question is whether its author's own qualification survives.
WordEverything turns on "[without exception / necessarily / simply / always / rightfully]", and that word commits the statement to more than it can defend.
Ally turnsThe statement's natural ally is [Hart / Devlin / Pepper / Rawls], yet he rejects its conclusion.
Case[Riggs / the 2007 retain-but-don't-enforce compromise / Ordinance 11 / the Jaffa Cakes case†] tests the statement at once.
ConcessionThe statement is right that [kernel]. It does not follow that [overreach], because [principle].
Self-application (once per script)The statement is itself [a philosophy / a moral verdict], so it cannot be true in the sense it claims.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
One statement, six openings

The statement: "Legislators must simply reflect majority moral opinion as accurately as possible."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Source: this is close to the view Devlin is often thought to hold. The question is whether his own qualification survives: he insists that the standard "does not depend on the counting of heads".
  • Word: everything turns on "simply". That word commits the statement to treating the legislator as a stenographer.
  • Ally turns: the statement's natural ally is Devlin, yet he rejects its conclusion. For the law-maker, majority opinion is "surely not enough".
  • Case: the 2007 retain-but-don't-enforce compromise tests the statement at once. The majority's view prevailed in the result, but not as the reason (7.6).
  • Concession: the statement is right that majority will settles who makes law in a democracy. It doesn't follow that it settles what the law should say, because legitimacy isn't the same as rightness.
  • Self-application: the statement is itself a moral verdict about legislators' duty. Ask whether it reflects majority opinion.

Pick one hook per essay.

1.2.2 The five theses

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
ThesisThe sheet's template
Numbered (default)I make [two / three] claims: (1) [limb 1]; (2) [limb 2]; (3) [limb 3].
DistinctionThe statement is right about [A] and wrong about [B]; the difference is [1.3 principle].
Who and what[The majority / the Constitution / the role] settles who decides, not what is right.
ConditionalIf "[word]" means [X], the statement holds but is trivial; if it means [Y], it is false, and [Y] is the reading it needs.
Two hatsAs an MP I would [vote against / amend]; as a judge I would [enforce it / read it down]; the answers differ because the roles ask different questions.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The same statement, with each thesis applied.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Numbered: I make two claims: (1) majority opinion is evidence legislators must weigh; (2) it cannot be their sole concern, because legislators are trustees.
  • Distinction: the statement is right about who decides, and wrong about what is right. The difference is distinction 1.3(1).
  • Who and what: the majority settles who decides, not what is right.
  • Conditional: if "reflect" means "take account of", the statement holds but is trivial. If it means "transcribe", it is false, and "transcribe" is the reading it needs.
  • Two hats: suits a bill question instead (12.6).

1.2.3 Steelman, closes, roadmap, lines, reformulation

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The remaining tools:

  • Steelman (120–150 words): the best case for the statement is [X], which [a Singapore example] supports. It shows [kernel], but not [overreach].
  • Close: verdict and principle (default): the statement is therefore [verdict], because [governing principle].
  • Close: back to the hook: read again, "[the opening word or case]" shows [what the essay established].
  • Close: actor (only if the question names one): for [the judge / the MP / the lawyer], this means [one concrete consequence].
  • Roadmap: none, or one sentence: I take the [two limbs] in turn, using the difference between [A] and [B].
  • Memorable lines, one per script:
    • A constitutional democracy can move moral questions between institutions, but cannot remove them.
    • Law is a floor, not a ceiling.
    • Easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory.
    • Thunder: "To simply point to the role is to give up explaining it."
  • Reformulation ("a defensible version would read …"): once per script, where one sentence repairs the statement.
✔ APPLICATION · To the same statementDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Steelman: the best case is equal respect. Counting every citizen's view equally treats them as equals, which Indranee Rajah's 2007 line, "we would go with the majority view, unless there is a reason to protect the minority position", supports. It shows that majority opinion matters, but not that it is the legislator's only concern.
  • Roadmap: "I take the two limbs, 'simply' and 'as accurately as possible', in turn, using the difference between who decides and what is right."
  • Close: verdict and principle: "The statement is therefore overstated, because majority will settles who decides, not what is right."
  • Close: back to the hook: "Read again, 'simply' shows the statement's error: legislators judge, as trustees."
  • Close: actor: "For the MP, this means voting on reasons she can defend to the minority."
  • Memorable line: A constitutional democracy can move moral questions between institutions, but cannot remove them.
  • Reformulation: "A defensible version would read: 'Legislators must weigh majority moral opinion, and decide on reasons they can defend to those who disagree.'"

31.3 Organising distinctions

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Each distinction gets a mini-hypo in one line: the statement it cracks, then how.

#DistinctionHome · fitsMini-hypo: the statement it cracksHow it cracks it
(1)who decides v what is right12, 11.5 · majority will, roles"The majority voted for it, so it is right."The vote settles who decides; whether it's right is a separate question.
(2)presupposed v operative9.8 · "necessarily""Morality necessarily decides every case."It is presupposed in every case (fidelity), but operative only in hard cases (Judge Ng, 9.8).
(3)floor v ceiling11.7, 10.5 · "sufficient", "rules only""If no rule forbids it, a lawyer may do it."Law is the floor (the discovery avalanche, 10.5).
(4)aim v mechanism6.10 · pluralism, harm principle"To avoid imposing a way of life, only harm may justify law."The aim survives, but the mechanism isn't necessary or neutral (6.10).
(5)punish v regulate v promote7.9 · "enforce morality""The state must not enforce morality."Which kind: jail, licence or curriculum? (7.9)
(6)validity v obligation8.7 · "law is law", obedience"It's valid law, so citizens must obey."Validity doesn't settle obedience (the Radio Decree, 8.7).
(7)observer v participant8.3 · "how the word is used""Historians call the Junta's decrees 'law', so they were."True for observers; a judge claims correctness (8.3).
(8)principle v policy9.2 · floodgates, courts v Parliament"Courts must refuse new claims to avoid floodgates."Floodgates as policy is for Parliament; as fairness in proportion to fault, it is principle (9.2).
(9)acceptable to all v sound6.4 · Rawls v Finnis and TSH"An argument everyone accepts is a good argument."Accessibility isn't soundness (the four MPs, 6.4).
(10)unjust system v rule v outcome†10.11 · defence work"A lawyer must never help a guilty man go free."Is the injustice in the system, the rule, or the outcome? (Teo, 10.11)
(11)usurpation v abdication12.2 · roles, non-enforcement"Judges must leave everything to Parliament."Rubber-stamping is abdication (Judge Bala, 12.2).
(12)accessible v accepted5.7 · Finnis, public reason"Finnis's goods are self-evident, so everyone must accept them."Accessible to reason isn't the same as accepted (the casino, 5.7).
(13)form v content3; 13.1"A published, clear law is a just law."Form (Fuller) v content (RF) (13.1.4).
(14)urges v ends5.6"The law should follow human nature."Urges or ends? (the 24-hour licence, 5.6)
(15)trustee v stenographer12.3"MPs must vote exactly as polls say."Trustee (12.3).
(16)mandated v compatible11.4"Positivism forbids judges using moral concepts."LP mandates little but allows more (Liu, 11.4.3).
(17)text-first v goal-first9.7"Dworkin and the crits do the same thing."Text-first v goal-first (Suri on appeal, 9.7).
(18)mindset v outcome10.10"Pepper and Thunder would act completely differently."Often the same act, for different reasons (10.10.4).

Also on the sheet: judge rival models by how persuasive and useful they are, not by proof (Liu, W11).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"Dworkin's model of judging is simply false; Kennedy's is simply true."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

You can't prove either model, because no one knows what goes on in judges' minds. Ask which model is more persuasive, which is more useful, and which better fits what a human being doing this work would likely experience (9.7, 14.22).

The ledger stops you repeating signatures across essays, and stops you missing the strongest example for each archetype.

HYPO LESSON 2 · ARCHETYPE 2 · ABOUT 48 MIN · 20 QUESTIONS

Hypos: LP v NLT, and why theory matters

⚡ BIG IDEA

Naming something "law" is an evaluation, so the choice between LP and NLT is a live one. Hard cases such as Riggs turn on a theory of law's grounds.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 2. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It is the sheet's wording, so it is what you will write in the exam.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 2 of the 7 Nov exam sheet. Section 2 is word-for-word the same in the Core and Theorist versions. Neither sheet was changed.

Every point in section 2 follows the same pattern: the rule as the sheet states it, then a hypothetical, then the application. A short Exam cue line at the end tells you which question words should send you to that block. The names, countries and statutes in the hypos are made up. The rules, cases and quotes come from the sheet. The coverage table at the end maps every line of section 2 to the hypo that covers it.

Abbreviations: LP = legal positivism; NLT = natural law theory; ALR = American legal realism; TSH = Tan Seow Hon; RF = Radbruch formula; † = from the slides.

12.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The sheet's Position: naming something "law" is an evaluation, so the choice between LP and NLT is a live one. Hard cases such as Riggs turn on a theory of law's grounds.

The sheet's Intro: LP has two theses (W1b slides 5–6†):

  1. law is a social fact, identified by its source rather than its merit;
  2. law has no necessary link with morality.

Both theses are coherent. But LP still has to evaluate whose recognition counts. And in Riggs the judges all agreed the law bound them, yet split over what it required. So theory decides hard cases.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Vaccine Payout

Ruritania's Vaccine Injury Compensation Act says: "Any person who suffers serious injury following a vaccination under the national programme shall be paid $500,000." Dev is deep in debt. Straight after his vaccination he injects a contaminant into his own arm, falls seriously ill, and claims the $500,000. He is later convicted of public mischief and fined $2,000. Every judge accepts that the Act is valid and binding, and on its words Dev qualifies.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The judges do not disagree about whether to obey the Act. They disagree about what the law is.

  • A judge who thinks the law is only the Act's words pays Dev.
  • A judge who thinks the law also includes the common-law principle that no one may profit from their own wrong refuses him.

Which of these is "the law" depends on a theory of law's grounds. So any statement that identifying law is neutral fact-finding fails on these facts. (2.8.1 works this case through the full Riggs card.)

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

the statement says identifying law is "neutral" or "just looking it up", or that theory is "optional".

22.1 Is LP merely descriptive?

📘 Learn 2.1 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: neutral, objective, merely describes, cross-purposes

2.1.1 LP and NLT are not at cross-purposes

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Some say the debate is at cross-purposes: LP tells us what law is, and NLT what it ought to be. TSH replies that on closer analysis both schools are asking the same question: what law is (TSH). NLT really does claim to say what law is, at least at the extremes (weak NLT: 2.3.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Marovian Land Decree

Marovia's Parliament follows the correct procedure to pass a Land Decree that confiscates, without compensation, every farm owned by a member of the Halani minority. Asha, a Halani farmer, puts one question to two professors: "Is the Decree law, so the bailiff can lawfully take my farm?"

  • Professor Lim, a positivist, says: "Yes. It was validly enacted. It is law, though wicked."
  • Professor Okafor, a natural lawyer, says: "No. It is so unjust that it is not law."

A commentator says the two professors aren't really disagreeing, because one is describing the law and the other is moralising.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The commentator is wrong. Asha asked one question, and the professors gave her opposite answers to it. Okafor is not saying what the law ought to be. He is saying what it is, and that the bailiff has no lawful power. Both professors are answering "what is law?" So there is a real dispute over the concept of law, not a division of labour.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"LP and NLT are at cross-purposes"; "LP says what law is, NLT what it ought to be".

2.1.2 Treating official recognition as conclusive is a choice

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

LP identifies law by looking at what courts and officials uphold. But treating that recognition as conclusive is itself a choice. Once the highest court upholds a manifestly unjust rule, the rule's injustice is "treated as irrelevant" (TSH).

Liu's slides make two further points (W1b slide 15†):

  • Circularity. LP finds law in what courts uphold, so its premise becomes its conclusion.
  • Evaluation. Equating what people regard as law with law "involves an evaluation, and is not merely descriptive".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Decree Reaches the Top Court

Asha challenges the Land Decree. Marovia's highest court holds that the Decree was passed in proper form, and upholds it. Professor Lim writes: "That settles it. I am only describing. The Decree is what Marovian officials treat as law, so it is law. I express no view on its merits."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Lim's "description" contains two evaluations.

  1. He chose the court's acceptance as the decisive test of law. That choice, not anything he observed, is what makes the Decree's injustice irrelevant.
  2. His argument is circular. He assumed that law is whatever officials uphold, then "found" that the Decree is law because officials uphold it. The premise became the conclusion.

He has described what Marovian officials regard as law and then equated that with law. That equation is an evaluation, not a description.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"LP is neutral", "objective" or "merely describes".

2.1.3 The steelman for LP, and why preferring it is still a value choice

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The best case for LP (Liu, W1):

  • lawyers "look up the books";
  • you must know what the law is before you can reform it;
  • LP arose in states without a shared moral base, where people needed a test of law that everyone could apply.

But preferring LP for a pluralist state is itself a value choice (2.1, point 3).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Client Who Wants a Straight Answer

Mei runs a café in a city-state of many faiths and ethnic groups. She asks her lawyer, Ravi, whether a new by-law makes her close by 11 pm. Ravi reads the by-law and says yes. Mei's cousin says Ravi should first ask whether the by-law is just. Ravi replies: "People here disagree about morality. If the test for law depended on everyone's moral views, no one would know what the rules are. I tell clients what the law is. Reform is a separate question."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Ravi's points are strong, and they are the steelman. He does have to know the law before he can argue for changing it, and a source-based test lets people of different faiths share one legal system.

But every reason Ravi gives is a value:

  • certainty;
  • peace among people who disagree;
  • keeping advice separate from reform.

So choosing LP because it suits a pluralist state is a value choice, not a neutral description. In an answer, concede the steelman, then show that it rests on an evaluation.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"lawyers just tell clients what the law is"; "in a diverse society only LP works".

2.1.4 The trap: "no necessary connection" still allows contingent ones

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

LP's second thesis says there is no necessary connection between law and morality, and "necessary" is the key word. Contingent connections are fine: morality can influence law, be incorporated into it, and critique it (W1b slide 7†). Riggs' maxim is a legal rule with moral content, and it troubles no positivist (Liu, W1). Some law, such as parking rules, needs no moral test at all.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Grossly Unfair Term

Ruritania's Contracts Act provides that "a contract term is void if it is grossly unfair". A student writes: "This proves LP is false. Here the law contains morality."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The student has fallen into the trap.

  • A positivist says the "grossly unfair" test is law because a recognised source, the Act, put it there. The moral content got in by a contingent choice: if Parliament repealed the clause, the test would drop out of the law.
  • LP denies only that law must contain morality, everywhere, by definition.
  • Ruritania's parking by-laws show the other side: they are valid law with no moral test at all.

To beat LP you have to show a necessary connection, for example extreme injustice defeating legality (2.3.2; section 8). A contingent one won't do.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

any argument of the form "law X contains a moral standard, so positivism fails"; "Riggs refutes positivism".

2.1.5 Against: Finnis's "rubbish heap"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Finnis doubts that law can be described from a "rubbish heap" of miscellaneous facts unless you use evaluative criteria to decide which facts matter. Description presupposes evaluation.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Visiting Researcher

Dr Sato is sent to a town to write "a purely factual description of its law". In a week she records:

  • a traffic warden's parking fines;
  • a gang's weekly "protection fees";
  • the chess club's rules;
  • a temple's dietary rules;
  • a magistrate's eviction order;
  • a parent's 10 pm curfew.

All are rules, all are backed by some pressure, and all are obeyed.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Nothing in the raw data tells Sato which of these are "law". To leave out the gang's fees but keep the warden's fines, she needs a criterion. It might be "rules that claim to serve the common good", or "rules officials accept as binding". Picking that criterion is an evaluation of what law is and what it is for. So LP cannot start from pure description: it must first evaluate which facts matter. That is Finnis's point.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"LP is merely descriptive"; "jurisprudence is just a description of rules".

32.2 Hart's internal "ought"

📘 Learn 2.2 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: mere commands, habit, Hart concedes moral evaluation

2.2.1 Law is more than commands obeyed out of habit

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Austin defines law as the command of a sovereign who is habitually obeyed and obeys no one, backed by a sanction (14.3). Hart says this misses law's internal "ought". A social rule has two aspects:

  • an external aspect: people regularly behave a certain way. On its own, that is a mere habit.
  • an internal aspect, the "critical reflective attitude": people criticise deviation, demand conformity, accept that criticism and demand as justified, and use words like "ought", "must", "right" and "wrong".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Saturday Movies and Red Lights

In the town of Bellhaven, most families go to the cinema on Saturday night, and most drivers stop at red lights. One Saturday Jun stays home, and nobody minds. That same night Jun drives through a red light. Other drivers honk, a passer-by shouts "You should have stopped!", a police officer fines him, and Jun's friends agree he deserved the fine.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Both are regular behaviour, but only one is a rule.

  • The cinema is a habit. No one treats staying home as a fault.
  • The red light has the internal aspect: deviation is criticised, conformity is demanded, the criticism is accepted as justified, and the language is "should".

An account of law as commands obeyed out of habit cannot tell these two apart. Hart's internal "ought" can.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"law is just commands backed by threats"; "law is obeyed from habit".

2.2.2 The "ought" need not be moral

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The internal "ought" need not be moral. Hart allows officials to accept the rules out of fear, self-interest or habit. What matters is that they use the rule as a standard. So Hart gets beyond mere habit without conceding that identifying law requires moral evaluation. (Liu's warning: don't write that Hart requires moral approval.)

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Reluctant Tax Judge

Judge Wong of the Ruritanian High Court thinks the new Wealth Levy Act is unfair to small family firms. She applies it anyway because Parliament passed it, and rules against a firm. In private she explains: "I want my pension, and that's how judges here do things." When a junior judge refuses to apply the Act because he dislikes it, Wong criticises his ruling as legally wrong.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Wong's motives are self-interest and habit, not moral approval. Yet she has the internal attitude: she uses "whatever Parliament enacts is law" as a standard, and she criticises the junior judge for departing from it. On Hart's account, that is enough for a rule of recognition to exist. So a statement that Hart's internal "ought" forces him to concede moral evaluation is wrong. Hart has moved past mere habit, but not into morality.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"Hart's internal point of view concedes that law rests on moral approval".

2.2.3 Dworkin's Nazi dilemma for Hart

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Dworkin: many officials of Nazi Germany obeyed Hitler "only out of fear". That poses a dilemma for Hart:

  • if obedience out of fear counts as acceptance, Hart's difference from Austin "becomes elusive";
  • if it doesn't, it seems there was "no law in Nazi Germany", which is not how most people use the word "law".

The reply (14.4): acceptance even from "fear, self-interest or habit" still treats the rules as standards.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Kessland Regime

In Kessland, judges and police enforce the Leader's decrees. Most officials obey only because people who dissent disappear. Yet in court, judges cite the decrees, criticise lawyers who ignore them, and overturn lower-court rulings that depart from them.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Dworkin's dilemma, applied:

  • Horn (a): if obeying out of terror counts as "acceptance", Hart is just Austin in more words.
  • Horn (b): if it doesn't count, Kessland had no law at all.

The reply takes horn (a) but denies that Hart collapses into Austin. Kessland's officials do more than fall into a pattern of fearful obedience. They use the decrees as standards: they cite them, criticise deviation and correct lower courts. That use is Hart's acceptance, whatever the motive behind it. So Kessland had law, wicked law, and that is the positivist's point: calling it law is what lets us condemn it plainly as "law but too evil to be obeyed" (8.2).

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"if officials obey out of fear, Hart is no different from Austin"; Nazi law.

42.3 Is NLT elitist?

📘 Learn 2.3 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: only the devout, religious faith, any judge strikes down

2.3.1 Natural law is known by reason, not revelation

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

NLT does not rest on moral truths that only the devout can see. Natural law, unlike divine law, can be apprehended by reason (TSH).

Aquinas's four kinds of law (W1b slide 13†):

KindWhat it is
Eternalgoverns all creation
Divinerevealed in scripture
Naturalhumans' share in eternal law, through practical reason
Humanlaid down in accordance with natural law

Grotius made natural law secular: it would have the same content even if God did not exist.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Prisoner-Torture Ordinance

Ruritania passes an ordinance that lets guards torture prisoners for entertainment. Two citizens argue that it is not law.

  • Sister Agnes cites scripture.
  • Ben, an atheist philosopher, argues from human vulnerability and the senselessness of pain inflicted for fun.

A columnist writes: "Natural law is a theory for priests. Only believers can know what it requires."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Ben reaches Agnes's conclusion without any revelation, which is exactly what NLT claims is possible. On Aquinas's scheme, scripture belongs to divine law. Natural law is what practical reason can grasp, and it is open to anyone. Since Grotius, its content is the same even if God did not exist. So the columnist has confused natural law with divine law, and the charge that NLT is only for "the devout" fails.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"NLT depends on religious faith"; "only the devout can know natural law".

2.3.2 NLT does not license any judge to strike down any law

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The versions of NLT and their limits:

  • Strong NLT: every rule must embody morality. That would have judges second-guessing tax law.
  • Weak NLT: a rule loses legal status only when it diverges from morality to an extreme degree, such as a law to execute all redheads (Liu, W1).
  • Radbruch formula: voids only intolerably unjust statutes (8.2–8.3). The strong connection thesis, on which a judge may refuse whatever he considers unfair, is one that "no serious non-positivist defends" (Alexy; 8.2).
  • Finnis: an unjust law is no nullity to disregard. It lacks only its prima facie power to bind in conscience, and there may still be a duty to obey it so as not to weaken a just system.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Judge Tan's Three Files

Judge Tan, a natural lawyer, has three files on her desk.

  • (a) The Income Tax (Amendment) Act raises the top rate from 22% to 24%. She thinks this is unfair to middle-income earners.
  • (b) The Licensing Act bans street hawking near malls. She thinks this is unjust to poor hawkers.
  • (c) The Public Order (Redheads) Act orders the execution of all redheads.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Strong NLT would let her refuse (a) simply because she disagrees with it. No serious natural lawyer defends that, and it would make law unworkable.
  • Weak NLT and the RF leave (a) and (b) as law. Only (c) diverges so far from justice that it loses legal status.
  • Finnis on (b): even if the Licensing Act is unjust, it is not a nullity she may ignore. It only lacks its prima facie power to bind in conscience, and there may still be a duty to comply so as not to weaken a just system.

So a statement that NLT lets "any judge strike down any law she dislikes" attacks a version no one holds.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"NLT lets judges strike down whatever they consider unjust".

2.3.3 Concede: who decides what natural law requires?

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

TSH admits there is "no easy answer" to who should pronounce on the content of natural law. Concede that judges' authority is doubtful below the extreme threshold (12.1). Keep NLT's force for intolerable injustice.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Sentencing Challenge

Ruritania's Constitution says no one shall be deprived of life or liberty "save in accordance with law". Kai was sentenced under a mandatory minimum sentence. He argues two things: that "law" here means law that conforms to natural law, and that mandatory sentences are unjust because they stop judges fitting the punishment to the offender. Thoughtful citizens and MPs disagree about whether such sentences are unjust.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even if Kai is right that "law" carries natural-law content, someone still has to decide what that content is. This issue is contested and nowhere near executing redheads. On an issue like that, an unelected court overruling Parliament has doubtful authority, and TSH concedes there is no easy answer. The honest response concedes the point: below the threshold, judges should hesitate. At the extreme, as with file (c) in 2.3.2, the authority worry fades, because "the more extreme the injustice, the more certain the knowledge of it" (Alexy; 8.3).

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"who decides what natural law requires?"; "NLT gives judges too much power".

52.4 Are Fuller and Dworkin natural lawyers in all but name?

📘 Learn 2.4 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: all but name

2.4.1 Fuller's thin, procedural natural law

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Fuller and Dworkin are NLT's allies, not natural lawyers in all but name, because neither lets injustice as such defeat validity. Fuller's is a thin "procedural natural law"†: legality demands rules "however fair or unfair they may be".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Well-Drafted Ban

Marovia replaces its Land Decree with a new Act: "From 1 January next year, no member of the Halani minority may buy farmland." The Act meets all eight of Fuller's desiderata (section 3):

  1. it is general, covering a class of people rather than named individuals;
  2. it is published;
  3. it is prospective, not retroactive;
  4. it is clear;
  5. it does not contradict other laws;
  6. it is possible to obey;
  7. it is kept stable;
  8. officials apply it exactly as written.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Every one of Fuller's requirements is met, so by Fuller's test Marovia is governing through law, even though the content is unjust. Fuller's morality is about how rules are made and applied, not about what they say: legality demands rules "however fair or unfair they may be". If Marovia had kept the ban secret or made it retroactive, Fuller's test would bite. Because unjust content alone does not defeat legality for Fuller, calling him a natural lawyer "in all but name" overstates. His is a procedural natural law, and that makes him an ally of NLT.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"Fuller (or Dworkin) is a natural lawyer in all but name".

2.4.2 Dworkin's judge must interpret the history he finds

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Dworkin's judge must "interpret the legal history he finds", not invent a better one. So a wicked legal history can produce a wicked answer, and intolerable injustice is left open. Integrity gives no exit from a wicked legal history (14.5).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Kessland's Eighty Years

For eighty years, every Kessland statute and case has denied the Doran minority the right to make contracts. A Doran trader sues to enforce a sale. Judge Reyes, a Dworkinian, looks for the reading of Kessland law that best fits and justifies the record.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Reyes must work with the history he finds. A reading that gives the Doran equal contract rights may be morally better, but it fits almost nothing in the record. If fit rules that reading out, integrity's best answer is still the wicked one. Unlike weak NLT, Dworkin offers no rule that intolerable injustice is not law. So Dworkin shares NLT's view that moral principle is among law's grounds, which makes him an ally. But he is not a natural lawyer "in all but name", because he leaves the extreme case open. Radbruch is the one who guards that outer limit (14.5; section 8).

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

as for 2.4.1.

2.4.3 Concede: weak NLT fails as an account of how lawyers use "law"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Dworkin finds even weak NLT "unpersuasive" as an account of usage, that is, as a theory of how all lawyers use the word "law". In Riggs, Gray seems to have agreed with Earl that the law would be better if it denied Elmer the inheritance, but not that the law therefore did deny it. Concede this, and defend NLT as a theory of law's grounds instead.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"The Law Is Against Her"

In a Ruritanian appeal, Judge Choo writes: "I agree that a better law would let the tenant stay. But the law as it stands says she must go." Lawyers on both sides find the sentence perfectly normal.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If NLT were a claim about how all lawyers use "law", Choo's sentence would contradict itself, because on that claim the morally better reading is the law. Yet lawyers say this kind of thing every day. So concede Dworkin's point: as a dictionary of usage, NLT fails. Then shift ground. NLT is a theory of what makes statements of law true, especially in the extreme cases where injustice defeats legality. Choo's tenant case is nowhere near that extreme.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"NLT misdescribes how lawyers talk"; "lawyers routinely call unjust laws 'law'".

62.5 Do judges disagree only about whether to obey?

📘 Learn 2.5 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: only about obeying, plain words, no law to apply
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

(The sheet lists "Terms" near the end of 2.5. It comes first here because the other hypos depend on it.)

2.5.1 Terms: empirical v theoretical disagreement

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • An empirical disagreement disputes whether agreed grounds of law are met. Is the statute in the book? Was it amended?
  • A theoretical disagreement disputes the grounds themselves. Do statutes and past decisions exhaust the law?

Two views hide theoretical disagreement:

  • the plain-fact view: law is only what institutions have decided in the past, so every question of law has an answer "in the books";
  • semantic theories: lawyers share hidden criteria for using the word "law".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Arguments About Speeding Fines
  • (a) In Lee's appeal against a speeding fine, the judges argue about whether the amendment lowering the limit to 60 km/h was gazetted before or after the day he was caught.
  • (b) In Dr Kumar's appeal against a fine under a limit that is clearly in force, the judges argue about whether the statute's words are the whole law, or must be read together with a common-law principle (2.5.2).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) is empirical. Everyone agrees that a gazetted statute is law. They dispute a fact: whether this one was gazetted in time.
  • (b) is theoretical. They agree on every fact about the statute and dispute what counts as law.

The plain-fact view can see only (a). It would recast (b) as an argument about whether the judges should depart from the law.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

any question about what judges disagree about.

2.5.2 Theoretical disagreement is not defiance

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Saying that judges only disagree about whether to obey the law mistakes theoretical disagreement for defiance. In Riggs all the judges accepted the law's authority but split over what it required. Saying there was "no law to apply" assumes the plain-fact view, when which arguments count as law is the very point in dispute.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Speeding Surgeon

Ruritania's Road Traffic Act says: "Any driver exceeding 70 km/h shall be fined $500." Dr Kumar, off duty, drives at 110 km/h to reach a cyclist who has collapsed, and saves his life. The Act has no emergency exception, but a long line of Ruritanian cases recognises a common-law defence of necessity to save life. All three appeal judges accept that the Act binds them.

  • Two hold that the Act must be read together with the necessity principle, and they quash the fine.
  • One holds that the words are plain and the fine must stand.

A newspaper headline reads: "Judges defy Parliament". A professor writes: "No law covered this. The majority simply made new law."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Both reactions miss what happened.

  • The headline: no judge refused to follow the Act. They disagreed about what the law, properly understood, required. The headline mistakes a theoretical disagreement for defiance.
  • The professor: "no law" assumes the plain-fact view, that only the statute's words count. But whether the necessity principle is part of the law is exactly what the judges were arguing about. Saying there was "no law" takes the dissent's side. It is not a neutral description.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"judges only disagree about whether to obey the law"; "once the plain words run out, there is no law to apply".

2.5.3 Agreed result, split grounds: the McLoughlin pattern

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

In McLoughlin the Lords agreed on the result but split over whether courts may let policy limit liability (2.8; 9.2). Agreement on an outcome can hide a theoretical disagreement about law's grounds.

LAWYER: "run both policy arguments" (9.2) means arguing both of these:

  1. policy fails on these facts (Wilberforce, Edmund-Davies, Russell);
  2. drawing policy lines is for Parliament, not the courts (Scarman).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Video-Call Drowning

Mr Ong's 12-year-old son is on a school trip abroad. A teacher supervising a swim is negligent and lets the boy drift out of his depth. At that moment another pupil is on a live video call with Mr Ong, and Mr Ong watches in real time as his son goes under and is dragged out unconscious. The boy survives with a brain injury, and Mr Ong develops a psychiatric illness. Every earlier successful nervous-shock claimant in Ruritania was physically at the scene or in its immediate aftermath.

The top court rules 5–0 that Mr Ong recovers, but the judges give different reasons:

  • three say policy may limit liability, but not here;
  • one says where to draw policy lines is "not justiciable";
  • one says reasonable foreseeability is the test, and any policy limit must not be arbitrary.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A headline saying "Court unanimous" hides a deep split. The judges disagree about whether policy is a legitimate ground of law at all. That is theoretical disagreement showing up in the reasons, not the result.

For counsel, Mr Ong's lawyer should run both arguments:

  1. even if courts may weigh policy, fear of a flood of claims does not justify denying this claim;
  2. in any case, drawing lines on policy grounds is for Parliament, not the courts.

Covering both wins over judges on both sides of the split. (2.8.2 works this case through the full McLoughlin card.)

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"the judges agreed, so there was no real disagreement"; "how should a lawyer argue a novel case?"

2.5.4 Dworkin: LP's two defences insult the judges

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

To protect the plain-fact view, LP has two defences, and Dworkin says each insults the judges:

  • The pretence defence. Judges only pretend to disagree about the law, to keep public faith in it. That shows judges as "well-meaning liars".
  • The borderline defence. Judges disagree only about a marginal use of the word "law", like arguing whether Buckingham Palace is a house. That shows them as "simpletons".

Dworkin's answer: Riggs and McLoughlin were not borderline cases but "pivotal" ones, testing what law is.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Commentators on the Speeding Surgeon

After Dr Kumar's case (2.5.2), two commentators write about it.

  • Commentator X: "The judges all knew there was no law. They dressed up a policy choice as legal reasoning so the public would keep believing in the rule of law."
  • Commentator Y: "They were only quibbling over whether the word 'law' stretches to a necessity principle at the edges, like arguing whether a palace is a house."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • X makes the judges well-meaning liars. There is no evidence they were pretending, and the dissenting judge plainly meant what he said.
  • Y makes them simpletons. Sensible people do not take a verbal quibble through years of appeals.

The better view is that Kumar's case was pivotal: the judges disagreed about the tests for what counts as law at all. Dworkin's comparison is two groups of critics arguing whether photography is art, in a way that shows they hold different views of what art is. That is genuine theoretical disagreement.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"judges only pretend to disagree"; "legal disagreement is merely verbal".

2.5.5 Qualify: Liu thinks Dworkin is unfair to LP

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Liu thinks Dworkin is unfair to LP. LP need not turn every disagreement into an empirical one, and soft positivism lets the rule of recognition adopt moral tests (Liu, W1).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Fairness Clause

Ruritania's Constitution says Parliament's laws are valid "only if not grossly unjust". The judges accept this as part of their rule of recognition. In a challenge to a new detention law, they split 3–2 over whether the law is grossly unjust.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A soft positivist can explain this split without calling it fake or merely empirical. The rule of recognition is a social fact (what officials accept), and here it has adopted a moral test. So the judges are disagreeing, in good faith, about whether that moral test is met, and LP can accommodate genuine disagreement that turns on moral argument. Use this to qualify Dworkin: he beats the plain-fact view, but not necessarily every positivist.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"Dworkin refutes positivism"; "LP cannot explain moral argument in court".

72.6 Is theory useless to lawyers?

📘 Learn 2.6 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: luxury, optional, irrelevant, no client needed, good dictionary, Jaffa Cakes

2.6.1 Citing theory is not using it (Fish)

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Fish grants the statement a kernel of truth: Rawls cited in court is likely to be regarded "at best as window dressing and at worst as showing off". Yet marshalling rules "takes place within an enterprise that is purposive". Without "some strong intuition of the general project", rehearsing the rules is "an empty gesture" (Fish). So calling theory a luxury confuses citing theory with using it.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Associate Who Quoted Rawls

Priya, a first-year associate, drafts a submission in a dispute over a late steel delivery and opens with a paragraph from Rawls on justice as fairness. The partner deletes it: "The judge will think we're showing off." A month later the firm acts for food-delivery riders. They argue that a statute giving "employees" paid sick leave covers them. The partner asks Priya: "What is this statute for? Who did Parliament think needed protecting, and from whom?"

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The partner was right the first time. Quoting Rawls in a steel case is window dressing. But the second question is theory in use: it asks what the state may do for workers, and why. Without that sense of "the general project", Priya could list the precedents on "employee" but not marshal them into an argument, and listing them would be an empty gesture. So "theory is a luxury" is true of citing theorists and false of using theory.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"legal theory is a luxury" or "irrelevant to practice"; "a good lawyer needs no philosophy".

2.6.2 Easy cases rest on a shared theory; hard cases on rival ones

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Easy cases rest on a shared theory (9.9), and hard cases on rival ones. Lawyers agree in easy cases because they share a practice of justification, not because no theory is involved.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Parking Fine and the Riders

Same firm. On Monday a client asks whether he must pay a parking fine issued under a validly made by-law. Everyone agrees that he must. On Friday the partner turns to the riders' case from 2.6.1, where the two sides read "employee" in rival ways.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Monday. No one argues about theory, but a theory is still at work. Everyone shares the view that validly made by-laws are law and bind, so nothing needs to be said.
  • Friday. The shared theory runs out. One side reads the statute as protecting anyone economically dependent on a platform. The other reads it as protecting only people under a traditional contract of service. The case is hard because the theories differ.

So when easy cases involve no talk of theory, that shows agreement on theory, not that theory is irrelevant.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"most cases are routine, so theory doesn't matter"; "no client needs philosophy".

2.6.3 The cake–biscuit lesson: philosophy turns up in unexpected places

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

In the Jaffa Cakes case† (United Biscuits (UK) Ltd, LON/91/160), the VAT tribunal used four philosophical moves:

  • core attributes;
  • what a settled class has in common;
  • thought experiments;
  • social context.

That amounts, indirectly, to a "philosophy of cakeness and biscuitness". The tribunal held Jaffa Cakes were cake, because stale cakes harden and stale biscuits soften. Both sides agreed on the factors but weighed them differently, which is the shape of most jurisprudential disputes (Liu, W1).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Sweet Bun Tax

Ruritania's Food Tax Act zero-rates "bread" and taxes "confectionery" at 10%. A bakery chain sells a soft milk bun with 18% sugar, a custard centre and a glazed top, packed in sixes and shelved in the snack aisle. The tax office says it is confectionery. The bakery says it is bread.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The tribunal has to make the same four moves.

  1. Core attributes: what makes bread bread (a staple flour-and-yeast dough?), and what makes confectionery confectionery (sweetness as the whole point?).
  2. Settled class: what do clear examples, such as a loaf and a doughnut, have in common?
  3. Thought experiment: would it still be "bread" without the custard?
  4. Social context: is it eaten as a meal or a treat, and where do shops put it?

Both sides will agree on these factors and weigh them differently. The tribunal cannot decide without a philosophy of what bread is. So philosophy cannot be avoided, even in a tax dispute.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"theory is optional"; any question that mentions Jaffa Cakes.

2.6.4 A good dictionary is not enough when the word is "law"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

TSH: a rule's purpose may settle what counts as a "vehicle", but a contested word like "law" brings in LP v NLT.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Toy Car and the Land Decree
  • (a) A park by-law says "No vehicles in the park". A child rides a battery-powered toy car along the path.
  • (b) Asha (2.1.1) asks whether the Marovian Land Decree is "law".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) The by-law's purpose, keeping the park safe and quiet, can settle the question without any theory of law. A slow toy car threatens neither, so it may well fall outside "vehicles".
  • (b) No dictionary, and no by-law's purpose, settles this one. Whether a manifestly unjust enactment is "law" is the LP v NLT question itself.

So "a good dictionary is all a lawyer needs" works for "vehicle" and fails for "law".

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"all a lawyer needs is a good dictionary".

2.6.5 You can't judge law good or bad without knowing what it is (Leff)

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Leff†: "[Y]ou can't know that a thing is not being done well until you know what it is that is being done". Judging excellence presupposes a theory.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Minister's Scorecard

A minister asks a consultant to grade Ruritania's criminal courts on "how well they're doing".

  • Court A has high conviction rates and fast trials.
  • Court B is slower, acquits more often, and gives long reasoned judgments.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The consultant cannot grade either court until she decides what criminal courts are for. If their point is controlling crime, Court A is doing well. If it is protecting the innocent and giving reasons citizens can accept, Court B may be doing better. Every judgment of how well a thing is done presupposes an account of its purpose, and that account is theory. So anyone who says law can be improved without theory has a theory, just an unexamined one.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"theory can't tell us whether the law is good"; "reform is practical, not theoretical".

2.6.6 Against: disagreement among theorists doesn't make theory useless

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The claim that theory cannot help anyone decide fails, because disagreement is not the absence of a fact (4.7). Disagreement no more disproves moral facts than disputes over the number of planets do. If the statement says the Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary, use 11.7.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"Ten Professors, Ten Answers"

A senior judge tells a law-school audience: "Ask ten legal philosophers whether the Riggs majority was right and you'll get ten answers. Theory can't help a judge decide anything."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The fact that theorists disagree shows the question is hard, not that it has no answer. People have disputed the number of planets, and there was still a fact of the matter. The judge also has to decide hard cases anyway: refusing theory just means deciding on an unexamined one. Answer the statement with 4.7, or with 11.7 if it is about the Constitution.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"theory cannot help anyone decide, because theorists disagree".

82.7 Singapore pragmatism

📘 Learn 2.7 in Lesson 2 →
🔑 Trigger words: prevailing philosophy, pragmatic, no blank slate
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The rule, in three steps
  1. Singapore's prevailing philosophy is often called pragmatism. When it kept s 377A in 2007, the Government called its approach "a pragmatic one that maintains Singapore's social cohesion".
  2. Yet pragmatism is itself a theory. TSH: in any "postmodern pragmatic" society, the view that law is whatever a court says "glosses over" the principles that should guide the court.
  3. So the claim that philosophy is unnecessary here fails: "The purpose of theory is to guide practice" (TSH).

AGAINST: "[I]n law, as in life, we simply cannot shun the question" of right and wrong (TSH).

Where the trigger "no blank slate" comes from: in 2007 the Government also refused to answer questions about what it would do if it were legislating from scratch: "We are not starting from a blank slate" (TSH, Pragmatism). That line is not on the current sheet, but it was checked against the reading on 4 Nov.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Unenforced Hotel-Room Law

The city-state of Port Meridian has an old law making it an offence for unmarried couples to share a hotel room. Some citizens want it repealed, and others want it kept. The Government keeps the law but announces that it will not enforce it, calling this "a pragmatic approach that keeps the peace between communities". It refuses to say what it would do if writing the law from scratch: "We are not starting from scratch." A columnist writes: "Port Meridian doesn't do philosophy. We do what works."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • It ranks values. The Government's choice puts social peace above legal clarity, keeps both camps on side instead of deciding the merits, and treats the existing law as the baseline. That ranking is a theory, a pragmatic one, and like any theory it can be defended or criticised.
  • Refusing a clean slate is itself a position. It gives the status quo weight.
  • "Whatever works" glosses over principles. If the columnist says law is "whatever works" or "whatever the court says", TSH's reply applies: that view glosses over the principles that should guide the decision.

Theory exists to guide practice and to judge it. So a pragmatic state still needs theory, and still cannot shun the question of right and wrong.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"Singapore is pragmatic, so legal philosophy is unnecessary here"; "Singapore's prevailing philosophy".

92.8 Case cards: Riggs and McLoughlin

📘 Learn 2.8 in Lesson 2 →
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Riggs turned on whether a clear statute has unstated exceptions. McLoughlin turned on whether policy may distinguish precedent. Each answer presupposes a theory of law.

2.8.1 Applying the Riggs card

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
RowRiggs v Palmer
FactsElmer, 16, poisoned his grandfather so that he would not revoke the will. Read literally, the statute of wills let Elmer inherit.
Held5–2: Elmer took nothing.
MajorityEarl: legislative intention, and maxims with "their foundation in universal law". The decision "takes from him no property".
DissentGray: the matter "does not lie within the domain of conscience". Courts cannot "add to the respondent's penalties".
LPGray's posited text (slide†). Or: Earl's maxim is itself posited common law with moral content, which LP accepts (Liu, W1). Or: a gap, filled by discretion.
DworkinTwo morally grounded theories. Gray's guards "an important principle of justice" (penalties fixed in advance). Earl's guards coherence.
ALRRules construed in different ways, or picked "from the mass available", fit results reached on other grounds.

Liu's two readings (he picks neither):

  • (a) Both sides argued about law, and the majority's law included common-law principle, so Dworkin overstates.
  • (b) The dispute was whether law is "always subject to universal fundamental principles of morality" (W1b slide 2†), as Earl's "universal law" suggests.

Either way, neither side kept to the four corners of the statute (W1).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Vaccine Payout, revisited (2.0)

Dev deliberately contaminated his own vaccination to claim $500,000 under an Act that says any person seriously injured after a vaccination under the national programme "shall be paid". He has been convicted and fined $2,000. The Ruritanian Court of Appeal splits 3–2.

✔ APPLICATION · Row by rowDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The issue. As in Riggs: does a clear statute have an unstated exception for someone who brings about the qualifying event by his own wrong?
  • Majority (Earl-style). Parliament cannot have meant to pay people who injure themselves in order to claim. Read the Act with the maxim that no one may profit from their own wrong. Refusing the claim takes nothing Dev already owned; it only stops him acquiring money through his wrong, so it is not an extra penalty.
  • Dissent (Gray-style). The words are plain, and Parliament has taken full control of the scheme. The $2,000 fine is the punishment the law fixed. Withholding $500,000 on top of it adds to his penalty, and that is for Parliament, not for a court's conscience.
  • LP reading. Three options:
    1. the dissent applies the posited text;
    2. the majority's maxim is itself posited common law with moral content, which LP accepts (2.1.4), so the majority can be positivist too;
    3. the Act is silent, leaving a gap the judges fill by discretion.
  • Dworkin reading. Both sides hold morally grounded theories of legislation. The dissent guards a principle of justice: penalties are fixed in advance by the legislature. The majority guards the law's coherence in principle. The disagreement is about what the law is.
  • ALR reading. The judges first decided whether Dev should get the money, then picked the canon (purposive or literal) that fit. The rules could be read either way, so the result came from somewhere else.
  • Liu's two readings.
    • (a) Everyone argued about law, and the majority cited a common-law principle as part of the law, so Dworkin overstates the drama.
    • (b) The real split is between the view that law is always subject to basic moral principles (the majority) and "the law is the law" (the dissent).
    • Either way, neither side kept to the Act's four corners: the dissent's point about fixed penalties is itself a policy and moral argument.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"unstated exception" or "literal v purposive" problems; "judges disagree only about whether to obey".

2.8.2 Applying the McLoughlin card

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
RowMcLoughlin v O'Brian
FactsShe was not at the scene. Hours later, in hospital, she saw her injured family, begrimed. A daughter died.
BelowTrial: shock not foreseeable. CA: foreseeable, but policy confines recovery to those at the scene.
Held5–0, reversing the CA: her shock was recoverable.
Majority on reasonsWilberforce, Edmund-Davies, Russell: policy may limit liability, but not here.
Split on reasonsNo dissent on the result. Scarman: line-drawing policy is "not justiciable". Bridge: stopping at decided cases is "an unwarranted abdication".
LPThe CA, as Dworkin reads it: the precedents ran out, so there was no law, and the task was repair by policy.
DworkinThe force of precedent was disputed. Scarman thought he was "bound by principles embedded in the precedents".
ALRReasons follow results. Yet the grounds split a unanimous House.

Wilberforce's "three elements":

  1. class: close ties of love and affection;
  2. proximity in time and space, including the "aftermath";
  3. means: sight or hearing, not someone else's report.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Video-Call Drowning, revisited (2.5.3)

Same facts as the hypo in 2.5.3; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATION · Stage by stageDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Trial judge. Distinguishes the precedents: shock to a parent in another country is not reasonably foreseeable. The claim fails.
  • Court of Appeal. Given live video, the shock is foreseeable. But policy confines recovery to people physically at the scene; otherwise anyone watching a live stream could sue (a flood of claims, fraud, insurance costs). The claim fails.
  • Top court, 5–0 for Mr Ong. Wilberforce's three elements:
    1. Class: father and son, close ties. Satisfied.
    2. Proximity in time: he saw it as it happened. Satisfied. Proximity in space: he was thousands of kilometres away, and the "aftermath" idea does not obviously cover that.
    3. Means: he saw it with his own eyes, not through someone's report, but on a screen. Whether live video counts as "sight" or is closer to a report is the hard question, so a Wilberforce-type judge must decide where the policy line falls.
  • Scarman-type judge. Where to draw this line is not justiciable. The principle, foreseeable harm to a close relative, decides the case, and Parliament may limit it.
  • Bridge-type judge. Reasonable foreseeability is the test. A line drawn at physical presence would be arbitrary, and stopping at decided cases would be "an unwarranted abdication".
  • LP reading (Dworkin's account of the CA). The precedents ran out, there was no law either way, and the court's job was repair.
  • Dworkin reading. The judges dispute the force of precedent. Are they bound by the principles embedded in earlier cases (Scarman), or only by what those cases held?
  • ALR reading. The result came first, from sympathy for the father, and the reasons followed. But ALR must explain why judges who agreed on the result split so sharply on the grounds. The split suggests the reasons mattered.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"when precedent runs out, judges legislate"; floodgates.

102.9 The conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The sheet's Conclusion: [The statement] is [wrong / partly right]. LP rightly ties law to sources, and Dworkin is unfair to paint it as blind to theoretical disagreement. But naming law is an evaluation, and rival theories split Riggs and the Lords' reasons in McLoughlin, so theory is not optional. A weak NLT earns its keep only at extreme injustice (section 8). Riggs needed no such extreme, only a choice of theory about law's grounds.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Putting the hypos together

Take the statement: "A good lawyer only needs to know what the law says. Legal theory is a luxury."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Concede. Ravi (2.1.3) is right that lawyers must know the sources first, and the fairness clause (2.5.5) shows LP can handle moral tests.
  • But. Professor Lim's "description" of the Land Decree was an evaluation (2.1.2). Dev's payout (2.8.1) and Mr Ong's claim (2.8.2) turn on rival theories of law's grounds. Even the sweet bun (2.6.3) needs a philosophy of bread.
  • Limit. Only the Redheads Act (2.3.2(c)) needs weak NLT's test of extreme injustice. Dev's case needs only a choice of theory.
