HYPO LESSON 3 · ARCHETYPE 3 · ABOUT 29 MIN · 19 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Rule of law and Fuller

⚡ BIG IDEA

The rule of law is a real but thin morality. It binds rulers and comes in degrees, but it cannot guarantee just laws.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 3. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It is the sheet's wording, so it is what you will write in the exam.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 3 of the 7 Nov exam sheet (identical in the Core and Theorist versions). Layout: the rule as the sheet states it, a made-up hypothetical, then the application. Lines tagged STEELMAN, AGAINST, QUALIFY, CONCEDE or JUDGE get their own short hypo, usually a twist on the block's main one. The Exam cue at the end of each block lists the question words that should send you there. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: RF = Radbruch formula; TSH = Tan Seow Hon; † = from the slides.

Fuller's eight desiderata, for reference (Liu W2; section 15.1): generality, promulgation, no abuse of retroactivity, clarity, non-contradiction, possibility of compliance, constancy, congruence between official action and declared rule.

13.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Position: the rule of law is a real but thin morality. It binds rulers and comes in degrees, but it cannot guarantee just laws.

Intro: for Fuller, total failure of one requirement leaves something "not properly called a legal system at all". Short of that, legality is "always a matter of degree". So legality restrains rulers and exposes their aims to criticism, but it cannot make bad laws just.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Islands
  • On Teral Island, the Governor keeps the entire criminal code in a locked safe. No one but him has read it. People are fined and jailed under rules they have never seen.
  • On Brannock Island, the code is published, but a few sections are badly drafted, and one licensing rule is rarely enforced.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Teral is a total failure of promulgation. On Fuller's view it is not a bad legal system but something "not properly called a legal system at all".
  • Brannock has a legal system with some defects. Legality there is "a matter of degree": better or worse, never all-or-nothing.
  • The limit. Publishing Teral's code would not make its content just. Legality makes rulers announce their rules and stick to them, but a published rule can still be wicked.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"the rule of law guarantees justice"; "the rule of law is mere efficiency"; "X is not a legal system at all".

23.1 Ranking

📘 Learn 3.1 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: rank them; not all equally important

3.1.1 Rank by branch of law and kind of rule

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Fuller lets priority vary by branch of law and kind of rule, so rank prospectivity in criminal law first.
  2. Fuller finds the retrospective criminal statute "universally condemned". Non-enforcement of s 377A strained congruence but left the system standing, so congruence for one rule ranks last.
  3. Yet breaches "tend to become cumulative": unclarity "may beget the necessity for retroactive laws". So a low rank never licenses neglect.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Minister's Audit

Ruritania's Law Minister asks you to rank three defects in its law, worst first.

  • (a) A new offence of "online disrespect to officials" has been applied to posts made last year, before the offence existed.
  • (b) One old licensing rule for street buskers is no longer enforced, though it stays on the books.
  • (c) The zoning code is so vaguely drafted that builders cannot tell what is allowed.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • First, (a). A retrospective criminal statute is the breach Fuller says is "universally condemned": people are punished for acts that were legal when done.
  • Last, (b). It is one rule. Officials ignoring it strains congruence, but the legal system as a whole still stands.
  • (c) sits in between, with a warning. Breaches are cumulative: when builders and courts can't tell what the code means, the government will soon need retroactive fixes to sort out the mess. So (c) can't be neglected just because it ranks below (a).

3.1.2 Requirements can conflict: curative retroactivity

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Liu's slide†: the requirements "may be in opposition". The standard example is curative retroactivity: a retroactive law that repairs another failure of legality.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Missing Stamp

Ruritanian law says a marriage certificate is valid only if it carries a state stamp. For six months the printing office runs out of stamps, so 3,000 couples marry with unstamped certificates, and all those marriages are void. Parliament passes a statute validating them retroactively.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The statute breaches non-retroactivity, but it cures earlier failures of promulgation and possibility (the couples could not comply). Here two requirements pull in opposite directions, and the retroactive law serves legality overall. "Curative" is no blank cheque, though: a regime that kills its opponents and then retroactively "validates" the killings is not curing a defect of form.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"rank Fuller's requirements"; "they are not all equally important".

33.2 Unenforced law

📘 Learn 3.2 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: sham; mockery; enforce fully or repeal; moral signpost

3.2.1 Open non-enforcement strains congruence, but isn't a sham

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Calling it "a sham" overstates. Open non-enforcement strains congruence, yet one rule, unlike a whole system, survives rare enforcement.
  2. TSH: the 2007 "overt announcement" "violated Fuller's requirement", but "showcased the competing value" of a symbolic message.
  3. So "enforce fully or repeal" is too stark. The law can exempt the trivial openly, as s 95† does for slight harm.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Midnight Noise Rule

Port Meridian's Public Order Act makes it an offence to play music outdoors after midnight. Many residents want it kept as a statement that the city values quiet; others want it gone. The Minister announces in Parliament: "The law stays as a signal of our values, but police will not proactively enforce it." A critic writes: "This makes the law a sham. Enforce it fully or repeal it."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Not a sham. The gap between the declared rule and what officials do strains congruence. But one rule that is rarely enforced does not collapse the legal system.
  • The trade-off. As TSH said of 2007, the announcement breaches Fuller's requirement but showcases a competing value: the law's symbolic message.
  • A middle path. "Enforce or repeal" ignores a third option: say openly in the law itself what is exempt. The Penal Code's s 95 does this for slight harm. Port Meridian could exempt, say, music below a set volume, so the declared rule and practice match.

3.2.2 STEELMAN: non-enforcement hands power to officials

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Perera: non-enforcement "places too much power in the hands of the Government and the AGC" (Hansard, 28 Nov 2022).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A year later, the police charge a well-known government critic for playing music at 12.30 am. No one else has been charged since the announcement.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This is Perera's worry made real. A law that stays on the books while officials choose when to use it hands them a weapon against people they dislike. That is the strongest argument for the critic's "enforce or repeal".

3.2.3 Tan Seng Kee and Liu's analysis

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Tan Seng Kee (CA 2022)†: the AG's 2018 assurance bound him until he gave clear notice (7.7). Liu (W2) splits the analysis in time:

  • Before the case, non-enforcement was official action, not a rule: a pure gap between law and practice. Treated as prosecutorial discretion, it also hit generality.
  • After it, officials' statements can silently change the law.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The critic in 3.2.2 argues in court that the Minister's announcement bound the police not to prosecute without first giving clear public notice. The court agrees and stops the prosecution.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The gain. The court has closed the gap: the announcement now has legal force, so declared rule and practice line up better.
  • The new cost (Liu). A ministerial statement has changed what the law means in practice without any amendment. A citizen reading the Act would not know this. That hurts clarity and constancy.

3.2.4 CONCEDE: TSH calls it a breach, not a strain

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

TSH is harsher: she calls it a breach, not a strain. Concede the breach, and defend only the trade-off.

✔ APPLICATION · To the Midnight Noise RuleDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Don't argue that there is no defect. Say: "Yes, this breaches congruence, as TSH says. My claim is only that the breach may be worth it for the symbolic value, and that it falls short of making the law a sham."

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"an unenforced law is a sham" or "a mockery"; "enforce it fully or repeal it"; "law as a moral signpost".

43.3 The tyrant, and what makes legality moral

📘 Learn 3.3 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: neither inner nor moral; a tyrant could follow it; guarantees justice; one rule fails

3.3.1 Legality is moral, but thin

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "A tyrant could follow it" is half right. Legality is moral but thin: at minimum it demands rules "however fair or unfair they may be".
  2. It is moral because:
    • reciprocity grounds the citizen's duty to obey;
    • it treats people as responsible agents†;
    • it binds even a self-seeking monarch.
  3. So "legality guarantees justice" fails: wicked aims can run through clear, public rules. Intolerable injustice needs the RF (8.3).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
General Vos's Decree

General Vos takes power in Kessland and wants to entrench himself. He publishes a clear, general, prospective decree: "From 1 March, all political parties other than the National Party are dissolved. Organising for a dissolved party is punishable by two years' jail." Officials enforce it exactly as written.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Half right. A tyrant can follow Fuller's requirements: the decree is general, public, clear and prospective.
  • But legality still did moral work. Because the rule is published in advance, citizens know exactly what will get them jailed, and can choose: comply, protest openly, or leave. That treats them as responsible agents. Vos has also tied his own hands: if he jails someone who did not organise for a dissolved party, he breaks the deal his own decree announced. That bond, reciprocity, is what grounds any duty to obey.
  • Not a guarantee. The decree's content is still unjust. If it were intolerably unjust, legality would not save it, and the question would be one for the RF (8.3).

3.3.2 STEELMAN: "the label seems misapplied"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Liu's slide†: "The label seems misapplied"; the concern "is really with efficacy".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A critic says: "Calling Fuller's eight principles a 'morality' is like saying a poisoner's craft has a morality because a good poisoner uses precise doses."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This is the best objection. A sharp knife is efficient, not moral, whether it cuts bread or a throat. Answer it with 3.3.1's two arguments: unlike sharpness, legality respects the people it governs as agents, and it binds the ruler through reciprocity. Neither of those is true of a poisoner's precision.

3.3.3 AGAINST: inner and outer morality decay together

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Fuller: the inner and outer moralities of law decay together "almost inevitably".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Two years on, Vos finds his own published rules inconvenient. He sets up special tribunals that ignore the code when it suits him, issues secret orders, and backdates new offences.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

As his aims grow more wicked, his respect for legality decays with them. Rulers who pursue evil ends tend to find clear, public, binding rules an obstacle. Fuller's point is that the two moralities rarely come apart for long. That is why a regime with wicked aims that also perfectly obeys all eight principles is rarer than the tyrant objection suggests.

3.3.4 When a single rule fails

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

For a single rule:

  • if it is secret or retroactive, it grounds no moral duty to obey;
  • if it is unclear, it is "less a law";
  • whether it is valid is a question for the RF (section 8), not for Fuller.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Vos issues three more orders: a secret order banning foreign newspapers; a retroactive order making last year's protests a crime; and an unclear order banning "disloyal attitudes".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The secret and retroactive orders: citizens owe no moral duty to obey rules they could not know, or that did not exist when they acted.
  • The unclear order: it is "less a law" than a clear one, because no one can guide their conduct by it.
  • Whether any of them is still law: keep this separate. Fuller speaks to their bindingness; validity is the RF's question (8).

3.3.5 CONCEDE: a regime can meet all eight and still be wicked

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Liu's slide†: a regime can meet all eight requirements and still be wicked. Concede that, but not that legality is morally empty.

✔ APPLICATION · To 3.3.1Decide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Vos's party ban meets all eight and is still wicked. Concede it openly. Then hold the line: legality's moral value (agency and reciprocity) is real even when the content is bad. It just isn't enough.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"Fuller's principles are neither inner nor moral"; "a tyrant could follow them"; "legality guarantees justice"; "what if one rule fails?".

53.4 Discretion

📘 Learn 3.4 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: rule of men; unfettered discretion; enforced only against critics

3.4.1 Only uncontrolled discretion becomes rule by men

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Every grant of discretion is a small surrender" overstates. Only uncontrolled discretion turns law into rule by men.
  2. Fuller condemns a 1934 Nazi statute, "undermined as it is by uncontrolled administrative discretion". Enforcement only against critics comes close to it.
  3. So Singapore's discretion fits legality if it is bounded by law and reviewable.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Gatherings Commissioner

Two cities give officials power over public gatherings.

  • Ruritania: "The Commissioner may ban any gathering he considers undesirable. His decision is final and needs no reasons." In practice he bans only opposition rallies.
  • Brannock: "The Commissioner may ban a gathering likely to cause serious public disorder. He must give written reasons, and his decision may be reviewed by the courts."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Ruritania has uncontrolled discretion: no standard, no reasons, no review, and it is used only against critics. That is rule by men dressed as law, close to the 1934 Nazi statute Fuller condemned, under which prosecution needed the consent of the Leader's representative.
  • Brannock also grants discretion, but bounded by a legal standard ("serious public disorder") and subject to review. That fits legality.

So the question is never "is there discretion?" but "is it controlled?"

3.4.2 JUDGE: review legality, not merits

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

JUDGE: review legality, not merits. Art 35(8)† prosecutorial discretion is subject to Art 12 (Ramalingam†). Liu (W2): discretion erodes generality by degree. Principled restraint is fine; protecting allies and punishing foes is not.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Two people commit the same offence together. The prosecutor charges one with a serious offence and gives the other, the son of a minister, a warning. The charged person seeks judicial review.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A judge should not second-guess the prosecutor's ordinary judgment calls, which would be merits review. But she can ask whether the discretion was exercised lawfully, including consistently with equality before the law (Art 12, as Ramalingam holds). Charging fewer people out of principled restraint erodes generality only slightly. Sparing allies and punishing foes means one law for the favoured, which legality condemns.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"discretion is rule by men"; "unfettered discretion"; "the law is enforced only against critics".

63.5 Mandatory sentences and presumptions

📘 Learn 3.5 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: purest expression of the rule of law; like cases alike
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Mandatory sentences look like "the purest expression of the rule of law", but they buy certainty, not justice.
  2. Fuller: Hart's "justice in the administration of the law" treats like cases alike "by whatever elevated or perverted standards the word 'like' may be defined".
  3. So "leaving nothing to judges" is just only if the line tracks real differences in harm or fault.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The $100 Line

Ruritania's Theft (Mandatory Sentences) Act says: "Any person who steals property worth more than $100 shall be imprisoned for five years." In one week:

  • Lina, a jobless mother, steals $110 of baby formula;
  • Marco, a professional fence, steals $40,000 of jewellery for resale.

Both get five years. The Minister says: "This is the rule of law in its purest form. Like cases are treated alike and judges have no discretion."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Certainty, yes. Everyone knows the sentence in advance.
  • Justice, not guaranteed. The Act treats Lina and Marco as "like" because both crossed $100. As Fuller says, like cases can be treated alike by "elevated or perverted" standards of likeness. Here the line ignores the real differences in harm and fault between them.
  • The test. A mandatory rule is just only if its line tracks real differences in harm or fault. This one doesn't, so its rule-of-law credentials buy predictability at the cost of justice.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"mandatory sentences are the purest expression of the rule of law"; "like cases must be treated alike".

73.6 Rules v standards

📘 Learn 3.6 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: same standard for those who cannot meet it; learner driver; clear rules

3.6.1 The reasonable-man dilemma

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Holding a learner driver to the ordinary standard is Fuller's reasonable-man dilemma. By analogy with strict civil liability, a "surcharge" on risky activity can justify it, but never in crime.
  2. Fuller's antinomy: aloof justice is "bound at times to be harsh", while intimate justice cannot be "evenhanded", so the law tempers the reasonable man.
  3. So "clear rules are always better" overstates. "Good faith" standards can clarify, and specious clarity can harm more than honest vagueness.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Sam's Second Lesson

Sam is on his second driving lesson. He panics at a junction, mounts the kerb and injures a pedestrian. Sam did his honest best, and his best was below what a competent driver would do. The pedestrian sues in negligence. Separately, prosecutors consider charging Sam with careless driving.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The civil claim. Holding Sam to a competent driver's standard asks the impossible of him. Fuller's answer is the surcharge analogy: the law isn't commanding Sam to drive like an expert, but attaching a cost to choosing to enter a risky activity, much as a sales tax attaches a cost to selling. That can justify the ordinary standard in tort.
  • The criminal charge. The surcharge logic does not carry over. Branding Sam a criminal for falling short of a standard he could not meet is exactly what Fuller warns against.
  • The antinomy. Judging Sam by his personal limits (intimate justice) can't be even-handed between drivers. Judging everyone by one objective standard (aloof justice) is sometimes harsh. The law has to tread a middle course.

3.6.2 The cases: Nettleship, Cook, Imbree

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Nettleship v Weston†: a learner owes the ordinary driver's standard. Cook v Cook† lowered the standard where the passenger knew the driver was a learner (later overruled: Imbree v McNeilly, 2008†).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Sam's instructor, sitting beside him, is also injured, and knew perfectly well that Sam was a nervous beginner.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Under Nettleship: the ordinary standard applies, even to a claim by the instructor.
  • Under Cook: a passenger who knew the driver was a learner would be owed only a reasonable learner's care.
  • After Imbree: Cook was overruled, so the ordinary standard is back.

The swing between the cases shows the dilemma at work: the law kept trying different middle courses.

3.6.3 Clear rules are not always better

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Fog Day

On a foggy morning, two possible traffic laws:

  • (a) "Do not exceed 50 km/h."
  • (b) "Drive with due care for the conditions."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Rule (a) is clear, but in thick fog 50 km/h is dangerous, and drivers obeying the rule may think they are safe. That is specious clarity. Standard (b) is vaguer, but everyone understands it, and it tells them what actually matters. Standards like "good faith" or "due care" can be the clearest option. So "clear rules are always better" overstates.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"the same standard for those who cannot meet it"; "learner driver"; "clear rules are always better".

83.7 Authority, reciprocity, crisis

📘 Learn 3.7 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: duty springs from authority; goodwill; crisis; simply majority will

3.7.1 The duty springs from reciprocity, not authority

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "The duty springs from authority" is the command view, which "confuses fidelity to law with deference for established authority".
  2. Reciprocity grounds the duty. Once government finally and completely ruptures it, "nothing is left on which to ground the citizen's duty".
  3. So goodwill cannot be enough: "No single concentration of intelligence, insight, and good will" can secure law's enterprise.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Prime Minister's Speech

Ruritania's Prime Minister tells citizens: "You must obey the law because we are your lawful government, and you can trust our good intentions." Meanwhile, building inspectors routinely let the PM's allies ignore the fire code, while fining everyone else.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Authority isn't the source. The PM treats obedience as owed to him, which confuses fidelity to law with deference to authority. The duty comes from reciprocity: the government asks citizens to follow rules, and implicitly promises to judge them by those same rules.
  • Rupture. Each favour to an ally breaks that promise a little. If the government broke it completely, nothing would be left to ground the citizen's duty.
  • Good intentions don't fix it. However wise the PM is, no single concentration of intelligence and goodwill can secure legality. It needs the cooperation of legislators, inspectors, courts and citizens.

3.7.2 The voter analogy

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Fuller: where officials disregard the rules, "at some point obedience becomes futile", like "casting a vote that will never be counted".

✔ APPLICATION · To the fire codeDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

An honest builder who keeps to the code while allies are waved through is like a voter who knows the count is rigged. Obeying is still possible, but it becomes futile.

3.7.3 AGAINST: "majority will, accurately expressed"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

If someone says law should simply express majority will accurately: tracking a shifting majority breaks constancy, like Rex's daily amendments.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A new party promises "law by daily poll": each week, laws change to match the latest survey.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Citizens could never plan, because the rules would keep moving. Like Rex's daily stream of amendments, a law that changes constantly is worse than no law. So accurately tracking the majority's will is not the same as the rule of law.

3.7.4 QUALIFY: crisis

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Crisis: "grim necessity" may justify hiding a weapons appropriation, but Fuller sees "no emergency" justifying a secret law "creating a new crime".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

During a border crisis, Ruritania's cabinet (i) secretly funds research into a new defence system, and (ii) passes a secret law making it a crime to "assist hostile interests", under which several people are arrested.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (i) can be justified by grim necessity. Secret spending tells no citizen how to behave.
  • (ii) cannot. A secret criminal law punishes people for breaking rules they could never know. Fuller can conceive of no emergency that justifies that.

So "it's a crisis" justifies some secrecy, never secret crimes.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"the duty to obey springs from authority"; "good government needs only goodwill"; "in a crisis, legality must give way"; "law is simply majority will".

93.8 Judge-made law

📘 Learn 3.8 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: never fully prospective; announced after the dispute; retrospective overruling
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Adjudication is partly retrospective, so "can never fully satisfy" holds in form. But a new rule may only confirm "views already widely held".
  2. In civil cases retrospective overruling is a price worth paying: purely prospective rulings would remove a private litigant's incentive to challenge bad precedent.
  3. Crime differs: a retrospective overruling would leave men "branded as criminals" for relying on a judicial interpretation.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Overrulings
  • (a) Civil. A 1990 Ruritanian case held that landlords owe no duty to repair dangerous stairs. In 2026 tenant Clara, hurt on her landlord's stairs, persuades the top court to overrule it.
  • (b) Criminal. In 2020 the top court held that the Betting Act does not cover online fantasy leagues, and thousands of people played. In 2026 it changes its mind.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Partly retrospective in form. Any new judge-made rule is announced after the events it decides, so it can never be fully prospective. But if most people already thought landlords should fix dangerous stairs, the ruling in (a) only confirms views already widely held.
  • (a) should apply to Clara herself. If the court overruled only for the future, Clara would win nothing, and no tenant would bother challenging a bad precedent. Retrospective effect is the price of letting private litigants fix bad law.
  • (b) is different. Applied retrospectively, the new ruling would brand people as criminals for acting on what the court itself told them was legal. In criminal law, the overruling should apply only to the future.

3.8.1 Abdul Nasir: constancy, not "branded as criminals"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Abdul Nasir† (CA 1997): life imprisonment means natural life, but only prospectively (8.6). This engages constancy, not "branded as criminals".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Ruritania's top court rules that "life imprisonment" means the rest of the prisoner's natural life, not 20 years as long assumed, and applies this only to future sentences.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

No one is turned into a criminal for past lawful conduct: the offenders' acts were already crimes. What changed is what an existing sentence means. That is a problem of constancy (the law's meaning shifting over time), which is why prospective application is the fair fix. It is not the "branded as criminals" problem from (b).

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"judge-made law can never be fully prospective"; "it is announced after the dispute"; "retrospective overruling".

103.9 Thin v thick; the Marxist challenge

📘 Learn 3.9 in Lesson 3 →
🔑 Trigger words: ruling-class slogan; instrument of power; whims of officials

3.9.1 Legal form binds rulers too

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Calling the rule of law "a slogan" for class power overstates, because legal form binds rulers too: "law cannot be built on law".
  2. Liu's slide† answers the Marxist: law "has its own character", applying legal criteria "with reference to standards of universality and equity" (on the crits: 9.3).
  3. So thin legality beats "the whims of its officials": published rules give notice and invite criticism.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Eviction Case

A student activist says: "The rule of law is a slogan for the rich. Landlords wrote the eviction laws, and the courts enforce them." The same month, Ruritania's largest property company tries to evict 200 tenants without the 60 days' notice the Act requires. The court rules for the tenants.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • A kernel of truth. The content of eviction law may well favour landlords.
  • But legal form binds the powerful too. Once the rules are law, the court applies them on standards of universality and equity, to the property company as to anyone. The company is bound by the very notice rule its industry wanted. That is law's "own character".
  • Better than whims. Because the notice rule is published, tenants knew their rights and could challenge the company, and anyone can see what the law demands and criticise it. Without published rules, the company and officials would simply do what they liked. So thin legality is worth having, even for critics of the law's content.

3.9.2 STEELMAN (Liu): dragging the monster into the light

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Liu (W2): law drags "the monster out into the light". A regime that nails its colours to the mast can be criticised, organised against and fled, while arbitrary power shows no pattern. Against: rules legitimise and spread evil ("it's the law").

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Compare two regimes persecuting the same minority.

  • Regime A publishes a decree: "Members of group Z may not hold public office."
  • Regime B has no rule at all. Members of group Z are quietly sacked, or disappear, at random.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • For legality (A): Z members know exactly what is being done to them. Outsiders can quote the decree and condemn it, opponents can organise around it, and people can decide to leave in time. Under B there is no pattern to criticise and no way to stay safe.
  • Against legality (A): the decree also lets clerks and neighbours say "it's the law", which spreads and normalises the persecution.

Liu's point is that it's a trade-off, and the visibility argument is on legality's side.

113.10 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Conclusion: the statement is right only in part. Legality binds rulers, respects subjects as agents, exposes their aims to criticism and comes in degrees, so "not a legal system at all" needs total failure. But legality is thin and cannot guarantee just laws. Intolerable injustice is the Radbruch formula's work.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Legality binds rulers: the property company (3.9.1).
  • Respects subjects as agents: Vos's published party ban (3.3.1).
  • Exposes aims to criticism: Regime A's decree (3.9.2).
  • Comes in degrees: Brannock against Teral (3.0).
  • Can't guarantee justice: the $100 line (3.5) and Vos's ban are legal in form and unjust in content.

HYPO LESSON 4 · ARCHETYPE 4 · ABOUT 22 MIN · 14 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Moral objectivity and scepticism

⚡ BIG IDEA

The sceptic's case is inconclusive, and its own demands presuppose moral truth. So the sceptic's conclusion fails. Fallibility calls for deliberation and provisional judgement, not for tolerance as dogma, or silence.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 4. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It is the sheet's wording, so it is what you will write in the exam.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 4 of the 7 Nov exam sheet (identical in the Core and Theorist versions). Layout: the rule as the sheet states it, a made-up hypothetical, then the application. Tagged lines (STEELMAN, AGAINST, TRAP, CONCEDE) get their own short hypo, often a twist on the block's main one. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: TSH = Tan Seow Hon; RF = Radbruch formula; † = from the slides.

14.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Position: the sceptic's case is inconclusive, and its own demands presuppose moral truth. So the sceptic's conclusion fails. Fallibility calls for deliberation and provisional judgement, not for tolerance as dogma, or silence.

Intro: the claim that morality is just opinion, or a social construct, is offered as a reason for tolerance, neutrality, or keeping morality out of law. But that conclusion is itself a moral demand the sceptic cannot ground. Disagreement and unprovability do not show there is no moral truth, and realism demands deliberation, not imposition.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Neutral Committee

A Ruritanian parliamentary committee is asked to decide whether to ban commercial surrogacy. Its chair opens: "Morality is just personal opinion, so this committee must stay neutral and not impose anyone's values."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The chair's "must" is a moral demand: it tells the committee what it ought to do, and binds people who disagree. If morality really were just personal opinion, the chair's demand for neutrality would be just his opinion too, with no more claim on the committee than anyone else's. So scepticism can't deliver the neutrality it promises. The better course: deliberate, hold conclusions provisionally, and demand stronger reasons the more coercive the law.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"morality is just opinion, so…"; "keep morality out of law".

24.1 Map

📘 Learn 4.1 in Lesson 4 →
🔑 Trigger words: just opinion; eye of the beholder; durian; nobody has proved; varies by culture

4.1.1 Sort the sceptic's claim first

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. The statement runs together three different positions:
    • relativism: cultures differ;
    • scepticism: there is no moral standard, or none we can know;
    • non-cognitivism: moral claims are mere sentiment.
  2. On Hume's non-cognitivism, a moral claim is like disliking durian: neither true nor false. Realists hold it can be true or false.
  3. So "nobody has proved it" bites only if proof means deduction, a test that natural science fails too.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four MPs on the Dog-Meat Bill

Ruritania debates a bill banning the sale of dog meat. Four MPs object:

  • MP A: "Whether this is wrong varies from culture to culture."
  • MP B: "There is no moral truth here, or if there is, we can't know it."
  • MP C: "Calling it wrong is like saying I dislike durian. It's just a feeling."
  • MP D: "Nobody has proved it is wrong."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • A is a relativist. Note that cultures differing doesn't show no culture is wrong.
  • B is a sceptic, in either the "no standard exists" or the "we can't know it" version.
  • C is a non-cognitivist, in Hume's way. On this view "it's wrong" is neither true nor false, like a taste. A realist says it is a claim about the act, which can be true or false.
  • D assumes proof means deduction. No one can deduce that the sun will rise tomorrow, yet science is not mere opinion. If deduction were the only proof, natural science would fail the test too.

Sorting the claims first lets you answer each one, instead of fighting a blur.

4.1.2 Liu's replies to the stock lines

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Liu's replies†: "shades of grey" is "not even an argument"; "merely opinions" assumes "the very point being contended".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

MP E adds: "It's not black and white. There are shades of grey. These are merely opinions."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • "Shades of grey" only says the question is hard. That is not an argument that there is no answer.
  • "Merely opinions" assumes that moral views are not statements of fact, which is the very point in dispute. It begs the question.

4.1.3 TRAP: "subjective" isn't "controversial"; moral ≠ legal realism

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

TRAP: "subjective" is not "controversial". Heliocentrism was once controversial, but never subjective. And moral realism is unrelated to legal realism (Liu, W3).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A student writes: "Whether dog meat should be banned is hugely controversial, so it's subjective. Like the legal realists, I think there is no objective answer."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Two errors.

  • Controversy ≠ subjectivity. People once fiercely disputed whether the earth goes round the sun, and there was still a fact.
  • Wrong "realism". Legal realism (ALR: judges decide by preference, then justify) has nothing to do with moral realism (moral facts exist). Mixing them up costs marks.

4.1.4 STEELMAN: Hume was no extreme relativist

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN: Hume seems no extreme relativist.

  • Reason as the "slave of the passions" may mean that shared emotions supply the premises.
  • He held that the rules of justice are "artificial" but "not arbitrary".
✔ APPLICATION · To MP CDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Treat MP C's Hume fairly. Even if moral claims rest on feelings, Hume thought humans share enough feelings that rules of justice are not arbitrary. So "it's just a feeling" does not get MP C to "anything goes".

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"morality is just opinion"; "in the eye of the beholder"; "nobody has proved it"; "it varies by culture".

34.2 Self-refutation

📘 Learn 4.2 in Lesson 4 →
🔑 Trigger words: all moral opinions are equally valid; who are you to judge; intolerant; social construct

4.2.1 The sceptic's demand refutes itself

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. The sceptic's "we must tolerate" or "no one may judge" is itself an objective moral demand, of exactly the kind the statement denies.
  2. A social construct that binds outsiders abandons subjectivism. If that binding rests on equal moral worth, the sceptic is a moral realist (TSH).
  3. So the statement defeats itself. True subjectivism, taken to its end, leaves its adherents no reply to genocide but force.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Banned Speaker

A university society cancels a talk by a visiting speaker who argues that some cultural practices are morally wrong. The society's statement says: "All moral opinions are equally valid. Who is he to judge other cultures? His view is intolerant, and intolerance must not be platformed."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The contradiction. If all moral opinions are equally valid, the speaker's opinion is as valid as the society's, and "intolerance must not be platformed" is just one more opinion. Yet the society treats it as binding on the speaker, who rejects it. That is an objective moral demand.
  • The realist premise. Ask why the speaker must tolerate other cultures. The likely answer, "because everyone has equal moral worth", is a claim that holds for everyone, whatever they believe. That is moral realism.
  • The end point. Imagine instead the speaker's own culture practising genocide. A consistent subjectivist could only say "your norms don't bind me". The other side can say the same back, and only force is left.

4.2.2 CONCEDE: self-refutation settles no content

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE: self-refutation binds only the sceptic who makes demands, and it settles no content. Further debate is "a squabble within the family of moral realists". Concede that realism must still argue for each norm.

✔ APPLICATION · To the Banned SpeakerDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Winning the self-refutation point doesn't show the speaker is right about which practices are wrong. It only shows that both sides are now realists, arguing about content. Each still has to give reasons for its view.

4.2.3 TRAP: TSH's domain is persuasion, not proof

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

TRAP: TSH's domain is moral persuasion, not proof that moral facts exist (Liu, W3). The sceptic who says no one is bound is consistent, but argues for nothing ("True skepticism", W3 slide 8†).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A different student says: "I'm a true sceptic. No moral rule binds anyone, so I make no demands, not even for tolerance."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

TSH's argument has no grip on this student, because the student makes no demands that could contradict themselves. So don't claim TSH proves moral facts exist. Instead show the cost: this student can argue for nothing at all, not even against the society cancelling talks. The position is consistent but useless in a debate about what law should do.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"all moral opinions are equally valid"; "who are you to judge?"; "imposing values is intolerant"; "morality is a social construct".

44.3 Appeals

📘 Learn 4.3 in Lesson 4 →
🔑 Trigger words: nobody can agree; we have been wrong before; it is safer; imposing values

4.3.1 Disagreement and past error

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. That nobody can agree shows that someone is wrong, not that there is nothing to be right about (4.7).
  2. TSH explains disagreement:
    • the mores of the times pervert reason;
    • weakness yields to passion;
    • self-interest, hardened by habit, dulls conscience.
  3. So "we have been wrong before" counsels slowness, not abstention: calling slavery an error presupposes a right answer.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Organ-Market Debate

Ruritania debates legalising the sale of kidneys. One MP argues: "Nobody can agree on this. Fifty years ago we thought homosexuality was a disease; we've been wrong before. It's safer for the law to say nothing."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • "Nobody can agree." If one MP says selling kidneys is wrong and another says it isn't, at least one is mistaken. Disagreement shows error somewhere, not the absence of truth.
  • Why people disagree. TSH explains it: the fashions of the time, weak will, and self-interest. Kidney brokers profit from one answer, and that can dull their judgement.
  • "We've been wrong before." Calling a past view an error assumes there was a right answer that we got wrong. The lesson is to move carefully and keep reasons open, not to refuse to decide.

4.3.2 STEELMAN: humility

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN: humility says the law should coerce only on what is widely shared. Yet that is a realist's case: genuine realism "entails a commitment to deliberation".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

"Only coerce where there's broad agreement" is a sound principle, but it is a moral principle about the limits of coercion, argued for on its merits. A realist can accept it, because a realist who knows they might be wrong deliberates before coercing.

4.3.3 Imposition

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

On imposition: "moral realists are not the only ones who can be bigoted and intolerant".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The MP says: "Realists are dangerous. They impose their values." A sceptic MP then shouts down every speaker who disagrees with legalisation.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Bigotry is a vice of character, not of metaethics. A sceptic can be intolerant, and a realist who holds views provisionally can be very open. So "realism means imposition" fails.

4.3.4 CONCEDE: the realist's weak point is access

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE: the realist's weak point is access. Consensus can err, and in 2007 both camps in the s 377A debate were "persons who think they are right, and absolutely so". Concede that realism settles no case on its own: it demands reasons.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Both sides of the organ-market debate may be equally sure they are right. Realism says one of them is wrong, but not which. So the honest answer concedes that being a realist doesn't settle the kidney question. It just requires both sides to give reasons rather than declare victory.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"nobody can agree"; "we have been wrong before"; "it is safer to stay out"; "imposing values".

54.4 Is–ought

📘 Learn 4.4 in Lesson 4 →
🔑 Trigger words: Hume showed; no ought from is; biology tells us nothing; studies show; natural; so legislators should

4.4.1 Facts alone settle nothing; facts plus an agreed ought do

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Hume's gap holds: the biological facts alone cannot settle whether a practice should be legal.
  2. Finnis draws no ought from facts. The basic goods are self-evident, and facts such as embryology show only how they apply.
  3. So "it tells us nothing" overstates: once an ought-premise is agreed, the facts fix the stakes.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Embryologist's Evidence

A committee on embryo research hears from Dr Ihara: "At about 14 days, the primitive streak forms." Two MPs react.

  • MP F: "So the law should allow research up to 14 days."
  • MP G: "Biology tells us nothing about what the law should be."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • MP F jumps the gap. The fact about the primitive streak doesn't, on its own, tell anyone what to do. MP F needs a moral premise, such as "research is permitted before a human individual exists", and hasn't stated it.
  • MP G overstates. If the committee agrees on an ought-premise, such as human life is a basic good that must not be directly attacked (Finnis), then embryology becomes crucial: it tells them when a human life is present, and so what is at stake in each kind of research.
  • Finnis's route. He doesn't derive "life is good" from biology. The good is self-evident, and the biology only shows how it applies.

4.4.2 Hume's two arguments, and the replies

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Hume's two arguments†:

  1. Wrongness lies "not in the act but in our sentiments", because reason knows only relations of ideas and matters of fact ("Statement X").
  2. There is no "ought" from an "is".

AGAINST, the replies:

  1. † "Is Statement X self-refuting?" Statement X is itself neither a relation of ideas nor a matter of fact, so by its own test it is neither true nor false.
  2. The gap is only logical. Agreed ought-premises (for example "the dignity of man") plus facts do yield oughts.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

MP G presses on: "Hume showed that only maths and facts can be true. Morality is neither, so it is just sentiment."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Turn Statement X on itself. "Only relations of ideas and matters of fact can be true" is not maths, and it is not an observable fact. By its own test, it is neither true nor false, so it can't show anything.
  • The gap is narrow. Hume shows you can't deduce an ought from facts alone. He does not show that facts are irrelevant once an ought-premise, such as human dignity, is shared.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"Hume showed you can't get an ought from an is"; "biology tells us nothing"; "studies show, so legislators should"; "it's natural".

64.5 Hidden judgement

📘 Learn 4.5 in Lesson 4 →
🔑 Trigger words: consensual and harms no one else; not wrong; victimless; the state should stay neutral

4.5.1 "Consensual and harmless, so not wrong" is a moral verdict

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Calling X not wrong because it is consensual and harms no one else is a moral verdict, not a neutral fact.
  2. The hidden premise is the primacy of autonomy, which rests on equal worth.
    • Unlimited, autonomy leaves everyone "equally worthless".
    • Limited, it is a moral law (TSH).
  3. So "the law should stay neutral" fails. Where harm stops, and whose consent counts, are moral choices. There is no "Switzerland of ambivalence" (Thio, 2007).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Kidney Contract

Ravi, deep in debt, agrees to sell a kidney to a wealthy buyer for $50,000. A columnist writes: "It's consensual and harms no one else. So it's not wrong, and the state should stay neutral."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • A moral verdict. "Consensual and harmless, so not wrong" is not neutral. It applies a principle: adults may do as they choose unless they harm others.
  • The hidden premise. That principle, the primacy of autonomy, rests on everyone's equal moral worth. If autonomy were unlimited, anyone could do anything to anyone, so everyone would be equally worthless. Once we add limits (bodily integrity, no exploitation), we have a moral law.
  • The choices hidden in "neutral". Is Ravi's consent real when he is desperate? Does "harm" include the long-term risk to Ravi himself, or the pressure on other poor people to sell? Answering those questions takes moral sides. Staying "neutral" means accepting the columnist's answers, so there is no Switzerland of ambivalence.

4.5.2 Finnis's charge

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Finnis's charge: appealing only to "what people subjectively prefer", then grounding that in the value of self-governance, is "outright self-contradiction".

✔ APPLICATION · To the columnistDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If the columnist says "the law should respect whatever people prefer, because self-governance is valuable", the second half is an objective value claim. The columnist has undercut "it's all subjective preference" in the act of defending it.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"consensual and harms no one else"; "victimless"; "not wrong"; "the state should stay neutral".

74.6 Whatever is enacted?

📘 Learn 4.6 in Lesson 4 →
🔑 Trigger words: law is whatever people say is law; whatever Parliament enacts; separation is safer

4.6.1 Nothing above the lawgiver

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. If law is whatever is enacted, nothing stands above the lawgiver. Liu asks whether that makes man "the ultimate lawgiver"† over his fellows.
  2. Saying citizens are safer if law may have any content is itself a moral claim about safety, liberty and power.
  3. So natural law stays a touchstone for criticising what is enacted, without denying that merely unjust enactments are law.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Citizenship Act

A commentator argues: "Law is whatever Parliament enacts. Keeping law separate from morality keeps citizens safe from moralising judges." Parliament then passes, by proper procedure, an Act stripping citizenship from anyone who criticises the government three times online.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Nothing above Parliament. On the commentator's view, the Act is law, and there is no higher standard by which to call it a defective law. The legislators become the ultimate lawgivers over their fellow citizens.
  • "Safer" is a moral claim. Safer for whom? The critics who lose their citizenship are not safer. The commentator is weighing safety, liberty and power, which is moral argument, not neutral description.
  • The touchstone. Natural law lets us say the Act falls short of what law should be. That does not mean every merely unjust law stops being law. Only the extreme case might (8).

4.6.2 Alexy: only the strong connection thesis risks legitimation

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Alexy: only the "strong" connection thesis risks uncritical legitimation. The weak one (the RF) keeps law open to critique. Hart's case for separation: 8.2.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The commentator replies: "If you tie law to morality, people will think every law is moral, and stop criticising."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • True of the strong thesis. If every law were necessarily moral, then calling something law would bless it.
  • Not true of the weak thesis. The RF says only that intolerable injustice is not law. Everything below that line is law and fully open to moral criticism. So the weak connection doesn't silence critics. (For Hart's own case for separation, use 8.2.)
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"law is whatever people say is law"; "whatever Parliament enacts"; "separating law and morality is safer".

84.7 The objectivity anchor (the reusable paragraph)

📘 Learn 4.7 in Lesson 4 →
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The paragraph, in its moves:

  1. Demanding tolerance or deference because morality is "just opinion", "personal" or "a social construct" defeats itself: the demand binds others, which abandons subjectivism.
  2. If the demand rests on equal moral worth, the sceptic is a moral realist.
  3. Disagreement no more disproves moral facts than disputes over the number of planets. The unproven is not the false.
  4. Refusing to act on a moral judgement may amount to acting on its opposite, so keeping morality out is itself a moral choice.
  5. Realism demands deliberation and provisional judgement, not imposition (TSH).

Where the sheet uses it: 4.1–4.3 and 4.5 (just opinion; nobody can agree; it is safer); 11.7 (personal morality; private conscience); 6.10 (equally valid); 7.5 (neutral); 10.4 (no one can say objectively).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Judge Who Keeps Morality Private

A judge hears a challenge to a law allowing landlords to refuse tenants of a particular religion. He writes: "Morality is personal, and judges may not disagree with Parliament about it, so I take no moral position." He upholds the law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the paragraph's moves on him.

  • Self-defeat. "Judges may not impose their morality" is itself a moral rule, binding on every judge, whatever they believe.
  • The realist premise. Why mustn't judges impose? If the answer is "because citizens have equal moral worth and deserve equal respect", he is a realist.
  • Disagreement. That people disagree about religious discrimination doesn't show there's no answer.
  • Refusing to judge is judging. By "taking no position" and upholding the law, he lets the discrimination stand. That is acting as if it were acceptable.
  • The better path. Deliberate, give reasons, and hold the judgement provisionally.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

any statement that relies on morality being subjective in order to reach a practical conclusion.

94.8 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Conclusion: the statement fails, or is overstated. Scepticism cannot deliver the tolerance, safety or neutrality it promises, since that promise is itself a moral norm, and its reasons are "inconclusive", though that proves no moral fact. The realist's weak point is access, not existence: consensus can err, and in 2007 both camps claimed moral truth. So hold moral judgements provisionally, and demand more of them the more coercive the law.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The promise is a norm: the Neutral Committee (4.0) and the Banned Speaker (4.2.1).
  • "Inconclusive" proves no fact: concede, with TSH's domain point (4.2.3), that refuting the sceptic doesn't prove moral facts exist.
  • Access: in the organ-market debate (4.3.4), both sides were sure.
  • More coercion, more demand: a criminal ban on selling kidneys needs stronger reasons than a regulatory licence would.

⚡ BIG IDEA

Finnis gives legislators real limits on the issue, and leaves much to prudence.
