Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 5 of the 7 Nov exam sheet (identical in the Core and Theorist versions). Layout: the rule as the sheet states it, a made-up hypothetical, then the application. Tagged lines get their own short hypo, often a twist on the block's main one. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: PR = practical reasonableness; TSH = Tan Seow Hon; † = from the slides. Requirement numbers in brackets, such as [7], are Finnis's nine requirements as listed in 5.2.

15.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Position: Finnis gives legislators real limits on the issue, and leaves much to prudence.

Intro: the statement assumes a theory of the good must either dictate how citizens live, or offer no guidance at all. Finnis shows a third path:

  • seven basic goods and nine requirements of practical reasonableness yield a few absolute limits, such as never intending to kill the innocent;
  • they also yield a common good that is a framework, not a life-plan.

Within those limits legislators choose prudently, and reasonable people may differ.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Bills on the Order Paper

Ruritania's Parliament has three bills before it:

  • (a) the Assisted Dying Bill, letting doctors give lethal injections on request;
  • (b) the Online Falsehoods Bill, letting a minister order corrections to false online statements;
  • (c) the Museums Bill, funding free entry to national museums.

A commentator says: "Finnis either tells Parliament exactly how everyone must live, or he's no help at all."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Finnis does neither.

  • (a) hits an absolute limit. Authorising doctors to kill intentionally, even on request, chooses directly against the basic good of life, so it is barred.
  • (b) is for prudence. Truth is a basic good, and deliberate falsehoods damage it, so the state may act. How, weighing chilling effects on free speech, is a judgement on which reasonable legislators differ.
  • (c) is facilitation. Free museums help citizens participate in knowledge and aesthetic experience. Whether to fund them, and how much, is a prudent choice, not a duty.

So the theory gives real limits, (a), and leaves wide room for prudence, (b) and (c).

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"Finnis would have the state dictate how citizens live"; "Finnis offers law-makers no guidance".

25.1 Goods and priorities

📘 Learn 5.1 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: basic goods; obviously good; just taste; rank the goods; golfer

5.1.1 Self-evident goods, no objective ranking

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Finnis's seven basic goods are self-evident, not inferred. Anyone reflecting on why they act can grasp a good such as knowledge as good "in itself".
  2. The goods are "all equally fundamental, though you can prioritise"†: "there is no objective hierarchy amongst them".
  3. So life-plans, not the state, rank the goods, and "the state must do the ranking" does not follow.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Culture Minister's Ranking

Ruritania's Culture Minister announces: "Knowledge matters more than play. From next year, all public arts and sport funding goes to universities. Playing football is a waste of a citizen's time."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • No objective ranking. For Finnis, knowledge and play are both basic goods, equally fundamental. Neither is objectively higher.
  • Prioritising is for life-plans. A scholar may reasonably put knowledge first; a footballer may reasonably put play first. The ranking depends on each person's temperament, capacities and opportunities.
  • So the Minister's premise fails. He assumes that because goods must be ranked, the state must rank them for everyone. Finnis gives the ranking to each person's plan of life. The state's job is to keep the conditions in which they can pursue their own (5.5).

5.1.2 The golfer

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Golfer: passing a drowning stranger is "indifference to the good of others whom one could easily help".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Ah Seng loves golf, and has made play his top priority. On the 7th hole he sees a child struggling in the water hazard. Helping would cost him two minutes. He plays on, saying: "Golf is my priority. That's my life-plan."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Having priorities is fine. Using them to ignore someone you could easily save is not. That is indifference to the good of others whom one could easily help, and it breaches [3], no arbitrary preference among persons. A life-plan ranks your own pursuits; it doesn't license treating another person's life as worthless.

5.1.3 The seven goods, and Liu's test

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The seven goods (W4 slide 3†): life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness and "religion". For "religion", "agnostic or negative" answers count.

The goods are pre-moral: morality comes in with the nine requirements. Liu's test (W4): strip out every use a good has for the other goods. Is something still left?

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A student says: "Play isn't a basic good. It's just a way of keeping healthy (life) and making friends (sociability)."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run Liu's test. Picture someone alone, playing a game of patience at midnight. It does nothing for their health and involves no friends, yet it still has a point: the game is enjoyed for its own sake. Something is left after the instrumental uses are stripped out, so play passes the test.

Note also that "religion" here isn't church membership. An atheist who has thought hard about their place in the universe, and concluded there is no God, participates in it.

5.1.4 QUALIFY: Liu's answers to four objections

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Liu (W4) answers four standard objections:

  • gossip is low-grade knowledge;
  • suicide shows life's deprivation, not its rejection;
  • lacking a good does not unmake it;
  • pleasure is an aspect of the goods, not their point.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

At a seminar, four objections are raised:

  • (i) "People love gossip. Is that the good of knowledge?"
  • (ii) "Some people choose to die. So life isn't good for everyone."
  • (iii) "My uncle has severe dementia and can't reason. So practical reasonableness isn't a universal good."
  • (iv) "Play is just pleasure."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (i) Gossip is still knowledge, just a low grade of it. Low participation is still participation.
  • (ii) People who want to die are usually suffering, already deprived of the good of life. That doesn't show that fuller life wouldn't be good for them.
  • (iii) The uncle lacking the good doesn't stop it being a good. That is exactly why the goods need protecting.
  • (iv) Play is enjoyable, and pleasure is one aspect of it. But a game can still be worth playing on a day it isn't fun, so pleasure isn't the point.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"who says these are goods?"; "it's just taste"; "the state must rank the goods"; the golfer.

35.2 The nine requirements as structure

📘 Learn 5.2 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: plan of life; detachment; commitment; efficiency; transpose to a legislature
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Nine requirements of practical reasonableness structure the pursuit of the goods. Most transpose to a legislature, though a state has no single life-plan (5.5).
  2. All nine bind together, each "fundamental, underived, irreducible". To Liu they read as prudent advice: neglecting (4) or (5) looks unwise rather than immoral (W5).

The nine:

  1. a coherent plan of life;
  2. no arbitrary preference among values;
  3. no arbitrary preference among persons (the Golden Rule);
  4. detachment: no fanatical policy;
  5. commitment: keep faith;
  6. efficiency, within reason (5.4);
  7. respect every basic value in every act (5.3);
  8. the common good (5.5);
  9. conscience.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Parliament's Year

Ruritania's Parliament, over one year:

  1. adopts a five-year legislative programme;
  2. passes a budget that funds roads and factories but cuts every library and park, with no stated reason;
  3. exempts MPs from a new tax that applies to everyone else;
  4. pursues "zero road deaths at any cost", banning all driving after dark;
  5. abandons a promised pension reform the moment it becomes unpopular;
  6. buys the cheaper of two equally good hospital IT systems;
  7. authorises police to torture a suspect to find a bomb;
  8. maintains courts, roads and schools so citizens can pursue their own plans;
  9. lets MPs vote against the whip where conscience forbids a bill.
✔ APPLICATION · Requirement by requirementDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Plan: the programme is the state's version of a coherent plan, but only a framework, since a state has no single life-plan for its citizens.
  2. Values: cutting every library and park with no reason arbitrarily discounts knowledge and aesthetic experience.
  3. Persons: exempting MPs is self-preference: they wouldn't accept it if others did it to them.
  4. Detachment: "zero deaths at any cost" is fanaticism. It gives one project (road safety) a weight only a basic value deserves, and crushes the rest.
  5. Commitment: dropping the pension reform at the first resistance fails to keep faith.
  6. Efficiency: choosing the cheaper equal system is efficiency within reason.
  7. Every value in every act: torture chooses directly against a basic good, which is barred whatever the stakes (5.3).
  8. Common good: maintaining the conditions of citizens' own pursuits is the common good as a framework (5.5).
  9. Conscience: no MP should vote for what they judge wrong.

Liu's doubt. Breaches (4) and (5) look unwise rather than immoral. Finnis would reply that each requirement is fundamental and irreducible, and binds along with the rest.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"apply Finnis's requirements to a legislature"; detachment; commitment; plan of life.

45.3 Absolutes and double effect

📘 Learn 5.3 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: shoot one hostage; scientist; a foreseen death is just as dead

5.3.1 Never take life "directly as a means"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. The seventh requirement yields absolutes, such as never taking life "directly as a means". So shooting one hostage to free ten is barred.
  2. Acts are individuated primarily by intention. Damaging a good as a means or an end differs from damaging it as a side effect. But plans cannot be characterised "ad lib".
  3. So "a foreseen death is just as dead" misses the point. Side effects are judged too, by fairness and commitments, not by a sum.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Bank Siege

A gunman holds eleven hostages in a bank. He tells the police commander: "Shoot that hostage, and I release the other ten. Refuse, and I kill all eleven." The commander refuses. Later the same day, in a separate incident, police shoot at a getaway car to stop it, knowing the hostage in the back seat may well be hit.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The demand to shoot is barred. Shooting the hostage is an act that, of itself, does nothing but kill an innocent person. The release of the ten would come from a separate, later act: the gunman's own free choice. Killing as a means is absolutely barred, whatever the numbers.
  • The car is different. The police intend to stop the car. The risk to the hostage is a side effect, not their aim. And they can't simply redescribe their plan however they like: if they aimed at the hostage to make the car stop, that would be killing as a means.
  • "A foreseen death is just as dead." True, but beside the point. Side effects aren't free: shooting at the car must still pass fairness. Would the commander think it reasonable if he were in the back seat? Was there another way? It is judged by those tests, not by adding up lives.

5.3.2 The scientist

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Scientist†: intending only knowledge, he takes a living person's heart. Even as a side effect, the death is "impermissible because unfair".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Dr Reyes wants to study a healthy beating heart. He removes one from a living, unconsenting patient. He says: "I don't intend the death. I only want the knowledge. The death is a side effect."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Grant him the description: his end is knowledge, his means is removing the heart, and death is a certain side effect. It still fails, because side effects are judged by fairness. No one would accept being killed for someone else's research, so the act is impermissible because unfair. Double effect is not a loophole.

5.3.3 The pregnancy cases

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Pregnancy cases† (as applied):

  • chemotherapy, or removing a cancerous womb, treats the mother, and the death of the unborn child is a side effect;
  • direct termination intends the death;
  • pre-eclampsia is hard (the sheet's own reading).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A hospital ethics committee has four files:

  • (i) a pregnant woman with aggressive cancer needs chemotherapy that will probably end the pregnancy;
  • (ii) a woman has a cancerous womb that must be removed while she is pregnant;
  • (iii) a woman requests a termination because the pregnancy is unplanned;
  • (iv) a woman has severe pre-eclampsia, and only delivery or termination will save her.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (i) and (ii) treat the mother's disease. The death of the unborn child is foreseen but not intended, so these are permissible if fair.
  • (iii) intends the death as the means to ending the pregnancy, so it is barred.
  • (iv) is hard. The "treatment" is the ending of the pregnancy itself, so it is difficult to say the death is merely a side effect. Say so in the exam rather than forcing an answer.

5.3.4 QUALIFY: Liu's verdict

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Liu (W5): the line is "honestly pretty artificial":

  • it is out of step with our intuitions, which is odd for principles claimed to be self-evident;
  • it is a poor guide when facing an attacker;
  • it heavily limits autonomy, since consent cures nothing.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A homeowner is attacked with a knife at 2 am. Finnis says she may act to disarm or deter, even foreseeing that the attacker may die, but may not aim to kill. A terminally ill man begs his doctor for a lethal dose, and is refused.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Can the homeowner really sort "aiming to disarm" from "aiming to kill" in two seconds? And the dying man's consent changes nothing for Finnis. Those are Liu's three criticisms in action. Use them to evaluate Finnis, while keeping his exposition and your critique distinct.

5.3.5 TRAP: double effect is Aquinas's; intention, not foresight

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

TRAP:

  • Double effect is Aquinas's. For Finnis, the casuists' doctrines "are not themselves the principles of practical reasonableness".
  • The line is intention, not foresight: a certain death can still be a side effect (W4 slide 9†).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Two errors to avoid in the exam:

  • don't call double effect "Finnis's ninth requirement", or say it is [7]. It is an older summary of hard cases, which Finnis treats as a useful reminder, not a principle;
  • don't say a side effect must be uncertain. The scientist (5.3.2) knew the death was certain, and it was still a side effect. What made it wrong was unfairness.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"shoot one hostage to save ten"; "a foreseen death is just as dead"; the scientist; abortion and medical cases.

55.4 Against utilitarianism

📘 Learn 5.4 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: greatest happiness; whatever makes them happy; maximise preferences; healthcare savings

5.4.1 "Not so much false as senseless"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Finnis calls the greatest happiness "intrinsically incoherent and senseless" outside "limited technical contexts". The goods are incommensurable, so act- and rule-utilitarianism are "not so much false as senseless".
  2. So maximising satisfied preferences is reasonable only inside the other requirements, as efficiency, and never as the measure of right.

Also on the sheet:

  • "Over a wide range of preferences and wants", maximising is reasonable. But sadists' preferences are discounted, and "certain intentional killings, frauds" are excluded.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Happiness Ministry

Ruritania creates a Happiness Ministry with one rule: "Adopt whatever policy produces the greatest total satisfaction of citizens' preferences." In its first month it faces three choices:

  • (i) which of two equally good bus routes to build;
  • (ii) whether to let a popular TV show stage real fights in which unwilling prisoners are hurt, because millions enjoy watching;
  • (iii) whether to secretly poison one terminally ill patient so his organs can save five others.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (i) Maximising is fine. Within a definite goal (getting people to work), comparing routes by how many people they serve is a technical calculation Finnis accepts.
  • (ii) The viewers' sadistic preferences don't count. The requirements discount them. No number of viewers outweighs that.
  • (iii) Excluded outright. It is an intentional killing, outside what any cost–benefit calculation may consider.
  • The deeper point. The Ministry's rule assumes life, friendship and knowledge can all be converted into one currency of "satisfaction" and added up. For Finnis that is like summing "the size of this page, the number six, and the mass of this book". The goods are incommensurable, so the calculation is not false but senseless.

5.4.2 The experience machine

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Nozick's experience machine, against pleasure as the point of it all: a sensible person "would not choose to plug into the experience machine at all", because "one wants to do certain things".

QUALIFY, Liu (W4): the class split about 14–10, so intuition is a fragile proof. Finnis needs only that turning the goods into units of pleasure loses something.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A start-up offers the "LifePod": plug in for life and you'll feel you are living a perfect life, writing novels and making friends, but none of it is real. A poll of law students finds 58% would plug in.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Finnis's claim: no sensible person would plug in, because we want to actually do things and be a certain kind of person, not just have the experiences.
  • Liu's worry: if 58% would plug in, the "obvious" intuition isn't obvious. Gambling on it is risky.
  • The rescue. Finnis doesn't need everyone to refuse. He needs only that something is lost when friendship or real achievement is converted into units of pleasure. Even a student who plugs in can accept that.

5.4.3 STEELMAN: efficiency is real, but life is not a cost

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN: efficiency is "a real requirement", so healthcare savings matter. But life is a basic good, not a cost to net off.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The Health Ministry proposes (a) switching to a cheaper but equally effective cancer drug, and (b) a rule that patients over 80 are never offered dialysis, "because the money saves more life-years elsewhere".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) is efficiency within reason, which Finnis accepts. Resources are limited.
  • (b) treats some people's lives as a cost to net off against others'. That converts life into units and drops a whole class of people from consideration, so it fails efficiency's limits, and [3] (no arbitrary preference among persons).
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"the greatest happiness of the greatest number"; "give people whatever makes them happy"; "maximise preferences"; healthcare savings.

65.5 From person to state

📘 Learn 5.5 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: transpose to the state; common good; minimal framework; online falsehoods; closer to liberalism

5.5.1 The common good is a set of conditions

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Finnis's common good is "a set of conditions" enabling members "to attain for themselves reasonable objectives".
  2. A state is no ship bound for one port: "Committing oneself to a life-plan is not at all like setting oneself to bake a cake".
  3. Yet it is "definite enough to exclude a considerable number of types of political arrangement, laws, etc.", so the claim that Finnis gives "almost no guidance" understates him.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ship of State

A Ruritanian party proposes a "National Life Plan": every citizen is assigned a career at 16, must attend state cultural events monthly, and must marry by 30. Its leader says: "A state is like a ship. It must steer everyone to one destination."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • No single destination. Finnis's common good is the conditions in which each person can pursue their own reasonable objectives: courts, roads, schools, public order. It is not a destination the state steers everyone towards.
  • Not like baking a cake. A life-plan isn't a project with one finished product, so there is no single plan the state could impose.
  • Still definite. The common good is definite enough to rule out the National Life Plan: assigning careers and forcing marriage destroy the very conditions in which people pursue their own goods. So Finnis gives real guidance: he excludes many kinds of law.

5.5.2 LEGISLATOR: Liu's working summary

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Liu's working summary†:

  1. law is a framework;
  2. it should facilitate the goods;
  3. public authorities must never intend to damage them;
  4. they may prohibit acts that do;
  5. then prudence (hate speech, fake news), weighing chilling effects "in particular places"†.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Online Falsehoods Bill

Port Meridian proposes a law letting a minister order the takedown of "false statements of fact" online.

✔ APPLICATION · Step by stepDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Framework: the state isn't deciding what citizens should believe. It is protecting conditions for public knowledge.
  2. Facilitate: a healthy flow of true information serves knowledge, sociability and practical reasonableness.
  3. Never intend damage: the state itself must not spread falsehoods or suppress truth.
  4. May prohibit: deliberate lies spread to deceive damage knowledge, so prohibiting them is justifiable in principle.
  5. Prudence: a broad ministerial power may chill honest speech. Whether that risk is serious depends on "particular places": how independent the courts are, how the power is likely to be used, and what review exists.

Finnis gives the frame; the final call is prudential.

5.5.3 CONCEDE: Finnis is less liberal than he looks

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE: Finnis is less liberal than he looks: the state must "favour the basic forms of good and ... discourage their contraries". Concede that he is not neutral. The state still keeps only peace and justice.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A liberal critic says: "So Finnis's state is basically neutral." Then Port Meridian taxes casinos heavily, funds marriage counselling, and bans the sale of hard drugs, citing the goods.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Finnis would let the state favour the goods and discourage what damages them, so he isn't neutral, and you should concede it. But even so, his state's role is limited to peace and justice. It is not making citizens integrally good, which is the job of families and churches. So he sits between strict liberal neutrality and a state that dictates virtue.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"transpose Finnis to the state"; "the common good"; "a minimal framework"; online falsehoods; "Finnis is closer to liberalism than he seems".

75.6 Human nature: urges or ends?

📘 Learn 5.6 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: human nature; follow nature; urges; live in the moment

5.6.1 Urges are not goods

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Following nature" can mean obeying urges or pursuing ends. The Stoics saw man as having "natural essences or ends", known by "the reflective intellect".
  2. Finnis infers nothing from urges. Many, like "the urge to gratuitous cruelty", answer to no good, and there is "no inference from fact to value".
  3. So "law should give people what they want" mistakes urges for goods: it is "unreasonable to live merely from moment to moment, following immediate cravings".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The 24-Hour Licence

A minister proposes letting bars serve alcohol 24 hours a day: "People clearly want to drink late. It's human nature. The law should follow nature and give people what they want."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Urges versus ends. The minister reads "nature" as "urges". The classical tradition reads it as the ends that reason can grasp.
  • No inference from urges. That people want something doesn't make it good. Some urges, like the urge to gratuitous cruelty, answer to no good at all. And Finnis draws no "ought" from facts about wanting.
  • Living in the moment. A law built on immediate cravings encourages exactly the life Finnis calls unreasonable: living moment to moment rather than by a coherent plan. The minister must argue that late drinking serves a good (play, sociability) and that the costs to others are justified. "People want it" isn't an argument.

5.6.2 Seligman and Tierney; Liu on the life-plan

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Seligman and Tierney: minds built for prospection fit the life-plan judged from one's death, but cannot ground it. Liu (W4): the plan sets policies ("greens at every meal"), not a deathbed test for each lunch. Finnis borrows Rawls's "rational plan of life".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A student says: "Finnis wants me to imagine my deathbed every time I choose lunch. That's absurd."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Liu's answer: the plan works through general policies. Decide once, "I eat healthily, so every meal includes greens", and lunch settles itself. And the psychology fits, since we are built to steer by imagined futures. But fitting our psychology doesn't prove the plan is reasonable: facts about how minds work can't ground an "ought" (5.6.1).

5.6.3 CONCEDE: Harris on facts and reflection

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE: Harris asks, of reflecting on our inclinations: "are not assumptions of fact about human nature inevitably going to form part of the content of the reflection?". Concede the mixture. Harris still calls it "reasoning" (16).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Finnis says we grasp the goods "from the inside", through our inclinations, without inferring them from facts. Harris's point is that facts about human nature inevitably feed into that reflection. Concede it: Finnis's method isn't fact-free. But it is still a form of reasoning, not mere feeling.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"follow human nature"; "give people what they want"; "live in the moment".

85.7 Finnis tested

📘 Learn 5.7 in Lesson 5 →
🔑 Trigger words: critically evaluate; self-evident; who decides; is gambling play?
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Finnis's weak points are his method and the seventh requirement:
    • self-evidence rests on intuitions shaped by upbringing;
    • the means/side-effect line is "artificial" (Liu, W4–5);
    • and accessible is not the same as accepted (is casino gambling play?).
  2. He replies that there is "no magic in the number seven", and that dissent may be "inculpably erroneous", not "perfectly reasonable".
  3. So concede to Rawls that reasonable disagreement limits what the state may coerce, even where Finnis is right about the good.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Casino Licence

Port Meridian considers licensing a second casino. Supporters say: "Gambling is play, a basic good. Finnis would back it." Opponents say: "It's not play; it's addiction and greed. Finnis would ban it." Both sides claim the goods are "self-evident".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Self-evidence under strain. Both sides find different things obvious, partly because of their upbringing. That is the weakness in Finnis's method.
  • Accessible ≠ accepted. The goods may be accessible to everyone's reason, but citizens plainly don't accept the same view of whether casino gambling is play.
  • Finnis's replies. The list is flexible ("no magic in the number seven"). And people who disagree may simply be mistaken without being blameworthy: "inculpably erroneous".
  • The concession to Rawls. Even if Finnis is right that compulsive gambling damages the goods, the depth of reasonable disagreement counsels restraint in using the criminal law. Regulating (licensing, limits, levies) may be more defensible than banning.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"critically evaluate Finnis"; "are the goods really self-evident?"; "who decides?"; "is gambling play?".

95.8 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Conclusion: Finnis gives legislators real limits: never intend to destroy a basic good, never treat one as worthless, and secure conditions in which each citizen pursues his own plan. Beyond that, the issue calls for prudence. And since his self-evidence rests on contested intuitions, and his means/side-effect line is, for Liu, artificial, disagreement about the goods counsels restraint in coercion. The statement is overstated: Finnis guides law-makers without dictating to them.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Never intend to destroy a good: the Assisted Dying Bill (5.0) and the bank siege (5.3.1).
  • Never treat one as worthless: the Culture Minister (5.1.1) and the over-80s dialysis rule (5.4.3).
  • Secure the conditions: the Ship of State (5.5.1).
  • Prudence: the Online Falsehoods Bill (5.5.2).
  • Restraint in coercion: the Casino Licence (5.7).

Hypos: Pluralist legislation, Rawls v Finnis

⚡ BIG IDEA

No law on the issue is neutral. Its reasons must be accessible to every citizen, sound on the merits and fitted to circumstances.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 6. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It is the sheet's wording, so it is what you will write in the exam.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 6 of the 7 Nov exam sheet (identical in the Core and Theorist versions). Layout: the rule as the sheet states it, a made-up hypothetical, then the application. Tagged lines get their own short hypo, often a twist on the block's main one. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: OC = overlapping consensus; OP = Original Position; TSH = Tan Seow Hon; † = from the slides.

16.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Position: no law on the issue is neutral. Its reasons must be accessible to every citizen, sound on the merits and fitted to circumstances.

Intro: the statement asks Parliament to take no side, or to rest only on grounds every citizen shares. Rawls rightly requires reasons each citizen could accept. But his neutrality is a neutrality of justification, not of outcome: permitting X still takes a moral side. Accessible is not the same as accepted, and process rests on substance. A law's reasons must be open to all, sound, and prudently fitted to circumstances.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Surrogacy Bill

Ruritania is deciding whether to allow commercial surrogacy. The Minister says: "Citizens deeply disagree, so Parliament will take no side. We'll simply allow it, and each citizen can decide for themselves."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Allowing it is a side. Permitting commercial surrogacy settles, for the law, that paying a woman to carry a child is acceptable. Opponents see the "neutral" option as a defeat.
  • What Rawls can rightly demand. Whatever Parliament decides, its reasons should be ones every citizen could accept, such as protecting women from exploitation or children's welfare, not "my faith forbids it" or "my philosophy of autonomy requires it".
  • What else is needed. The reasons must also be sound (true claims about exploitation and welfare) and fitted to Ruritania's circumstances (how its clinics and courts actually work).
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"the state should take no side"; "only grounds every citizen can share".

26.1 Rawls

📘 Learn 6.1 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: grounds every citizen can share; majority; civility

6.1.1 More than a majority, less than unanimity

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Rawls asks more than a majority, and less than unanimity. Power is legitimate only under constitutional essentials all citizens "may reasonably be expected to endorse".
  2. Public reason binds:
    • judges "more strictly";
    • officials and candidates;
    • citizens, when voting as if they were legislators;
    • on constitutional essentials and basic justice, "so far as possible". It never binds churches or the media.
  3. So "civility, not justifications" inverts Rawls. Civility is a moral duty to justify. When officials and citizens follow public reason, the majority's enactment is "legitimate law".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Who Must Give Public Reasons?

During Ruritania's surrogacy debate, five people speak:

  • (i) a bishop, in a sermon, says surrogacy offends God;
  • (ii) a newspaper editorial calls opponents "dinosaurs";
  • (iii) an MP, in the House, argues it exploits poor women;
  • (iv) a judge, striking down a regulation, cites her religious convictions;
  • (v) a citizen, alone in the voting booth, votes in a referendum on his faith's teaching alone.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (i) and (ii) are free. Churches and the media belong to the "background culture", which public reason doesn't bind.
  • (iii) is doing it right. Exploitation of poor women is a political value any citizen could accept.
  • (iv) breaks it most seriously. Public reason binds judges "more strictly".
  • (v) breaks it too. When voting, Rawls asks citizens to think as if they were legislators, and give only public reasons.
  • The result. If the officials and voters do follow public reason, then whatever the majority enacts is legitimate law, even for those who lost. That isn't unanimity (some will still disagree), but it is more than a bare majority (the reasons must be ones all could reasonably accept).

6.1.2 AGAINST: Finnis's dilemma

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST, Finnis's dilemma (W5b slide 3†):

  • read predictively, the test ("may reasonably be expected to endorse") gives "a particularly gross form of veto";
  • read normatively, it judges the merits, as calling rationalist believers "mistaken" does.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A small, loud group says it will never endorse any surrogacy law at all.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Predictive reading. If "may reasonably be expected to endorse" means "will in fact agree", that group has a veto over the law, which is absurd.
  • Normative reading. If it means "ought, if reasonable, to agree", then Rawls must judge whether the group's objection is any good. That is a judgement on the merits, which his theory claimed to avoid.

Either way, Rawls's test is in trouble.

6.1.3 QUALIFY: TSH and Finnis on majorities

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY:

  • TSH: Rawls "surely does not mean to equate public reason with majority views". So he must show that pro-choice votes are not unreasonable.
  • Finnis: excluding moral truth leaves the gravest questions to "sheer power of numbers" (14.10).
✔ APPLICATION · To surrogacyDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If the bill passes 60–40, that alone doesn't show it rests on public reason. Rawls must still show the losing side's arguments weren't reasonable. Otherwise, as Finnis says, it's just numbers.

6.1.4 The basis of Rawls's view

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The basis: Rawls's deepest divide is between the view that there is one reasonable good (from Plato to Aquinas, "the dominant tradition") and reasonable pluralism. Political power is "the power of free and equal citizens as a collective body".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Rawls's whole test starts from the claim that reasonable people will always disagree about the good life. If you share the older view, that reason can find one true good, you'll find his test too timid. That divide, not any single issue, is where Rawls and Finnis really part.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"only grounds every citizen can share"; "the majority decides"; "civility".

36.2 Not neutral

📘 Learn 6.2 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: takes no side; neutral fact

6.2.1 "Taking no side" takes a side

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "The state takes no side" is a moral position. Even Rawls concedes that "our actions nevertheless imply" a view on salvation.
  2. Even Rawls's filter is moral. "Unreasonable" means refusing fair terms of cooperation, not being false, and who counts as reasonable is the very dispute (6.11).
  3. So neutrality is unattainable. Even MOE's "secular" sexuality curriculum "reflects the national posture on the heterosexual family" (Masagos, 2022).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Religion-Free Curriculum

Port Meridian's schools decide to "stay neutral" by never mentioning religion in class: no teaching about any faith, and no religious holidays marked.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Not neutral in effect. A child taught for twelve years as if religion didn't matter learns something about religion. Rawls himself concedes that what the state does implies a view on salvation, even if it doesn't intend one.
  • The filter is moral. If a group objects and Port Meridian calls it "unreasonable", that judgement rests on a moral standard: willingness to accept fair terms.
  • Every curriculum has a stance. As the Masagos line shows, even a "secular" curriculum reflects some view, there of the family.

6.2.2 AGAINST: Finnis on method

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST, Finnis on method: Rawls's "thin theory" of the good is "arbitrary", a "radical emaciation of human good". What the Original Position rejects is not thereby unjust.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A Rawlsian planner says: "Behind the veil of ignorance, no one would choose principles that favour friendship or art, so the state may give them no special value."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The thin theory. Finnis replies that counting only liberty, opportunity, wealth and self-respect as goods, and treating knowledge, play and friendship as of no account, is not neutral. It is an impoverished view of the good.
  • The veil proves less than claimed. Even if principles chosen behind the veil are fair, principles not chosen there aren't shown to be unjust.

6.2.3 TRAP: "unreasonable" ≠ false

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

TRAP:

  • A doctrine holding "outside the church there is no salvation" may be true. It is unreasonable only because it "proposes to use the public's political power" to enforce itself.
  • Tolerance need not be a tenet of a doctrine. The doctrine need only not be hostile to reciprocity (Liu, W6).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Two churches in Port Meridian each teach "outside our church there is no salvation". Church A campaigns to make its doctrine the law. Church B teaches it to members but accepts equal rights for all.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Don't write that Rawls calls Church A's doctrine false. He doesn't. Church A is unreasonable because it wants state power to enforce its doctrine on others. Church B, with the same belief, is reasonable: it doesn't preach tolerance as a doctrine, but it isn't hostile to fair terms.

6.2.4 AGAINST: liberal neutrality favours the already-established

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST, slide 9†: liberal neutrality favours doctrines already "institutionally and socially reinforced". Rawls: political liberalism is "itself a moral conception".

✔ APPLICATION · To the curriculumDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A "neutral" curriculum built around individual choice suits the views most already at home in Port Meridian's institutions, and those of people who value choosing among ways of life. Faiths that see life as received rather than chosen are disadvantaged. Rawls's own reply concedes that his view is a moral one.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"the state takes no side"; "permitting it is neutral"; "it's a neutral fact".

46.3 Overlapping consensus v modus vivendi

📘 Learn 6.3 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: what the faiths share; overlap of convictions; modus vivendi

6.3.1 The OC is not Devlin's shared morality, and not a truce

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Legislating what the faiths share" is Devlin's shared morality, not Rawls's OC. The OC is a consensus of reasonable doctrines on a political conception of justice.
  2. Each doctrine affirms that conception on its own moral grounds, so it holds "regardless of shifts in the distribution of political power", as a modus vivendi cannot.
  3. So the OC is no "modus vivendi in philosophical dress", though "reasonable" decides who belongs.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Settlements on Kessland Island

Kessland Island has two faith communities, the Arans and the Belts.

  • 1950: after a civil war, they sign a treaty giving each equal worship rights. Each side signs only because it can't win. Each says privately it would suppress the other if it could.
  • 2026: both communities teach equal religious liberty. The Arans say God gave everyone free conscience. The Belts say forcing belief is unfair. A census shows the Arans will soon be 70% of the population, and they say nothing would change.

A politician proposes: "Let's make law out of whatever the two faiths' teachings share."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • 1950 is a modus vivendi. It rests on a balance of power and would collapse when power shifts.
  • 2026 is an overlapping consensus. Each community affirms equal liberty on its own moral grounds, and the test is whether it survives a power shift. The Arans' answer shows it does.
  • The politician has Devlin, not Rawls. "Whatever the faiths share" is shared morality, which could include all sorts of moral rules. Rawls's OC is only about a political conception of justice.
  • The catch. Who counts as a "reasonable" doctrine eligible for the consensus is decided by Rawls's own standard (6.11).

6.3.2 QUALIFY: Finnis on the abortion "consensus"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, Finnis: pro-choice writers share no view of the unborn, so there is no "overlapping consensus" except in the result.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If three pro-choice writers reach the same law by three incompatible routes about what the unborn is, they agree only on the outcome. That is closer to a coalition than to a consensus on principle.

6.3.3 The OC is on principles, not reasons; tolerance works outside it

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • The OC is on principles, not reasons. The Golden Rule can be held as divine teaching or as reciprocity (Liu, W5). Secular doctrines join too (Kant, Mill).
  • Tolerance works outside the overlap: "I may be right, yet legislating it would be unfair" (Liu, W6).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

An Aran also believes alcohol is sinful, a view the Belts don't share.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Inside the overlap: both communities agree on equal liberty, for different reasons. That is enough.
  • Outside it: the Aran's view on alcohol isn't in the overlap. Tolerance means saying: "I may be right that drinking is wrong, but making it a crime would be unfair to the Belts." So the Aran keeps the belief, but doesn't legislate it.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"legislate what the faiths share"; "an overlap of convictions"; "it's just a modus vivendi".

56.4 Sorting reasons

📘 Learn 6.4 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: whose morality is admissible; four MPs

6.4.1 By kind, by motive, by merit

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Rawls and Finnis differ on more than whose morality is admissible:
    • Rawls sorts reasons by kind;
    • Chua (Singapore's 1969 Health Minister) sorted them by motive;
    • Finnis and TSH sort them by merit.
  2. Rawls treats secular comprehensive arguments "the same way" as religious ones, but admits Catholic common-good views "expressed in terms of political values".
  3. So the lines blur. In TSH's Catch-22, religious reasons would fail Rawls's test, while Chua dismissed medical ones as a facade. That is a test "more far-reaching than Rawls's".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four MPs on Assisted Dying

Ruritania debates legalising assisted dying. Four MPs oppose it.

  • MP A: "Scripture says life is God's gift; only He may take it."
  • MP B, a strict Kantian: "Killing is always wrong, because persons are ends in themselves."
  • MP C, a Catholic: "Legalising it will pressure the elderly and disabled to die, and weaken the trust between doctors and patients."
  • MP D, a devout believer, cites medical studies on palliative care. The Minister dismisses her: "Your studies are a facade for your religion."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Rawls (by kind): A and B both argue from comprehensive doctrines, one religious, one secular, and both fail public reason, equally. C passes: although C is Catholic, the argument is expressed in political values (protecting vulnerable citizens, the doctor–patient relationship). D's studies are public reasons too.
  • Chua (by motive): the Minister rejects D because of D's faith, whatever her argument. That excludes even public reasons, which is more sweeping than Rawls. It is TSH's Catch-22: religious arguments fail, and non-religious arguments from religious people are written off as a facade.
  • Finnis and TSH (by merit): ask whether each argument is good. Are C's and D's claims about pressure and palliative care true?

6.4.2 CONCEDE: merit-sorting rests on disputed premises

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE, Rawls: sorting by merit rests on disputed premises. TSH replies that process too rests "on substantive values". Concede that merit settles truth, not coercion (5.7).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even if MP B's Kantian argument is sound, judging it so is a contested call, which is Rawls's point. TSH's reply is that Rawls's own process also rests on contested values. Concede both: being right about the merits doesn't by itself justify coercing those who disagree.

6.4.3 Liu on what public reason is not

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Liu (W6):

  • a bad reason is not a non-public one;
  • a motive is not the justification;
  • a Kantian's "all lying is wrong" is barred too;
  • public reason moves with the background culture.
✔ APPLICATION · To the four MPsDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • MP C's argument might be weak, but weak doesn't mean non-public.
  • MP D's motive (faith) is not her justification (the studies).
  • MP B is barred like MP A, so public reason isn't anti-religious.
  • As views in the wider society shift, what counts as a public reason can shift too.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"whose morality is admissible?"; "four MPs"; "religious arguments in Parliament".

66.5 Abortion

📘 Learn 6.5 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: nobody can say when life begins; stand aside; free not to have one; slavery; compromise

6.5.1 A permissive law is not neutral

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "A permissive law is neutral" fails. Chua said learned men "have not been able to agree", then declared that an early conception "is not a human being".
  2. If nobody can say when life begins, then TSH's hunter (after Brown), unsure what moves behind a bush, should not fire.
  3. So Parliament cannot stand aside: permission "settles the metaphysical question". Argue for limits from accessible consequences.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Late-Limit Bill

Ruritania's Health Minister proposes allowing abortion on request up to 24 weeks. In the debate she says: "Experts can't agree when life begins, so Parliament won't take a view. Women who object are free not to have one." In the same speech she adds: "In any case, a 12-week foetus is not yet a human being."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • She settled what she said couldn't be settled. Like Chua in 1969, she says no one can say when life begins, then says a 12-week foetus isn't a human being.
  • The hunter. If we really don't know whether the foetus is a person, the cautious course is not to fire. A hunter who shoots at movement in a bush without checking it isn't a person is irresponsible.
  • Permission settles the question. The law forbids killing the innocent. Permitting abortion therefore treats the foetus as not an innocent person in the relevant sense. Standing aside is not available.
  • The constructive route. An opponent can still argue for limits from reasons any citizen could accept: health risks, how often late terminations are actually needed, support for adoption.

6.5.2 Rawls's two positions, and Finnis's reply

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Rawls first called a doctrine denying the first-trimester "qualified right" "to that extent unreasonable". He later said Catholics "need not exercise" the right, by then accepting arguments against the right, framed in political values, as public reason. For Finnis, "need not exercise" is a slave-owner's reply: "mere impudence or thoughtlessness".

✔ APPLICATION · To the Minister's "free not to have one"Decide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Finnis's point is that this answers nothing for someone who believes the foetus is a person. It is like telling an abolitionist "you needn't own slaves". The objector's concern isn't their own conduct but the victim.

6.5.3 AGAINST: TSH on Macedo's "middle ground"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST, TSH: Macedo's "fairly close call" middle is no neutral midpoint; it stems from non-cognitivism. A pro-life middle (a ban, plus aid to women, easier adoption, and penalties on providers rather than women) "would be rejected by pro-choicers", as she reports Wolfe and George.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A backbencher proposes a "compromise": abortion on request to 16 weeks, then only for medical reasons. Another MP proposes a different "compromise": a ban, plus full support for pregnant women, easier adoption, and penalties only on providers.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Each side calls its own proposal the middle. TSH's point is that any "middle" assumes how much the unborn's life weighs against the woman's choice. So "split the difference" is not a neutral position. It already takes a view of the question.

6.5.4 AGAINST: Finnis turns reciprocity on Rawls

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST, Finnis turns reciprocity on Rawls. Children reared for paedophiles and killed painlessly in their sleep plainly fail reciprocity. So he asks "why Rawls draws the boundary of justice, fairness and reciprocity at birth", and why "the child a week before birth" faces "the uttermost coercion".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Rawls's reciprocity is meant for free and equal citizens. But Finnis's horrifying example shows we think justice covers people who can't yet take part, such as young children. So why stop at birth? A foetus a week before birth and a newborn a week after differ mainly in location. Rawls owes a reason for the line.

6.5.5 CONCEDE: TSH on who counts as human

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE, TSH: our consensus on human worth "does not currently extend to the details of who is entitled to be treated as human". Argue for circumspection, not victory.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even a strong pro-life argument can't claim the debate is won. Everyone agrees humans have equal worth, but they disagree about who counts. So the honest conclusion is caution: hesitate before declaring the question settled, either way.

6.5.6 TRAP: Finnis's article is not an argument that abortion is wrong

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

TRAP (Liu, W6): Finnis's article is no argument that abortion is wrong. It tests Rawls's promise of fair terms that don't settle deep questions. Rawls and Reiman assume the unborn is not a person; otherwise it would be owed fair terms.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In an exam, don't write "Finnis proves abortion is murder". Write: "Finnis shows that Rawls's 'neutral' permissive answer quietly assumes the unborn is not a person, so it doesn't sidestep the deep question." That is the method critique the article makes.

6.5.7 Slide 7's decision tree

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Slide 7†'s decision tree:

  1. Is the unborn a clump of cells?
  2. If not, must the woman "house" it (Thomson's violinist)?

Either branch settles a moral question. Finnis: Thomson lends such views a "reasonable" status they lack.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A pro-choice MP says: "Even if the foetus is a person, no one can be forced to use her body to keep another alive. If you woke up plugged into a famous violinist's kidneys, you could unplug."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The first branch ("just cells") answers the metaphysical question directly.
  • The violinist argument tries to avoid it, but it still makes a moral claim: that the woman has no obligation to house even a person. Either way, a moral answer is given.
  • Finnis adds that Thomson's argument, which he calls a bald assertion, gets treated as more reasonable than it is.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"nobody can say when life begins"; "the state should stand aside"; "you're free not to have one"; "slavery"; "compromise".

76.6 Finnis for law-makers

📘 Learn 6.6 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: never v should; rank the goods
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The sheet says only "See 5". Use the archetype 5 file: absolute limits (5.3), no state ranking of the goods (5.1), and prudence (5.5).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Quick hypothetical

An MP says "Finnis says the state must never allow X, and should always promote Y". Sort it:

  • "never" belongs to the absolutes of [7], such as never intending to kill the innocent;
  • "should" belongs to prudence and facilitation;
  • and the state doesn't rank the goods for citizens.

86.7 Religion

📘 Learn 6.7 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: religious arguments; faith condemns it; exemption

6.7.1 Religious arguments aren't barred for being religious

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Public reason bars no argument for being religious. The Good Samaritan may be cited, if public reasons follow "in due course".
  2. Finnis's basic good of religion, open to "agnostic or negative" answers, supports religious freedom. Rawls protects it because denying basic liberties "normally" breaks reciprocity.
  3. So "ban it because a faith condemns it" fails, though TSH warns that a "national interest" test may leave religion "little practical impact".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Bystander Bill and the Tattoo Ban
  • (a) An MP introduces a bill requiring bystanders to call emergency services when they see someone injured. She opens with the parable of the Good Samaritan, then argues that it would save lives and costs bystanders almost nothing.
  • (b) Another MP proposes banning tattoo parlours "because my faith teaches that marking the body is sinful".
  • (c) A religious minority asks for an exemption from a new law, so it can keep its traditional head-coverings in court.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) passes. Citing scripture is allowed, provided public reasons follow in due course. Here they do: lives saved, at trivial cost.
  • (b) fails. "A faith condemns it" is not a reason every citizen could accept.
  • (c) has support from both theorists, for different reasons. For Finnis, religion is a basic good, open even to agnostic answers, that the state should respect. For Rawls, denying basic liberties like religious freedom normally breaks reciprocity.
  • TSH's warning. If every law must serve "national interest and collective good", religious perspectives may in the end have little practical effect, even when they are allowed to be voiced.

6.7.2 TSH: "is this begging the question?"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

TSH: political values render religious perspectives "nugatory" wherever an issue counts as metaphysical. Whether an issue is political is itself contested (polygamy), as Liu's slide asks: "Is this begging the question?" (W5a slide 7†).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A man asks Ruritania to recognise his polygamous marriage. The government says: "Marriage is a political matter, the orderly reproduction of society, so only political values count." He replies: "For me, marriage is a religious matter, and my faith permits it."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Whether marriage is "political" is exactly what's in dispute. Labelling it political settles the question against the religious view before any argument begins. That is TSH's point, and the slide's question.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"religious arguments have no place"; "ban it because a faith condemns it"; "exemption".

96.8 The whip

📘 Learn 6.8 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: party discipline; conscience; one clear voice
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. A whipped House "may not be representative of the majority opinion" (TSH), so "one clear voice" need not show what justice requires.
  2. For TSH, lifting the whip "on certain occasions" is "an option", with each member encouraged to see his role "in deciphering higher law". Another option is judicial.
  3. So a free vote serves conscience, not necessarily public reason. Treating s 377A as "policy", not conscience (Shanmugam, 2022), is itself a moral judgement.

Also on the sheet: precedent: abortion free votes in 1969 and 1974, "arguably an endorsement" of considering religious perspectives (TSH).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Euthanasia Vote

Ruritania's ruling party holds 80% of seats. Its leaders whip MPs to vote for an assisted dying bill: "The House must speak with one clear voice." Several MPs privately believe the bill is gravely wrong. The leader says: "This isn't a conscience issue. It's health policy."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • One voice isn't the majority's voice. A whipped 80% may not reflect what most MPs, or citizens, actually think, so the result doesn't show what justice requires.
  • Lifting the whip is an option. TSH suggests letting MPs vote freely on certain occasions, each considering their role in working out what the higher law requires. Singapore did so on abortion in 1969 and 1974.
  • A free vote serves conscience. It doesn't guarantee public reason: MPs voting freely might still give only religious reasons.
  • "Policy, not conscience" is itself a judgement. Calling the bill mere "health policy" decides that it raises no grave moral question, which is a moral call in itself.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"party discipline"; "a conscience vote"; "Parliament must speak with one clear voice".

106.9 Close

🔑 Trigger words: make people better
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Moral truth, not neutrality, limits legislation. But "the law's task is to make people better" overreaches.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Improvement Act

A minister proposes an "Improvement Act": every adult must read one approved book a month and attend a monthly ethics class, "because the law's job is to make people better".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Moral truth does limit law. Finnis's absolutes are real (5.3), and neutrality is impossible anyway (6.2).
  • But this overreaches. Even Finnis's tradition gives the state a limited role: to keep peace and justice, not to make people integrally good. That is for families, churches and individuals. And forcing virtue undercuts the very practical reasonableness it aims at, since you can't make someone good by compulsion.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"the law's task is to make people better".

116.10 Aim and mechanism

📘 Learn 6.10 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: equally valid; objectively necessary; wrongdoer; only then; fixed conception of the good life

6.10.1 The aim and the mechanism come apart

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. The statement's aim (not imposing a fixed conception of the good life) and its harm-to-others mechanism come apart.
  2. The mechanism is:
    • not necessary, since Hart's paternalism answers defective consent, not immorality (7.2);
    • not neutral, since Rawls files Mill's liberalism among the comprehensive doctrines.
  3. So the statement keeps its aim only by dropping its mechanism. Finnis supplies substance, Rawls discipline, Hart a presumption against coercion.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Draft Constitutional Clause

A reform commission proposes: "Because all moral opinions are equally valid, the state shall not impose any fixed conception of the good life. Only when conduct harms others is coercion objectively necessary against the wrongdoer, and only then may the law intervene."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The aim is fine. Not imposing one way of life on everyone is a reasonable goal.
  • The mechanism isn't needed for it. The state can avoid imposing a way of life and still pass some protective laws, such as a cooling-off period for payday loans. As Hart shows, that kind of paternalism protects people whose consent may be defective; it doesn't impose a view of the good life (7.2).
  • The mechanism isn't neutral. "Only harm to others counts" is Mill's liberal philosophy, which Rawls himself classes as one comprehensive doctrine among others.
  • Keep the aim, drop the mechanism. Use Finnis for the substance of what law protects, Rawls for the discipline of giving public reasons, and Hart for a presumption against coercion.

6.10.2 The loaded words

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The statement's own words carry hidden commitments:

  • "Objectively" presupposes moral realism;
  • "wrongdoer" presupposes a wrong;
  • "others" raises who counts (6.5);
  • "equally valid" defeats itself (4.7).
✔ APPLICATION · To the clauseDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The clause says opinions are equally valid, then speaks of what is "objectively necessary" against a "wrongdoer". That assumes there are objective wrongs. And "harms others" leaves open whether the unborn, animals or future generations are "others". Each word assumes what the clause's opening sentence denies.

6.10.3 Liu's model: read the sentences as a chain

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Liu's model (W9): read the sentences as a chain. Sentence (2) is the means to (1), and "only then" makes it the only means.

  • Finnis: there is a range of valid opinions, not one, and protecting others is a ground for coercion, not the only one.
  • Rawls: "equally valid" holds a priori, and not for unreasonable doctrines.
  • Critics: toleration is itself imposed.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Answer the clause link by link:

  • Is "not imposing a way of life" (1) best served by "only harm to others" (2)?
  • Is (2) the only way?
  • Finnis says there are other grounds.
  • Rawls says "equally valid" can't extend to unreasonable doctrines.
  • Critics say the clause imposes toleration while claiming to impose nothing.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

multi-sentence statements with "equally valid", "objectively necessary", "only then", "wrongdoer", "fixed conception of the good life".

126.11 Freestanding yet overriding

📘 Learn 6.11 in Lesson 6 →
🔑 Trigger words: freestanding; overriding; contradictory
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Freestanding" means derived from no comprehensive doctrine, not value-free: the conception is "political (but of course moral)".
  2. On constitutional essentials and basic justice, political values normally override, because they are "very great values", governing "the basic framework of social life". Reasonable doctrines can support them, and the cooperative virtues are "political capital".
  3. So there is no contradiction for the reasonable. But for dissenters, the label "reasonable" does the overriding, and TSH asks what standard grounds it.

STEELMAN: Masagos echoes Rawls: decisions apply "secular, universal values and not individual religious beliefs" (2022). Even Finnis agrees in part: 14.10.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Overridden Believer

Jun, a devout citizen, says: "Rawls claims his political values are 'freestanding', independent of my faith. Yet on basic questions they override my faith. How can something independent of my beliefs have authority over them? It's contradictory."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • "Freestanding" isn't "value-free". The political conception doesn't come from any one religion or philosophy, but it is openly moral.
  • Why it overrides. It governs the basic framework within which everyone lives together, and the values at stake (fair cooperation, equal liberty) are very great. Jun's own faith may well endorse them for its own reasons, which is the OC. Then there's no contradiction: Jun accepts the override from inside his faith.
  • The real problem. If Jun's faith does not endorse them, Rawls calls him "unreasonable", and that label does the overriding. TSH asks what standard justifies the label. If it isn't just majority opinion, it looks like an objective moral standard of the kind Rawls says he avoids.
  • The steelman. Singapore's ministers speak the same way ("secular, universal values"), so the idea has real-world appeal.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"freestanding"; "overriding"; "Rawls's view is contradictory".

136.12 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Conclusion: the statement is wrong, overstated or partly right. Rawls rightly demands coercion justifiable to every citizen, and his "unreasonable" condemns refusing fair terms, not error. But neutrality cannot deliver it: any law on the issue takes a moral side, as Finnis's abortion test case shows. Pluralism asks equal respect for persons, not equal validity for opinions. Reasons must be accessible, sound and prudently fitted to circumstances.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Justify coercion to all: who must give public reasons (6.1.1).
  • "Unreasonable" ≠ wrong: Church A and Church B (6.2.3).
  • Neutrality fails: the Surrogacy Bill (6.0) and the Late-Limit Bill (6.5.1).
  • Persons, not opinions: Jun (6.11) deserves respect even if his view is rejected.
  • Accessible, sound, fitted: MP C's argument (6.4.1), tested on its merits and on Ruritania's facts.
