HYPO LESSON 7 · ARCHETYPE 7 · ABOUT 32 MIN · 20 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Enforcement of morals

⚡ BIG IDEA

Every answer to whether law should enforce morality, repeal included, takes a moral stand. The real question is which reasons justify which degree of coercion.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 7. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It is the sheet's wording, so it is what you will write in the exam.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 7 of the 7 Nov exam sheet (identical in the Core and Theorist versions). Layout: the rule as the sheet states it, a made-up hypothetical, then the application. Tagged lines get their own short hypo, often a twist on the block's main one.

Some blocks (7.4–7.7, 7.11) are about Singapore's real s 377A debates. For those, the hypo is either an invented analogue (Ruritania's old law against unmarried cohabitation), with a "Singapore link" line in the application, or a columnist's claim about the real events that you test against the sheet's facts. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: TSH = Tan Seow Hon; † = from the slides.

17.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Position: every answer to whether law should enforce morality, repeal included, takes a moral stand. The real question is which reasons justify which degree of coercion.

Intro: the statement treats harm, autonomy or majority feeling as a neutral test of when law may coerce. None is neutral, because what counts as harm, and whose feelings count, are moral questions. The issue is which reasons justify how much coercion.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Veridine

A new hallucinogen, "veridine", becomes popular in Ruritania. Parliament has three options:

  • (a) jail anyone who uses it;
  • (b) allow sale only on prescription;
  • (c) do nothing, since "the state should take no side".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Every option takes a stand. (a) says the state may punish people for what they do to themselves. (b) says it may protect people whose choices may be impaired, without punishing them. (c) says neither reason is good enough. Each answer rests on a moral view.
  • Match reasons to coercion. Jail, (a), needs the strongest justification; prescription-only, (b), a lesser one. So the question is not "enforce morality: yes or no?" but which reason supports which level of coercion.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"should law enforce morality?"; "harm is the only neutral test".

27.1 Harm as plain fact

📘 Learn 7.1 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: Wolfenden got it right; only harm to others; plain matter of fact; a sham

7.1.1 Harm is not a plain fact

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Harm is a plain matter of fact" fails. What counts as harm, and who counts as an "other", are moral questions.
  2. Hart's real question is whether the bare fact that positive morality condemns X is any reason to punish it.
  3. So "the quarrel is a sham" fails. Both sides moralise, but they hold "divergent critical principles" (Hart), not merely rival moral codes.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Bare-Knuckle Club

In a warehouse, consenting adults hold private bare-knuckle fights. Broken jaws and concussions are common. No one under 21 is admitted, and no spectators are allowed. A committee member says: "Wolfenden got it right. Harm to others is a plain matter of fact, and here there's none, so the law has no business here. The rest of this debate is a sham, because everyone is just moralising."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Not a plain fact. Is a broken jaw that the fighter consented to "harm to others"? What about a fighter's children, who depend on his income, or the public hospital that treats him? Whether those count is a moral choice, not something you observe.
  • Hart's real question. It isn't whether the fights are wrong, but whether the bare fact that most Ruritanians condemn them is any reason to punish them.
  • Not a sham. Yes, both sides argue morally. But they disagree about critical principles, such as whether liberty may be restricted without harm, not just about which acts are wrong. That is a real dispute.

7.1.2 STEELMAN: liberty as a value

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN: Mill: "over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign"†. Hart: liberty may be "a value in itself".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The strongest case for the fighters is that it is their bodies and their risk. Freedom to choose, even badly, has value in its own right, and lets people experiment with how to live. Make this case before attacking it.

7.1.3 AGAINST: what concerns others?

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST:

  • Liu: what "concerns others? Everything?"†
  • Wolfenden itself guards decency and the vulnerable.
  • Devlin: Wolfenden's own bans on "corruption" presuppose a public morality.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The club's defenders also want the law to ban anyone under 21 from fighting, and to ban recruiting "vulnerable" young men from homeless shelters.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Almost everything concerns others, at some remove: families, hospitals, the young men who watch. So "only harm to others" doesn't draw a sharp line.
  • Even the defenders protect morality. Their own rules (protecting the young, banning the exploitation of vulnerable recruits) are exactly what Wolfenden did. Devlin's point is that a ban on "corrupting" the young only makes sense if society has a view about what is corrupt. So Wolfenden's approach already presupposes a public morality.

7.1.4 TRAP: this is not a debate about positivism

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

TRAP: this is not positivism. Hart and Devlin agreed the laws were law, and argued about what the law should be. Hart's thought is modular, so a positivist could back Devlin (Liu, W7, W9).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Don't write "Hart, as a positivist, rejects legal moralism". Positivism is a theory of how to identify law. Whether the club should be banned is a question about what law should be, and a positivist could take either side.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"Wolfenden got it right"; "only harm to others"; "harm is a plain matter of fact"; "the Hart–Devlin quarrel is a sham".

37.2 Paternalism, and the offence line

📘 Learn 7.2 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: protect adults from themselves; sale and consumption; offensive; public decency

7.2.1 Hart's paternalism protects defective consent

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Never protect adults from themselves" is Mill's anti-paternalism, pushed to lengths Hart says "may now appear to us fantastic".
  2. Hart's paternalism protects defective consent, not virtue. It supports restricting sale, not obviously jailing the user it is meant to protect.
  3. So "the line is easy to draw" fails. Paternalism and offence both turn on whose choices and feelings count.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Veridine, revisited (7.0)

Parliament debates two clauses: Clause 1 bans the sale of veridine except on prescription. Clause 2 makes using it punishable by jail. A Millian MP says: "Adults must never be protected from themselves, so both clauses are wrong."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The Millian view looks extreme today. Hart says Mill's anti-paternalism can now look "fantastic". People choose from transitory desires, with clouded judgement, under subtle pressure. Consent obtained that way is defective.
  • Clause 1 fits Hart. Restricting sale protects buyers whose consent may be impaired, without punishing them.
  • Clause 2 doesn't, obviously. Jailing the very user you claim to protect is hard to justify as protection. It looks more like punishing them.
  • The line is contested. Whose consent counts as defective is a judgement call, which is why the line is not easy to draw.

7.2.2 FOR: Hart on drugs

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

FOR, Hart: punishing drug supply "even to adults, except under medical prescription" is explicable as protecting buyers. "Transitory desires", clouded judgement and subtle pressure weaken consent.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This is Hart's own example, and it matches Clause 1 exactly. Use it to show paternalism isn't legal moralism: the law protects the buyer, and doesn't punish wickedness.

7.2.3 AGAINST: TSH on targets, and the offence line

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST:

  • TSH: morals pick the targets (apotemnophilia v dangerous sports).
  • Hart's offence ground covers public indecency, not distress at "the bare knowledge" of private acts.
  • Teetotallers: 12.6.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist
  • (i) Ruritania bans surgeons from amputating a healthy limb at the request of a person with apotemnophilia (a desire to be rid of a healthy limb), but allows free solo climbing, which kills more people.
  • (ii) Residents complain they are distressed just to know that veridine parties happen in private homes.
  • (iii) Teetotallers complain about public drinking at outdoor festivals.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (i) Morals pick targets. Both choices involve consent to serious self-harm. Why ban one and not the other? TSH: because a moral view (one is degrading, the other admirable) picks the target. So paternalism isn't morally neutral either.
  • (ii) Bare knowledge isn't enough. Hart's offence ground covers public acts that affront decency, not distress at merely knowing what others do in private. If bare knowledge counted, the only liberty left would be to do what no one objects to.
  • (iii) The teetotallers. Public drinking does offend teetotallers, yet the law ignores them. Deciding which public offences count needs majority opinion or morality, so even the offence line isn't neutral (12.6).
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"never protect adults from themselves"; "punish sale but not consumption"; "it's offensive"; "public decency".

47.3 Devlin's jury box, rightly read

📘 Learn 7.3 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: majority disgust; revulsion; act swiftly; behind closed doors; Clapham omnibus; right-minded man

7.3.1 Devlin's premise without his safeguards

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Majority disgust is reason enough" borrows Devlin's premise but drops his safeguards.
  2. Devlin refuses to count heads. He wants slowness and, "more tentatively", privacy. He does not want a majority to act swiftly, or to ignore closed doors.
  3. So "majority feeling is the voice of the community" fails. Disgust is only "a good indication", and Devlin also demands "a deliberate judgement that the practice is injurious to society".

From Devlin's text:

  • Devlin 15: for the law-maker, majority opinion is "surely not enough". The standard "does not depend on the counting of heads". It is what twelve people chosen at random "might after discussion be expected to be unanimous" on (Pollock's "practical morality").
  • Devlin 17: it is "not nearly enough" that "a majority dislike a practice". Disgust counts only if "deeply felt and not manufactured", and those "swayed simply by disgust" would be "wrong".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Suspension Parties

A viral video shows a private party where consenting adults are suspended from hooks through their skin. A snap poll finds 65% of Ruritanians "disgusted". An MP says: "The man on the Clapham omnibus is revolted. Majority disgust is reason enough. Let's ban it this week, private parties included."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Not counting heads. Devlin rejects a 65% poll as the test. He asks what twelve random jurors would be unanimous on after discussion, and a deeply divided issue may fail that.
  • Disgust is a sign, not the test. It must be deeply felt, not stirred up by a viral video, and even then it is only an indication. Devlin also demands a calm, deliberate judgement that the practice injures society.
  • Slowness and privacy. "Ban it this week" ignores Devlin's caution about acting quickly on a new matter. Reaching into private parties ignores his (tentative) respect for privacy.

So the MP is using Devlin's name while discarding his safeguards.

7.3.2 STEELMAN: no society can do without disgust

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN, Devlin: "No society can do without intolerance, indignation, and disgust" (17).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The best case for the MP is that moral feelings carry information. Real, widely shared revulsion can signal that a fundamental norm is at stake. Grant that much before showing the MP has gone too far.

7.3.3 AGAINST: no unanimity, and critical morality

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST:

  • On a contested issue, there is no expected unanimity.
  • Hart: critical morality must test that judgement (his racist society).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

In a different society, juries would be unanimously disgusted by mixed-race couples.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The unanimity test cuts against banning contested practices. On the suspension parties, twelve random jurors would probably split, so Devlin's own test isn't met.
  • Unanimity isn't enough anyway. Where a whole society shares a prejudice, as with mixed-race couples, unanimous disgust shows only what that society feels. Hart's point is that we need critical principles to test whether the feeling is a good reason.

7.3.4 What Devlin actually attacked

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Devlin attacked Wolfenden's approach, not its conclusion. He gave no "opinion one way or the other" (2), and "eventually" backed decriminalisation (Shanmugam, 28 Nov 2022; Liu, W9). Though in 1959, repeal's difficulty was "strongly militating against" change (18).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A student writes: "Devlin opposed decriminalising homosexuality, so he'd back the suspension ban."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Two mistakes.

  • Devlin's lecture argued only that protecting society is an acceptable kind of reason. He declined to give a view on Wolfenden's conclusions, and later supported decriminalisation.
  • His 1959 remark was about the difficulty of repeal, not a verdict that the conduct must be criminal.

So don't assume Devlin's theory dictates a ban.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"majority disgust is enough"; "revulsion"; "act swiftly"; "even behind closed doors"; "the man on the Clapham omnibus"; "the right-minded man".

57.4 Disintegration

📘 Learn 7.4 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: chain reaction; inevitably; end of society; slippery slope

7.4.1 Trivial or unproven

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Repeal begins the end of society" is trivial if a society just is its present morality, and unproven as a prediction.
  2. Hart: nothing shows that private deviation threatens society "like treason". There is "much evidence against it".
  3. So "inevitably" overstates. Only the principled slope bites, and Art 156 now shields marriage laws from fundamental-liberties challenge.

Liu's four readings of "disintegration"†:

ReadingVerdict
Society is its moralityTrivial. Hart: "absurd"; change is like "a peaceful constitutional change".
Empirical collapseHart: there seems to be no permissive drift in Europe.
Interpersonal bonds (George)The loss "may not be regrettable" to those who reject a shared life.
Principled slopeLawrence to Obergefell; Masterpiece Cakeshop, Bull v Hall†. Contrast Art 156.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Cohabitation Law

Ruritania has an old law making it a crime for unmarried couples to live together. A bill proposes repealing it. An opponent says: "Repeal will start a chain reaction. It will inevitably lead to the end of our society."

✔ APPLICATION · Reading by readingDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Society is its morality. If "our society" just means "our current moral code", then any change "ends" it, but only by definition. That's trivial. Changing a rule is more like a peaceful constitutional amendment: the same society, moving on.
  2. Empirical collapse. The opponent must show that countries which allowed cohabitation descended into lawlessness. Hart's point is that there's no such evidence.
  3. Loosened bonds. Perhaps people will share less of a common way of life. But couples who don't share that ideal won't see the loss as a loss.
  4. Principled slope. This is the strong version. If repeal rests on the principle that cohabitation isn't wrong, that same principle may later be used to demand equal treatment with marriage in tax, adoption and the courts. A constitutional shield for marriage laws would stop the slope at that point.

Singapore link: this is the s 377A debate. The principled slope runs from Lawrence (decriminalisation) to Obergefell (marriage), and on to Masterpiece Cakeshop and Bull v Hall (service providers). Art 156 now shields Singapore's marriage laws from fundamental-liberties challenges.

7.4.2 STEELMAN: immorality is like subversion

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN, Devlin: immorality, like subversion, is "capable in their nature of threatening the existence of society". Reply: that gives the law jurisdiction, not a reason to punish X.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Grant Devlin that society may in principle legislate against some immorality, as it does against treason. That doesn't show cohabitation is the kind of immorality that threatens society. Jurisdiction to act is not a reason to act here.

7.4.3 QUALIFY: whose morality?

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, whose morality? s 377A's origin looked like "happenstance" (Shanmugam, 2022): it dates only from 1938. But keeping it in 2007 was a choice.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Historians show that Ruritania's cohabitation law was copied from a colonial statute in 1931 after a two-minute debate.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

That weakens any claim that the law expresses Ruritania's deep morality. But keeping it today is a fresh choice that must be defended on its merits. An accidental origin neither condemns nor saves it.

7.4.4 QUALIFY: Liu on change and fragmentation

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, Liu (W9):

  • recast as mere change, the thesis cannot justify harsh sanctions;
  • Devlin fears fragmentation;
  • he presupposes a consensus that pluralist Singapore, unlike 1950s England, may lack, or may keep only by coercion.

Most jurists, Liu thinks, side with Hart.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If the opponent retreats to "repeal will change our society", that is true, but it can't justify jailing cohabiting couples, since change isn't a disaster. Devlin's real fear, a society splintering into many views, presupposes a single shared view to start with. A society of many faiths may never have had one, or may hold one only through the very law at issue.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"a chain reaction"; "inevitably"; "the end of society"; "a slippery slope".

67.5 Is repeal neutral?

📘 Learn 7.5 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: takes no side; neutral; stands aside; leaves each citizen free
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Repeal takes no side" fails. Withdrawing the criminal law rests on a moral judgement about what the state may punish.
  2. Finnis: every society "takes a public stand" on abortion. Shanmugam called repeal "the right thing to do", which is itself a verdict.
  3. So "repeal is neutral" holds only weakly. Withdrawal is not endorsement, but its reasons are never neutral.

FOR, Shanmugam (2022): a crime "generally" needs "a public order or public interest issue" (16.3). Private consensual adult acts raise no "law-and-order concerns" (also Faishal).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Minister's Repeal Speech

Ruritania's Minister repeals the cohabitation law. In one speech he says both: "By repealing, the state takes no side and leaves each citizen free," and "Repeal is the right thing to do."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • He took a side. "The right thing to do" is a moral verdict. And repeal rests on a judgement that cohabitation is not the kind of conduct the state may punish.
  • The weak sense in which he's right. Repealing a crime isn't the same as endorsing cohabitation. The law withdraws; it doesn't celebrate.
  • His best reason. It is Shanmugam's: crime generally needs a public-order or public-interest issue, and private consensual adult conduct raises none. That reason is a principle, not neutrality.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"repeal takes no side"; "the state stands aside"; "leaves each citizen free".

77.6 2007

📘 Learn 7.6 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: majority opinion; what prevailed; the 2007 compromise; live and let live
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. In 2007, majority feeling prevailed, with Devlin's slowness and privacy: s 377A was kept but not proactively enforced.
  2. Proponents met "no harm" and "religious only" with other grounds and with spill-over arguments, largely avoiding Devlin's treason and disintegration theses (perhaps two speeches came closer).
  3. So "majority feeling decides" describes the 2007 result, not its reasons:
    • debate had moved "from arguments of toleration and privacy to arguments about rights";
    • its motive (deference to the majority, or protecting what was right) was a "point of equivocation";
    • by 2022, tolerance had shifted.

AGAINST:

  • Spill-over to marriage and adoption: in TSH's words, "tangible harm in the form of public consequences".
  • Thio: harm can be "both physical and intangible". Per TSH, she explained that homosexuality could be viewed as contrary to biological design.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Columnist's Claim

A columnist writes: "In 2007 Singapore simply let majority feeling decide s 377A. MPs said 'most people are disgusted', and that was that. It was pure Devlin."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Test the claim against the record.

  • Partly right about the result. The majority view did prevail, and in a Devlin-like way: slowly (keep the law), and with respect for privacy (no proactive enforcement).
  • Wrong about the reasons. Proponents didn't mainly argue "disgust" or "disintegration". They answered "it harms no one" and "your reasons are only religious" with other grounds, chiefly spill-over: retention protects marriage and adoption from later challenge. TSH calls that "tangible harm in the form of public consequences", and Thio said harm can be intangible.
  • The debate had changed. It wasn't Hart–Devlin's toleration-and-privacy debate but a rights debate. Was the government deferring to the majority, or defending what it thought right? TSH calls that a point of equivocation.
  • It didn't last. By 2022 tolerance had shifted, and the law was repealed.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"majority opinion prevailed in 2007"; "the 2007 compromise"; "live and let live".

87.7 Consistency and non-enforcement

📘 Learn 7.7 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: arbitrary; inconsistent; sham; enforce fully or repeal; unenforced; moral signpost
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Neither inconsistency nor non-enforcement alone makes s 377A arbitrary or a sham.
  2. Devlin concedes "There is no logic to be found in this": each crime is weighed on its own, so the fact that adultery is legal proves nothing.
  3. So "enforce fully or repeal" is too stark. Announced non-enforcement breached Fuller's congruence, yet still sent "a symbolic message".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Adultery Is Legal

Ruritania keeps its cohabitation law but announces that police won't proactively enforce it. Adultery, which arguably breaks up more families, is not a crime at all. A critic says: "This is arbitrary and inconsistent. Either enforce it fully or repeal it. An unenforced law is a sham."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Inconsistency proves little. Devlin admits the criminal law follows "no logic" across offences: adultery is left alone largely because it is too hard to police. Each offence must be judged on its own merits, so "adultery is legal" doesn't show the cohabitation law is arbitrary.
  • Non-enforcement isn't a sham, but it has a cost. It breaches congruence (3.2). Yet the law still sends a symbolic message about the value placed on marriage, which is the trade-off (3.2).

7.7.1 AGAINST: the sword hanging over people

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST: an unenforced law gives police and prosecutors "formidable discriminatory powers" (Hart). It is "a sword hanging over" gay men (Shanmugam).

✔ APPLICATION · To RuritaniaDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A cohabiting couple can't be sure the policy won't change, or that a particular officer won't act. That standing threat, and the power it hands officials to pick targets, is the strongest objection to keeping the law unenforced.

7.7.2 QUALIFY: policing varies

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY: TSH: policing varies with the offence. A 2007 MP: some laws, eg nudity visible to the public eye, are hard to police.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The critic assumes a law is a sham unless it is fully enforced. But many laws are enforced patchily because of their nature (public nudity, for example), and no one calls them shams. Enforcement difficulty alone doesn't settle whether a law should exist.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"arbitrary"; "inconsistent"; "a sham"; "enforce it fully or repeal it"; "an unenforced moral signpost".

97.8 Wrong before; order v good

📘 Learn 7.8 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: we were wrong before; slavery; keep order, not make people good; how severely

7.8.1 Past error doesn't mean abstention

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "We were wrong before" defeats itself: calling a past law an error presupposes a right answer.
  2. As Siew argued in 2007, disgust once defended slavery. That warrants Devlin's slowness and Hart's demand for reasons, not abstention.
  3. So "keep order, not make people good" fits Devlin's legal "minimum". Stephen punishes vice as such, and Finnis aims at the common good.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Campaigner's Speech

A campaigner against the cohabitation law says: "Ruritania once banned interracial marriage, and the majority were disgusted by it then. We were wrong before, so we can never trust moral judgements in law. The law should keep order, not make people good."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Self-defeating. Calling the old ban "wrong" assumes there was a right answer. So past error can't mean "never judge". It means "judge carefully".
  • What it does support. Disgust has backed injustice before (Siew's slavery point). That supports Devlin's slowness and Hart's demand for real reasons before criminalising, not abandoning moral judgement altogether.
  • "Keep order, not make people good". Each theorist reads this differently:
    • Devlin: the criminal law sets a minimum, not the maximum of good conduct;
    • Stephen: the law should punish vice as such;
    • Finnis: law aims at the common good, the conditions in which people can flourish.

7.8.2 Whether to punish and how severely

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Hart: whether to punish and how severely are "distinct and independent questions", so a harsh penalty needs its own case.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Instead of repealing, Ruritania raises the cohabitation penalty from a $500 fine to two years in jail.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even if some sanction were justified, the jump to jail needs its own justification. That something may be punished doesn't show it may be punished harshly.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"we were wrong before"; "slavery"; "law should keep order, not make people good"; "how severely?".

107.9 The coercion gradient: punish, regulate, promote

📘 Learn 7.9 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: enforce morality; regulate private behaviour; their own lives; promote; defend marriage
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Enforcing morality" can mean punishing, regulating or promoting, and the justification needed rises with the coercion used.
  2. Hart: coercion is "prima facie objectionable". It punishes offenders, constrains everyone else, and in sexual matters may cause "misery of a quite special degree".
  3. So "legislators should not enforce morality" fails as stated, since all law promotes some morality. But it holds for punishing private consensual conduct for immorality alone.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Gambling Laws

Ruritania considers three responses to gambling:

  • (a) jail anyone who plays private poker for money;
  • (b) license casinos and charge citizens an entry levy;
  • (c) fund school lessons on the risks of gambling.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The gradient. (a) punishes, (b) regulates, (c) promotes. The justification needed is highest for (a) and lowest for (c).
  • Hart on (a). Jail punishes the players, constrains everyone else who might play, and, as Hart notes, criminal law in intimate or personal matters can cause special misery. It needs strong reasons.
  • The statement fails as stated. Even (c) promotes a moral view, that gambling is risky and unwise, so "never enforce morality" would ban almost all law. Its true core is narrower: don't punish private, consensual conduct merely because it is thought immoral.

7.9.1 CONCEDE: promotion coerces too

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE: promotion coerces too (curricula, media rules, adoption). Rawls: appeals to monogamy "as such" reflect comprehensive doctrines, though he leaves the question open. Concede that promotion needs public reasons (6.1). Liu reads the 2022 package as arguably Rawlsian (13.2).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Ruritania's curriculum teaches that "marriage is the ideal family", media rules restrict scenes showing cohabiting couples, and adoption favours married couples.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Promotion isn't free of coercion. Children must sit the lessons, broadcasters must obey the rules, and cohabiting couples lose out in adoption. So promotion also needs public reasons, ones any citizen could accept. "Marriage as such is better", resting on a faith or philosophy, isn't one; arguments about child welfare might be. Liu's view is that Singapore's 2022 package (repeal plus Art 156) can be read as Rawlsian in this sense.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"legislators should not enforce morality"; "regulate private behaviour"; "people should live their own lives"; "promote"; "defend marriage".

117.10 Sin, crime and religion

📘 Learn 7.10 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: religious grounds; sin; a faith condemns it; without exception
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. In any secular society, as Pritam Singh said in 2022, "sin and crime are separate categories".
  2. Even Devlin concedes that law "can no longer rely on doctrines in which citizens are entitled to disbelieve", so a faith-based ban needs a secular reason.
  3. So a ban "without exception" fails twice: one faith cannot alone justify coercing others, and the ban would catch sacramental or temple use.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Alcohol Petition

A large faith group in Ruritania petitions for a total ban on alcohol: "Our faith teaches that drinking is a sin, so the law should forbid it, without exception."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Sin ≠ crime. That a faith calls something a sin doesn't make it a crime in a secular state. Citizens of other faiths, or none, are entitled to disbelieve the doctrine, and even Devlin accepts that the law can't rest on it.
  • A secular reason is needed. For example, drink-driving deaths or liver disease. That reason would then have to justify the specific measure.
  • "Without exception" fails twice.
    • One faith's teaching can't justify coercing everyone else.
    • A total ban would also catch communion wine and religious offerings, so it would burden other faiths' practices.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"ban it on religious grounds"; "it's a sin"; "a faith condemns it"; "without exception".

127.11 Polls are not a mandate

📘 Learn 7.11 in Lesson 7 →
🔑 Trigger words: poll; 85% at least somewhat support; most citizens; let the people decide
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. A poll showing disapproval is no mandate to criminalise. In 2007, Hri Kumar noted, the 70% who "frowned on" it were never asked about criminalising.
  2. TSH's dilemma: if there is a right to the conduct, following the majority is oppression; if there isn't, it is democracy. So the moral question returns.
  3. So majority support is evidence to weigh, never a reason that settles what the law should be.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The 85% Survey

A survey finds that "85% of Ruritanians at least somewhat support" keeping the cohabitation law. An MP says: "Let the people decide. The survey settles it."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • What was actually asked? "Somewhat support keeping the law" may mean mild disapproval of cohabitation, not support for prosecuting couples. Like the 2007 70% who frowned on homosexual conduct, these respondents may never have been asked whether it should be a crime.
  • TSH's dilemma. If cohabiting couples have a right to live together, then letting 85% override it is oppression. If they have no such right, deferring to the majority is democracy. Either way, you need to answer the moral question first, so the poll can't settle it.
  • So treat the poll as evidence of what people think, to weigh alongside other reasons. It is never decisive on its own.

7.11.1 STEELMAN: majority rule treats citizens as equals

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN: majority rule treats citizens as equals (Indranee, 2007: 16.3; 12.3).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The best case for the MP: counting every citizen's view equally is itself a form of respect. Concede the value of that, then show it doesn't answer whether a right is being overridden.

7.11.2 CONCEDE: consensus gauges, not grounds

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE: consensus gauges, not grounds. In Liu's map of the 2007 replies, majority opinion "can be an indication of objective morality"†. Yet majorities erred on slavery, and TSH admits a "catch".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

An 85% view may be tracking something true about the moral question, so it isn't worthless. But majorities have backed slavery. So use consensus as a gauge of where moral truth may lie, never as the ground that makes something right.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"a poll shows…"; "85% at least somewhat support"; "most citizens"; "let the people decide".

137.12 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Conclusion: the statement is right, wrong, or only partly right. No answer, repeal included, is neutral, and Hart v Devlin is a moral quarrel, not a positivist one. Harm, defective consent or public offence may justify punishment. Majority feeling is evidence, never the reason, and Devlin's disintegration thesis suits a society in deep agreement, not a pluralist one. Promotion needs public reasons. Singapore's 2022 package fits: a Wolfenden-like presumption (public order or public interest) for crime, and Art 156 for marriage.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • No answer is neutral: Veridine (7.0) and the Minister's repeal speech (7.5).
  • A moral quarrel, not a positivist one: the TRAP (7.1.4).
  • Harm, defective consent, offence: the Bare-Knuckle Club (7.1), Clause 1 (7.2) and the teetotallers (7.2.3).
  • Majority feeling is evidence only: the Suspension Parties (7.3) and the 85% Survey (7.11).
  • Disintegration needs consensus: the Cohabitation Law (7.4.4).
  • Promotion needs public reasons: the curriculum twist (7.9.1).

HYPO LESSON 8 · ARCHETYPE 8 · ABOUT 32 MIN · 16 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Unjust laws, Radbruch and retroactivity

⚡ BIG IDEA

An unjust law stays law unless it is intolerably unjust. But validity never settles whether the judge or citizen should obey it.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 8. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It is the sheet's wording, so it is what you will write in the exam.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 8 of the 7 Nov exam sheet (identical in the Core and Theorist versions). Layout: the rule as the sheet states it, a made-up hypothetical, then the application. Tagged lines get their own short hypo, often a twist on the block's main one. Most hypos use Valdoria, an invented state that was ruled by a Junta from 2005 to 2015 and is now a democracy. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: RF = Radbruch formula; LP = legal positivism; TSH = Tan Seow Hon; † = from the slides.

18.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Position: an unjust law stays law unless it is intolerably unjust. But validity never settles whether the judge or citizen should obey it.

Intro: the statement runs two questions together:

  1. is the statute law?
  2. must anyone obey it?

Answer them separately. Unjust law stays law unless intolerably unjust (Radbruch, Alexy), and validity never settles obedience (Hart).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Curfew Decree

During the Junta years, Valdoria passed a Curfew Decree: anyone outdoors after 9 pm could be jailed for a year. A student writes: "The Decree was valid law, so citizens had to obey it."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Question 1: was it law? On Radbruch's and Alexy's view, a harsh but not intolerable injustice stays law. A one-year curfew penalty is harsh, but probably below that threshold, so it was law.
  • Question 2: did citizens have to obey? Validity doesn't answer this. Hart: whether to obey a valid law is a separate moral question. A citizen sheltering a fleeing protester after 9 pm might be morally right to break the curfew.

The student ran the two questions together.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"an unjust law is no law"; "if it is law, it must be obeyed".

28.1 The grudge informer

📘 Learn 8.1 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: Nazi statute; denounced her husband; could never shelter

8.1.1 Who bears the cost of past injustice

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Whether the Nazi statute was "law" decides who bears the cost of past injustice.
  2. Hart left two honest options: let her go, or punish her under "a frankly retrospective law". The latter, Fuller replies, voids the Nazi laws as applied to informers "for purposes of that statute at least".
  3. So "she could never shelter behind a Nazi statute" can hold even if the statute was law. On Alexy's reading, Bamberg voided no statute.

The facts: in 1944 she denounced her husband's anti-Hitler remarks. He was sentenced to death, but sent to the front instead. In 1949 she was convicted under the 1871 Criminal Code.

Fuller defends the courts:

  • if all the Nazi statutes were law, the informers were "guiltless";
  • the real issue seems to be who does "the dirty work";
  • the courts, "living participants" in an emergency, could not wait, and waiting risked self-help.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Landlord Who Informed

In 2012, under the Junta's Insult Decree (death for "disparaging the Leader", even in private), landlord Kovač reported his tenant for joking in his own flat that the Leader was a fool. Kovač wanted the flat back. The tenant was sentenced to death, commuted to ten years' hard labour. In 2020, democratic Valdoria prosecutes Kovač for unlawfully depriving a person of liberty, under the Criminal Code of 1900, which was never repealed. Kovač's defence: "I acted lawfully under the Insult Decree."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Three routes.

  • Radbruch: the Insult Decree was so intolerably unjust that it wasn't law. So Kovač's act was never lawful, and he can be convicted under the 1900 Code.
  • Hart: be honest about the dilemma. Either (a) let Kovač go, because what he did was lawful at the time, or (b) pass a statute that openly makes his conduct punishable after the fact. Fuller's reply: option (b) itself treats the Insult Decree as void, at least for informers. So the real question is who does the dirty work, courts or Parliament. And Valdoria's courts, facing angry victims now, may not be able to wait.
  • Alexy's reading of the real case: a court could convict without declaring the Decree void at all, through a criminal-law route (Kovač indirectly caused an unlawful deprivation of liberty). So "he can't shelter behind the Decree" doesn't require denying it was law.

The stakes: if the Decree was law, the tenant bears the cost of the injustice. If it wasn't, Kovač does.

8.1.2 QUALIFY: Alexy on Bamberg

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, Alexy: Bamberg convicted her on "a controversial criminal law construction", which he leaves open.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If you rely on Alexy's version of the real case, flag that the construction (an indirect deprivation of liberty, punishable even though the court that sentenced him acted "legally") was controversial. Don't present it as settled law.

8.1.3 Liu on the open statute; Alexy's "evident" reply

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Liu (W10):

  • any open form of retroactive statute will do, for example a statute saying it is no defence to invoke the named Nazi laws;
  • though she did report under what was procedurally law.

Alexy's "evident" reply fits here: the formula defeats a defence, and creates no new liability.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Valdoria's Parliament passes: "In any prosecution under the 1900 Code, it is no defence to rely on the Insult Decree."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Liu: that is an honest, open way of doing what Hart asks. It owns the retroactivity, so the precise wording doesn't matter. But note the unfairness from Kovač's side: when he acted, he was using what was procedurally law.
  • Alexy: the RF isn't inventing a new crime. The 1900 Code already made the act a crime. The formula only strips away a defence based on an evidently unjust decree, and evident injustice means Kovač could have known.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"the Nazi statute was law, so she was innocent"; "she denounced her husband"; "she could never shelter behind it".

38.2 Hart's best case

📘 Learn 8.2 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: law is law; no law at all; speak plainly; simply refuse; considers unfair

8.2.1 Validity leaves the moral question open

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Hart answers the claim that judges raised on "law is law" will never resist: validity leaves open "the final moral question" of obedience.
  2. Speaking plainly, the decree is "law but too evil to be obeyed", a condemnation "everyone can understand".
  3. So "he should simply refuse whatever he considers unfair" states the strong connection thesis, which "no serious non-positivist defends" (Alexy).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Judge Varga's Training

Judge Varga trained under a professor who taught "law is law". A commentator says: "Positivist judges like Varga will never resist the Junta's laws. If you're told law is law, you obey." Another commentator says: "Varga should simply refuse to apply any Junta law she considers unfair."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • To the first commentator (Hart): knowing that the Insult Decree is law doesn't tell Varga whether to apply it. That is "the final moral question", and she must answer it as a moral agent. The plain verdict is that it is "law but too evil to be obeyed", a condemnation "everyone can understand".
  • To the second: "refuse whatever you consider unfair" is the strong connection thesis, that any unfair law isn't law. Even non-positivists like Alexy reject it: only extreme injustice defeats legality.

8.2.2 STEELMAN: honesty

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN: Hart's best point is honesty. Denying evil law the name breeds the romantic optimism that all values fit one system, and "insincerity" about a dilemma.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If Varga says "the Insult Decree isn't law" and refuses it, she hides the hard choice: she is overriding something that functioned as law. Hart wants her to say openly that she is disobeying a law for moral reasons, and accept what follows. That honesty is his strongest card.

8.2.3 Fuller's reply

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Fuller: Radbruch saw the dilemma. LP gives fidelity to law no "coherent meaning", and Hart's dilemma, as Fuller states it, "makes no sense".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Fuller would say Hart's picture, a valid law that you must obey as law but may disobey as a moral agent, leaves "fidelity to law" empty. If law can have any content, what exactly is Varga being faithful to? For Fuller, fidelity makes sense only to a system that meets the inner morality of law.

8.2.4 AGAINST: "an extraordinary naïveté"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST: that LP disarmed German lawyers is "an extraordinary naïveté". Elsewhere, "law is law" went with "the most enlightened liberal attitudes".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Blaming Varga's positivist training for the Junta's success ignores the fact that in other countries the same slogan sat comfortably with liberal politics. The cause of the judges' compliance lies elsewhere (fear, careerism, sympathy with the regime), not in a theory of how to identify law.

8.2.5 QUALIFY: purpose and cross-purposes

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY:

  • Radbruch (1946) wrote to arm judges against the next tyranny. Hart (1958): the formula is useless during the regime and unneeded after it (Liu, W11).
  • Hart and Fuller talk across purposes: a wicked regime that meets all eight desiderata leaves the formula question open (Liu, W10).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Timing. Radbruch's aim was to give future Vargas a legal ground to refuse. Hart's reply: during the Junta, no court would accept it, and after the Junta a new Parliament can simply legislate.
  • Cross-purposes. Imagine the Junta had published every decree clearly and in advance. Fuller's "no real law" argument wouldn't apply, and the Radbruch question would still be waiting. So Fuller and Hart aren't quite answering the same question.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"law is law"; "it was no law at all"; "speak plainly"; "the judge should simply refuse whatever he considers unfair".

48.3 Alexy's replies

📘 Learn 8.3 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: how the word is used; any neutral standpoint; eye of the beholder; reaching back; determined tyranny

8.3.1 Observer v participant

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Alexy grants "that is simply how the word is used" to observers. But a judge applying Ordinance 11, a citizenship decree, joins a procedure that claims correctness.
  2. So "the decree is law" holds only for observers. A judge refusing it on legal grounds must call it "prima-facie law but in the end not law at all".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Citizenship Ordinance

In 2008, the Junta issued an Ordinance stripping citizenship from every member of the Kel minority living abroad, and seizing their property. In 2021, Kel exiles sue to recover their property.

  • A foreign historian writes: "In 2008, the Ordinance was Valdorian law."
  • Judge Petrov must decide the exiles' claim.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The historian is an observer. Describing what Valdorian officials treated as law, she can call it law, and Alexy grants this.
  • Petrov is a participant. When she decides, her ruling claims to be correct. If the Ordinance's injustice is extreme, she can't correctly apply it. So she says it was "prima-facie law but in the end not law at all", and rules for the exiles.

8.3.2 The five objections, applied

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Alexy's replies to the five objections. (Liu: use two of them in an answer. The language objection is the weakest, and effectiveness is speculative both ways.)

ObjectionAlexy's replyApplied to the Citizenship Ordinance
ClarityAdequacy before simplicity. At the extreme, the ethical problem is also a legal one."It was law, but evil" is simpler. But for Petrov, whether the exiles own their property is a legal question, so a purely moral verdict won't decide the case.
EffectivenessLargely conceded. If lawyers share a consensus, resistance gains legal grounds; risk effect (12.5).The formula wouldn't have stopped the Junta. But if Valdorian lawyers had shared the RF, an official refusing the Ordinance would have had a legal argument, and the risk of later liability might have deterred some.
Certainty"The more extreme the injustice, the more certain the knowledge of it". Only an absolutist objects.Stripping citizenship from a whole minority is not a borderline case. The formula only bites where injustice is obvious, so certainty is barely affected.
RelativismIn rights-steeped states, a rights consensus should thwart Hoerster's "Nazi morality" judge. The minimum core is unargued here.Couldn't a judge with Junta values call the new democratic laws unjust? In a state steeped in rights, the shared consensus checks him. But Alexy doesn't fully argue for the minimum core.
Democracy, dispensabilityCore area only, otherwise there'd be no judicial review. Nulla poena may be unamendable (art 79(3), 57). Singapore: 11.7.The RF applies only to the core of extreme injustice, so it doesn't let judges override ordinary democratic choices.

8.3.3 CONCEDE: candour is the strongest objection

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE: Hart's candour objection is "the strongest argument against" non-positivism, "but not its downfall" (Alexy). Two answers:

  • exempt past actors via nulla poena; or, better,
  • the injustice was so "evident" that the legal position is "simply determined".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

For a Junta official who enforced the Ordinance, Petrov's ruling looks like retroactive judgement, which is Hart's point. Concede it. Alexy's best answer: the Ordinance was evidently unjust, so the official could have known it lacked legal force. Nothing was sprung on him later. Alternatively, protect past actors from punishment through nulla poena, while still denying the Ordinance effect today, for example in the property claim.

8.3.4 The real Ordinance 11

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Ordinance 11 (Reich Citizenship Law) deprived people of citizenship (W10 slide 9†) on racist criteria. The Federal Constitutional Court (1968) found its injustice "intolerable" and "evident": such destruction "has nothing in common with law and justice". It is not the informer statutes (1934, 1938), which Liu once confused it with (W10).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Keep your examples straight in the exam:

  • the informer case (8.1) involves the 1934 and 1938 statutes;
  • Ordinance 11 is Alexy's citizenship example, and the Valdorian Ordinance above is modelled on it.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"that is simply how the word 'law' is used"; "from any neutral standpoint"; "in the eye of the beholder"; "reaching back"; "against a determined tyranny".

58.4 Does the label matter?

📘 Learn 8.4 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: a quarrel about words; his conscience belongs to his private life; lawbreaker

8.4.1 It decides who may refuse, and who may shelter

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. The label is a definitional quarrel, and neither side is less honest: Hart judges by effect, Alexy by concept (Liu, W11). But it is no mere quarrel about words. It decides who may lawfully refuse, and who may shelter behind the statute.
  2. Even Hart, though the wife's fate might be the same either way, holds that candour is "not just one among many minor virtues".
  3. So "his conscience belongs to his private life" restates pre-war Radbruch, the view Hart says he recanted.

How each actor fares, depending on the label:

ActorIf it is law (LP, Hart)If it is not law (Radbruch, Alexy)
Judgeapplies it, or refuses on moral grounds: confusion at "its height"refuses on legal grounds (Alexy)
Legislatorbound only by the master rule (Week 13†)legislates to a higher standard
Lawyermay refuse, but "what he refuses to obey is still the law" (Alexy 44, on LP)should denounce it as having "no legal character" (Hart on Radbruch)
Citizena refuser is a lawbreaker; an obeyer acted lawfully, but is morally open to criticisma refuser is still punished (8.7); an obeyer has no shelter if the injustice was "evident" (Alexy)
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ordinance, Four Ways

Take the Citizenship Ordinance (8.3.1) in 2008. Four people face it:

  • Judge Horvat, asked to confirm a seizure;
  • MP Novak, voting on an amendment;
  • lawyer Babić, asked to draft eviction notices;
  • clerk Jurić, ordered to stamp the seizure orders.

A commentator says: "Whether we call it 'law' is just a quarrel about words. Each person's conscience is a private matter."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Judge Horvat. If it's law, she either applies it or refuses on purely moral grounds. Fuller calls a court refusing what it admits is law moral confusion at "its height". If it isn't law, she refuses on legal grounds.
  • MP Novak. If it's law, he is bound only by the rule of recognition. On the non-positivist view, he must legislate to a higher standard.
  • Lawyer Babić. If it's law, he may refuse, but what he refuses is still law. On Radbruch's view, he should denounce it as having no legal character at all.
  • Clerk Jurić. If it's law, refusing makes him a lawbreaker, while stamping is lawful (though morally open to criticism). If it isn't law, refusing is still punished while the Junta lasts, and stamping gives him no later shelter, because the injustice was evident.

So the label changes legal outcomes; it isn't just words. And "conscience is private" is exactly the pre-war Radbruch view that Radbruch himself abandoned.

8.4.2 AGAINST: words shape attitudes

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST, Fuller:

  • words here have "a powerful effect on human attitudes";
  • Nazi law failed legality itself: the Roehm statute, "the party in the streets".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Calling the Ordinance "law" lends it dignity in officials' eyes. And for Fuller, the Junta's system, with its secret orders, retroactive "validations" and party thugs acting outside any rule, may have failed the inner morality of law so badly that "law" was barely the right word anyway.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"this is a quarrel about words"; "his conscience belongs to his private life"; "the refuser is a lawbreaker".

68.5 A stable democracy

📘 Learn 8.5 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: unelected veto; substitutes his own morality; for Parliament to repeal; must never invalidate

8.5.1 A narrow check, tested by broad consensus

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. In a stable democracy, the formula is a narrow check, not an unelected veto. Legislation stands unless intolerably unjust (TSH).
  2. For TSH, judges must show intolerable injustice by broad historical consensus. Racial genocide and slavery qualify. Abortion limits did not in 1973, nor, for now, do opposite-sex marriage laws.
  3. So "judges must never invalidate a law on grounds of justice" holds for ordinary injustice, which is Parliament's to repeal, but not for genocide.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Judge Lim's Four Challenges

Ruritania is a stable democracy. Judge Lim is asked to strike down four laws on grounds of injustice:

  • (a) a law raising the voting age from 18 to 21;
  • (b) a law allowing creditors to keep defaulting debtors as unpaid servants until the debt is worked off;
  • (c) a law restricting abortion after 12 weeks;
  • (d) a law defining marriage as between a man and a woman.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) is ordinary injustice, if any. It is for Parliament to repeal. A judge substituting her view would be an unelected veto.
  • (b) is slavery in substance. Broad historical consensus condemns it as intolerably unjust, so the formula applies.
  • (c) and (d) are matters on which, by TSH's test, there is no broad historical consensus that they are intolerably unjust. Abortion limits weren't in 1973, and opposite-sex marriage laws aren't now.

So only (b) can be struck down on these grounds. The statement that judges must never invalidate is right for (a), (c) and (d), and wrong for (b).

8.5.2 AGAINST: TSH on Arts 9 and 12

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST, TSH:

  • since constitutional supremacy rests most soundly on "equal moral worth", Arts 9 and 12 "may legitimately import a higher law (including Radbruch's formula)";
  • consensus generally checks "idiosyncratic personal ideologies".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In a system like Singapore's, Judge Lim needn't treat the formula as a foreign import. Constitutional guarantees of life, liberty and equality can carry it. And the consensus requirement stops her using it to impose her personal politics.

8.5.3 CONCEDE: TSH's catch, and judicial oligarchy

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE, TSH's "catch":

  • "decades on", the formula could be used to impose a worldwide trend on same-sex marriage;
  • where consensus has, for realists, "gone dreadfully wrong", while a local legislature tries to do right, using it is "problematic and not merely ineffective".

CONCEDE also: amid judicial oligarchies, consensus may "reflect the views of select groups of judges".

Concede both. Then accept TSH's reply: "an autocrat, a few oligarchs, or even a brute majority" would do no better.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Forty years on, most of the world's top courts hold that law (d) is intolerably unjust. Ruritania's Parliament still disagrees.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The catch. The consensus test would now point Judge Lim towards striking down (d). If the global consensus were mistaken, the formula would be imposing an error on a legislature trying to do right.
  • Oligarchy. And the "consensus" might really be the view of a small circle of judges citing each other.
  • The reply. Concede both risks. But every alternative decision-maker (an autocrat, a few oligarchs, or a brute majority) can also get it wrong. Broad consensus remains the best available check.

8.5.4 QUALIFY: Liu on the formula's role

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, Liu (W11; Alexy): because it draws on common morality, the formula is a transitional safeguard, "primarily a tool of resistance". It is idle once morality has fully shifted.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The formula is built for the moment when a regime breaks sharply with shared morality, like the Junta. In a stable democracy, where laws track the public's moral views, it has little to do. So it is mainly a tool of resistance, not a tool of routine review.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"an unelected veto"; "the judge substitutes his own morality"; "it's for Parliament to repeal"; "judges must never invalidate".

78.6 Retroactivity

📘 Learn 8.6 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: retrospective laws are always unjust; life imprisonment; overnight
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Retrospective laws are always unjust" confuses a cost with a verdict. A curative statute may be "essential to advance the cause of legality".
  2. The core case is the new crime, "commanding a man today to do something yesterday", which even Hart grants may be "odious".
  3. So the statement nearly holds for new crimes. But a longer term is "less so", and civil overruling is a price worth paying (3.8).

Also on the sheet:

  • Keep apart: "branded as criminals" concerns overruling a reading under which conduct was not criminal; Abdul Nasir† (3.8) engages constancy.
  • Liu's test (W2): retroactivity is abuse when it undermines guidance (bad faith, frequency, after-the-fact punishment). Leniency (MDA re-sentencing) is not abuse, though fairness to prisoners is external morality. The common law is retroactive by default.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Retroactive Laws

In one session, Ruritania's Parliament passes four laws with retroactive effect:

  • (a) validating wills witnessed by only one person during a pandemic lockdown, when two witnesses were impossible;
  • (b) a new crime of "panic buying", applied to purchases made last March;
  • (c) raising the maximum sentence for burglary from 5 to 7 years, applied to burglaries already committed;
  • (d) letting prisoners serving mandatory death sentences apply for re-sentencing under a new, lighter regime.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) is curative. It repairs a failure of possibility (no one could find two witnesses), so it advances legality.
  • (b) is the core abuse. It commands people today to have done something differently yesterday. Even Hart calls this odious.
  • (c) is less bad. Burglary was already a crime, and people had notice of that. It still punishes after the fact, so it needs strong justification, but it is not the same as (b).
  • (d) is leniency. It doesn't undermine anyone's ability to plan, so it isn't abuse, though the reason for it (fairness to prisoners) is an argument from external morality, so say so.
  • Keep the labels apart. "Branded as criminals" is about a court overruling a reading under which conduct was legal. A change to what an existing sentence means, as in Abdul Nasir, is a constancy problem.

So "always unjust" holds nearly for (b), and fails for (a) and (d).

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"retrospective laws are always unjust"; "life imprisonment"; "overnight".

88.7 Obey or disobey?

📘 Learn 8.7 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: obligation to obey; has done nothing wrong; will they be punished; fidelity means deference; highest court

8.7.1 Three questions, five theorists

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. The statement merges three questions: a legal duty to obey, and moral duties to obey or to disobey.
  2. Fidelity is not deference: Rex's subjects stayed "faithful to him as king", not to his law, "for he never made any".
  3. So "the citizen who obeys has done nothing wrong" holds legally for Hart, and for Radbruch only below the threshold. Morally it stays open.
TheoristLegal dutyMoral duty to obeyMoral duty to disobey
Hartyesnot settled by validitypast "a certain degree of iniquity" (Bentham, Austin)
Fullerby degree; none on total failurefrom reciprocity; none once "finally and completely" ruptured"no simple principle" short of rupture, as under Hitler
Radbruch, Alexynone past intolerable injustice or betrayed equality†below that, law is open to moral critiquejudges and lawyers: deny it legal character
Aquinasnone: "a corruption of law"none, except, perhaps, to avoid "scandal or some particular danger"unstated in Harris
Finnisnot a nullitynot prima facie; it can arise lest a system on the whole just weakenapplied: never choose "directly against a basic value"
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Radio Decree

The Junta's Radio Decree required citizens to report any neighbour who listened to foreign radio. Petra refused to report her neighbours. Tomas reported his. After the Junta falls, Tomas says: "I obeyed the law. I did nothing wrong."

✔ APPLICATION · Theorist by theoristDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Hart: the Decree was law, so Tomas had a legal duty, and Petra broke the law. But validity doesn't settle the moral question. Past a certain degree of iniquity, there is a moral duty to resist, and Petra may have been right.
  • Fuller: if the Junta's legal system was badly degraded (secret orders, retroactive decrees), any duty to obey weakened with it. If the government had wholly ruptured reciprocity, nothing was left to ground the duty.
  • Radbruch and Alexy: if the Decree was intolerably unjust, it imposed no legal duty at all. Tomas can't shelter behind it.
  • Aquinas: an unjust law is "a corruption of law". Obedience is owed, perhaps, only to avoid scandal or danger.
  • Finnis: the Decree isn't a nullity, but it carries no prima facie moral bindingness. Reporting neighbours for persecution may well choose directly against basic goods, which Tomas must never do.

So Tomas's "I did nothing wrong" holds legally on Hart's view, and on Radbruch's only if the Decree was below the threshold. Morally, it is very much open.

Fidelity ≠ deference. If Tomas says "being faithful to law means obeying whoever rules", Fuller's reply is that Rex's subjects stayed loyal to Rex as king, but couldn't be faithful to his law, because he never made any. Fidelity to law is owed to a system of rules, not to the person in charge.

8.7.2 CITIZEN: will they be punished?

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CITIZEN: punished? While the regime lasts, yes, either way. The refuser "must reckon with the usual consequences" (Hoerster).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Whatever the theory says about legal validity, the Junta will still jail Petra for refusing. Calling the Decree "not law" doesn't protect her during the regime. That is Hoerster's point.

8.7.3 JUDGE: the highest court says "law"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

JUDGE: what if the highest court says it is law?

  • For observers and LP, it is law.
  • For participants, the court's ruling "lays claim to correctness" (Alexy). So at extreme injustice, a later court or a lawyer may call it legally wrong. Below that, it is law.
  • For lower courts, see 15.10.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

In 2010, the Junta's Supreme Court upheld the Radio Decree as valid.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A historian can record that the Decree was law, because the top court said so. But the court's ruling claimed to be correct. Because the Decree was extremely unjust, a 2021 court or a lawyer can say the 2010 ruling was legally wrong, not merely immoral. For an ordinary unjust law, the top court's ruling would simply settle it.

8.7.4 STEELMAN: why obey at all? (Liu's pigeon feeder)

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN, why obey at all? Liu's pigeon feeder (W10):

  • deterrence makes her comply, but it is no moral reason;
  • "others will copy" justifies punishing her, not her obeying;
  • fair play does give a reason: she gains from institutions others uphold, and fairness between citizens (Rawls) asks her to keep laws she rejects.

Assume the duty: the topic is its exceptions. Every reason to obey is moral. Legality only says the rule is law, so a positivist has the same reasons (W10).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Mrs Goh feeds stray cats, in breach of a town by-law, because she believes she has a moral duty to them. She is willing to pay any fine.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Not reasons: escalating fines may stop her, but that is not a reason to obey. And "others will copy" explains why the town fines her, not why she should obey.
  • A real reason: fair play. She benefits every day from rules others keep even when they disagree (clean streets, traffic order), so fairness asks her to keep this one too.
  • The positivist point. That reason is moral. Knowing the by-law is valid only tells her it is law, so positivists and natural lawyers have exactly the same reasons to obey.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"is there an obligation to obey?"; "the citizen who obeyed did nothing wrong"; "will they be punished?"; "fidelity means deference"; "the highest court has spoken".

98.8 Radbruch's betrayal-of-equality limb†

📘 Learn 8.8 in Lesson 8 →
🔑 Trigger words: racist statute; discriminates by race or faith; not even an attempt at justice

8.8.1 Does it even attempt justice?

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Radbruch's second limb asks not how unjust the statute is, but whether it attempts justice at all. Where equality "is deliberately betrayed", the statute "lacks completely the very nature of law"†.
  2. So "the judge must apply it" fails for a statute aimed at one race. Morally, too, no role excuses applying "a facially racist law" (Thunder).

Radbruch's tiers (W10 slide 2†):

  1. positive law prevails "even when its content is unjust";
  2. at an "intolerable level", it is "flawed law" that "must yield to justice";
  3. where equality is betrayed, it is no law at all.

Liu (W10): tier 2 is no nullity, but the outcome is the same.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Residence Act

Ruritania's Parliament passes a Residence Act: "No member of the Halani race may reside within the capital." It carries no penalty beyond eviction. Judge Tan is asked to grant an eviction order against a Halani family.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The question isn't degree. Eviction is less harsh than death. But the Act doesn't even attempt justice: it singles out a race and deliberately betrays equality, which is the core of justice. On Radbruch's third tier, it "lacks completely the very nature of law". So Judge Tan has no law to apply.
  • The tiers compared. Under tier 2 (intolerable injustice), the Act would be "flawed law" that yields to justice, rather than a nullity. Either way, as Liu notes, Judge Tan refuses the order.
  • Morally. Thunder: no professional role, judge or lawyer, excuses applying a facially racist law.

8.8.2 CONCEDE: "equality" is contested

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE: "equality" is contested (Westen, as LMS (CA) noted). Confine the limb to deliberate, facial betrayal, tested as in 8.5. For unjust outcomes, see 1.3(10).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A different Act requires all civil servants to pass a test in the national language. Halani citizens fail at higher rates, and claim it betrays equality.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

This law doesn't single out a race on its face. Its unequal outcome comes from a neutral rule. Because "equality" means many contested things, Radbruch's limb should be kept to deliberate, facial betrayal like the Residence Act, tested by broad consensus as in 8.5. Unequal outcomes from neutral rules belong to other arguments (1.3(10)), not to the claim that the law has no legal character.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"a racist statute"; "it discriminates by race or faith"; "not even an attempt at justice".

108.9 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Conclusion: the statement is overstated. Validity never settles what the actor should do. A law that survives the formula is shown not to be intolerably unjust, never to be just: that question stays with Parliament and conscience. Deviating can be unjust too: the judge's morality may be wrong (Hoerster's "Nazi morality" judge), and Radbruch himself warned of "frightful dangers".

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Validity doesn't settle obedience: the Curfew Decree (8.0) and Petra and Tomas (8.7).
  • Surviving the formula ≠ just: the voting-age law (8.5.1(a)) is still open to criticism in Parliament.
  • Deviating can be wrong too: imagine a former Junta judge, still on the bench, refusing to apply Valdoria's new equality laws because he thinks they are unjust. That is Hoerster's worry. Radbruch's own warning shows the formula must stay narrow.
