ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 9 of the 7 Nov exam sheet. Sections 1–12 are the same in the Core and Theorist versions, except for one cross-reference in 9.8: Core points to 14.5, Theorist to 15.9. Layout: the rule as the sheet states it, a made-up hypothetical, then the application. Tagged lines get their own short hypo, often a twist on the block's main one. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: ALR = American legal realism; CLS = critical legal studies (the crits); HIWTCO = Kennedy's "how-I-want-to-come-out"; RF = Radbruch formula; TSH = Tan Seow Hon; † = from the slides.

19.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Position: the statement overstates. Judges justify by fit and political morality, and rules leave some cases open, not all.

Intro: the statement treats adjudication as politics in robes.

  • Realists rightly show that canons and ratios leave some cases open.
  • Crits rightly show that principles meet counterprinciples.
  • But a judge cannot predict his own ruling. He must justify it, by the reading that best fits and justifies the law (Dworkin).

So rules leave some cases open, not all, and political morality, not preference, closes them.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Cases in One Morning

Judge Koh of the Ruritanian High Court hears two cases.

  • (a) A driver was clocked at 92 km/h in a clearly marked 60 zone. He has no defence.
  • (b) A rider for a delivery app claims she is an "employee" under the Employment Act, which doesn't define the word for platform work.

A commentator says: "Judging is just politics in robes. Judges decide what they want, then dress it up."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) is closed by the rule. No honest reading lets the driver off. Rules don't leave every case open.
  • (b) is genuinely open. The canons point different ways, and the precedents can be read narrowly or widely, as the realists say.
  • Even in (b), Koh must justify. She has to give the reading of "employee" that best fits the Act and the case law and best justifies them, for example the Act's purpose of protecting dependent workers. That is political morality, argued in public reasons, not her private preference about riders.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"judging is politics"; "judges decide first and rationalise after".

29.1 American legal realism

📘 Learn 9.1 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: decide first, prediction, canons, ratios read narrowly or widely

9.1.1 A judge must justify, not predict

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Realism rightly says that canons and ratios leave hard cases open. But a judge must justify, not predict.
  2. Practitioners may predict, "but judges themselves cannot. They must purport to justify". "Alas, I must find for the defendant" predicts nothing on its face.
  3. So "law is prediction" holds at most for counsel. Llewellyn called realism "a method nothing more".

FOR, Cheng San GRC (GE 1997)†:

  • candidates stood inside polling stations;
  • s 82(1)(d) barred waiting "outside", and (e) loitering "within a radius of 200 metres" (pre-2023);
  • read literally, only "outside" was barred; read purposively (the mischief, and "at or near"), being inside was too;
  • the AG advised that no offence was committed.

Precise canons, uncertain outcome (Liu, W11).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Candidate in the Polling Hall

Ruritania's Elections Act says: "(a) No person shall wait outside a polling station. (b) No person shall loiter within 100 metres of a polling station." On polling day, candidate Tan stands all day inside the polling hall, smiling and nodding at voters. He is charged.

  • His counsel tells him: "Under the literal rule, you'll probably be acquitted. 'Outside' means outside."
  • The prosecutor argues the purposive rule: the mischief is candidates influencing voters at the booth, and being inside is worse than being outside.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The realists are right that the canons conflict. Both the literal rule and the mischief rule are respectable canons, and they give opposite answers. The rules alone don't settle it.
  • Counsel may predict; the judge may not. Counsel's job is to forecast. The judge can't decide by forecasting her own decision. She must give reasons: which canon fits this Act and why, such as the purpose of free voting.
  • "Alas". If she writes "Alas, I must convict", she presents the conviction as compelled by law, not predicted. A realist can call that a pose, but the duty to justify is real.
  • Realism as method. Llewellyn himself called realism a method, a way of studying courts, not a theory that tells judges what to do.

9.1.2 QUALIFY: flimsy rulings are costly

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, Liu: ALR oversimplifies. A judge can write any decision, but reputation, reversal, time and credibility (Denning) make a flimsy one costly.

Kennedy's correction: law is a "medium" that constrains like bricks, relative to one's project. Moving it costs "work and the credibility risk".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The judge personally thinks Tan should be convicted. She could write two lines: "Inside is near enough to outside. Convicted."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Liu's costs. A two-line ruling invites reversal on appeal, damages her reputation, and spends her credibility (Denning was admired, but seen as always pushing the limits).
  • Kennedy's bricks. The statute's words are like bricks. She can build different things with them, but turning "outside" into "inside" takes real argumentative work, and carries a risk to her credibility.

So the realists' "anything goes" is too quick.

9.1.3 QUALIFY: weak and strong realism

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, the weak and strong readings:

  • on Harris's minimal reading, "'rules' are not all that matter";
  • in its extreme form, all legal reasoning is "mere surface talk".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The weak reading is plainly true of Tan's case: the judge's sense of the Act's purpose matters, not just its words. The strong reading would say her reasons are irrelevant decoration. That is much harder to believe, given the costs in 9.1.2. Concede the weak form; reject the strong one.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"judges decide first"; "law is a prediction of what courts will do"; "canons cancel out"; "ratios can be read narrowly or widely".

39.2 Dworkin v ALR

📘 Learn 9.2 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: precedent runs out, judges legislate, floodgates, social goals

9.2.1 A theoretical disagreement, not a gap

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Saying that the judge legislates once precedent runs out mistakes a theoretical disagreement about law's grounds for a gap.
  2. In McLoughlin, all five Lords allowed the appeal, yet they split. Scarman held line-drawing policy "not justiciable"; Edmund-Davies called that "as novel as it is startling".
  3. So leaving floodgates to Parliament is Scarman's contested view. Defend it as a choice, not as the case's lesson.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Rescue Volunteer

A train derails. Ravi, a passer-by with no relation to anyone on board, spends three hours pulling injured passengers from the wreck, and develops severe post-traumatic stress. No Ruritanian case has allowed a claim by an unrelated rescuer who wasn't in personal danger. The defendant rail company argues: "If he can sue, every bystander can. The floodgates will open."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • No gap. A realist says precedent has run out, so the judges will simply legislate. But the judges are really disagreeing about what the law's grounds are. Are earlier cases bound by an underlying principle (foreseeable harm to those drawn into the danger), or only by their facts?
  • The McLoughlin split. One judge, like Scarman, may say: the principle covers Ravi, and limiting it for floodgates reasons is for Parliament. Another, like Edmund-Davies, says courts may weigh policy, but carefully.
  • Scarman's view is a choice. You can defend it, but present it as your view of the judicial role, not as what McLoughlin decided.

9.2.2 AGAINST: is floodgates policy or principle?

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST, is floodgates policy or principle (Week 1b slide 3†)?

  • As policy: court congestion and insurance costs, which lie beyond "the limits of the forensic process" (Scarman).
  • As principle: liability out of proportion to fault.
✔ APPLICATION · To RaviDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • If the rail company says "courts will be swamped and premiums will rise", that is policy, and on Scarman's view not for judges.
  • If it says "it is unfair to make us liable to an unlimited number of strangers for one moment's carelessness", that is principle: a claim about justice between the parties, which courts may weigh.

How you classify the argument decides whether the court can consider it.

9.2.3 QUALIFY: Bridge

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, Bridge weighed the policy grounds offered, found them "wholly insufficient", and called stopping at decided cases "an unwarranted abdication".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A Bridge-type judge would hear the rail company's floodgates argument, find it far too weak to deny Ravi a remedy, and say that refusing to go beyond existing cases simply because they are the existing cases would be abdicating the judicial role.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"when precedent runs out, judges legislate"; "floodgates"; "courts should pursue social goals".

49.3 CLS v Dworkin

📘 Learn 9.3 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: neutral framework, exceptions prove the rule, drawn up by an elite, tear it down

9.3.1 Principles meet counterprinciples

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Unger rightly denies that contract law is a neutral framework. Each principle meets a counterprinciple that the dominant view files as an anomaly.
  2. With its exclusions, exceptions and repressions, the dominant contract theory rules far less than it claims (Unger).
  3. Yet "tear it down" overreaches. Condemning hidden interests needs a non-subjective standard, which Finnis's basic goods supply (5.1).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Deactivated Rider

A delivery platform's standard terms let it "deactivate any rider at any time without reasons". Suri, a rider for five years who depends on the app for all her income, is deactivated the day after complaining about pay. She argues the term is unconscionable, given the gross inequality of bargaining power. The platform says: "Contract law is a neutral framework. She agreed. Unconscionability is a narrow exception that proves the rule."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The principle: freedom of contract. Parties choose their terms.
  • The counterprinciple: unfair bargains shouldn't be enforced (duress, undue influence, unconscionability, inequality of bargaining power).
  • Unger's point. Nothing in the doctrine says which is the rule and which the exception. Calling fairness an "exception" reflects the existing power structure, which treats platforms' control as normal. And the theory's own exclusions (labour law), exceptions (fiduciary duties) and repressions (long-term relationships like Suri's) show it governs far less than it claims.
  • But "tear it all down" goes too far. To say the platform's control is unjust, and not just one interest among others, you need a standard that isn't merely subjective. Finnis's basic goods (Suri's livelihood, her sociability as a worker) can supply one.

9.3.2 FOR: doctrine legitimates hierarchy

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

FOR: doctrine legitimates hierarchy "even when it is deployed by someone who thinks he is forwarding progressive causes": hidden interests (Week 1b slide 17†). Crits generally distance themselves from Marxist instrumentalism.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even Suri's lawyer, arguing unconscionability, accepts that the platform's terms are the normal starting point, and asks only for an exception. That framing legitimates the platform's control. Crits don't say law is simply the capitalist's tool (that would be Marxist instrumentalism). They say it makes these arrangements look natural.

9.3.3 STEELMAN: fit crowns the past

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN, the crit's best point is conservatism. Fit crowns the past's dominant principle and files fairness (duress, undue influence: Week 11 slide 14†) as exceptions. The fixes become "arbitrarily selective" (Unger).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The court rescues Suri on unconscionability. A month later, another rider, Hamid, with almost identical facts but a slightly better-paid contract, loses.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A Dworkinian judge asks which reading best fits the past cases. If most past cases favour freedom of contract, fit keeps that principle on top and treats fairness as an occasional repair. So relief is patchy: Suri wins, Hamid loses, for no principled reason. That is Unger's "arbitrarily selective" correction, and the crits' strongest charge against Dworkin.

9.3.4 AGAINST: Harris on incremental justice

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST, Harris: the liberal must show that reformed legalism yields more "incremental justice" than "deconstruction for its own sake".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The liberal reply to the crits is practical. Suri did win, through ordinary doctrine. The challenge for the liberal is to show that steady reform within legal reasoning helps more riders than exposing contradictions without offering a working alternative.

9.3.5 QUALIFY: ALR v CLS

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, ALR v CLS (Liu, W1): both give the same description, that law is politics. They split on "what next?":

  • ALR keeps the system, given good judges;
  • CLS would remake it, exposing class interests.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • A realist looking at Suri's case says: "The judge's sympathies decided it. Get good judges."
  • A crit says: "The whole structure of contract law favours platforms. Change the structure, not just the judges."
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"contract law is a neutral framework"; "the exceptions prove the rule"; "law is drawn up by an elite"; "tear it down".

59.4 Precedent and theory

📘 Learn 9.4 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: like cases alike, stare decisis, authority for argument
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Precedent cannot replace theory. Treating like cases alike needs a test of which differences matter, and that test is moral.
  2. Was a mother reaching hospital two hours later like one at the scene? Only a principle, foreseeability or physical risk, can say.
  3. So "precedent, not justice, makes law fair" fails. Stare decisis is itself contested (strict or relaxed), and needs justification.

AGAINST: relaxed precedent yields when "sufficiently wrong" (Law's Empire). Interpretation "must contain a doctrine of mistake".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Two Mothers
  • Precedent: a mother who watched her son drown in front of her recovered damages for nervous shock.
  • New case: Mrs Wee was at work when her daughter drowned at a public pool. She arrived 90 minutes later and saw her daughter's body.

The pool's counsel says: "Precedent requires treating like cases alike. These cases are unlike: she wasn't there."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Like or unlike? It depends on the principle behind the precedent.
    • If the principle is foreseeable psychiatric harm to close relatives, the cases are alike: a mother seeing her dead child is foreseeable shock, wherever she was standing.
    • If the principle is being in physical danger or at the scene, they are unlike.
  • The choice is moral. Choosing the principle means asking what makes a claim deserve compensation, which is a moral question. Precedent alone can't answer it.
  • Stare decisis is contested too. Should the court follow a precedent it thinks wrong (strict), or only give it weight (relaxed)? That is itself a question needing justification. On Dworkin's relaxed view, a precedent that is sufficiently wrong may yield, so any theory of precedent needs a doctrine of mistake.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"treat like cases alike"; "stare decisis makes law fair"; "precedent, not justice".

69.5 The right answer

📘 Learn 9.5 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: single right answer, whatever coheres, never refuse an unjust statute

9.5.1 Possible in principle, but no threshold

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. A single right answer is possible in principle. Interpretation neither finds law ready-made nor invents it, so one reading can be best.
  2. But fit "will often fail to produce a unique interpretation", and then "substantive political theory" decides.
  3. So "he need never refuse an unjust statute" fails. Dworkin gives no threshold; the Radbruch formula, gauged by TSH's broad historical consensus, does (15.13).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Judge Reyes and the Strikers' Pensions

Ruritania's Parliament passes an Act stripping the pensions of all public workers who took part in a lawful strike. Two readings of an ambiguous section fit the Act equally well: one applies it only to future strikes, the other to strikes in the last ten years. Judge Reyes, a Dworkinian, says: "There is always a single right answer, and I need never refuse a statute, however unjust."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • A right answer is possible. If fit narrows the field, the best reading may be the one that shows the Act in its best light, perhaps applying it only to future strikes, since that fits the law's wider respect for reliance.
  • Fit runs out. Here both readings fit. Reyes must use political theory (fairness, reliance) to choose, which is what Dworkin says happens.
  • "Never refuse" is the weak point. If the Act were intolerably unjust, Dworkin gives Reyes no threshold at which to refuse it. The RF does: refuse only if the injustice is intolerable, judged by broad historical consensus (15.13). Stripping pensions for a lawful strike is unjust, but probably not intolerable on that test.

9.5.2 CONCEDE: beliefs other judges need not share

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE, Dworkin: a judge's best reading rests on "beliefs other judges need not share". Concede that there is no demonstrable answer. Insist that the choice is political, not personal (9.8).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Another judge might honestly prefer the ten-year reading. Concede that Reyes can't prove his reading to her. But his choice rests on public principles (reliance, fairness), not on his personal tastes. That is the difference between political and personal judgement.

9.5.3 QUALIFY: when the practice includes the formula

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, Liu (W11):

  • where the practice itself includes the formula, a Dworkinian judge can fit and still refuse extreme injustice;
  • fit is a matter of degree (Denning; the German nullity courts).

TSH's catch: 8.5.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Ruritania's courts have long held that statutes are read subject to "fundamental principles of justice", and once refused a racist statute.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In that legal culture, refusing an extremely unjust statute fits the practice. So Reyes can be both a Dworkinian and a judge who refuses at the extreme. Fit is a matter of degree: Denning, and the post-war German courts that voided Nazi laws, claimed fit with deeper principles of justice. TSH's catch (8.5) still applies: the "consensus" behind the formula could itself go wrong.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"there is a single right answer"; "whatever coheres is law"; "a judge need never refuse an unjust statute".

79.6 Judge-variance study

📘 Learn 9.6 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: outcomes vary by judge, change the bench
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. A realist reads the variance findings as fact scepticism confirmed. But they indict judges who fail to justify, not Dworkin's normative theory.

On rule v fact scepticism (W11 slide 8†):

  • Llewellyn's "paper rules";
  • Frank's "upper courtitis": the fact-finder decides whether a rule applies;
  • Liu: appeal only moves the discretion up a level (W11).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Asylum Study

A study of Ruritania's immigration tribunal finds that, for similar cases, one adjudicator grants asylum 12% of the time and another 78%. A columnist says: "This proves law is whatever the judge you draw wants. Change the bench and you change the law."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The realist reading. This looks like fact scepticism: adjudicators decide whether an applicant's story is credible, so the rule's application turns on the fact-finder.
  • Rule scepticism and fact scepticism. Llewellyn's rule scepticism says the "paper rules" don't decide cases. Frank's fact scepticism says even if rules were clear, the fact-finder controls whether they apply, and that focusing only on appeal courts is "upper courtitis".
  • What the study really shows. That some adjudicators are failing to decide by justified standards. That is a criticism of them, judged by the very standard Dworkin sets (decide by the best justification). It doesn't refute his account of how judges ought to decide.
  • Liu's point on appeal. Appeal doesn't remove the discretion. It moves it up a level, to the appeal judges.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"outcomes vary by judge"; "change the bench, change the law".

89.7 Synthesis

📘 Learn 9.7 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: answers the realists, victory to the crits
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Dworkin's judge answers the realists: he must justify by fit and value, and cannot predict his own ruling.
  2. But fit may crown freedom of contract and file fairness as an anomaly. Harris reads Unger's jibe at "a pre-established harmony" as aimed at Dworkin.
  3. So "victory to the crits" follows only if value is subjective. Liu's third option, natural law, would say which principle should win (Riggs?: Week 11 slide 15†).

QUALIFY, Liu (W11): Dworkin is text-first. The judge brings his political theory but owes his duty to that law, close to Fuller's fidelity. The crits are goal-first, moulding the text to the transformative aim. The work can overlap; the starting point differs.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Suri on Appeal

Suri's case (9.3) reaches the Court of Appeal. Three judges write:

  • Judge A (Dworkinian): "I must find the reading of contract law that best fits and justifies it. Fit favours freedom of contract; fairness protects only the vulnerable in extreme cases. Suri wins narrowly."
  • Judge B (crit): "My goal is to shift contract law towards protecting workers. I'll read the authorities to make fairness the governing principle."
  • Judge C (natural lawyer): "Contract law exists to serve human goods. A term that lets one party destroy another's livelihood on a whim fails that purpose."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • A answers the realists. He doesn't predict; he justifies.
  • The crits' objection to A. Fit with the past keeps freedom of contract on top, and treats fairness as a convenient anomaly. That is Unger's "pre-established harmony", the assumption that the law already hangs together.
  • Do the crits win? Only if choosing between freedom and fairness is just preference. C shows the third option: an objective account of the good can say which principle should win, as the Riggs majority's appeal to principle suggests.
  • Text-first v goal-first. A and B may reach the same result, but A starts from the law and is bound by it, while B starts from the goal and works the law towards it.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"Dworkin answers the realists"; "victory goes to the crits".

99.8 Is theory "necessarily" implicated?

📘 Learn 9.8 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: necessarily, always, every case, common law and statutes, constitutional democracy
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Theories of law are always implicated: a judge who claims simply to apply the statute has already taken a side on what counts as law.
  2. Morality is always presupposed (legality; reasons to defer to clear words), but it is an operative ground only in hard cases and at intolerable injustice.
  3. So "necessarily implicated" holds for theory, and for morality as a presupposition, but not for morality as the ground of every decision.

Where morality enters, for each theorist:

  • Hart: at most, where the rules run out;
  • Fuller: in fidelity, viewed with the judge's "responsibility for making law what it ought to be";
  • Dworkin: in every proposition of law (Core 14.5; Theorist 15.9).

FOR, Riggs: two morally grounded theories of one statute. Earl's "intention of the makers" against Gray's "What power or warrant have the courts to add to the respondent's penalties".

STEELMAN, Hart: rules have a "core of central meaning" where morality sits idle. LMS refused to judge a law's object without legal standards (TSH). Reply: restraint is itself a theory of judging.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"I Simply Apply the Statute"

Judge Ng says at a conference: "In my court, theory and morality never come into it. I simply apply the statute." That week she decides:

  • (a) a parking fine under a clear by-law;
  • (b) a case where a son who assaulted his mother claims under her insurance policy as "next of kin".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Theory is always there. Even in (a), "apply the statute" assumes a theory of what counts as law: that validly made by-laws are law, and that clear words govern. In (b), deciding whether the plain words or the purpose governs is to take a side, as in Riggs (Earl's intention of the makers against Gray's refusal to add to the penalty).
  • Morality is presupposed, not operative, in (a). Judge Ng's deference to clear words rests on moral reasons (fair notice, democratic authority). But it doesn't decide the parking case: the by-law does.
  • Morality is operative in (b). It is a hard case, where fit leaves room and moral principle helps decide.
  • The steelman. Hart is right that most cases, like (a), sit in the core of settled meaning. Singapore's LMS court likewise declined to judge a law's object without legal standards. But a policy of restraint is itself a theory of how judges should judge.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"theories of law are necessarily implicated in every case"; "always"; "common law and statutes"; "in a constitutional democracy".

109.9 Why judges converge

📘 Learn 9.9 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: shared backgrounds, converge, what apart from rules
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Judges converge less because of shared backgrounds than because they share a practice of justification.
  2. Harris reports Llewellyn: a lawyer who "soaked himself in the 'folkways'" of an appellate court could predict outcomes "eight times out of ten".
  3. So easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory. The tenth case is where that theory is argued, not predicted.

Also on the sheet:

  • FOR: ALR's "underlying ethical pluralism" (Week 1b slide 16†). Kennedy: shared rule-application is "not in fact objectivity", though he sometimes "can't budge" a rule.
  • AGAINST, Dworkin: hard cases are "perhaps just" those where fit yields no unique reading.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The 90% Court

Ruritania's Court of Appeal is unanimous in 90% of its cases. A columnist says: "That's because all the judges went to the same two schools and the same law firms. Shared backgrounds, not law, explain it."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • A better explanation. The judges share a practice of justification: they agree on what counts as a good legal argument. That is why a lawyer steeped in the court's ways can predict about eight cases in ten.
  • The tenth case. In the remaining cases, the shared theory runs out, and the judges argue about it. Those are the hard cases.
  • For the realists. Kennedy warns that shared application isn't the same as objectivity: a homogeneous bench can agree on something that only looks objective. Yet he also admits he sometimes can't budge a rule, so the rules do bite.
  • For Dworkin. The hard cases may be exactly those where fit gives no unique answer.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"judges converge because of shared backgrounds"; "what, apart from rules, decides cases?".

119.10 Chain novelist, author and critic

📘 Learn 9.10 in Lesson 9 →
🔑 Trigger words: chain novel, author, critic, one coherent story
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. The artist interprets as he creates; the critic creates as he interprets. Yet "there is a difference between interpreting while creating and creating while interpreting".
  2. Each chain novelist after the first has "the dual responsibilities of interpreting and creating". After the second, "no single author" has intentions that decide.
  3. So the judge, "a partner in a complex chain enterprise", has a duty "to interpret the legal history he finds, not to invent a better history".

Also on the sheet:

  • QUALIFY: fit has "no algorithm", and value is political, not aesthetic (Dworkin's "political hypothesis").
  • AGAINST: Kennedy's judge works the field toward "how-I-want-to-come-out" (13.1).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Writing Class

A creative-writing class writes a novel in turn, one chapter each. Writer 1 introduces a detective. Writer 5 inherits four chapters that hint the detective is the murderer. Writer 5 would love to make it a romance instead. Meanwhile Judge Lee inherits forty years of Ruritanian cases on employers' liability for their workers' torts.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Writer 5's dual job. She must interpret the story so far (what kind of novel is this?) and create the next chapter. She can't ignore the clues and switch to romance. No single earlier author's intention decides: she must read what the chapters together have become.
  • Judge Lee is in the same position. He must interpret the case law he inherits and add the next chapter, making the law the best it can be, but it must be this law's best version, not a better history invented from scratch.
  • The qualifications. There is no formula for how well a reading must fit. And "best" here means best in political morality (justice, fairness), not most beautiful.
  • Kennedy's contrast. Kennedy's judge starts from how he wants the case to come out and works the field towards it. Writer 5, on that model, would decide on romance first, then hunt for clues to justify it.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"the judge as chain novelist"; "author or critic?"; "one coherent story".

129.11 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Conclusion: the statement is overstated. Rules leave some cases open, not all, and the cost of a flimsy ruling keeps most judges close to them. Where cases are open, judges must justify by fit and political morality, starting from the text, not the goal: neither prediction nor preference. Theory is always implicated and morality always presupposed, but morality decides only where fit runs out or injustice becomes intolerable.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Some cases open, not all: the speeding driver v the rider (9.0).
  • Flimsy rulings cost: the two-line ruling twist (9.1.2).
  • Fit and political morality: Judge Reyes (9.5).
  • Text-first: Judge A on Suri (9.7).
  • Morality decides only at the margins: Judge Ng's two cases (9.8).

Hypos: Lawyering (Pepper, Thunder, Kennedy)

⚡ BIG IDEA

The statement fails. The lawyer's role is moral. Law sets a floor, and prudence, dialogue and rare objection decide the hard cases above it.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 10. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo

  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.

Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 10 of the 7 Nov exam sheet. Sections 1–12 are the same in the Core and Theorist versions, except for one cross-reference in 10.11: the Theorist version adds "(15.12)". Layout: the rule as the sheet states it, a made-up hypothetical, then the application. Tagged lines get their own short hypo, often a twist on the block's main one. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: LP = legal positivism; NLT = natural law theory; RF = Radbruch formula; † = from the slides; S13 = Session 13. "Q95", "Q100" and "Q103" are the practice-bank questions the sheet names.

110.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Position: the statement fails. The lawyer's role is moral. Law sets a floor, and prudence, dialogue and rare objection decide the hard cases above it.

Intro: the statement assumes the lawyer's role can be sealed off from morality, the view Thunder caricatures as "just focus on the law". Yet even Pepper defends that role morally, by appeal to autonomy and equality. So reject or qualify it: the role is moral, bounded by law, and its hard cases call for prudence, dialogue and, rarely, refusal.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"Just Focus on the Law"

A senior partner tells a new associate: "Your job is the law. Morality is the client's business, not yours."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Even Pepper disagrees with the reasoning, though not the conclusion. His case for the "amoral" role is itself moral: lawyers should serve clients fully because clients have a right to autonomy, and equal access to the law.
  • So the role is moral from the start. The law sets the floor (the associate must never help a client break it). Above the floor, hard cases need judgement: prudent advice, moral dialogue with the client, and, in rare cases, refusing to act.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"a lawyer's role is amoral"; "just focus on the law".

210.1 The floor

📘 Learn 10.1 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: turn away a client, distaste, abuses his position, hidden bodies

10.1.1 Choice of client, and Pepper's dilemma

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Turning a client away abuses his position" overstates Pepper. Choice of client is "troubling if it leads to foreclosure of a person's access to the law".
  2. Pepper's best case is a dilemma. Conduct "sufficiently 'bad'" should, it seems, be "made explicitly unlawful". If it isn't, why impose "the happenstance" of one lawyer's conscience?
  3. So "the client's conscience must govern" is itself a moral claim. And to spot Pepper's "extreme cases", the lawyer must weigh morality all the time, so the role is less amoral than it looks (Liu, S13: like Radbruch's judge, though a refused client can find another lawyer).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Payday Lender

Wen, a solo lawyer in a city with hundreds of firms, is asked by a payday lender to draft loan agreements at the highest interest rate the law allows, aimed at low-income borrowers. It is entirely lawful. Wen finds it distasteful and declines. The lender says: "You've abused your position. You're denying me the law."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Not an abuse. For Pepper, choice of client is troubling only if it shuts someone out of the law. The lender can easily hire another of the city's lawyers, so its access isn't foreclosed.
  • Pepper's dilemma, though, has force. If high-interest lending is bad enough, Parliament should ban it. If Parliament hasn't, why should Wen's personal conscience decide which lawful business gets served?
  • But the lender's own argument is moral. "The client's choices must govern" is a claim about what the lawyer ought to do.
  • Liu's point. To know when a case is "extreme" enough to refuse, Wen must weigh morality all the time. So even the Pepper model isn't truly amoral. It resembles Radbruch's judge, who must watch for intolerable injustice, except that a refused client, unlike a litigant, can find another lawyer.

10.1.2 AGAINST: the statement's verbs are moral

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST:

  • The statement's verbs, "abuses" and "denies", are moral premises.
  • Thunder: Pepper's role is "rendered morally impotent for the sake of a moral principle".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The lender says Wen "abused" her position and "denied" it access. Both verbs assume a moral standard for lawyers. And Thunder's charge is that Pepper strips the lawyer's moral agency in the name of a moral principle (autonomy), which is self-undermining.

10.1.3 QUALIFY: Pepper's four zones of autonomy

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, Pepper's four zones of autonomy, which together form "a meaningful field":

  1. practising at all;
  2. choice of client;
  3. dialogue;
  4. objection, "an ever present option".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even on Pepper's own model, Wen has room for her conscience:

  1. she could choose not to practise;
  2. she can turn the lender away;
  3. if she takes it on, she can raise her concerns with it;
  4. in an extreme case, she can refuse a specific task.

10.1.4 Hidden bodies (Q95 only)

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Hidden bodies (Q95 only): objection "should be rarely exercised", but may reveal "the live victim".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A criminal client tells his lawyer, in confidence, that he left a kidnapped child locked in a basement, still alive.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Pepper says conscientious objection should be rare. But this is the extreme case it exists for. Disclosure could save a live victim. (In the real hidden-bodies case the victims were already dead. Pepper's footnote draws the line between not revealing a dead body and revealing a live victim.) Even a Pepper lawyer may break ranks here.

10.1.5 TRAP: Pepper ≠ LP

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

TRAP, Pepper ≠ LP:

  • LP only identifies law, and a moral decision remains (Hart v Radbruch). So a positivist may side with Pepper or Thunder.
  • Pepper is hard to square with NLT, for which finding the law already involves morality (Liu, S13).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Don't write "Pepper is a positivist, so…". Wen could be a positivist and still think, with Thunder, that she must weigh morality in choosing clients. Positivism tells her what the law is, not how to practise. A natural lawyer, by contrast, would find Pepper's "law without morality" picture hard to accept at all.

10.1.6 AGAINST: inequality, and the replies

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST, inequality: the rich buy more law, so a moral filter could level it. The replies (Pepper; Liu, S13):

  • access to justice;
  • distribution is not content;
  • filters may hurt the poor more.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A critic says: "Wen should filter. The lender is rich and can buy endless legal help. Moral filtering by lawyers evens things up."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Access to justice. The better fix is legal aid and pro bono for borrowers.
  • Distribution ≠ content. Unequal access to lawyers is a problem about how legal services are distributed, not about what lawyers may do for clients.
  • Filters can backfire. Rich clients can always find a less scrupulous lawyer. A poor client stuck with one affordable lawyer suffers most from that lawyer's moral filter.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"turning a client away"; "distaste"; "abuses his position"; "hidden bodies".

310.2 The effluent case

📘 Learn 10.2 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: enforcement risk, what officials will actually do, full access
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Advising on enforcement risk is "accurate" and "useful to the client" (Pepper). The trouble is what realism does to Pepper's limit, "the law".
  2. In Pepper's effluent case (the limit is .050 g/l, but anything up to .075 is ignored), a client without "strong moral guidance" faces "no pressure to obey the law as written".
  3. So if law is only what officials will actually do, the promise not to encourage lawbreaking holds only by emptying the word "law".

Also on the sheet:

  • AGAINST, Thunder: autonomy may yield to "the beauty of our shared environment" and others' health.
  • QUALIFY, Liu (S13): the example is "lopsided". No lying by omission, and probably the standard of care, require telling the client both figures. Weighing morality to reach "tell" is Thunderian, while Pepper tells without asking.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Noise Limit

A factory's licence caps night-time noise at 65 dB. Everyone in the industry knows inspectors only act above 75 dB, because of budget cuts. The factory owner asks his lawyer, Daniel: "What's the real limit?"

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Pepper: telling the owner about the 75 dB practice is accurate and useful. It is information the client is entitled to.
  • The realism problem. If "the law" just means what inspectors actually do, then 75 dB is the law. Daniel's promise not to help the client break the law becomes empty, since nothing between 65 and 75 counts as breaking it. And a client with no strong moral compass will feel no pull towards 65.
  • Thunder: the owner's freedom to run his factory may have to give way to neighbours' sleep and health. A good lawyer would raise that.
  • Liu: the example is lopsided. Honesty forbids misleading by omission, and the standard of care probably requires Daniel to give both numbers anyway. Most lawyers would reach "tell" by weighing morality, which is a Thunderian method. Pepper would tell without asking the moral question at all.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"advise on enforcement risk"; "the law is what officials will actually do"; "full access to the law".

410.3 Moral dialogue

📘 Learn 10.3 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: moral dialogue, cost, criminal defendant, corporate officer
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Moral dialogue is a real answer only in part. It makes the lawyer a "moral educator" without judging or policing the client (Pepper).
  2. Its limits are Pepper's own: "it is expensive", and a criminal defendant "will be less open to the dialogue than will the corporate officer".
  3. So dialogue works where it matches Thunder's prudence and tact. For his lawyer, it is ordinary practice, not a repair.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Clients, One Afternoon

Lawyer Priya has two meetings.

  • (a) A company's HR director wants to make 40 staff redundant the week before their annual bonuses vest. It is lawful.
  • (b) A man charged with assault wants Priya to cross-examine the complainant about her past relationships, to make her look unreliable. That is lawful, within limits.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) suits dialogue. The HR director has time, is used to discussing reputation and fairness, and may change course if Priya raises the morale and fairness costs. Priya educates without dictating.
  • (b) is harder. A defendant facing prison is understandably less open to hearing about the complainant's dignity. Every hour of dialogue also costs him money.
  • So dialogue is a partial fix. For Thunder, raising such points tactfully isn't a special repair to an amoral role. It is just what a good, prudent lawyer does.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"moral dialogue"; "it costs too much"; criminal defendant v corporate officer.

510.4 Compartments

📘 Learn 10.4 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: soldiers, separate compartments, chaos, no one can say objectively

10.4.1 Thunder rejects the "dramatic bifurcation"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Lawyers are like soldiers" is the "dramatic bifurcation" Thunder rejects: "to simply point to the role is to give up explaining it".
  2. Pepper fears the moralising lawyer will turn "policeman, judge, and/or deceiver". Thunder holds that the lawyer stays accountable "as a human being".
  3. So "no one can say what a virtuous lawyer would do" overstates. Roles are "not completely idiosyncratic", and prudence applies the virtues (4.7).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Soldier Analogy

A litigator, Marcus, says: "Lawyers are like soldiers. We follow orders inside our role. If we each brought our own morality, there'd be chaos. And anyway, no one can say objectively what a 'virtuous' lawyer would do."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • "It's my role" explains nothing. Saying "it's my role" doesn't explain why the role is worth doing, or how to do it well.
  • Pepper's worry. A moralising lawyer might police, judge, or deceive his own client. That is a real risk.
  • Thunder's reply. Marcus is still a human being who answers for what his work serves.
  • Not chaos. Lawyering has known purposes (justice, fair process), so its virtues aren't arbitrary. Prudence applies them case by case. And "no one can say objectively" is the sceptic's move that 4.7 answers.

10.4.2 CONCEDE: the office lawyer tests Thunder

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE: Pepper's office-lawyer model tests Thunder. Thunder's function ("ensuring the accused a fair trial") fits courts better than offices. Concede that; justice and public order still reach advice.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Marcus moves to a corporate firm, drafting supply contracts. There is no accused and no trial.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Thunder's account of the lawyer's purpose, ensuring the accused a fair trial, doesn't obviously apply. Concede it. But office advice still serves justice and public order: honest contracts and lawful structures. So Thunder's view still reaches Marcus's desk.

10.4.3 QUALIFY: roles matter, but no "pocket universe"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY: Thunder accepts role morality. The police officer owes "courtesy and compassion rather than with cold-hearted mechanical precision". But a role is no "pocket universe" (Liu). The lawyer interprets it constantly by the good life, where Pepper steps outside it only in extremes (S13).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Thunder agrees roles matter. A police officer has duties a civilian doesn't. But the officer should carry them out with compassion, not mechanically. Likewise Marcus interprets his role every day in light of what a good life is. On Pepper's model, by contrast, he only steps outside his role in rare extreme cases.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"lawyers are like soldiers"; "separate compartments"; "it would be chaos"; "no one can say objectively".

610.5 Rules only

📘 Learn 10.5 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: conduct rules, nothing more nothing less, as written, too vague
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "If no rule forbids it, a lawyer may do it" mistakes a floor for the whole. Conduct rules presuppose a purpose (16).
  2. Thunder calls codes "legalistic": mostly general rules, not aspirations. The lawyer's function is not "to slavishly observe the letter of the law".
  3. So "serving justice is too vague" overstates. Thunder admits "substantial disagreement on particular cases", but norms "exploited" against justice are "subverted".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Discovery Avalanche

Big Corp is sued by a small supplier for $80,000. Big Corp's lawyer serves 4,000 discovery requests, knowing the supplier can't afford to answer them and will drop the case. No professional conduct rule expressly forbids this. The lawyer says: "Nothing in the rules stops me. 'Serving justice' is too vague to apply."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The rules are a floor. They exist to make litigation fair and efficient. Using them to crush a smaller party defeats their own purpose.
  • Thunder on codes. Professional codes are legalistic. A lawyer's job isn't to obey their letter slavishly while ignoring what they are for.
  • Vagueness doesn't excuse. Thunder admits lawyers will disagree about many cases. But using discovery rules to bury a claim on its merits is not a hard case. It turns a fairness norm against fairness, which subverts it.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"conduct rules, nothing more, nothing less"; "as written"; "serving justice is too vague".

710.6 The guilty client

📘 Learn 10.6 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: acquittal, believed guilty, technicality, refuse any part
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Winning an acquittal for a client believed guilty is wrong" fails: defending the accused is the role working.
  2. Thunder's lawyer serves by "ensuring the accused a fair trial". For Pepper, full access to the law is "clearer and more dramatic" in criminal cases.
  3. So "he must refuse any part" fits an unjust system, or invoking an intolerably unjust rule such as a racist statute. It doesn't fit a just rule's unjust outcome† (10.11).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Unlawful Search

Lawyer Hannah believes her client stole the jewellery. The police found it during a search without a warrant, so the court excludes it, and the client is acquitted. A journalist writes: "Hannah helped a thief walk free on a technicality. She should have refused any part in it."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The role was working. The exclusion rule protects everyone from unlawful searches, and Hannah's job is to make sure the accused gets a fair trial. On Thunder's view she acted as a good lawyer. On Pepper's, criminal defence is the clearest case for full access to the law.
  • When refusal fits. If the trial were in a corrupt regime's court (an unjust system), or if the defence depended on an intolerably unjust rule (say, a statute excluding a witness's evidence because of her race), refusal could be right.
  • Not here. The exclusion rule is just. An unjust outcome from a just rule is not a reason to refuse (10.11).
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"winning an acquittal for a client believed guilty"; "a technicality"; "he must refuse any part".

810.7 Junior lawyers

📘 Learn 10.7 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: junior lawyers, lawful instructions, superiors, public officials
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Juniors following lawful instructions bear no moral responsibility" fails: legality settles what may be done, not who answers for it.
  2. Thunder's "lazy lawyer" will "tend to take for granted the standards and expectations of his peers and superiors". Courage resists "pressure to conform".
  3. So the junior shares responsibility. Raise it in dialogue first, and refuse only where the instruction would seriously harm others.

Also on the sheet:

  • AGAINST, Thunder: the amoral lawyer "loses the right and indeed the duty to take at least some responsibility" for what his work serves.
  • Mei (Q100 and Q103 only): pleading the time bar is lawful, yet the win may be unjust, so dialogue first. The concealed defect endangers the public, so objection (10.1).
  • JUDGE: Kennedy's five courses are a judge's (12.4; 15.10), not a junior's.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Aisha's Two Instructions

Aisha, a second-year associate, gets two instructions from her partner.

  • (a) Plead the limitation period against an elderly widow who filed her claim against the client three days late.
  • (b) Draft a settlement with a confidentiality clause that would stop the claimant revealing a known brake defect in the client's cars, which are still on the road.

Aisha thinks: "Both are lawful, and I'm only following instructions, so it's not on me."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Lawful ≠ no responsibility. Legality says what Aisha may do, not whether she answers for it. Thunder warns against the "lazy lawyer" who simply absorbs the standards of superiors. Courage means resisting the pressure to conform.
  • (a): dialogue first. Pleading the time bar is lawful, and limitation periods serve real purposes. But the result may be unjust to the widow, so Aisha should raise it with the partner (could the client settle?), not refuse outright.
  • (b): objection may be warranted. Silencing evidence of a defect that endangers the public risks serious harm to others. That is the kind of case where refusing, as conscientious objection (10.1), becomes right.
  • Thunder's AGAINST. If Aisha adopts a purely amoral stance, she gives up both the right and the duty to take responsibility for what her work serves.
  • Not Kennedy's five courses. Those are options for a judge whose sense of the law conflicts with how he wants to decide (12.4). Aisha's position is different: she can raise concerns, or refuse.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"junior lawyers following lawful instructions"; "superiors"; "public officials".

910.8 Lawyers' training and outlook

📘 Learn 10.8 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: conscience at the door, law school, argue any side, theory isn't relevant
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "Leave your conscience at the door" describes an outlook lawyers are trained into. It doesn't justify it.
  2. Pepper reports "We are all realists now" as "a comment often heard from contemporary law professors".
  3. So "theory isn't relevant" is itself an unexamined theory: the realist lawyer already advises "breach as cost".

Also on the sheet: Kennedy: "progressive-minded people", fearing conversion "without choice", ask "Will law school warp my mind?".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Moot Coach

A first-year law student is told by her moot coach: "Leave your conscience at the door. A good advocate can argue any side. And forget jurisprudence; theory isn't relevant to practice." A year later, she advises a client: "Breaching this contract will cost you $50,000 in damages, but you'll make $200,000, so breach."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Describing isn't justifying. The coach describes how lawyers are trained. That doesn't show the training is right.
  • "We are all realists now". The student's advice treats breach of contract as just a cost, which is exactly the realist view of law that Pepper says many law professors hold. So she has a theory after all, just one she never examined.
  • Kennedy. He notes that idealistic students fear exactly this: that law school will change their minds without their choosing.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"leave your conscience at the door"; "law school trains you to argue any side"; "theory isn't relevant".

1010.9 Transactional work

📘 Learn 10.9 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: transactional work, no opposing counsel, no judge
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. In criminal defence, the law "may allow more": implying that a truthful witness lied brings no liability. Similar half-truths used to sell a termite-ridden house may be misrepresentation.
  2. So the statement holds in part. Realism is likelier from a lawyer advising "a large corporate enterprise", where no judge or opposing counsel checks the client.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Half-Truths
  • (a) Defence counsel cross-examines a witness she believes honest, suggesting he may be mistaken or lying, to raise reasonable doubt. That is allowed.
  • (b) A conveyancing lawyer, drafting the sale of a termite-ridden house, writes the disclosure so that it hints the house is "structurally sound" without saying so.
  • (c) A lawyer advises a large company alone, on a restructuring that shifts risk onto suppliers. No one else is in the room.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) is permitted by the adversarial system. A judge and prosecutor are there to test the case.
  • (b) may be misrepresentation. The buyer has no judge and may have no lawyer to catch the half-truth.
  • (c) is where realism tempts most. Advising a big corporation alone, with no judge or opposing counsel to check it, the lawyer is likeliest to treat the law as whatever the client can get away with.

So the statement that lawyers in transactional work may act more freely is only partly right. In fact, they need more care, because no one else is checking.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"transactional work"; "no opposing counsel"; "no judge".

1110.10 Thunder's diagnosis, and the natural-teleological view

📘 Learn 10.10 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: why we hold such views, purpose of law, hired gun, just do your job

10.10.1 Realism plus neo-Kantianism

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Thunder traces the amoral view's appeal "in large part" to "the unwitting collaboration of legal realism and neo-Kantian morality".
  2. Neo-Kantianism tends to make role-based reasons "morally suspect", prudence ("the bread and butter of the legal profession") amoral, and right conduct separate from the good life.
  3. Realism gives the view "a congenial philosophical home". Against both, law is "intended ultimately (though not always immediately)" for ends "naturally good for man".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Hired Gun

A senior partner tells juniors: "We're hired guns. Just do your job. What the law is for isn't our business. A lawyer's ethics are the conduct rules, full stop."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Thunder's diagnosis explains why this sounds plausible.

  • Realism teaches that law is just what officials will do, so "what law is for" seems an idle question.
  • Neo-Kantian ethics treats morality as universal duties for everyone alike. That makes role-based reasons look suspect, treats prudence (lawyers' daily judgement calls) as morally neutral, and separates right conduct from living a good life.
  • Thunder's alternative. Law is ultimately for ends naturally good for human beings: peace, justice, flourishing. A lawyer who serves those ends well is a good lawyer and a good person, not a hired gun.

10.10.2 STEELMAN: Pepper's reply

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN, Pepper: providing access to law makes the lawyer "a good person".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The partner's best defence is Pepper's. By giving clients full access to the law, he serves their autonomy, which is itself a moral good. So the "hired gun" is doing good, not just following orders.

10.10.3 CONCEDE: a diagnosis is not a refutation

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE: a diagnosis is no refutation, and Thunder is "less concerned to counter Pepper's argument blow by blow". Liu doubts the neo-Kantian half, and adds a likelier source: the intuition that a lawyer should not substitute his judgement for the client's, which Thunder shares (S13). Concede, and use 10.1 to answer it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Explaining why the partner holds his view doesn't show it is wrong. Liu suspects the real source is simpler than neo-Kantianism: the sense that it isn't a lawyer's place to override a client's choices. Thunder shares that intuition. So concede the point, and answer the partner with 10.1's arguments: the "amoral" role rests on moral claims, and spotting extreme cases requires constant moral weighing.

10.10.4 QUALIFY: same act, different reasons

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, same act, different reasons (Liu, S13). A Thunder lawyer may disclose a live victim, either as part of the role or because duties "as a human being" trump it. A Pepper lawyer may too, but only as extreme-case objection. The gap is mindset, not necessarily outcome, and the positive law sets how wide it is.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Back to the kidnapped child (10.1.4). Two lawyers both disclose.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The Thunder lawyer may say either "a good lawyer serves the law's purposes, so disclosure is part of my role", or "my duty as a human being outweighs my duty as a lawyer".
  • The Pepper lawyer says: "My role demands silence, but this is the rare extreme where I object."

Same act, different reasoning. How often the two lawyers' actions would differ depends on how much the professional rules already require.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"why do lawyers hold this view?"; "the purpose of law"; "hired gun"; "just do your job".

1210.11 Liu's three scenarios†

📘 Learn 10.11 in Lesson 10 →
🔑 Trigger words: racist statute, coerced evidence, hide behind the system, institutional wrong
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Ask in order†:
    1. Is the system, by and large, just?
    2. If so, is this rule intolerably unjust?
    3. If not, is this outcome unjust?
  2. Calling an unjust result the institution's wrong, not the lawyer's, only moves the question†. Is the institution justified by truth-finding, by dignity, or by replacement costs?
  3. Only truth and dignity make the lawyer's part good rather than merely excused. Pepper names both as defences of the adversary system.

Also on the sheet: Pepper limits client autonomy "by the law, not by the lawyer's morality". If the RF denies a racist statute legal character, even Pepper's lawyer may refuse.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Files on Lawyer Teo's Desk
  • File 1: defend a client in Kessland's Junta courts, where verdicts are fixed in advance.
  • File 2: in a just Ruritania, a landlord wants to evict a tenant under an old, still unrepealed statute that lets landlords evict tenants of one particular race.
  • File 3: in a just Ruritania, Teo's client confessed under coercion. The confession is excluded, and a guilty man will likely walk free.
✔ APPLICATION · Asking the questions in orderDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • File 1: the system is not just. Teo's participation helps legitimise a sham. The case for refusing, or acting only to protect the client from the system, is strongest.
  • File 2: a just system, but an intolerably unjust rule. A racially targeted eviction statute fails the RF (8.8). Even on Pepper's view, client autonomy is limited by the law, so if the statute isn't law, Teo may refuse.
  • File 3: a just system, a just rule, an unjust outcome. Teo may say "the acquittal is the institution's wrong, not mine". But that only moves the question: is the institution justified?
    • If by truth-finding (excluding coerced confessions makes verdicts more reliable) or by dignity (no one should be forced to incriminate himself), Teo's part is good. Pepper cites both.
    • If only by replacement costs ("changing the system would cost too much"), his part is merely excused.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"a racist statute"; "coerced evidence"; "hiding behind the system"; "it's the institution's wrong".

1310.12 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Conclusion: the statement is overstated. Pepper and Thunder are closer than their labels:

  • Pepper defends the role morally, and keeps a right of objection, which needs a lawyer weighing morality throughout;
  • Thunder accepts role morality, and that no legal system is perfect.

They differ in mindset more than outcome, and the more robust the conduct rules, the narrower the gap (Liu, S13). The live question is how often conscience may override the role: rarely and openly, after dialogue, where serving the client would subvert the law's point.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Pepper's moral defence: the payday lender (10.1).
  • Weighing throughout: Liu's point in 10.1.1.
  • Same act, different reasons: the kidnapped child (10.10.4).
  • Conduct rules narrow the gap: the noise limit (10.2), where the standard of care already requires telling.
  • Rarely, openly, after dialogue: Aisha (10.7): dialogue on the time bar, objection on the brake defect.
