HYPO LESSON 11 · ARCHETYPE 11 · ABOUT 29 MIN · 16 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Constitution and judicial role

⚡ BIG IDEA

The statement is overstated. The Constitution relocates, rather than settles, the NLT v LP debate. Courts should presume a law valid, save at intolerable injustice.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 11. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It is the sheet's wording, so it is what you will write in the exam.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 11 of the 7 Nov exam sheet (identical in the Core and Theorist versions). Layout: the rule as the sheet states it, a made-up hypothetical, then the application. Tagged lines get their own short hypo, often a twist on the block's main one.

This archetype is about Singapore's Constitution, so most hypos imagine invented bills or cases under the real Articles (Art 4, 5(2), 9(1), 12, 15, 156). The bills are made up; the cases and quotes come from the sheet. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: LP = legal positivism; NLT = natural law theory; RF = Radbruch formula; BHC = TSH's "broad historical consensus" test; TSH = Tan Seow Hon; YVK = Yong Vui Kong; LMS = Lim Meng Suang; TEH = Tan Eng Hong; S14 = Session 14; † = from the slides.

111.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Position: the statement is overstated. The Constitution relocates, rather than settles, the NLT v LP debate. Courts should presume a law valid, save at intolerable injustice.

Intro: the statement assumes a supreme, written Constitution settles what law is. It doesn't:

  • Art 4 is a master rule only because it is accepted;
  • Part 4's "law", "life", "liberty" and "equal" are contested moral terms.

So qualify it: courts should presume validity, yet void intolerable injustice.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
"The Constitution Has Settled It"

A law student writes: "Singapore has a written, supreme Constitution. Whatever complies with it is law, and whatever conflicts with it is void. So the NLT v LP debate doesn't matter here."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Art 4 depends on acceptance. Art 4 is supreme only because judges and officials treat it as supreme. A document can't make itself supreme.
  • Part 4 needs interpreting. Whether a law deprives someone of "life" or "liberty" otherwise than "in accordance with law", or treats people un"equal"ly, requires deciding what those words mean. That is where NLT and LP part ways.
  • So the debate moves inside the Constitution. It hasn't gone away. The sensible position: presume statutes valid, and strike down only the intolerably unjust.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"the Constitution settles what law is"; "the written Constitution makes the debate irrelevant".

211.1 Supremacy

📘 Learn 11.1 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: Art 4; supreme law; settled it; check the text

11.1.1 A master rule exists because it is accepted

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Art 4 makes the written Constitution supreme. But a master rule exists only because it is accepted: "We may not infer it from the written text alone" (TSH).
  2. So "the Constitution sets the criteria of validity" holds only formally. Part 4's moral terms force a choice of school (11.2, 11.3).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ignored Constitution

Imagine a country, Valdoria, whose written constitution says it is supreme. For decades, its judges ignore the constitution and treat the President's decrees as the highest law.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In Valdoria, the real master rule is "the President's decrees are supreme", because that is what officials actually accept. The text's claim to supremacy changes nothing. Singapore's Art 4 is the master rule because Singapore's officials accept it, not because it says so. And even accepted, it only tells you where to look. What Part 4's moral words require is still open.

11.1.2 AGAINST: LP and morally loaded concepts

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST: LP "does not shed light upon such morally loaded concepts" (TSH). Should the state define "'person', 'life' and 'liberty' when it is not the giver of life?"

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Suppose Parliament passes an Act defining "person" in Art 9 to exclude anyone in a permanent coma. LP can tell you the Act was validly passed. It can't tell you whether Parliament has the moral standing to decide who counts as a "person". TSH's point is that these words point beyond the text.

11.1.3 QUALIFY: basic features

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY: Teo Soh Lung (HC) rejected the basic features doctrine, and YVK (2015) left it open. TSH relies on equal moral worth: even a genocide amendment falls to the RF.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Imagine Parliament, with a two-thirds majority, amends the Constitution to permit the killing of a named ethnic group.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

On Teo Soh Lung's view, there are no unamendable basic features, so the amendment is formally valid. TSH's answer doesn't need basic features. Constitutional supremacy rests on equal moral worth, so an amendment authorising genocide is intolerably unjust and falls to the RF, whatever its pedigree.

11.1.4 TRAP: "the Constitution includes morality, so NLT wins"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

TRAP: never argue that the Constitution includes morality, so NLT wins. That makes you "an LP who is very happy that morality is now part of the positive law" (a student's line Liu endorsed, S14). TSH's own thesis: "constitutionalism is an affirmation of a higher law".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If you write "Art 12's 'equal protection' is a moral idea, so the Constitution proves natural law right", a positivist simply agrees: the positive law has incorporated a moral standard (2.1.4). To make a real NLT point, argue like TSH that constitutionalism itself affirms a higher law that would bind even without the text.

11.1.5 CONCEDE: the master-rule point doesn't do much

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE, Liu: in practice, the master-rule point "doesn't necessarily lead to much". What matters is how theory shapes judges' duty to law (S14).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Concede that showing Art 4 rests on acceptance doesn't, by itself, change any case. The real difference is in how a judge sees her duty: as a positivist applying whatever the master rule picks out, or as a natural lawyer reading the Constitution's moral terms in light of a higher law.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"Art 4"; "the Constitution is the supreme law"; "the Constitution has settled it"; "just check the text".

311.2 Art 9(1) "law"

📘 Learn 11.2 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: validly passed; fair trial only; invent rights; caning; international norms

11.2.1 "In accordance with law"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Reading "law" as "whatever is validly passed" begs the question: what would breach Art 9 that isn't in force? (TSH)
  2. On my application of TSH's test, caning for third-time littering survives the other readings, and falls under the RF only if broad historical consensus condemns it. Arguably none does.
  3. So stopping at fair-trial rules is a choice of theory, not of text. The RF adds only a floor against intolerable injustice.

The readings of "law" in Art 9(1):

ReadingAuthority
Validly passedJabar dictum; YVK (2010)†: not about constitutionality; Nguyen read it to include constitutional validity
Natural justiceOng Ah Chuan left substantive fairness open; YVK (2015)†: procedural; TEH (HC): Art 12 imports none
Not absurd or arbitraryYVK (2010)† suggested it; TSH: TEH's plea failed on evidence, not principle
International lawNguyen: statute beats custom; YVK (2010)†: read consistently where possible; no inhuman-punishment bar adopted
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Littering (Caning) Bill

Suppose Parliament validly passes an Act making caning mandatory for anyone convicted of littering a third time. A convicted man argues that this deprives him of "personal liberty" otherwise than "in accordance with law" under Art 9(1).

✔ APPLICATION · Reading by readingDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • "Validly passed": if "law" just means any validly passed Act, Art 9 can never be breached by a statute, which is TSH's point: it begs the question. (Nguyen read "law" to include constitutional validity, which is itself circular here.)
  • "Natural justice": he gets a fair trial, so the procedural reading is satisfied.
  • "Not absurd or arbitrary": caning for repeated littering is harsh, but it has a rational aim (deterrence), so it probably isn't arbitrary.
  • "International law": Singapore's courts read statutes consistently with international law where possible, but a clear statute beats custom, and they have adopted no bar on inhuman punishment.
  • The RF: the law falls only if broad historical consensus condemns caning for littering as intolerably unjust. Arguably no such consensus exists.

So the Act survives. And stopping at the "fair trial" reading is a choice about how to read "law", not something the text forces.

11.2.2 FOR: no rights "out of whole cloth"

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

FOR, YVK (2015): courts cannot create a right absent from the Constitution "out of whole cloth", as natural law, so there is no right against caning. (No ruling on natural law's view of caning; George: 12.1.)

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The government's best case: the Court of Appeal refused to invent an unwritten right against caning from natural law. On that view, the convicted man can't invoke natural law to add a right the text doesn't contain.

11.2.3 AGAINST: TSH on what the court rejected

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST:

  • TSH: the CA targeted US substantive due process, "the antithesis of natural law theory".
  • LMS: no privacy right. Art 9 covers unlawful deprivation of life, and detention. YVK (2015)† adds unlawful use of force.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

TSH says the YVK court was really rejecting American-style judicial rights-creation, which is the opposite of natural law, not natural law itself. And Art 9 already covers unlawful force, which includes caning, so whether caning is "in accordance with law" is squarely within Art 9.

11.2.4 STEELMAN: each judge a law unto himself

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN: richer readings risk making "each judge a law unto himself". TSH replies that letting manifest injustice stand "defeats the very purpose of certainty".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The risk is real: if "law" means "just law", each judge applies her own idea of justice. TSH's reply is that certainty exists to serve justice, so leaving a manifestly unjust law in place defeats the point of certainty. That is why the RF floor is narrow: it applies only to manifest injustice.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"'law' in Art 9 means whatever is validly passed"; "Art 9 only guarantees a fair trial"; "judges would be inventing rights"; caning; "international norms".

411.3 Art 12

📘 Learn 11.3 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: intelligible line; legitimate object; unelected legislators; left-handed drivers

11.3.1 The LMS test

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. For LMS (CA), an intelligible line rationally related to the law's object usually suffices, since courts are not "mini-legislatures".
  2. On a double fee for left-handed drivers, the CA asks whether the line rationally serves its aim. The HC would also void an "inherently bad" aim.
  3. So "judges who probe the object become legislators" overstates. The RF voids only intolerable injustice, which is a narrower ground than Wednesbury unreasonableness.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Left-Handed Drivers' Fee

Suppose a regulation doubles the licence fee for left-handed drivers. The stated aim is "road safety", based on one old study suggesting left-handers react more slowly.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The CA's test (LMS). Is there an intelligible line (left-handedness), and is it rationally related to the object (road safety)? If the study is junk, the rational link fails. The court won't second-guess whether road safety is a good aim, since it isn't a mini-legislature.
  • The HC's extra step. The High Court would also strike down an aim that is "inherently bad". Suppose the real aim were to "discourage left-handedness": that would fail.
  • Not judicial legislation. Probing the object this far isn't the court legislating. The RF goes further only at intolerable injustice, which is narrower than Wednesbury unreasonableness. Courts don't strike down laws merely for being unwise.

11.3.2 FOR: a threshold test

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

FOR, LMS (CA):

  • the test is a threshold test;
  • there is no free-standing review of legitimacy, only a "limited element of illegitimacy";
  • Wednesbury is rejected;
  • use Art 12(2).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The Court of Appeal's approach is deliberately modest. It asks whether the line makes sense, not whether the law is fair. Art 12(2) lists specific forbidden grounds (religion, race, descent, place of birth), and left-handedness isn't among them, so the general threshold test applies.

11.3.3 QUALIFY: not cleanly LP v NLT

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY: this is not cleanly LP v NLT.

  • "Extreme illogicality and/or incoherence" fails a limb, and a ban on women driving "might" fail limb two.
  • TSH calls the test "a manifestation of the workings of natural law".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A different regulation bans women from driving, citing "family stability".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Even the modest LMS test would likely catch this. A link between women driving and family instability is so far-fetched that the line fails for extreme illogicality. So the "positivist" threshold test still makes judgements of reason and coherence, which is why TSH calls it natural law at work.

11.3.4 AGAINST: equality is empty without a higher law

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST, TSH: "Equality is empty of content without a higher moral law". The question is which differences are "morally significant", so moral arguments are not "extra-legal" under Art 12(1). Without them, laws treating everyone "equally badly" pass (W13 slide 18†).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Parliament passes a law forbidding all drivers from driving after 8 pm, to save fuel.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

No one is singled out, so there is no unequal line to test. Art 12 is silent, even though the law treats everyone equally badly. And for the left-handed fee, deciding whether left-handedness is a "morally significant" difference is a moral question. Equality only has content once you have a view of which differences matter.

"an intelligible line rationally related to the object"; "a legitimate object"; "judges as unelected legislators"; left-handed drivers.

511.4 Four walls

📘 Learn 11.4 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: within its own four walls; foreign values; universal morality

11.4.1 Four walls needn't exclude universal standards

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Reading the Constitution primarily "within its own four walls", as Colin Chan did (TSH; LP, per Liu's slide†), need not exclude universal standards.
  2. Reading Haw Tua Tau charitably, TSH finds that fairness "was universal, though its specific manifestation varied according to local conditions".
  3. So "universal morality" need not mean foreign values, if it is confined to manifest injustice (11.5).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Foreign Precedent

A litigant challenging a Singapore law cites a European court's ruling on the right to a fair hearing. The Attorney-General replies: "Our Constitution must be read within its own four walls, not by importing foreign values."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The four-walls approach (Colin Chan) is a sound starting point: read Singapore's Constitution in light of Singapore's text and history.
  • But it needn't exclude universal standards. On TSH's reading of Haw Tua Tau, fairness is universal, though how it is applied depends on local conditions.
  • So the litigant's real argument isn't "follow Europe". It is "the basic fairness every legal system owes its people requires this", applied in Singapore's way, and only at the level of manifest injustice.

11.4.2 CONCEDE: higher law cuts both ways

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE: higher law cuts both ways. A "true-blue Thomist" may get judges with "quite a different view of dignity" (Lawrence; TSH). Concede: no wide review, only a narrow trigger.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A conservative natural lawyer who invites judges to apply "universal morality" may get judges whose view of dignity points the other way, as the US Supreme Court's Lawrence decision did for some. Concede that risk, and confine the trigger to manifest injustice.

11.4.3 QUALIFY: Liu on TSH's narrow LP

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, Liu (S14): TSH's LP is too narrow. LP mandates little but allows more.

  • Where the text points to a moral concept, an LP judge may follow it outward, as "commercial reasonableness" imports trade practice.
  • A purposive LP judge may read the Constitution as guarding individuals.

TSH replies: then "Reference to natural law" is "mandatory". And can he stop at popular morality?

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A positivist judge reading Art 12's "equal" can follow that word out into moral reasoning, just as a commercial judge reads "reasonable" by looking at trade practice. So positivism doesn't confine judges to the four walls. TSH's reply: if the judge must look outside the text, natural law is unavoidable. And if he stops at popular morality, what stops majorities defining "equal" however they like?

"within its own four walls"; "foreign values"; "universal morality".

611.5 Who decides (courts)

📘 Learn 11.5 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: for Parliament, not the courts; ballot box; unelected judges; activism
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Contested rights are for Parliament, but only until "the threshold of injustice in Radbruch's formula is met" (TSH).
  2. So "judges must never invalidate a law for injustice" goes too far. Rubber-stamping is a vice too (12.2), and intolerable injustice must fall.

Also on the sheet:

  • STEELMAN: Rajeevan (HC 1998), per TSH: the legislature "rightfully determines the rights of the individual" absent specific guarantees.
  • Threshold (BHC: 15.13): met for genocide and slavery; not for Roe, Obergefell, or Women's Charter s 12. The catch: 11.7.
  • QUALIFY: LMS left Hart v Devlin to the Legislature (16). TSH: only "if no constitutional right was at stake".
  • LEGISLATOR: where "objective morality is not clear", a deliberative democracy "can take a stand through its legislature" (12.3).
  • Close, Liu's last slide†: "Who decides? … We are back where we started. But, wiser."
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Petitions

The High Court receives three challenges:

  • (a) to a law allowing debt bondage (working off debts as unpaid servants);
  • (b) to the Women's Charter s 12 definition of marriage;
  • (c) to a law raising the drinking age to 21.

The government argues: "These are for Parliament and the ballot box, not unelected judges."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a): the threshold is met. Debt bondage is slavery in substance, and broad historical consensus condemns it. A court that rubber-stamped it would abdicate.
  • (b): the threshold is not met. There is no BHC that the current marriage definition is intolerably unjust, so it is for Parliament.
  • (c): ordinary policy. It is plainly for Parliament.
  • The steelman. Rajeevan holds that, absent specific guarantees, Parliament rightly decides individuals' rights, which supports deference on (b) and (c).
  • LMS and Hart–Devlin. The Court of Appeal left the Hart–Devlin question to Parliament. TSH's qualifier: that is right only if no constitutional right is at stake.
  • Where morality is unclear, as on (b), a deliberative democracy takes its stand through its legislature (12.3).
  • The catch (11.7): consensus can shift or go wrong. As Liu's last slide says, we end up asking who decides, but wiser.

"it's for Parliament, not the courts"; "the ballot box"; "unelected judges"; "judicial activism".

711.6 Art 156

📘 Learn 11.6 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: repeal; marriage; leave it to Parliament; courts are binary
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. In 2022, change through Parliament came. s 377A went, and Art 156, intended as "a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism" (TSH), shielded man–woman marriage laws from Part 4.
  2. So "leaving it to Parliament" moved the question rather than removing it: a two-thirds majority (Art 5(2)) put those laws beyond Part 4 (11.7).

Also on the sheet:

  • FOR, Shanmugam: courts "can only make binary decisions" (Hansard, 29 Nov 2022).
  • QUALIFY, TSH: repeal was for risk, not unconstitutionality, so laws that differentiate are "not incoherent in principle". After UKM, s 377A "failed to do the work", which "might explain the change of tactic".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Columnist's Claim

A columnist writes: "By repealing s 377A in Parliament and adding Art 156, Singapore took the question away from the courts and settled it democratically. That's what 'leave it to Parliament' means."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Partly right. The change did come through Parliament, as the "leave it to Parliament" view wanted, and Shanmugam's point was that courts can only strike down or uphold, while Parliament can craft a package.
  • But the question moved, not vanished. Art 156 was itself a constitutional decision, made by a two-thirds majority under Art 5(2), which places marriage laws beyond Part 4's rights. So the question became "who holds two-thirds?" rather than "what do the rights require?".
  • TSH's reading. The government repealed s 377A because of the risk of a court striking it down, not because it was unconstitutional. So keeping other laws that differentiate is not inconsistent in principle. And after UKM, s 377A was no longer doing the work of protecting the marriage framework, which may explain the switch to Art 156.

811.7 The Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary?

📘 Learn 11.7 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: neither philosophy nor personal morality; always sufficient; I just apply the law; my morals are private; without exception

11.7.1 The statement is itself a legal philosophy

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. The statement is itself a legal philosophy: too moralised for the positivist, and too amoral for the natural lawyer.
  2. Hart, positivism's ablest defender, rejects its conclusion: "Law is not morality; do not let it supplant morality".
  3. So "compliance always gives sufficient moral guidance" fails. Law is a floor, not a ceiling, and its open terms need theory.

Also on the sheet:

  • Dilemma: Hart's penumbral judge may have to reach beyond the law; Dworkin's judge finds the answer in community morality that is also law. Theory either way.
  • LAWYER: law is a floor: it "is concerned with the minimum and not with the maximum" (Devlin). Pepper's own premise implies the same (10.1).
  • Art 5(2): a "special two-thirds majority" amends most provisions (TSH), with no express core like the Basic Law's art 79(3) (implied limits: 11.1). So treating compliance as moral guidance hands judgement to whoever holds two-thirds.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Judge's Speech

A newly appointed judge says: "In Singapore, the Constitution gives us everything we need. I need neither philosophy nor personal morality. If I follow the Constitution, I will always act rightly. My morals are private."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • It's a philosophy. "The Constitution is always sufficient moral guidance" is a theory of law and morality. A positivist would reject it as too moralised (positivists say legal and moral duty can come apart). A natural lawyer would reject it as too amoral (it ignores any higher law).
  • Hart agrees. Even positivism's champion says: law is not morality, so don't let it replace morality.
  • The open terms. When the judge must decide what "equal" means, Hart's model has her exercising discretion in the penumbra, and Dworkin's has her finding community morality in the law. Either way, she uses theory.
  • The floor. As Devlin says, law sets the minimum, not the maximum. A lawyer who does only what the law demands has not done everything that is right.
  • Two-thirds. Most of the Constitution can be amended by two-thirds of Parliament, with no protected core. If compliance were always morally sufficient, morality would be whatever two-thirds of MPs decide.

11.7.2 STEELMAN: most cases are routine

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN: personal morality is subjective, so keep it out. Most cases are routine: "to be occupied with the penumbra is one thing, to be preoccupied with it another".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The judge's best point is that most of her cases (contracts, sentencing within ranges) never require moral theory. Hart's line warns against obsessing over the hard edge. Concede that, then insist the hard edge still exists.

11.7.3 AGAINST: refusal as fidelity

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST:

  • A natural-law judge refusing manifest injustice "expresses his fidelity to law", and is "not merely acting according to his conscience" (TSH).
  • Subjectivism defeats itself: 4.7.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The judge assumes that any moral reasoning would be her private conscience. TSH's reply: refusing manifest injustice is fidelity to law properly understood, not personal preference. And "morality is subjective, so keep it out" is itself a moral claim (4.7).

11.7.4 Without exception: Art 15

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Without exception: try an as-applied Art 15 challenge, though Art 15(4), read literally, lacks the "necessary" test of ICCPR art 18(3) (TSH): 12.6.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A law bans alcohol "without exception", catching communion wine.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

A church could bring an as-applied challenge under Art 15 (freedom of religion). But on TSH's reading, Art 15(4) doesn't require restrictions on religion to be "necessary", unlike the ICCPR. So the challenge is weak on the text, even if strong morally (12.6).

11.7.5 CONCEDE: TSH's catch

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE, TSH's catch (8.5): consensus is a gauge, not a ground.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If you argue the judge should refuse intolerable injustice judged by broad consensus, concede that consensus only indicates injustice. It can be wrong (8.5.3).

911.8 Legitimacy, basic features, separation of powers

📘 Learn 11.8 in Lesson 11 →
🔑 Trigger words: what makes it legitimate; consent; unamendable; basic features; separation of powers; gatekeeper

11.8.1 Acceptance can't found legitimacy

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. "The people's acceptance" cannot found legitimacy. The framers' will "begs the question of why it should continue to bind us", and treating non-revolt "as acquiescence is artificial" (TSH).
  2. "Only by understanding our co-equal dignity under natural law is our consent meaningful". NLT answers this from within, while LP must borrow another moral or political theory (Liu, S14).
  3. So "NLT defeats the separation of powers" fails. On the weak thesis, morality overrides only at the Radbruch threshold, and TSH agrees that a "representative legislative mandate should generally prevail over judicial opinion on contentious moral norms".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Student's Two Claims

A student argues:

  • (i) "The Constitution is legitimate because the people accepted it in 1965, and no one has revolted since."
  • (ii) "Natural law would let judges overrule Parliament on any moral issue, so it destroys the separation of powers."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (i) fails. Why should the framers' choice in 1965 bind citizens born decades later? And treating "no revolt" as consent is artificial: people stay quiet for many reasons. Consent means something only if we are equals in dignity, which is a natural-law premise. A positivist must borrow some other moral or political theory to explain legitimacy.
  • (ii) fails. Weak NLT lets morality override law only at intolerable injustice. On contested moral questions, TSH agrees that Parliament's mandate should generally prevail over judges' opinions.

11.8.2 QUALIFY: Liu's two further answers

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

QUALIFY, Liu's two further answers (S14):

  1. reason converges, so, properly applied, all three branches reach one result;
  2. NLT v LP asks what law is; the separation of powers asks how power is organised. So a democrat or a dictator could hold either.
✔ APPLICATION · To (ii)Decide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If moral reasoning done well converges, a natural-law Parliament and a natural-law court shouldn't clash. And the two questions are separate: a positivist can be a dictator's lawyer, and a natural lawyer can be a committed democrat.

11.8.3 AGAINST: the gatekeeper problem

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

AGAINST, the gatekeeper problem:

  • an LP judge defers, leaving the legislature as moral gatekeeper;
  • an NLT judge tests law against a higher law, so the conflict is real (Radbruch);
  • German courts applied the formula to a fallen regime's laws (Liu, W11);
  • whether Singapore's judges hold it is "debatable", and they prefer a constitutional basis;
  • against a sitting legislature, it is untested (S14).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Concede that there is a real difference. Under NLT, the court is a backstop gatekeeper. But the German use of the formula was against a regime that had already fallen. Using it against a sitting Parliament has never been tested in Singapore, and Singapore's judges would look for a constitutional peg (Arts 9, 12) rather than invoke natural law directly.

11.8.4 Basic features

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Basic features:

  • Kesavananda (India) held some features of the constitution unamendable. Those suggested include "the separation of powers" and its "secular character" (TSH).
  • The doctrine was rejected in Singapore (11.1).
  • Liu: it is easier for NLT, because a good constitution has a telos that some amendments would destroy.
  • TSH: argue from natural law, not by "second-guessing the intention of the constitution-framers".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

A two-thirds majority amends the Constitution to abolish the courts' independence.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

India's Kesavananda doctrine would void the amendment as destroying a basic feature. Singapore has rejected that doctrine. A natural lawyer has a better argument than guessing what the framers intended: the Constitution exists for an end (protecting citizens' equal dignity under law), and an amendment that destroys judicial independence defeats that end. As Liu says, NLT finds this argument easier to make.

"what makes the Constitution legitimate?"; "consent"; "unamendable"; "basic features"; "separation of powers"; "who is the gatekeeper?".

1011.9 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Conclusion: the statement is overstated. Art 4 and Part 4 relocate, rather than settle, the NLT v LP debate, so judges choose a theory whenever they read "law" or "equal". The Constitution narrows the practical gap between NLT and LP judges, and makes Radbruch's formula rarely needed, but leaves open the extreme case, our attitude to law, and who decides by what standard (Liu, S14). Judges should presume validity but void intolerable injustice. No clause relieves anyone of conscience.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • A theory is chosen: the Littering (Caning) Bill (11.2) and the Left-Handed Drivers' Fee (11.3).
  • The gap narrows: most of the hypos come out the same for NLT and LP judges.
  • The extreme case: the genocide amendment (11.1.3) and debt bondage (11.5).
  • Who decides: Art 156 (11.6).
  • Conscience: the judge's speech (11.7).

HYPO LESSON 12 · ARCHETYPE 12 · ABOUT 19 MIN · 13 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Roles, who decides

⚡ BIG IDEA

The statement is right as a presumption. Roles have limits, but where they lie is contested, and abdication is a vice too.

The theory behind these hypos is taught in Lesson 12. Do that lesson first if the rules below look unfamiliar.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It is the sheet's wording, so it is what you will write in the exam.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 12 of the 7 Nov exam sheet (identical in the Core and Theorist versions). Layout: the rule as the sheet states it, a made-up hypothetical, then the application. Tagged lines (OFFICIAL, JUDGE, LAWYER, LEGISLATOR, STEELMAN, CONCEDE, QUALIFY) get their own short hypo, often a twist on the block's main one. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: RF = Radbruch formula; BHC = TSH's "broad historical consensus" test; NLT = natural law theory; LP = legal positivism; TSH = Tan Seow Hon; YVK = Yong Vui Kong; † = from the slides.

112.0 The archetype in one line

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Position: the statement is right as a presumption. Roles have limits, but where they lie is contested, and abdication is a vice too.

Intro: the statement treats each role's limits as settled. Roles do have limits: a constitutional democracy divides power. But:

  • where a role ends is contested, and drawing the line is a moral judgement;
  • refusing one's own work is as much a vice as taking someone else's;
  • refusing extreme injustice is fidelity, not usurpation.

Frame (for roles questions): the statement is almost verbatim George, as TSH reports him: at least in a "basically just regime", natural law requires "that judges and other officials respect the limits of their own authority". The statement drops the proviso and adds lawyers.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Statement on the Paper

An exam question says: "Judges, officials and lawyers must respect the limits of their own roles, and leave to others what is rightfully theirs. Discuss."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Spot the source. This is George's claim, with two changes. It drops "in a basically just regime", and it adds lawyers.
  • Agree as a presumption. In a just democracy, judges shouldn't legislate, officials shouldn't make policy, and lawyers shouldn't police their clients' morals.
  • Then push back three ways:
    1. who decides where a role ends is itself contested;
    2. a judge who rubber-stamps everything fails her role as surely as one who legislates;
    3. a judge who refuses to apply a law ordering genocide isn't overstepping her role. She is being faithful to law.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"respect the limits of their roles"; "leave to others what is rightfully theirs"; "who decides?".

212.1 Source and frame

📘 Learn 12.1 in Lesson 12 →
🔑 Trigger words: limits of their own authority; rightfully others'; who decides?; for Parliament, not the courts

12.1.1 A role's limits come from a theory of the role

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. The statement assumes we know where roles end. For George, allocating authority is a determinatio: a prudent choice among morally acceptable options.
  2. TSH's reply is the question George leaves open: "who rightfully decides on whether it is prudentially made?".
  3. So "what is rightfully others'" assumes its own answer. A role's limits come from a theory of the role.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Euthanasia Case

A terminally ill man asks Ruritania's top court to declare that the ban on assisted suicide breaches his right to life and liberty. The government says: "Whether to allow assisted dying is rightfully Parliament's decision, not the courts'."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • George. How a society divides authority between courts and Parliament is a determinatio: there are several morally acceptable ways to do it, and the choice is prudent rather than dictated by natural law.
  • TSH's question. But who decides whether that division was prudently made? The government's "rightfully Parliament's" assumes the answer.
  • So the court needs a theory of its role. Is it to protect individuals against majorities on fundamental rights, or to defer on contested moral questions? Only then can it say what is "rightfully" Parliament's.

12.1.2 STEELMAN: Rajeevan and YVK

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

STEELMAN:

  • Rajeevan (11.5): the legislature rightly determines individual rights, absent specific guarantees.
  • YVK (2015), citing George: "some have contended" that natural law requires judges "to respect the boundaries of authority".
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The government's best case is that Singapore's courts themselves have adopted this deference. Rajeevan gives Parliament the lead on rights the Constitution doesn't specifically guarantee. YVK even notes the natural-law argument for judges keeping within their bounds. So deference isn't anti-natural-law.

12.1.3 CONCEDE: TSH's impasse

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE, TSH's impasse binds my side. Natural law condemns vesting authority in "a random group of bandits", but cannot say who decides. Still, the proviso, "impasse notwithstanding, must be right in principle".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If you argue that the court may override Parliament at extreme injustice, concede that natural law can't tell you exactly who should decide hard cases. It only rules out the absurd, like handing power to bandits. But George's proviso (respect role limits only "in a basically just regime") is right in principle. In an unjust regime, deference loses its basis.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"respect the limits of their own authority"; "leave to others what is rightfully theirs"; "who decides?"; "for Parliament, not the courts".

312.2 Twin vices: usurpation and abdication

📘 Learn 12.2 in Lesson 12 →
🔑 Trigger words: usurp; leave it to Parliament; non-enforcement; just focus on the law

12.2.1 Every role can fail twice

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Every role can fail twice: by doing others' work (usurpation) or by refusing its own (abdication). The statement names only the first.
  2. TSH names both for judges: in bad faith they "would either engage in judicial legislation, or rubber-stamp whatever law Parliament passes".
  3. So "respecting the limits of one's role" is half the duty. The other half is doing the role's own moral work.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Two Judges
  • Judge Ang strikes down a tax law because she thinks a flat tax is fairer.
  • Judge Bala upholds every law that comes before him, including one letting police detain anyone indefinitely without charge. He says: "It's not my place."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Ang usurps. She does Parliament's work, deciding tax policy.
  • Bala abdicates. He refuses the court's own work, which is to check laws against the Constitution and against intolerable injustice.
  • The lesson. The statement warns only against Ang's error. TSH names both failings: legislating from the bench, and rubber-stamping. Respecting your limits is only half of doing your job well.

12.2.2 The twin vices by role

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
RoleThe sheet's exampleHypothetical twistApplication
OFFICIALs 377A (2007), kept but not proactively enforced: arguably Parliament abdicated, and the executive quasi-legislated (7.7).Ruritania's Parliament keeps a law it won't defend, and the Attorney-General announces it won't be prosecuted.Parliament avoided deciding (abdication), and the executive in effect changed the law by announcement (usurpation).
JUDGEBridge's "unwarranted abdication" (McLoughlin 441; 9.2).A judge refuses a novel claim only because no earlier case has allowed it.Refusing to develop the law when principle requires it is abdication.
LAWYERScreening clients usurps (Pepper); "just focus on the law" abdicates (Thunder).One lawyer refuses all clients whose politics she dislikes. Another drafts anything lawful without a thought.The first takes over the court's and Parliament's job of deciding who gets the law's help (usurpation, on Pepper's view). The second gives up his own moral agency (abdication, on Thunder's view).
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"usurp"; "leave it to Parliament"; "non-enforcement"; "just focus on the law".

412.3 The legislator's hat

📘 Learn 12.3 in Lesson 12 →
🔑 Trigger words: majoritarian will; sole concern; as accurately as possible; poll; referendum; whip

12.3.1 Trustee, not stenographer

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Majority will settles who may make law in a democracy, not what the law is or should say.
  2. Devlin, the statement's natural ally, tells law-makers that majority opinion "is surely not enough". His standard "does not depend on the counting of heads".
  3. So the legislator does what "the sole concern" forbids: he judges, as a trustee, not a stenographer.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The MP's Pledge

A new MP pledges: "My sole concern is to reflect my voters' will as accurately as possible. I'll vote however the latest constituency poll says, on every bill."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Majority will has a role. It explains why he is the one who gets to vote. It doesn't tell him how to vote on a bill to, say, cut legal aid.
  • Even Devlin. The MP might cite Devlin, but Devlin says counting heads isn't enough: legislators must judge what is truly beyond the limits of tolerance.
  • So he is a trustee. He must use his own judgement on his voters' behalf, not simply transcribe a poll.

12.3.2 STEELMAN, LEGISLATOR and QUALIFY

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • STEELMAN: equal respect amid disagreement, and a fear of juristocracy (TSH). Poa (2022) sought a referendum, marriage being "a matter of social norm".
  • LEGISLATOR: Masagos to Poa: MPs must "come to a decision even, and perhaps especially, for difficult and polarising social issues" (2022).
  • QUALIFY: TSH: non-NLT legislators "may not regard themselves as bound" by higher standards. Liu: "need not" ≠ "will not". A legislator who wants good, not merely valid, laws weighs morality (14.4's minimum content; Hart v Devlin). LP uses morality in one dimension (good law); NLT in two (good law, and law at all).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

The MP, facing a divisive bill on the definition of marriage, says: "This is a social norm. Let's hold a referendum." A minister replies that MPs must decide hard questions themselves. A third MP, a positivist, says: "Since law needn't be moral, I'm not bound by any higher standard."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The referendum idea has a real basis: treating citizens as equals when they disagree, and preferring the people to judges (Poa's argument).
  • The minister's reply (Masagos): MPs are elected precisely to decide hard and polarising issues, not to hand them back.
  • The positivist MP. He's right that, as a positivist, he need not treat any higher standard as binding on legality. But that doesn't mean he won't weigh morality. If he wants good laws, and not merely valid ones, he must, just as Hart did in arguing against Devlin. The difference is that positivists use morality in one dimension (is it a good law?), while natural lawyers use it in two (is it a good law, and is it law at all?).
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"majoritarian will"; "the legislator's sole concern"; "as accurately as possible"; "a poll"; "a referendum"; "the whip".

512.4 The judge's hat

📘 Learn 12.4 in Lesson 12 →
🔑 Trigger words: if passed, would you enforce it?; strike down; refuse; validly passed; applying the law

12.4.1 The judge's ladder

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. The judge asks not whether the law is wise, but what it is and what fidelity to it requires.
  2. Climb a ladder:
    1. validity;
    2. then interpretation by principle and purpose;
    3. then discretion within the statute;
    4. refusal only at the Radbruch threshold.
  3. So "I would enforce it" is a moral conclusion, reached through a theory of the judicial role, not an escape from morality.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Curfew for Under-16s

Ruritania passes a law: "No person under 16 may be in a public place after 10 pm. Breach is punishable by a fine of up to $1,000, payable by the child." Judge Lee thinks the law is unwise. A 15-year-old is charged for walking home from a late hospital visit to her mother.

✔ APPLICATION · Up the ladderDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Validity. It was properly passed, and it's constitutional on its face.
  2. Interpretation. Read by principle and purpose (keeping children safe, not punishing necessity), does "in a public place" cover a child walking straight home from a hospital? A purposive reading may exclude it.
  3. Discretion. If it does apply, the statute says "up to $1,000", so the judge can impose a nominal fine.
  4. Refusal? The law is unwise, but nowhere near intolerable injustice, so refusal is off the table.

So Judge Lee enforces the law, gently. And that decision rests on a moral theory of her role: fidelity to valid law, read by its purpose.

12.4.2 Kennedy's five courses

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Kennedy's five courses (15.10):

  • He endorses or excludes none of them "a priori".
  • The public's "devil's compact" (defend the decision as plausibly legal, change it, or withdraw) presupposes a determinacy that "initiates know is false".
  • He finds it "unconvincing" that the rule of law means obeying it.

Candour, my standard, bars his covert last two. Refusal line: genocide and slavery; not Roe.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The twist

Judge Lee, a crit like Kennedy, wants the girl acquitted, but the field won't budge: the words plainly cover her. Her options:

  1. apply the law, and write an opinion denouncing it;
  2. withdraw from the case;
  3. acquit, openly saying the law is wrong;
  4. acquit using an argument she thinks implausible;
  5. find, falsely, that the girl wasn't in a public place.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Kennedy refuses to rule any of these in or out in advance. He thinks the public's picture (the judge must either show the law supports her, change her mind, or step aside) assumes the law is more determinate than insiders know it is.
  • A candour standard rules out 4 and 5, because both are covert: a bad-faith argument, and a false finding.
  • The refusal line. Option 3 is open only at the Radbruch threshold (genocide, slavery). A curfew, or Roe-type issues, don't reach it.
  • So Judge Lee should take option 1, or perhaps option 2.

12.4.3 CONCEDE: TSH's catch

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

CONCEDE, TSH's own catch: concede the risk. Her reply: 8.5.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

If consensus decides where the refusal line falls, consensus could one day move it somewhere mistaken. Concede that. Then use TSH's reply (8.5.3): any other decision-maker is no more reliable.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"if passed, would you enforce it?"; "strike it down"; "refuse"; "it was validly passed"; "I'm only applying the law".

612.5 The official's and the junior's hat

📘 Learn 12.5 in Lesson 12 →
🔑 Trigger words: officials tasked with enforcing; lawful instructions; superiors; junior; deference
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. Officials owe fidelity to law, not deference to rank: "mere respect for constituted authority must not be confused with fidelity to law" (Fuller).
  2. In a rogue state, Alexy's risk effect reaches "a judge or another office-holder", "neither a saint nor a hero": if non-positivism prevails, he risks later prosecution.
  3. So "obeying lawful instructions" is not blameless: "to simply point to the role is to give up explaining it" (Thunder).

Also on the sheet:

  • CONCEDE: Thunder grants that virtue under-determines cases (10.5): dialogue first, refusal only at the extreme.
  • Thunder's librarian, mistreating customers under "official library policies", cannot plead the role.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Clerk Jurić, Again

Under the Junta, clerk Jurić (8.4) is ordered by his superior to stamp seizure orders confiscating the Kel minority's property. He's no hero. He just wants to keep his job.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Fidelity ≠ deference. Jurić owes fidelity to law, not obedience to whoever outranks him. Respecting authority is a different thing.
  • The risk effect. Alexy's point is aimed at ordinary office-holders like Jurić, "neither a saint nor a hero". If non-positivism becomes the accepted view, then after the Junta falls, the seizure orders may be held never to have been law, and Jurić may face prosecution. That prospect gives him a reason to refuse now.
  • "I was just doing my job" explains nothing. As Thunder says, pointing to your role doesn't explain why the role justifies what you did.
  • The concession. Thunder admits that being virtuous doesn't settle every case. So for a less extreme instruction, Jurić should raise concerns first, and refuse only at the extreme.
  • Thunder's librarian. A librarian who is rude to customers because "official library policies" say so can't hide behind the role either. Roles shape how you act, but don't excuse acting badly.
🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"officials tasked with enforcing"; "lawful instructions"; "superiors"; "a junior"; "deference".

712.6 The two-hats problem frame

📘 Learn 12.6 in Lesson 12 →
🔑 Trigger words: a bill proposes; would you vote for it?; if passed, would you enforce it?; Ruritania
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  1. As an MP, I would vote against the bill and propose narrower measures. As a judge, I would apply it if validly enacted, refusing only at the Radbruch threshold.
  2. The bill's scope does the damage: it reaches consumption as well as sale, and, "without exception", catches communion and temple wine.
  3. The answers differ because the roles ask different moral questions: what the law should be, and what fidelity to it requires.

The grounds, steelmanned and tested:

GroundSteelmanTest, then verdict
FaithAddiction subverts practical reasonablenessDenying worship "normally" breaks reciprocity: a voice, not a ground
HarmHart accepts paternalismIt protects buyers: license, not jail
Poll85% at least "somewhat"Not Devlin's "real feeling of reprobation" (17): evidence, not mandate

Also on the sheet:

  • Yaacob Ibrahim (2005): "drinking and other activities that Muslims consider vices are not banned". Critics' teetotallers: offence is selected morally.
  • JUDGE: read literally, Art 15(4) has no "necessary" test (TSH), so an as-applied claim is weak. The law is harsh, not intolerable (no BHC condemns prohibition), so apply it.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Ruritanian Prohibition Bill

A bill in Ruritania proposes: "The sale and consumption of alcohol is prohibited, without exception. Breach is punishable by up to two years' imprisonment." Its supporters cite:

  • a faith that teaches drinking is sinful;
  • the harm alcohol causes;
  • a poll showing 85% "at least somewhat support" it.

The question: as an MP, would you vote for it? As a judge, if it passed, would you enforce it?

✔ APPLICATION · As MP: vote against, and propose narrower measuresDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Faith. Steelman: addiction does undermine practical reasonableness, a basic good. But a faith's teaching can't by itself justify coercing citizens who don't share it. And the bill would stop other faiths' worship (communion wine, temple offerings), which normally breaks reciprocity. The faith gets a voice in the debate, not a ground for the law.
  • Harm. Steelman: Hart accepts paternalism. But Hart's paternalism protects buyers whose consent may be impaired, which supports licensing and controlling sale, not jailing drinkers.
  • Poll. Steelman: 85% is a lot. But "somewhat support" isn't Devlin's "real feeling of reprobation", and a poll is evidence, not a mandate (7.11).
  • Singapore comparison. In 2005, Singapore's minister Yaacob Ibrahim noted that drinking and other activities Muslims consider vices are not banned. And teetotallers' offence at drinking is one the law chooses to ignore, which shows that which offences count is a moral choice (7.2.3).
  • The fix: licensing hours, taxes, drink-driving laws, and an exemption for religious use.
✔ APPLICATION · As judge: apply it, if validly enactedDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Art 15. A church could bring an as-applied challenge. But read literally, Art 15(4) lacks the "necessary" test, so the claim is weak.
  • The RF. Prohibition is harsh, but no broad historical consensus condemns it as intolerable, so refusal isn't justified.
  • The result. The judge applies it, reading it as narrowly as its words allow.

Why the answers differ. The MP asks what the law should be. The judge asks what fidelity to a valid law requires. Different roles, different moral questions.

🎯 EXAM CUE · QUESTION WORDS THAT SEND YOU HERE

"a bill proposes…"; "would you vote for it?"; "if passed, would you enforce it?"; Ruritania.

812.7 Conclusion, applied

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Conclusion: no role ends moral duty. The statement is right that roles have limits, but drawing them is itself a moral judgement, and the vice is not only taking others' work but refusing one's own.

✔ APPLICATION · Applied to the hyposDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Roles have limits: Judge Ang (12.2.1).
  • Drawing them is moral: the Euthanasia Case (12.1.1).
  • Refusing your own work is a vice: Judge Bala (12.2.1) and the stenographer MP (12.3.1).
  • No role ends moral duty: Clerk Jurić (12.5), and the MP and judge on the Prohibition Bill (12.6).

How to work through a hypo

ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 13 of the 7 Nov exam sheet.

  • 13.1–13.2 (comparisons and current controversies) are in both versions.
  • 13.3–13.6 (Core cards A–D) are in the Core version only.

Layout: the rule as the sheet states it, a made-up hypothetical, then the application.

  • For the comparison rows, one scenario shows what the two theorists share and where they split.
