Abbreviations: LP = legal positivism; NLT = natural law theory; RF = Radbruch formula; TSH = Tan Seow Hon; † = from the slides.

113.1 Comparisons

13.1.1 LP v Rawls: pluralism

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • Shared: both bracket contested morals. LP finds law in sources; Rawls finds legitimacy in shared political values.
  • Split: neither is neutral. Acceptance is LP's test, and "reasonable" is Rawls's filter. Finnis: some basic rights have one right answer.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A religious minority objects to a new Ruritanian law requiring all schools to teach evolution.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • LP says: "It was validly enacted, so it is law. Whether it is wise is another question." That brackets morality.
  • Rawls says: "It is legitimate if justified by public reasons, such as scientific literacy for citizens." That brackets comprehensive doctrines.
  • Neither is neutral. LP's verdict rests on its choice of official acceptance as the test (2.1.2), and Rawls's on who he counts as "reasonable" (6.11).
  • Finnis would add: on some basic rights there is one right answer, and bracketing it isn't fair.

13.1.2 Autonomy: Mill, Hart, Finnis, Pepper

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • Shared: all four value autonomy and bound it. Mill bounds it by harm to others. Pepper's first-class citizenship serves it.
  • Split: Hart allows some paternalism. Finnis bounds autonomy by practical reasonableness. Pepper bounds it by law alone, "not by the lawyer's morality", save in "extreme cases".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

An adult wants to sell his kidney, and asks his lawyer to draft the contract.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Mill: his body, his choice, unless others are harmed.
  • Hart: desperate sellers may have defective consent, so restricting the sale is justified paternalism.
  • Finnis: autonomy is exercised well only within practical reasonableness. Selling a kidney for cash may treat a basic good (life and bodily integrity) as a mere means.
  • Pepper: if it's lawful, the lawyer drafts it. Only the law, not the lawyer's morals, limits the client, except in extreme cases.

13.1.3 Kennedy v the chain novel

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • Shared: both put the judge inside inherited materials. Fit and value constrain Dworkin's judge; work and credibility risk constrain Kennedy's.
  • Split: Kennedy starts from "how-I-want-to-come-out", Dworkin from the text (Liu, W11). Kennedy answers "always a right answer" with felt indeterminacy and "free ethical or political choice", disclaiming a verdict.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A judge hears a case on whether striking workers may block a factory gate.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Both judges must work with forty years of picketing cases.
  • Dworkin's judge reads them to find the principle that best fits and justifies them.
  • Kennedy's judge decides first that he wants the workers to win, then works the cases towards that result, paying in effort and credibility.
  • Where they part. Kennedy reports moments when the law felt genuinely open, and he chose freely. He won't claim his account is the right one.

13.1.4 Fuller v the RF

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • Shared: both deny that enactment alone settles legality. Fuller tests form; the RF tests content.
  • Split: Fuller grades by degree (an unclear statute is "less a law"). The RF voids only "intolerable" injustice.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Valdoria's Junta passes (a) a vaguely worded ban on "disloyal attitudes", and (b) a clear decree confiscating a minority's homes.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Fuller says (a) is "less a law", because no one can follow it. He has less to say about (b): its form is fine.
  • The RF passes over (a)'s vagueness, but voids (b) if its injustice is intolerable.
  • Both reject "it was enacted, so it's law, full stop".

13.1.5 Religious freedom: Finnis v Rawls

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • Shared: both protect religious freedom, neither neutrally. Finnis protects it as a basic good; Rawls as equal liberty of conscience.
  • Split: Rawls takes "the truths of religion off the political agenda". Finnis values inquiry, "whatever the answer".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A sect asks for an exemption from compulsory schooling, to teach children at home in its scriptures.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Both start sympathetic.
  • Rawls protects the sect's liberty of conscience without asking whether its beliefs are true. Religion's truth is off the agenda. But children's education as future citizens is a political value that may limit the exemption.
  • Finnis protects the sect because seeking answers about ultimate questions is a basic good, even if the answers are agnostic or negative. But he would also weigh the children's own good of knowledge.

13.1.6 Whose morality (obscenity, immoral contracts)?

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • Shared: it must be beyond the judge's preference:
    • Devlin's right-minded man;
    • Hart's critical morality (Devlin too invokes a "critical principle");
    • NLT's objective morality.
  • Split:
    • Devlin: honest belief, "right or wrong";
    • TSH's second "option", "not favoured in Rajeevan": judges may filter incoherent opinions.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A court must decide whether a contract to pay for a "companion" is void as contrary to public morals.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • None of the theorists lets the judge use her personal taste.
  • Devlin's judge asks what the right-minded person honestly believes, right or wrong.
  • Hart asks whether a critical principle justifies voiding it.
  • NLT asks what objective morality requires.
  • TSH's alternative lets the judge set aside popular opinions that are incoherent. Singapore's Rajeevan didn't favour that option.

13.1.7 Finnis v liberalism

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • Shared: the common good is "a set of conditions", and the state's role is "only to maintain peace and justice".
  • Split: Finnis isn't neutral: reason requires us "to favour the basic forms of good". He is liberal in means, not ends.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Port Meridian considers funding public libraries and taxing casinos heavily.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • A liberal and Finnis agree that the state should create conditions (libraries, order) in which citizens pursue their own lives, without making them good.
  • But Finnis openly favours knowledge (libraries) and discourages what damages the goods (heavy casino taxes) because they are good or bad. A neutral liberal would need another reason. That is the sense in which Finnis is liberal in means, not ends.

13.1.8 Finnis v Fuller

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • Shared: they are complementary: Fuller covers procedure, Finnis substance (Liu, W5).
  • Split: for Finnis, law "treats them as partners in public reason" by promulgation, clarity, generality and stability. And Finnis can condemn punitive retroactivity by its effects.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Ruritania retroactively raises penalties for a tax offence.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Fuller condemns it as a breach of legality's inner morality.
  • Finnis agrees that law must treat citizens as partners in public reason (essentially Fuller's list), and can also condemn the law by its effects on the goods of those punished. Procedure and substance work together.

13.1.9 Fuller v Hart on validity

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • Shared: compatible.
  • Split: Fuller tests form. Hart takes what officials accept, so Ordinance 11 may pass (Liu, W10).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The Junta's published, clear Citizenship Ordinance (8.3).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Hart: officials accepted it, so it was law, though too evil to obey.
  • Fuller: a clear, published, general ordinance passes his tests of form, so he can't easily deny it was law.
  • So the two are compatible here. Both may call it law; it is the RF that would deny it.

13.1.10 Hart v Devlin

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • Shared: both usually spare private acts (7.3).
  • Split: they are not fully reconciled. Devlin can punish what meets none of Hart's grounds (cruelty to animals; Hart explains that law by the animals' suffering) (Liu, W9).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A man privately tortures his own pet, and no one sees.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Devlin: it is beyond the limits of tolerance, even in private, so it may be punished.
  • Hart: it is not harm to other people, not paternalism, and not public offence. But he explains the cruelty law by the animal's suffering, so he agrees with the result for a different reason.
  • Where they'd split. On private conduct that disgusts but harms no one, not even an animal, Devlin could punish and Hart couldn't.

13.1.11 Devlin v Rawls and Finnis

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • Shared: shared ground, and "reasonable" judgement.
  • Split: Rawls needs only enough overlap, while Devlin needs deep agreement. Devlin's reasonable man feels; Finnis's reasons (Liu, W7).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A society of many faiths debates banning gambling.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Rawls needs only enough common ground for a political conception of justice.
  • Devlin needs a deep shared morality, and a pluralist society may not have one.
  • Devlin's "reasonable man" reacts with feeling (disgust). Finnis's reasonable person reasons from the basic goods. They might reach the same verdict on gambling by very different routes.

213.2 Current controversies

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
  • s 377A repeal and Art 156 (2022)†: s 377A went, and Art 156 shielded man–woman marriage laws from Part 4, both from 3 Jan 2023. → Theory: the coercion gradient. Punishment was withdrawn; marriage was promoted (15.7, 7.9, 11.6).
  • QUALIFY: Hart's lines survive. Non-consensual acts, acts with young persons and public indecency stay crimes; only private consensual adult conduct is freed (Shanmugam, 2022). Liu's exercises: 16.5.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Columnist's Two Claims

A columnist writes: "The 2022 package means the law no longer cares about sexual morality at all."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Wrong about "no longer cares". On the coercion gradient (7.9), the state stopped punishing private consensual conduct, but moved to promoting a view of marriage (Art 156). That is a shift in kind of enforcement, not an end to it.
  • Wrong about "at all". Hart's lines remain in the criminal law: non-consensual acts, acts with minors, and public indecency are still crimes. Only private, consensual adult conduct was freed.
  • For the theorist exercises, see 16.5.
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

:::quiz ? HYPO · APPLY | A columnist: "The 2022 package means the law no longer cares about sexual morality at all." Reply? + Punishment was withdrawn, but marriage was promoted || On the coercion gradient, punishment was withdrawn but marriage was promoted (Art 156), and Hart's lines remain for non-consensual acts and the young. A shift in kind, not an end.

  • The columnist is right, since s 377A was repealed || Promotion and Hart's lines remain.
  • s 377A is still in force, though unenforced || It was repealed from 3 Jan 2023.
  • Art 156 criminalises same-sex conduct || It shields marriage laws from Part 4.

> Punish v promote.

3Core cards (Core version only)

:::

413.3 Core A: law-making and morality

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

For legislator questions.

Spine: no law on a moral question is neutral. Permitting, punishing and promoting all take a stand. So pluralism cannot mean neutrality. It means discipline on three things:

  • reasons: accessible to every citizen, and sound on the merits;
  • coercion: graded to the strength of those reasons;
  • forum: the legislature decides, as a trustee, not a stenographer.

13.3.0 Flaws F1–F4: how to attack a statement

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT
FlawSignal wordsMove
F1 gaptherefore, however, only then, lesthook word, thesis distinction
F2 absoluteonly, all, simply, mustthe word, conditional
F3 self-refutation—self-application once, numbered
F4 equivocation—concession, conditional
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
A Statement with All Four Flaws

"All moral opinions are equally valid; therefore the state must remain neutral, and only harm to others can ever justify coercion. Legislators must simply follow what society thinks."

✔ APPLICATION · Flaw by flawDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • F1 gap: hook on "therefore". Even if opinions were equally valid, it doesn't follow that the state can be neutral. Distinguish the two theses: equal validity of opinions v equal respect for persons.
  • F2 absolute: attack "only", "must", "simply". Turn each into a conditional: "harm to others is a strong presumption, but not the only ground", and "society's view is evidence legislators should weigh, not an instruction".
  • F3 self-refutation: apply the statement to itself, once, and number the step. (1) If all moral opinions are equally valid, then so is the opinion that the state should not be neutral. (2) So the statement's own demand for neutrality has no special claim.
  • F4 equivocation: "what society thinks". Concede one meaning ("legislators should listen to public opinion"), then go conditional on the other ("but if it means the majority's view must decide, that confuses who decides with what is right").

13.3.1 P1 "The state should be neutral"

🔑 Trigger words: not endorse moral values; take no side; fixed conception; moral truth
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: neutrality of outcome is impossible, and even Rawls's neutrality of justification rests on moral values. The defensible kernel is narrower: the state should not make one comprehensive doctrine official, or coerce on reasons only its adherents can accept.

Alignments:

  • Hart: partly;
  • Devlin: rejects;
  • Rawls: partly; the natural ally, but in the weak form only;
  • Finnis: rejects the strong form, accepts a limit.

→ 6.2, 7.5, 6.10.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"The state should never endorse moral values. On surrogacy, it should take no side."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Outcome neutrality is impossible. Allowing or banning surrogacy takes a side either way (6.0).
  • Even Rawls's justification-neutrality rests on values such as fairness and equality.
  • What survives: Ruritania mustn't make one faith's view of family the official doctrine, or ban surrogacy on reasons only that faith accepts.
  • Theorists: Rawls is the closest ally, in the weak form. Devlin would reject the idea. Hart would agree only partly (he still defends critical moral principles). Finnis rejects strong neutrality, but accepts that the state shouldn't impose a full life-plan.

13.3.2 P2 "Moral opinions are equally valid"

🔑 Trigger words: equally valid; denial of moral truth; suspension of judgment; skeptical
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: equal validity defeats itself and cannot deliver the tolerance it promises. What survives is fallibility, which counsels deliberation, provisional judgement and caution in coercion, not silence.

Alignments:

  • Hart: rejects;
  • Devlin: partly; a dangerous ally;
  • Rawls: partly (Liu's reading);
  • Finnis: rejects, but not in favour of a single right answer on everything.

→ 4.2, 4.7.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"On euthanasia, all moral opinions are equally valid, so Parliament should suspend judgement."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Self-defeat. If all opinions are equally valid, "Parliament should suspend judgement" is no more valid than "Parliament should ban it". So the statement defeats itself (4.2).
  • What survives is fallibility. Parliament should deliberate, decide provisionally, and be cautious about using the criminal law. It shouldn't be silent.
  • Theorists:
    • Devlin is a dangerous ally: his cultural relativism treats each society's morality as valid for it, which supports enforcing the majority's view, not tolerance.
    • Rawls partly fits: on Liu's reading, he treats reasonable doctrines as equally entitled in politics.
    • Hart and Finnis reject it, though Finnis allows a range of reasonable answers.

13.3.3 P3 "Only harm to others justifies coercion"

🔑 Trigger words: only; protect others; wrongdoer; objectively necessary
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: harm to others is the right presumption for punishment, but it isn't the only ground, and it isn't a neutral fact. What counts as harm, and who counts as an "other", are moral questions.

Alignments:

  • Hart: partly;
  • Devlin: rejects;
  • Rawls: it's the wrong test;
  • Finnis: partly; a ground, not the only one, and no ban on everything that fails to pursue a good.

→ 7.1, 7.2, 6.10.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"Only harm to others justifies coercing a wrongdoer. So the state can't restrict the sale of veridine (7.0)."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The right presumption, but not the only ground. Hart himself adds paternalism, which justifies restricting sale to protect buyers with defective consent (7.2).
  • Not neutral. Is a user's family an "other"? Is a public hospital?
  • Theorists:
    • Rawls would say the test is wrong in kind: the question is whether the reasons are public, not whether there is harm.
    • Finnis accepts harm as one ground, but not as the only one, and he wouldn't ban everything that fails to pursue a good.
    • Devlin rejects the harm-only test entirely.

13.3.4 P4 "A right to decide intimate matters"

🔑 Trigger words: fundamental decisions; own destinies; intimate relationships; child rearing; private behaviour
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: the right is real, but it is itself a moral claim with moral limits. It rules out punishing private consensual conduct for its immorality alone. It doesn't rule out regulation or promotion, and it can't settle cases where a third party, the child or the unborn, is at stake.

Alignments:

  • Hart: largely agrees;
  • Devlin: rejects in principle, often agrees in practice;
  • Rawls: partly;
  • Finnis: partly.

→ 4.5, 7.9.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"Everyone has a right to decide intimate matters, including how to raise their children, so the state may not require vaccination or schooling."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The right is real where only the adults are concerned: the state shouldn't jail them for private consensual choices.
  • But it is a moral claim (4.5), and it stops where a third party is at stake. The child's health and education are the child's own goods.
  • Regulation and promotion remain open. The state can require schooling (regulation) and run vaccination campaigns (promotion).
  • Theorists:
    • Hart largely agrees with the core;
    • Devlin rejects it in principle, but would usually leave private adult conduct alone in practice;
    • Rawls and Finnis each accept part.

13.3.5 P5 "Majority or societal morality"

🔑 Trigger words: majority; majoritarian will; certain groups; minority rights; poll
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: the majority settles who decides, not what is right. Majority feeling is evidence to weigh, never the reason that settles the law. And protecting minorities is itself a moral judgement, not an escape from one.

Alignments:

  • Hart: rejects it as a reason;
  • Devlin, the natural ally, refuses to count heads;
  • Rawls: rejects;
  • Finnis: rejects, from the other side.

→ 7.3, 7.11, 12.3.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"A poll shows 70% oppose a minority group's festival in a public park, so the law should ban it."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The majority decides who makes law, through elections, not whether a ban is right.
  • The poll is evidence, not a mandate (7.11).
  • Protecting the minority is a moral judgement about equal respect, so it isn't neutral either.
  • Theorists:
    • Devlin, the supposed ally, refuses to count heads (7.3);
    • Hart and Rawls reject majority feeling as a reason;
    • Finnis rejects it because the question is what is truly good, not what most people think.

13.3.6 P6 "Enforcing morality is (il)legitimate"

🔑 Trigger words: legislating morals; unjust; illegitimate; intractable moral conflicts
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: enforcing morality is not illegitimate as such, since every law enforces some morality. What can make it unjust is the reasons used, the coercion chosen, and who bears it. So the limits are moral and prudential, not sceptical.

Alignments:

  • Hart: partly;
  • Devlin: agrees;
  • Rawls: partly;
  • Finnis: agrees.

→ 7.5, 7.9.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"Legislating morality is illegitimate, because moral conflicts are intractable. So Ruritania should not criminalise cruelty to animals."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Every law enforces some morality. An animal cruelty law enforces the view that animals' suffering matters. So "legislating morality is illegitimate" proves too much.
  • The real question. Are the reasons accessible and sound (animals' suffering: yes)? Is the coercion proportionate? Who bears it?
  • Intractability counsels restraint, not abstention.
  • Theorists: Devlin and Finnis agree that enforcing morality is legitimate in principle. Hart and Rawls accept parts of the claim.

13.3.7 Pivots and repaired statements (Core A)

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Pivots:

  • neutrality is impossible (6.5, 7.5);
  • the coercion gradient (7.9);
  • majority is not legitimacy (7.11, 12.3);
  • scepticism answered (4.7);
  • "fixed" is a matter of degree: no theorist imposes one complete life-plan, and every theorist fixes some limits.

Repaired statements (use one per script):

ThemeRepaired statement
NeutralityLegislators should treat all citizens, not all opinions, as equal, and coerce only on reasons every citizen can examine.
HarmLegislators should presume against punishing conduct that harms no one else, and need stronger reasons the more coercive the law.
AutonomyChoices about one's intimate life deserve strong protection from punishment, but not immunity from all regulation, or from the state's promotion of other goods.
MajorityThe majority decides, but must decide on reasons it can defend to the minority.
EnforcementEnforcing morality is legitimate when its reasons are accessible and sound and its coercion proportionate. Scepticism is no objection, but fallibility is a reason for restraint.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The statement is "The state must not impose a fixed conception of the good life."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Pivot on "fixed". No theorist imposes a complete life-plan (even Finnis's state is a framework), and every theorist fixes some limits (even Mill bans harm to others). So "fixed" is a matter of degree.
  • Conclude with the repaired neutrality line: "Legislators should treat all citizens, not all opinions, as equal, and coerce only on reasons every citizen can examine."

513.4 Core B: judges, lawyers and morality

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

For judge and lawyer questions.

Spine: no judge or lawyer works without theory or morality:

  • identifying the law is already an evaluation;
  • hard cases turn on rival theories of law's grounds;
  • every role is justified by what it is for.

But that makes legal work neither preference nor private conscience. Morality is:

  • presupposed always;
  • operative at the margins (hard cases, intolerable injustice);
  • disciplined by role: fit and candour for judges, the law as a floor for lawyers.

13.4.1 Q1 "Judges only apply the law"

🔑 Trigger words: no substantive moral judgments; only what the law is; I just apply the law
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: morality is always presupposed in judging, and sometimes operative. It is presupposed in legality, and in every claim that a ruling is correct. It is operative in hard cases and at intolerable injustice. A judge concerned "only with what the law is" already holds a theory of what law is.

Alignments:

  • Hart: partly agrees;
  • Dworkin: rejects;
  • realists: reject, for a different reason;
  • TSH: rejects for constitutional cases.

→ 9.8, 11.2, 11.3.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"Judges make no substantive moral judgements. They decide only what the law is." Test it on Judge Ng's two cases (9.8): a parking fine, and the insurance claim by a son who assaulted his mother.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The parking fine: morality is presupposed (deference to clear rules) but not operative.
  • The insurance claim: a hard case, where moral principle helps decide.
  • Theorists:
    • Hart partly agrees: most cases are core cases;
    • Dworkin rejects: law is interpretive, all the way down;
    • the realists reject it, because they think judges decide on preference anyway;
    • TSH rejects it for constitutional cases, where "law", "equal" and "liberty" carry moral content (11.2, 11.3).

13.4.2 Q2 "Adjudication is politics"

🔑 Trigger words: politics; pretence; rules don't decide; essentially
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: adjudication is political in Dworkin's sense: where fit runs out, judges choose between principles of political morality. It isn't politics in the partisan sense that "pretence" needs. Rules leave some cases open, not all, and judges must justify, not predict.

Alignments:

  • realists: partly;
  • Unger and the crits: agree in part;
  • Kennedy: partly, the most honest witness;
  • Dworkin: rejects the partisan reading.

→ 9.1, 9.3, 9.7.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"Adjudication is essentially politics. Legal reasoning is a pretence." Test it on Suri's case (9.3, 9.7).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Political in Dworkin's sense. Choosing between freedom of contract and fairness is a choice of political principle.
  • Not partisan. Judge A justified his choice publicly by fit and value, rather than pretending.
  • And many cases aren't open at all (the speeding driver, 9.0).
  • Theorists:
    • Kennedy is the most honest witness: he admits his politics, but shows how much work and risk the law imposes;
    • the crits agree in part;
    • the realists partly;
    • Dworkin rejects the partisan reading.

13.4.3 Q3 "Theory is irrelevant to practice"

🔑 Trigger words: theory isn't relevant; just do your job; no practical need
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: true in a weak sense: lawyers rarely cite theory, and most cases are easy. False in the strong sense: every lawyer acts on a theory of what law is and what the role permits, and the only choice is between examined and unexamined theory.

Alignments:

  • Fish: partly;
  • Dworkin: rejects;
  • Thunder: rejects, and names the source;
  • positivism: rejects, even on its own terms.

→ 2.6, 10.8, 10.10.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"A practising lawyer has no practical need for legal theory. Just do your job." Test it on the associate who quoted Rawls (2.6.1) and the student who advised "breach as cost" (10.8).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Weakly true. Quoting Rawls in a steel case was window dressing (Fish partly agrees).
  • Strongly false. "Breach as cost" is realist theory in action. Thunder names the source: realism plus neo-Kantianism (10.10). Dworkin rejects the statement. And even positivism is a theory of law the lawyer is relying on.

13.4.4 Q4 "Lawyers serve clients within the law"

🔑 Trigger words: client; lawful; adversarial system; hired gun
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: the lawyer's role is itself moral, and law sets its floor, not its ceiling. Above the floor, prudence, dialogue and rare objection decide hard cases. Pepper and Thunder differ more in mindset than in outcome.

Alignments:

  • Pepper: agrees, on moral grounds;
  • Pepper's own limits undercut him;
  • Thunder: rejects;
  • Liu's three scenarios: a test, not a side.

→ 10.1, 10.2, 10.11.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"A lawyer's only duty is to serve the client within the law. She is a hired gun in an adversarial system." Test it on Aisha's two instructions (10.7) and Teo's three files (10.11).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Pepper agrees, but for moral reasons (autonomy, equal access). His own outlets (objection, choice of client) concede that the role has moral limits.
  • Thunder rejects it.
  • Liu's three questions sort Teo's files: is the system just, is the rule intolerably unjust, is the outcome unjust? They don't take a side between Pepper and Thunder.
  • Above the floor: dialogue for Aisha's time bar, objection for the brake defect.

13.4.5 Q5 "Stay within your role"

🔑 Trigger words: limits of their own authority; usurp; officials; for Parliament, not the courts
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: right as a presumption: a constitutional democracy divides power, so roles have limits. But where a role ends is contested, abdication is as much a vice as usurpation, and refusing extreme injustice is fidelity, not usurpation.

Alignments:

  • George and TSH: agree, then ask who decides;
  • TSH's twin vices add the missing half;
  • Fuller: fidelity is not deference;
  • Alexy and Kennedy: the outer limit.

→ 12.1, 12.2, 12.5.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"Judges and officials must respect the limits of their authority, leaving contested issues to Parliament." Test it on Judges Ang and Bala (12.2) and Clerk Jurić (12.5).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The presumption holds against Ang, who usurps.
  • But Bala's rubber-stamping is the twin vice.
  • Jurić owes fidelity to law, not deference to rank (Fuller).
  • At the outer limit, Alexy's risk effect and Kennedy's options show that refusing extreme injustice is part of the role, not a breach of it.

13.4.6 Q6 "Law and justice"

🔑 Trigger words: rule of law; essence; certainty, procedure; necessarily connected
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: justice is the rule of law's point and its outer limit. Certainty and procedure are its everyday content. Validity never settles obedience, and only intolerable injustice defeats legal character.

Alignments:

  • Fuller: partly;
  • Hart: separates them, for candour;
  • Radbruch and Alexy: a narrow link;
  • TSH: disciplines the link for courts.

→ 3.3, 8.2, 8.5.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"The essence of the rule of law is certainty and procedure. Justice has nothing to do with it." Test it on Vos's party ban (3.3) and the Residence Act (8.8).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Certainty and procedure are the everyday content. Vos's ban is clear and public, which matters (Fuller partly agrees).
  • But justice is the point and the outer limit. The Residence Act is intolerably unjust, so Radbruch and Alexy deny it legal character.
  • Hart keeps law and justice apart, for the sake of candour.
  • TSH disciplines the link: courts may use it only on broad historical consensus (8.5).

13.4.7 Pivots and repaired statements (Core B)

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Pivots:

  • presupposed, not always operative (9.8);
  • easy cases rest on a shared theory (9.9);
  • floor, not ceiling (11.7);
  • twin vices (12.2);
  • judge's hat (12.4);
  • practical need: concede that extremes are rare. The law still leaves several lawful paths, above all for lawyers, and cannot choose between them (11.1, 10.7).

Repaired statements (use one per script):

ThemeRepaired statement
JudgesJudges should not decide by personal conviction. They bring political morality to bear through fit and candour, and override the law only at intolerable injustice.
PoliticsAdjudication is political in the sense of political morality, not partisanship. Where the rules leave a case open, judges must justify, not pretend.
TheoryLawyers need not cite theory, but they cannot practise without one. The choice is between examined and unexamined theory.
LawyersA lawyer serves the client within the law, but the law is a floor: dialogue above it, and refusal only at the extremes.
RolesLegal actors should respect the limits of their roles and do their roles' own moral work, refusing only intolerable injustice.
Rule of lawJustice is the rule of law's point and its outer limit. Certainty and procedure are its everyday content.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"There is no practical need for lawyers to engage with morality; extreme cases almost never arise."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Concede that extremes are rare.
  • Then pivot. Even in ordinary work, the law leaves a lawyer several lawful paths. Aisha could plead the time bar or suggest settlement (10.7), and the law can't choose between them. Morality does that work.
  • Close with the repaired lawyers line.

613.5 Core C: what law is, and what we owe it

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

For nature-of-law and citizen questions.

Spine: people make law, so its sources can be found by looking. But deciding that sources are all that count is an evaluation, and finding the law never settles what it should be or what anyone should do. Keep three questions apart:

  1. what counts as law: sources, plus, for non-positivists, a narrow moral limit;
  2. what the law should be: reasons, not facts about opinion;
  3. what I owe it: a moral question on every theory, with a strong default of obedience.

13.5.1 L1 "Law is a social fact"

🔑 Trigger words: made by human beings; social fact; what people accept; whatever is enacted
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: law's sources are facts, and usually a lawyer needs no more. But deciding that sources are all that count is an evaluation. Law is a social fact only on a theory of what law is.

Alignments:

  • Hart: agrees, more narrowly;
  • natural law: accepts the premise, denies the conclusion;
  • Dworkin: rejects;
  • TSH and Liu: naming law is an evaluation.

→ 2.1, 2.5.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"Law is made by human beings, so it is simply a social fact: whatever people accept as law." Test it on Professor Lim and the Land Decree (2.1.2).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The sources are facts. For a normal client question, looking them up is enough.
  • But choosing official acceptance as the test made the Decree's injustice irrelevant, which is an evaluation (TSH, Liu).
  • Theorists:
    • Hart agrees, in a narrower form: only officials' acceptance counts, not "people's";
    • natural law accepts that humans make law, but denies that this makes it a mere fact;
    • Dworkin rejects the whole idea.

13.5.2 L2 "No necessary link between law and morality"

🔑 Trigger words: absurd; necessarily connected; law is law
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: "absurd" fails: a narrow necessary link is a serious position. But the link that survives is weak. Only extreme injustice defeats legal character, and ordinary unjust laws stay law.

Alignments:

  • Hart: agrees, with care;
  • Fuller: rejects, thinly;
  • Radbruch and Alexy: reject, narrowly;
  • Finnis and weak natural law: reject "absurd", keep the distinction.

→ 2.3, 8.2, 8.3.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"It is absurd to say law and morality are necessarily connected. Law is law." Test it on Judge Tan's three files (2.3.2).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • "Absurd" overstates. It is a serious position that file (c), the Redheads Act, is not law.
  • But the surviving link is weak. Files (a) and (b), unjust but not extreme, remain law.
  • Theorists:
    • Hart agrees with the statement, carefully;
    • Fuller rejects it in a thin, procedural way;
    • Radbruch and Alexy reject it, narrowly;
    • Finnis rejects "absurd", but keeps the distinction between unjust law and no law.

13.5.3 L3 "Facts about opinion settle the debate"

🔑 Trigger words: positions and views; solely concerned; as a matter of fact; naturally follows
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: facts about what people think are evidence to weigh, and they fix the stakes. They cannot settle what the law should be, because no ought follows from an is alone.

Alignments:

  • Hart: rejects;
  • Devlin: the nearest ally, but stops short;
  • Rawls: starts from a fact, ends with a norm;
  • Finnis: rejects outright.

→ 4.4, 6.3, 7.1.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"As a matter of fact, most citizens hold traditional views on marriage. It naturally follows that the law should reflect them."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The facts matter. They show what is at stake, and how a law would be received.
  • But "it naturally follows" jumps the is–ought gap (4.4).
  • Theorists:
    • Devlin comes closest, but even he requires a deliberate judgement that the practice harms society;
    • Rawls starts from the fact of reasonable pluralism, but ends with a norm of public reason (6.3);
    • Hart and Finnis reject the inference.

13.5.4 L4 "Law is simply will or power"

🔑 Trigger words: simply an expression; majoritarian will; command; whatever Parliament enacts
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: will makes law only through rules that officials accept, and that also bind the will. Law is more than what the strongest or the most want, which is why we can criticise them by it.

Alignments:

  • Austin: agrees, crudely;
  • Hart: rejects;
  • Fuller: rejects;
  • TSH: rejects for Singapore.

→ 3.7, 12.3, 14.3.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"Law is simply an expression of whatever Parliament wills."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Will acts through rules. Parliament's will becomes law only through rules of recognition that officials accept, and those rules also bind Parliament (manner and form, the Constitution).
  • And we can criticise Parliament by law's own standards. Fuller's reciprocity (3.7) shows how: when Parliament breaks the rules it announced, we can say so.
  • Theorists:
    • Austin fits the statement, crudely (law as command);
    • Hart rejects it (law needs the internal point of view);
    • TSH rejects it for Singapore: Art 4 makes the Constitution, not Parliament's will, supreme (14.3).

13.5.5 L5 "Valid law must be obeyed"

🔑 Trigger words: validly-enacted; obligation to obey; recipe for disaster; chaos
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: there is a strong default of obedience, but it is a moral default: validity only tells us the rule is law. It can be defeated, but only by grave injustice, not by disagreement.

Alignments:

  • Hart: separates validity from obedience;
  • Fuller: grounds the duty in reciprocity;
  • Radbruch and Alexy: a default, then a threshold;
  • Aquinas and Finnis: conscience, with a brake.

→ 8.7, 3.7.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"Validly enacted laws must be obeyed. Anything else is a recipe for chaos." Test it on Mrs Goh and the cat by-law (8.7.4) and Petra and the Radio Decree (8.7.1).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Mrs Goh should obey. There is a strong moral default, from fair play and reciprocity, and her disagreement doesn't defeat it.
  • Petra may be right to disobey. Grave injustice can defeat the default.
  • Not chaos. Every theory confines disobedience to grave cases.
  • Theorists:
    • Hart separates the legal and moral questions;
    • Fuller grounds the duty in reciprocity;
    • Radbruch and Alexy set a default, then a threshold;
    • Aquinas and Finnis give conscience a role, with a brake: obey to avoid scandal, or lest a just system weaken.

13.5.6 L6 "A moral link licenses private disobedience"

🔑 Trigger words: own moral reasoning; justifiably disobey; conscience; who decides
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

VERDICT: the licence, if it is one, is not peculiar to those who link law and morality. Every theory leaves room for moral refusal, and every serious one confines it. The real problem is who decides.

Alignments:

  • Hart: the same licence, stated honestly;
  • Alexy: rejects the target;
  • TSH: accepts the question of who decides;
  • Fuller: the risk runs both ways.

→ 8.2, 8.7, 12.1.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"If law is linked to morality, every citizen can disobey whenever their own moral reasoning says a law is unjust."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Hart gives the same licence. He says some valid laws are too evil to obey (8.2). He just states it honestly, as a moral choice.
  • Alexy rejects the target: his link applies only at extreme injustice, not whenever a citizen disagrees.
  • TSH accepts that the real question is who decides (12.1).
  • Fuller: the risk runs both ways. Blind obedience to wicked law is as dangerous as too much private judgement.

13.5.7 Pivots and repaired statements (Core C)

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Pivots:

  • what people made is not what they should make (4.4);
  • a social fact is not public opinion: sources v positive morality (12.3);
  • three questions about obedience (8.7);
  • threshold, not licence (8.2, 8.5).

Repaired statements (use one per script):

ThemeRepaired statement
Social factLaw's sources are matters of social fact, but what law should be is not, and facts about opinion are evidence to weigh, never the answer.
Necessary linkLaw and morality may be separable in identifying most law, but validity never settles obedience. Extreme injustice is the narrow case where the two questions meet.
DisobedienceCitizens owe a strong moral duty to obey, which grave injustice can defeat and mere disagreement cannot.
WillMajority will settles who may make law, within rules that bind it. It does not settle what the law should say.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"Law is a social fact, so public opinion is the law." Use the pivot "a social fact is not public opinion".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The social facts that identify law are officials' practices of recognising sources (statutes, cases), not the public's moral views, which are positive morality (12.3). Then close with the repaired social-fact line.

713.6 Core D: testing a theory on a new issue

🔑 Trigger words: soundness; "[X]'s theory"; bear on this debate; the best way
▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Spine: a theory is not refuted by needing moral judgement, or by failing to dictate an answer. Each of these four supplies a question, not a verdict:

  • Rawls asks which reasons;
  • Finnis asks what the act does to a basic good;
  • Hart asks what justifies this coercion;
  • Devlin asks what society can tolerate.

So test a theory three ways:

  1. does it hold together?
  2. does it give a defensible answer on the hard case?
  3. does it beat its rivals?

Tasks:

  • Assess a theory: cards 14.8, 14.10, 14.13, 14.15.
  • Apply it: say what it rules out, what it requires and what it leaves open (16.5).
  • Compare: "best" needs a rival, a job and a cost.

Pivots:

  • needing moral judgement is fatal only if the theory promised to avoid it (14.13);
  • a framework needs inputs, so "demands" is usually wrong;
  • sound means it holds together, answers the hard case and beats its rivals;
  • Hart limits punishment most tightly, but says little on promotion (7.9).

Repaired statements (use one per script):

ThemeRepaired statement
AutonomyAutonomy deserves great weight in the common good, but it demands no particular law. Parliament must decide on reasons those who disagree can examine, and protect those whose consent is least free.
HartHart's theory needs moral judgement, which is no objection to it, and it is the tightest limit on punishment we have. It is not a complete account of what law may do.
Named theory[Theory] sets a sound discipline on [reasons / coercion], but its contested premise means it cannot settle [the issue] alone.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Assisted Dying Question

"Hart's theory demands that Ruritania legalise assisted dying. Assess the soundness of Hart's theory, and whether it is the best way to approach this debate."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Apply each theory's question:
    • Hart: what justifies coercing a doctor who helps a competent, consenting patient die? Harm to others? Paternalism, if the patient's consent may be impaired by depression or pressure? Public offence: none.
    • Rawls: are the reasons for and against public?
    • Finnis: does it choose directly against life? Yes, so it is barred.
    • Devlin: can society tolerate it?
  • "Demands" is wrong. Hart's framework needs inputs, such as how free terminally ill patients' consent really is. So it doesn't demand legalisation; it supplies a question.
  • Soundness, three ways:
    1. Hart's view holds together;
    2. it gives a defensible answer on the hard case (perhaps legalise, with strong safeguards against defective consent);
    3. it beats Devlin on pluralist ground. Against Finnis, the cost is that it treats life as a good a person may waive.
  • "Needs moral judgement" is no objection, since Hart never promised to avoid it (14.13).
  • Gaps. Hart says little about promotion (should the state fund palliative care over assisted dying?) (7.9).
  • "Best" needs a rival, a job and a cost. Hart is best for the job of limiting punishment. The cost is his silence on promotion.
  • Close with the repaired Hart line.
