HYPO LESSON 14 · SECTION 14 · ABOUT 62 MIN · 28 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Theorist bank

⚡ BIG IDEA

Every theorist card runs purpose, claim, strength, critique and verdict. Each hypo makes you use every line of one card on one set of facts.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It is the sheet's wording, so it is what you will write in the exam.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 14 of both 7 Nov sheets.

  • Most cards are identical in the two versions.
  • 14.8, 14.10, 14.13 and 14.15 differ. Both versions are given here, marked [Theorist] and [Core].
  • 14.9, 14.14, 14.17, 14.20, 14.21 and 14.28 are in the Theorist version only.
  • The only other differences are TEST cross-references: in 14.5, the Theorist version adds "→ 15.9"; in 14.19, Core reads "→ 8.3" and Theorist "→ 15.8".

For each card: the card (its lines, as the sheet states them), then one hypothetical, then an application that uses every line of the card. Many hypos reuse the anchor cases from the archetype files, so you meet the same facts from the theorist's side. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: LP = legal positivism; NLT = natural law theory; RF = Radbruch formula; BHC = broad historical consensus; TSH = Tan Seow Hon; † = from the slides.

114.1 Fish

🔑 Use: 2.6, 10.5, 10.8
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: is theory useless to a lawyer, beyond doctrine and tactics?
  • CLAIM: practice marshals doctrine inside a purposive enterprise, informed by a vision of how the state may and may not use its monopoly of legalised violence.
  • STRENGTH: Searle's football: brute description misses the game. An expert's field is "already configured" by understanding what is at stake.
  • CRITIQUE: the complaint Segal reports, that law school, jurisprudence included, never taught the tricks of the trade → reply: the tricks "would not amount to much" without knowing "what the trade is".
  • SAY: "surely a practice but it is also a subject".
  • VERDICT: Fish is right that practice presupposes a view of the state's force, but he never says which view is true.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Training Head's Memo

A firm's head of training writes: "Trainees should learn the tricks: how to draft a winding-up petition, how to time an injunction. Jurisprudence is a waste of their time." That week, a trainee drafts a petition that will let a bank seize a small family's home.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim. Every step of the trainee's petition uses the state's power to force a family out. Knowing when that use of force is justified (proportionate, procedurally fair) is a view about legalised violence, and it shapes how the petition should be argued.
  • Strength (Searle). Described in brute terms, the trainee is just filling in a form. Only someone who understands what is at stake (debt, homes, the state's force) sees what the form is doing.
  • Critique and reply. The memo voices Segal's complaint: law school should teach the tricks. Fish's reply: tricks without knowing what the trade is would not amount to much.
  • Say: law is "surely a practice but it is also a subject".
  • Verdict. Fish shows the trainee needs a view of the state's force, but not which view is right. For that, use Finnis, Rawls or Hart.

214.2 NLT and Aquinas

🔑 Use: 2.1, 2.3, 2.8, 8.7, 11.2
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: must law meet a higher, reason-known standard to bind?
  • CLAIM: human law binds as it derives from natural law, by deduction or by determination. Law contrary to natural law is defective as law.
  • TEST:
    • Aquinas: an unjust law is "a corruption of law", though obedience is owed "perhaps, in certain special cases", to avoid scandal or danger;
    • Finnis: it merely lacks its prima facie power "to bind in conscience" (18);
    • TSH: a manifestly unjust law "is not law".
  • CRITIQUE: TSH asks who may "pronounce on the content of higher law" → reply: discernment, unlike fiat, must cohere and stay revisable.
  • VERDICT: natural law explains why some enactments fail as law, but must first settle who decides.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Three Ruritanian Laws
  • (a) Murder is a crime.
  • (b) The speed limit on highways is 90 km/h.
  • (c) Every citizen must report any relative who practises a minority religion.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim.
    • (a) is derived from natural law by deduction: don't kill the innocent.
    • (b) is a determination: natural law says "protect life on the roads", but the exact number is a reasonable choice, like an architect picking one design for a house.
    • (c) contradicts natural law, so it is defective as law.
  • The three readings of (c):
    • Aquinas: a corruption of law, though a citizen might obey it in special cases to avoid scandal or danger.
    • Finnis: it lacks the power to bind in conscience, but it isn't simply void.
    • TSH: a manifestly unjust law is not law.
  • Critique and reply. Who says (c) is unjust? TSH presses that question. The reply: a judgement that (c) is unjust must cohere with everything else we know, and stay open to revision. It is not mere say-so.
  • Verdict. NLT explains why (c) fails as law, but still has to settle who gets to declare it so (12.1).

314.3 Austin

🔑 Use: 2.2, 8.7, 11.1, 12.3
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: what is law, as a fact, without moral premises?
  • CLAIM: law is the command of a sovereign, habitually obeyed and obeying no one, backed by a sanction.
  • STRENGTH: candour: "the existence of law is one thing; its merit or demerit is another".
  • CRITIQUE: Hart: habits miss the internal "ought", and power-conferring rules enable rather than require → reply: Dworkin grants that Austin's main idea, restated by Hart, "has never wholly lost its grip on jurisprudence".
  • SG: against "that sovereign is simply Parliament": Art 4 voids statutes to the extent they are inconsistent with the Constitution (TSH; 11.1).
  • VERDICT: Austin is honest that wicked law gets enforced, but habit or fear cannot explain why officials treat law as binding.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Warlord and the Will
  • (a) A warlord controls a valley. Villagers habitually obey his orders, backed by beatings, and he obeys no one.
  • (b) In Singapore, a woman makes a will signed before two witnesses.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim. On Austin's test, (a) is law: the commands of an habitually obeyed sovereign, backed by sanctions.
  • Strength. Austin can say candidly: "It is law. Whether it is good law is another question."
  • Critique. But the villagers obey out of fear and habit. Nobody treats the warlord's orders as standards they ought to follow, so Hart's internal "ought" is missing. And (b) doesn't fit at all: the rule on witnesses commands no one. It enables her to make a valid will.
  • Reply. Dworkin admits that Austin's core idea, refined by Hart, still grips jurisprudence.
  • Singapore. If someone says Singapore's "sovereign" is simply Parliament, Art 4 answers that statutes inconsistent with the Constitution are void. Parliament is not an unlimited Austinian sovereign.
  • Verdict. Austin is honest that bad law gets enforced, but fear and habit can't explain why judges treat law as binding.

414.4 Hart: The Concept of Law

🔑 Use: 2.1, 2.2, 11.1, 11.7, 12.3
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: why do lawyers say "ought", if law is neither command nor morality?
  • CLAIM: law is the union of primary duty rules and secondary rules of recognition, change and adjudication, which officials accept from an internal point of view.
  • TEST: a system exists when primary rules are generally obeyed, and officials accept secondary rules. The secondary rules cure uncertainty, rigidity and diffuse pressure. Soft positivism lets the rule of recognition contingently adopt moral tests.
  • CRITIQUE 1: Dworkin: many Nazi officials obeyed Hitler "only out of fear". If that is acceptance, Hart nears Austin; if not, there was "no law in Nazi Germany" → reply: acceptance even from "fear, self-interest or habit" still treats rules as standards.
  • CRITIQUE 2: TSH: only officials need accept, so Hart "may not be very different from the power view", and LP "is not necessarily democratic" → reply: describing law is not praising it.
  • SAY: "critical reflective attitude"; "the sheep may end in the slaughter-house" (Hart).
  • TRAP: Hart's "minimum content of natural law" is no legality test. Men "are not members of suicide clubs", so every society needs rules against violence, theft and deceit: a practical necessity, unlike Radbruch's override (Liu, W10). Harris: a "'sociological' conception", consistent with "institutionalising slavery or racial oppression".
  • VERDICT: Hart maps a working legal system most accurately, yet deciding what the map shows is already an evaluation.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Island Settlement

Two hundred shipwrecked people settle an island.

  • Year 1: they live by customs (don't steal, share water). Disputes arise: is there a custom about fishing rights? Nobody can change a bad custom, and enforcement is by angry crowds.
  • Year 3: they agree that rules written in the Council Book are binding, that the Council may change them, and that three elders settle disputes.
  • Year 10: a faction takes over the Council. Its officials accept the Book as binding; most settlers obey only out of fear.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim and test.
    • Year 1 has only primary rules, with three defects: uncertainty (is there a fishing rule?), rigidity (no way to change customs) and diffuse pressure (mob enforcement).
    • Year 3 adds secondary rules: recognition (the Book), change (the Council) and adjudication (the elders). Now there is a legal system, because the rules are generally obeyed and officials accept the secondary rules.
  • Soft positivism. If the Book said "no rule is valid if grossly unfair", the rule of recognition would contain a moral test.
  • Critique 1 (Dworkin). In Year 10, do officials obeying only out of fear count as "accepting"? Reply: if they use the Book as a standard to judge conduct, criticising and correcting, that is acceptance, whatever their motive.
  • Critique 2 (TSH). Only officials need to accept. The settlers may be sheep led to the slaughter-house, so Hart's system isn't necessarily democratic. Reply: Hart describes; he doesn't praise.
  • Say: "critical reflective attitude".
  • Trap. That the island needs rules against violence, theft and deceit (Hart's minimum content) is a practical necessity for survival, not a test of legality. Harris notes that such a "natural law" is consistent even with slavery.
  • Verdict. Hart's map fits the island best. But calling the Year 10 regime "law" is already an evaluation.

514.5 Dworkin

🔑 Use: 2.4, 2.5, 9.2, 9.5, 9.10
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: why do judges disagree about the law, and what constrains them in hard cases?
  • CLAIM: law is interpretive. Judges read the legal record by fit and political value, so law is political, but never personal or partisan.
  • TEST: a reading must "both fit that practice and show its point or value". Where several readings fit, political morality decides. (The Theorist version adds "→ 15.9".)
  • STRENGTH: it explains theoretical disagreement, which the plain-fact view cannot, though Liu thinks this unfair to LP (2.5).
  • CRITIQUE: realists and crits: fit leaves readings open, so "value" is the judge's politics → reply: Dworkin concedes that fit "will often fail to produce a unique interpretation", not that law is "personal or partisan".
  • CONCEDE: a judge's best reading rests on "beliefs other judges need not share", and integrity gives no exit from a wicked legal history (2.4). Concede both; Radbruch guards the outer limit (14.19).
  • SG: LMS (CA) invoked "a central motif" of Dworkin's theory to disregard extra-legal considerations "uniquely within the purview of the Legislature". Principle v policy is TSH's surmise.
  • SAY: "deeply and thoroughly political".
  • VERDICT: Dworkin best explains how principle constrains hard cases, granted that fit often cannot settle them alone.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The "Reasonable Rent" Clause

Ruritania's Tenancy Act lets tribunals reduce rent that is "unreasonable". Two tribunal members disagree over a 40% rent rise in a gentrifying area: one says market rates make it reasonable; the other says tenants' security makes it unreasonable.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim and test. Each member offers a reading that fits the Act and the past decisions, and shows the Act's point: market efficiency, or tenants' security. Where both fit, political morality decides which reading is best.
  • Strength. This explains their disagreement as a dispute about the law's grounds, not a gap. (Liu would add that soft positivism can explain it too.)
  • Critique and reply. A realist says each member is just voting their politics. Dworkin concedes that fit often won't produce a unique answer, but holds that the choice must rest on principles about what tenancy law is for, not on partisanship.
  • Concede. The winning reading rests on beliefs the other member needn't share. And if Ruritania's tenancy law had a wicked history (say, excluding a minority), integrity alone gives no way out; Radbruch's formula is the outer limit.
  • Singapore. In LMS, the Court of Appeal relied on a central idea of Dworkin's to leave extra-legal considerations to the Legislature. TSH surmises that the court meant the principle v policy distinction.
  • Say: law is "deeply and thoroughly political", in the sense of political morality.
  • Verdict. Principle constrains the tribunal, but fit alone can't settle it.

614.6 Fuller

🔑 Use: 3, 8.4, 2.4, 13.1
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: what separates law from naked power, and why do failures of form wrong citizens?
  • CLAIM: law is the enterprise of subjecting human conduct to the governance of rules, with an inner morality of eight desiderata.
  • TEST: → 15.1. Total failure in one desideratum yields something "not properly called a legal system at all". Otherwise, a legal system's existence is "always a matter of degree".
  • STRENGTH: it binds lawmakers first: being at the top of the chain of command "intensifies" their duty of legality.
  • CRITIQUE: Liu's slides†: "Is it about morality at all? The label seems misapplied"; perhaps it is efficacy (W2 slide 17) → reply: legality respects responsible agents (W2 slide 17†), and grounds the duty to obey by reciprocity (3.3).
  • CONCEDE: legality is thin: a clear, public, prospective law can still be wicked. Concede it; let the Radbruch formula test content (13.1).
  • SAY: "no greater legal monstrosity than a secret statute"; "no less an undertaking than being a lawgiver".
  • TRAP: "Not all cases are hard" concerns legality, not adjudication. Fuller did not adopt the Radbruch formula; he asks "how much of a legal system survived".
  • VERDICT: Fuller shows legality is a genuine but modest morality binding rulers, not that it makes their laws just.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Parliament's Secret Annex

Ruritania's Parliament passes a Public Safety Act whose Schedule of offences is kept secret "for security reasons". Separately, it passes a clear, published law excluding a minority from public jobs.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim and test. The secret Schedule fails promulgation. If all criminal law were secret, there would be no legal system at all. Here it is one Act, so the system survives, but degraded: legality is a matter of degree.
  • Strength. Parliament, at the top of the chain of command, has an intensified duty of legality. It can't excuse itself as judges and police can't either.
  • Critique and reply. Is this just about efficacy, about whether the law works? No: a secret offence denies citizens the chance to choose as responsible agents, and breaks the reciprocity that grounds their duty to obey.
  • Concede. The published job-exclusion law passes Fuller's tests and is still wicked. Concede that legality is thin, and let the RF test its content.
  • Say: "no greater legal monstrosity than a secret statute". Balancing the eight requirements is "no less an undertaking than being a lawgiver".
  • Trap. If you write about which cases are easy or hard, that concerns legality (whether citizens can follow the rules), not how judges decide. And Fuller didn't adopt the RF. Facing the Junta's laws, he would ask how much of a legal system survived.
  • Verdict. Genuine but modest.

714.7 TSH: moral subjectivism

🔑 Use: 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.5, 4.7
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: is morality a matter of personal or cultural opinion, and can subjectivists argue with anyone?
  • CLAIM: subjectivists cannot hold others to any standard independent of their belief without ceasing to be subjectivists, so their moral dialogue is gravely limited.
  • TEST: does a sceptic's premise bind someone who rejects it? A relativist who binds outsiders invokes a "meta-cultural standard". If it honours equal moral worth, he "is a moral realist".
  • STRENGTH: the genocide hypothetical: "Moral dialogue in fact breaks down". If all may do as they please, "everyone becomes equally worthless". Concede limits, and the subjectivist is "just another moral realist".
  • CRITIQUE: epistemic sceptics (TSH's second kind): who knows the moral facts? → reply: a legitimate variant, but a dead end for law-making. Finnis's goods offer a way forward (Liu, W3; 14.8). Realism "entails a commitment to deliberation", with judgements held "more provisionally".
  • CONCEDE: she shows that subjectivists' moral dialogue is "gravely limited", not which realist content is right. The rest is "a squabble within the family of moral realists".
  • VERDICT: TSH shows that a subjectivist who argues or demands must turn realist, and that subjectivism's case is inconclusive, not that moral facts exist. How we know what is right is left to deliberation.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Two Islands Dispute

The people of Aster Island believe it is right to enslave anyone born on neighbouring Brin Island. Brin's government, whose official philosophy is cultural relativism, protests: "You must respect our people's right to govern themselves."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Test. Brin's protest binds Aster, which rejects it. That is a meta-cultural standard (cultural self-determination). If Brin grounds it in equal moral worth, Brin is a moral realist.
  • Strength. If Brin stays a true relativist, it can only say "our norms don't bind you", and Aster can say the same back. Dialogue breaks down, leaving force. And if everyone may do as they please, everyone is equally worthless.
  • Critique and reply. A Brin philosopher says: "Moral facts may exist, but who can know them?" That is a legitimate position, but it leaves Brin with nothing to argue. Finnis's basic goods offer a way to make progress, and realism, properly held, means deliberating with provisional judgements.
  • Concede. TSH shows Brin must argue as a realist. She doesn't show which realist view is right; that is a squabble within the realist family.
  • Verdict. It is a persuasion argument, not a proof that moral facts exist.

814.8 Finnis

🔑 Use: 5, 6.2, 6.5, 2.3, 4.4
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
[Theorist] card
  • PURPOSE: what makes choices and laws reasonable, without deriving "ought" from nature?
  • CLAIM: seven self-evident basic goods and nine requirements of practical reasonableness yield moral norms, and a common good that rules out many laws.
  • TEST: → 15.3, 15.4. A requirement plus the circumstances gives: this act ought (not) to be done (W4 slide 11†).
  • STRENGTH 1: the goods are grasped, not inferred: "there is no inference from fact to value".
  • STRENGTH 2: the state's role is "not ... to make people integrally good but only to maintain peace and justice", on principles "accessible to all people whatever their religious beliefs".
  • CRITIQUE: Liu's slides† doubt self-evidence and the seventh requirement (W4 slide 13). Harris: facts about human nature creep back in (15–16) → reply: "we are not dealing with logical necessities", yet it is still reasoning.
  • CONCEDE: accessible is not accepted: reasonable people dispute the list and its use. Concede that this limits the coercion he can justify (5.7).
  • VERDICT: Finnis gives lawmakers usable limits and a facilitative state, but his self-evidence rests on contested intuitions, and Liu finds the seventh requirement artificial.
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
[Core] card

(replaces the above in the Core version):

  • PURPOSE: the same.
  • TEST: → 15.3, 15.4.
  • STRENGTH: Finnis gives legislators real limits without a state life-plan: the common good is "a set of conditions", and "there is no inference from fact to value". He can say why some things are wrong even if most people approve.
  • CRITIQUE:
    • self-evidence rests on intuitions shaped by upbringing (Liu);
    • accessible is not accepted;
    • the means and side-effect line is "honestly pretty artificial", and since consent cures nothing, it is a heavy limit on autonomy (Liu) → reply: there is "no magic in the number seven", "we are not dealing with logical necessities", and dissent may be "inculpably erroneous", not "perfectly reasonable".
  • VERDICT: reasonable disagreement limits what the state may coerce, even where Finnis is right about the good.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Assisted Dying Bill (5.0), Finnis's Way

Ruritania's Assisted Dying Bill would let doctors give lethal injections on request. 70% of citizens approve.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim and test. Life is a basic good. The seventh requirement bars choosing directly against it. In these circumstances, a lethal injection is chosen as the means to end suffering, so it ought not to be done. Authorising it is not something the state may do.
  • Strengths.
    • Finnis doesn't infer "life is good" from biology. It is grasped directly.
    • He can explain why the Bill is wrong even though 70% approve.
    • And he doesn't need a state life-plan: the state's role is peace and justice, the common good as a set of conditions, on reasons accessible to everyone regardless of religion.
  • Critiques.
    • Is life's goodness really self-evident, or is that intuition shaped by a Catholic upbringing?
    • Harris says facts about human nature creep into the reasoning.
    • The means/side-effect line is artificial: a doctor may give a large dose of painkiller foreseeing death (side effect), but not intending it.
    • And the dying man's own consent counts for nothing.
  • Replies. The list isn't sacred ("no magic in the number seven"). It isn't logical deduction, but it is still reasoning. Those who disagree may be mistaken without being blameworthy.
  • Concede. Accessible isn't accepted. Many reasonable citizens reject Finnis's view of life.
  • Verdict. Even if Finnis is right, the depth of reasonable disagreement limits how far the state should coerce. So a Finnisian legislator might vote against the Bill, while being cautious about jailing desperate relatives who help a loved one die.

914.9 Seligman and Tierney [Theorist only]

🔑 Use: 5.6, 5.1
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: does human nature push us by urges, or pull us towards ends (Topic 4: "follow nature")?
  • CLAIM: minds are built for prospection. Memory and emotion serve planning, so we are pulled by ends, not pushed by the past.
  • STRENGTH: it fits Finnis's first requirement: living merely "from moment to moment, following immediate cravings" is unreasonable.
  • CRITIQUE: Hume and Finnis: psychology cannot ground norms (14.8) → reply: the essay shows how goods appear in experience, not that they are goods.
  • TRAP: only a summary is in the folder: paraphrase, never quote.
  • VERDICT: Seligman and Tierney make Finnis's planner look true to life: an illustration, never a proof.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Student's Proof

A student writes: "Seligman and Tierney prove Finnis right. Science shows humans are built to plan, so we ought to live by a plan of life."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim and strength. The research does fit Finnis: we spend more time imagining futures than recalling the past, which makes the plan of life natural to us, and living moment to moment looks against the grain.
  • Critique and reply. But "we are built to plan" is a fact. "We ought to plan" doesn't follow from it (Hume), and Finnis himself denies any inference from fact to value. The research shows how goods appear in experience, not that they are goods.
  • Trap. Only a summary of the essay is in the folder, so paraphrase it. Don't put words in quotation marks.
  • Verdict. Use it as an illustration, never as a proof.

1014.10 Rawls

🔑 Use: 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.11, 13.1
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
[Theorist] card
  • PURPOSE: when is coercion legitimate among citizens who reasonably disagree about the good?
  • CLAIM: power is fully proper only under a constitution whose essentials all citizens, as free and equal, may reasonably be expected to endorse.
  • TEST: → 15.5.
    • Scope: constitutional essentials, basic justice and bordering questions, "so far as possible", in the public political forum.
    • Reciprocity: offer reasons others "might also reasonably accept", not merely understand, as Servetus understood Calvin.
  • STRENGTH: not secularism. Public reason is not "secular reason", and the proviso admits religious argument if public reasons follow "in due course".
  • CRITIQUE 1: Finnis: the principle is "illegitimate, unreasonable, and uncivil", leaving the gravest questions to "sheer power of numbers or influence" → reply: Finnis grants the reciprocity ideal "seems broadly reasonable"; the dispute is who is reasonable.
  • CRITIQUE 2: TSH: unless Rawls counts heads, "reasonable" needs a standard "external to the citizens" → reply: his standard is moral though political, not a head-count.
  • VERDICT: Rawls sets the right discipline for public argument, though deciding who counts as reasonable already takes a moral side.
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
[Core] card
  • PURPOSE: the same.
  • TEST: → 15.5. Reciprocity: offer reasons others "might also reasonably accept".
  • STRENGTH: Rawls explains how a law can bind people who reject its premises. He favours no doctrine a priori, and public reason is not "secular reason": secular comprehensive doctrines are limited in the same way.
  • CRITIQUE:
    • Finnis's dilemma: read as a prediction, the test gives "a particularly gross form of veto"; read as a norm, it judges merits;
    • Finnis calls the principle "illegitimate, unreasonable, and uncivil", leaving the gravest questions to "sheer power of numbers or influence";
    • "reasonable" needs a standard "external to the citizens" (TSH);
    • on abortion, Rawls moved from "to that extent unreasonable" to saying Catholics "need not exercise" the right → reply: his standard is moral though political, not a head-count, and Finnis grants the reciprocity ideal "seems broadly reasonable". The dispute is who is reasonable.
  • VERDICT: Rawls sets the right discipline for public argument, but deciding who counts as reasonable already takes a moral side, and public reason may still end in a vote.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Servetus Test

In a debate on surrogacy (6.0), MP Lim says: "I'll explain my faith's view so clearly that every citizen will understand why I oppose it."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim and test. Surrogacy touches basic justice (exploitation, children's welfare), so public reason applies so far as possible. Being understood isn't enough: Calvin's reasons for burning Servetus were understood by Servetus. Lim must give reasons others might reasonably accept, such as the risk of exploiting poor women.
  • Strength. Lim may still mention his faith, if public reasons follow in due course. A secular MP arguing from a comprehensive philosophy of autonomy faces the same limit, so it isn't secularism.
  • Core strength. If the law passes on public reasons, it binds even citizens who reject its premises.
  • Critiques.
    • "Might reasonably accept": predicted, or deserved? The first gives a veto; the second judges merits.
    • Finnis: it leaves the gravest questions to numbers.
    • TSH: "reasonable" needs an external standard.
    • Core adds: on abortion, Rawls himself shifted, from "unreasonable" to "need not exercise".
  • Replies. The standard is moral, not a head-count, and Finnis accepts the reciprocity ideal itself.
  • Verdict. It is the right discipline for Lim's argument. But labelling opponents "unreasonable" takes a moral side, and (Core) the debate may still end in a vote.

1114.11 TSH: religion and public reason

🔑 Use: 6.4, 6.5, 6.7
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: in a multi-religious democracy, may law-makers rely on religious arguments?
  • CLAIM: judge arguments by their accessibility and merit, not their religious motive. Bracketing a metaphysical question already answers it.
  • CRITIQUE: Rawls: using state power against reasonable dissenters is "unreasonable or worse" → reply: she asks only for accessible reasons; "the delineation of a political sphere is artificial".
  • CONCEDE: her close: consensus on human worth "does not currently extend" to who counts as human. She suggests a "pragmatic strategy" of arguing from consequences. Concede that principle alone may not move Parliament.
  • SAY: "shatters the illusion of an accommodative solution".
  • VERDICT: TSH exposes the unfairness of sorting arguments by motive, but not how a divided Parliament should settle contested questions.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Abortion Review Campaign

A coalition, partly religious, campaigns for Ruritania to lower its abortion limit from 24 to 20 weeks. A minister dismisses them: "These are religious people with religious motives."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim. The minister is sorting by motive. TSH says judge the arguments themselves: are they accessible (foetal pain research, viability) and sound? And keeping the "when does life begin" question out of the debate already answers it, by permitting abortion at 24 weeks.
  • Critique and reply. A Rawlsian says the coalition wants to use state power against reasonable dissenters. TSH replies that she asks only for accessible reasons, and that the line between "political" and "metaphysical" is artificial.
  • Concede. Society hasn't agreed on who counts as human, so arguing from principle may not move Parliament. Her pragmatic strategy: argue from consequences everyone accepts, such as women's health data.
  • Say: the debate "shatters the illusion of an accommodative solution".
  • Verdict. She shows the minister's dismissal is unfair, but not how a split Parliament should finally decide.

1214.12 Mill and Wolfenden

🔑 Use: 7.1, 7.2, 7.5
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: what may the criminal law prohibit: only harm to others, or private immorality too?
  • CLAIM: coercion is justified only to prevent harm to others. Private immorality that neither harms nor offends in public is not the criminal law's concern.
  • TEST: Wolfenden: preserve public order and decency, protect from the offensive or injurious, and safeguard the vulnerable against exploitation or corruption.
  • STRENGTH: in Hart's words, free choice may be "a value in itself", or valuable because it lets individuals "experiment" in living.
  • CRITIQUE 1: Devlin: consent is no defence to murder or assault, so the law already enforces moral principle → reply: Hart: such rules can be paternalist, not moralist.
  • CRITIQUE 2: TSH: "harm" and "self-regarding" are indeterminate, and if only legal interests count, "there appears to be circularity" → reply: the harm line needs moral argument, openly made.
  • SG: Shanmugam (2022): Singapore's position is "broadly similar" to Wolfenden's (7.5).
  • SAY: "not the law's business" (Wolfenden).
  • VERDICT: Mill and Wolfenden rightly make liberty the default, but cannot draw the harm line without moral argument.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Sex-Work Review

Ruritania reviews its laws on sex work. A committee proposes to:

  • (a) decriminalise private, consensual adult sex work;
  • (b) keep street solicitation an offence;
  • (c) keep severe penalties for trafficking and for exploiting minors.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim and test. (a) follows Mill: private, consensual adult conduct is "not the law's business". (b) protects public order and decency. (c) safeguards the vulnerable against exploitation. Together, they are Wolfenden's model.
  • Strength. Adults' free choice has value in itself, and lets people live as they judge best.
  • Critique 1. Devlin: the law already denies that consent excuses assault, so it enforces morality. Hart's reply: that rule protects people (paternalism), not morality as such.
  • Critique 2. TSH: is a sex worker's long-term psychological harm "self-regarding"? Is a client's family "harmed"? If "harm" means only harm to legal interests, the test is circular. Reply: the line can be drawn, but only by moral argument, made openly.
  • Singapore. Shanmugam said Singapore's position is broadly similar to Wolfenden's.
  • Verdict. Liberty is the right default, but drawing the harm line takes moral argument.

1314.13 Hart: Law, Liberty, and Morality

🔑 Use: 7.1, 7.2, 7.4, 7.9
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
[Theorist] card
  • PURPOSE: may the criminal law enforce morality as such, beyond preventing harm to others?
  • CLAIM: coercion is prima facie objectionable, and needs a countervailing good. Paternalism and public decency can supply one, but bare moral condemnation cannot.
  • TEST: → 15.7.
    1. It is a question of critical morality about enforcing positive morality.
    2. There are two costs: punishing offenders, and coercing those who never offend.
    3. Paternalism, where consent is defective.
    4. Decency: punish the public act.
  • STRENGTH: bigamy, if punished to protect religious feelings from a public act, is punished "neither as irreligious nor as immoral but as a nuisance". Whether to punish turns on contestable estimates of offence against freedom lost.
  • CRITIQUE: TSH: "a critique could be made" that paternalism is "in the ultimate analysis, based on morals" → reply: Hart grants that applying his grounds takes moral judgement. He denies only punishing immorality as such (Liu, W9).
  • VERDICT: Hart wins the case against punishing private immorality as such, though moral judgement still decides where his paternalism and decency bite.
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
[Core] card
  • PURPOSE: the same.
  • TEST: → 15.7.
  • STRENGTH: Hart asks the right question: is the bare fact that positive morality condemns conduct any reason to punish it? He finds no evidence for disintegration, which merits "no more respect than the Emperor Justinian's statement" on earthquakes. Bigamy is punished "neither as irreligious nor as immoral but as a nuisance".
  • CRITIQUE: TSH:
    • paternalism is "in the ultimate analysis, based on morals", since morals pick its targets (apotemnophilia v dangerous sports);
    • "harm" is indeterminate, and if only legal interests count, "there appears to be circularity";
    • decency has the same problem: teetotallers can be offended too → reply: Hart grants that applying his grounds takes moral judgement. He denies only that immorality as such is a reason to punish (Liu).
  • VERDICT: Hart wins against punishing private immorality as such, but moral judgement still decides where his paternalism and decency bite.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Mock Wedding

Ruritania makes bigamy a crime. Raj, already married, lives with a second partner and holds a full church-style wedding ceremony with her, with guests and a cake. A second couple in the same position simply live together, with no ceremony, and commit no crime.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim and test.
    1. The question is one of critical morality: is the community's condemnation of bigamy a reason to punish Raj?
    2. Punishment costs Raj his liberty, and threatens everyone else.
    3. No defective consent is involved, so paternalism doesn't apply.
    4. Decency: the law punishes the public ceremony, which offends those for whom marriage is sacred.
  • Strength. That explains why only Raj, and not the cohabiting couple, is punished. He is punished "neither as irreligious nor as immoral but as a nuisance". (Core adds: Hart asks the right question, whether bare condemnation is any reason, and there is no evidence that tolerating private arrangements disintegrates society.)
  • Critique. TSH: why protect these religious feelings, but not teetotallers' offence at public drinking (Core)? And why ban surgery for apotemnophilia but allow dangerous sports? Morality picks the targets.
  • Reply. Hart accepts that applying his grounds needs moral judgement. He rejects only punishing immorality as such.
  • Verdict. Hart wins on Raj's private cohabitation. But where the "public offence" line falls is a moral call.

1414.14 Stephen [Theorist only]

🔑 Use: 7.8
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: may criminal law punish vice as such? Stephen's reply to Mill.
  • CLAIM: Stephen holds what Hart calls the extreme thesis: enforcing morality is valuable in itself. Devlin, "for most of his essay", holds the moderate one: a shared morality as "the cement of society".
  • CRITIQUE: Hart: a "non sequitur". What to punish and how severely are "distinct and independent questions" → reply: Hart still lets wickedness be "a partial determinant" of severity.
  • SAY: "a persecution of the grosser forms of vice" (Stephen).
  • VERDICT: Stephen is a useful foil. Beside his extreme thesis, Devlin's moderate one and Finnis's "peace and justice" limit look narrow.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Two Burglars

Two burglars steal the same amount. Ana stole to feed her children. Bo stole to fund gambling, and mocked his elderly victim. Bo gets a longer sentence. A commentator says: "So the criminal law punishes vice: Stephen was right."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim. Stephen would say yes: criminal law is "a persecution of the grosser forms of vice", and enforcing morality is good in itself. Devlin, more moderately, defends shared morality as what holds society together.
  • Critique. Hart: it's a non sequitur. That we grade sentences by wickedness doesn't show we punish because of wickedness. Whether to punish burglary (harm) and how severely (partly wickedness) are separate questions.
  • Reply. Hart still allows wickedness to be a partial factor in severity, which is why Bo gets longer.
  • Verdict. Next to Stephen, Devlin (protect society) and Finnis (only peace and justice) look narrow.

1514.15 Devlin

🔑 Use: 7.3, 7.4, 15.6
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
[Theorist] card
  • PURPOSE: may society enforce its shared morality by law, and how is it found?
  • CLAIM: Devlin holds that society may use law to protect the shared morality that holds it together, against conduct beyond the limits of tolerance.
  • TEST: → 15.6. The reasonable, not rational, man in the jury box: what any twelve people chosen at random "might after discussion be expected to be unanimous" on. Not majority opinion, and not every citizen's assent: it "does not depend on the counting of heads" (15).
  • STRENGTH: consent is no defence to murder, since the offence is "against society" (6–7).
  • CRITIQUE 1: Hart: no evidence; it merits "no more respect than the Emperor Justinian's statement" on earthquakes → reply: deviation and subversion are only "capable in their nature" of threatening society, and "If morality is changed, the law can be changed". But if only "capable", why harsh sanctions now (Liu, W9)?
  • CRITIQUE 2: TSH, for moral realists: treating secular moral judgement as "simply a feeling" (17) "comes close to" non-cognitivism → reply: her charitable reading, an objective "reasonable", she herself finds "overly generous" (Devlin's relativism).
  • SAY: "invisible bonds of common thought" (10).
  • TRAP: Devlin argues as a cultural relativist (Liu, W7). Monogamy binds as "built into the house in which we live" (9). Honest belief, "right or wrong", makes immorality "a question of fact". Privacy is only "to be taken into account".
  • VERDICT: Devlin rightly denies law's moral neutrality, but wrongly lets common feeling, not reason, fix what it enforces.
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
[Core] card
  • PURPOSE: the same.
  • TEST: → 15.6.
  • STRENGTH: Devlin rightly denies that law is morally neutral: consent is no defence to murder because the offence is "against society", and "No society can do without intolerance, indignation, and disgust".
  • CRITIQUE:
    • Hart: no evidence that private deviation threatens society;
    • Devlin argues as a cultural relativist (Liu): monogamy binds because it is "built into the house in which we live", so a persecuting society has the same claim;
    • pluralist Singapore may lack the consensus he presupposes → reply: he says only that immorality is "capable in their nature" of threatening society, and "If morality is changed, the law can be changed". But if only capable, why harsh sanctions now (Liu)?
  • SAY: "invisible bonds of common thought".
  • TRAP: honest belief, "right or wrong", makes immorality "a question of fact". Privacy is only "to be taken into account".
  • VERDICT: Devlin leaves much to individual morality in practice, but he lets common feeling, not reason, fix what the law enforces.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Suspension Parties (7.3), Devlin's Way

Back to the private hook-suspension parties.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim and test. Would twelve random Ruritanians, after discussion, be unanimous that these parties are beyond the limits of tolerance? Not a 65% poll, and not universal assent. If unanimity is unlikely, Devlin's test isn't met.
  • Strength. Devlin is right that law isn't morally neutral: consent wouldn't excuse a murder, because murder offends society. Core adds: no society can do without indignation and disgust.
  • Critiques.
    • Hart: no evidence that tolerating private parties threatens society; that claim is as unsupported as Justinian's earthquakes.
    • TSH: calling moral judgement "simply a feeling" is close to non-cognitivism.
    • Core adds: a pluralist society may lack the deep consensus Devlin needs, and his relativism gives a persecuting society the same claim.
  • Reply. Devlin says only that immorality is capable of threatening society, and that the law can change when morality does. But then why jail anyone now?
  • Trap. For Devlin, what the right-minded person honestly believes, right or wrong, is the morality the law may enforce: immorality becomes a question of fact. Privacy is only a factor. He is a relativist, not a realist.
  • Say: society is held together by "invisible bonds of common thought".
  • Verdict. In practice, Devlin would probably leave the parties alone (Core). In principle, he lets feeling, not reason, decide.

1814.18 Hart: separation (1958)

🔑 Use: 8.1, 8.2, 8.7
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: should an iniquitous rule be denied the name of law, or called law and condemned?
  • CLAIM: Hart separates law as it is from law as it ought to be: validity never settles whether to obey.
  • TEST: if punishment needs retroactivity, choose openly "between two evils", by statute.
  • STRENGTH: plain speech: "law but too evil to be obeyed" is among the most powerful moral criticisms, because it is the simplest.
  • CRITIQUE 1: Fuller: positivism "never gives any coherent meaning" to fidelity to law, and the question then seems to be "who should do the dirty work" → reply: only a statute sacrifices a principle openly; the bridge to obedience is moral (8.7).
  • CRITIQUE 2: Alexy: where the injustice was evident at the time, the court ascertains the law then in force, so there is no covert retroactivity → reply: even Alexy calls candour "the strongest argument against" non-positivism, "but not its downfall".
  • SAY: "not just one among many minor virtues".
  • TRAP: Bamberg voided no 1934 statute, as Hart supposed. He later conceded the error (Alexy).
  • VERDICT: Hart wins on labels for observers and historians. A judge deciding today needs more than candour.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Kovač the Informer (8.1), Hart's Way

Same facts as the hypo in 8.1; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

  • Critique 2 (Alexy). If the injustice was evident in 2012, a 2020 court finding the Decree void is just stating what the law was then, so nothing is covertly retroactive. Reply: even Alexy admits candour is the strongest objection.
  • Say: candour is "not just one among many minor virtues".
  • Trap. In the real informer case, the Bamberg court did not void the Nazi statute. Hart got that wrong, and later admitted it.
  • Verdict. For a historian describing 2012, Hart's labels win. For a 2020 judge deciding Kovač's case, candour alone isn't enough.

1914.19 Radbruch and Alexy

🔑 Use: 8.3, 8.4 (Theorist adds 15.8)
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card

    • necessity after a regime collapses;

Same facts as the hypo in 8.3; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

  • Strength 1. Petrov's ruling claims to be correct, and an extremely unjust norm can't be correctly applied.

    • necessity: after the Junta fell, courts had to deal with its laws;

  • Critique and reply. Hart: Radbruch misunderstood liberalism. Fuller: Radbruch saw the real dilemma, between order and good order.

  • Trap. Radbruch himself warned of the dangers, and preferred a retroactive statute for informers. "Not law" at tier 2 is Alexy's reading. BHC is TSH's test, not Alexy's.
  • Verdict. A narrow backstop, if the minimum core holds.

2214.22 Kennedy

🔑 Use: 12.4, 15.10, 13.1
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card
  • PURPOSE: what is judging like when the law and the judge's sense of justice conflict?
  • CLAIM: Kennedy's judge is neither simply bound nor free. Law is a medium that constrains, but what it rules out depends on the judge's project.
  • TEST: the strikers' lie-in. The rule first "just applies itself". The judge then works it towards "how-I-want-to-come-out", paying in time and "legitimacy cost".
  • STRENGTH: legality requires building the best case for the other side. What would betray it is "the wrong attitude at the end". Sometimes the rule is "a felt objectivity" he "can't budge".
  • CRITIQUE: Hart, against rule sceptics: rules have a "core of central meaning" → reply: how much of a field is open, in itself, is "simply unanswerable".
  • SAY: "free to deploy work in any direction"; "the field is me, resisting myself".
  • TRAP: five courses, never three (15.10, 12.4). Against "always a right answer", he sets the experience of "free ethical or political choice", not a thesis.
  • VERDICT: Kennedy describes judging more honestly than he justifies it. He shows the choice is moral, then leaves it "for another time".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Eviction Order

Judge Okafor, who sympathises with tenants, hears a landlord's claim to evict a family that is two months behind on rent after the father lost his job. The tenancy statute seems clearly to allow eviction.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim and test. At first, the statute "just applies itself": eviction. Okafor's HIWTCO is "the family stays". She works the materials: perhaps the landlord's notice was defective, or a hardship provision can be stretched. That costs time, and risks her credibility.
  • Strength. To be faithful to legality, she must build the landlord's best case, and test her first impression against it. Only the wrong attitude at the end, deciding against what she concludes the law requires, betrays legality. And she may find the rule simply can't be budged.
  • Critique and reply. Hart: "pay rent or be evicted" has a core of settled meaning. Kennedy: how much of the field is open can't be answered in the abstract. It depends on the work.
  • Say: she is "free to deploy work in any direction", yet "the field is me, resisting myself".
  • Trap. If the law won't budge, Kennedy lists five courses, not three (12.4.2). And he doesn't claim there's never a right answer. He reports his experience of free choice.
  • Verdict. Honest about the choice; silent on how to make it.

2314.23 Pepper

🔑 Use: 10.1, 10.3, 15.11
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card

  • CLAIM: Pepper argues that lawful help is morally justified, because access to law serves autonomy and equality. The client, not the lawyer, is accountable.
  • TEST: → 15.11. Law is "a public good available to all"; autonomy is "a moral good"; access needs lawyers, so screening means "rule by an oligarchy of lawyers".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Tax Scheme

A wealthy client asks lawyer Farah to structure a lawful but aggressive scheme that shifts profits offshore to pay almost no tax. Farah thinks it is immoral.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Claim and test. The tax law is a public good available to everyone. The client's autonomy in arranging his affairs is a moral good, and he needs a lawyer to use the law. If Farah refused because of her personal morals, lawyers would become an oligarchy deciding who gets the law.
  • Strength. If such schemes are bad enough, Parliament should ban them. Screening by lawyers would add a second inequality (a lawyer's approval) on top of the first (who can pay).
  • Critique 1. If the client thinks of law as just costs (realism), and Farah applies no morality, nothing restrains him. Pepper's replies: Farah can raise her concerns, refuse the client at the outset, or, in an extreme case, object.
  • Critique 2. Why is an unjust result acceptable as "the system's" wrong rather than Farah's? Pepper answers: because the system gives everyone first-class citizenship.
  • Say: "morality comes through the door as part of the client". Pepper's model is "not comfortable, but good".
  • Verdict. Pepper justifies the client's access to law, not every service Farah might be asked to provide. Her conscience survives.

The card

Same facts as the hypo in 14.23; reread them first.

2514.25 TSH: Constitutional Jurisprudence

🔑 Use: 11.1, 11.7, 12.1
▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The card

The Detention Challenge

A man detained for 30 days without charge under a new Public Order Act argues that this deprives him of "personal liberty" otherwise than "in accordance with law" (Art 9(1)). The government replies: "The Act was validly passed, and Art 4 says the Constitution is supreme, not natural law."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Gambling Ban

Ruritania bans all private gambling, with jail terms. A court upholds the ban, a lawyer is asked to defend a poker player, and citizens must decide whether to obey.

✔ APPLICATION · Reading the grid acrossDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Aquinas. If the ban is unjust, it is a corruption of law. Rulers decide, for the common good. Obey only to avoid scandal.
  • Hart. The ban is law. May it be justified? Only by harm, paternalism or decency, and private poker fails all three, except perhaps paternalism for addicts. Obedience is a moral question.
  • Fuller. Is the ban public, clear and followed by officials? If it is enforced only against some players, ask how much legality survives.
  • Finnis. The state keeps peace and justice, and may ban acts that intend harm to a good. Is casual poker such an act? Probably not. Disobedience may be limited, lest a just system weaken.
  • Dworkin. The judge must read the ban in its best light, by fit and value.
  • Rawls. The ban needs public reasons, not one faith's condemnation of gambling. Citizens should vote as ideal legislators.
  • Devlin. Is private poker beyond the limits of tolerance, judged by the jury box? Unlikely.
  • Radbruch and Alexy. The ban isn't intolerably unjust, so it is law.
  • Kennedy. A judge who hates the ban works the field; if it won't budge, he picks among five courses.
  • TSH. The moral question can't be shunned. The legislature decides, and the court strikes down only at the BHC threshold, which isn't met here.
  • Pepper. Parliament decided; the lawyer serves the client within the law.
  • Thunder. The lawyer, by prudence, serves justice. The role is no excuse for a racist law, but this isn't one.

2814.28 Cross-examination lines [Theorist only]

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

The six lines:

  1. Hart to Devlin: why preserve a persecuting society whose "disintegration" might be "morally better than its continued existence"?
  2. Fuller to Hart: if positivism gives fidelity no coherent meaning, what does a judge owe a secret or retroactive Nazi statute?
  3. TSH to Alexy: if consensus nearly refutes relativism, what may a judge do once it goes "dreadfully wrong" while a legislature "purports to do right locally"?
  4. Finnis to Rawls: if public reason brackets moral truth, are the gravest questions not left to "the status quo established by sheer power of numbers"?
  5. Kennedy to Dworkin: when fit runs out and value is contested, is the chain novelist's best reading more than "free ethical or political choice"?
  6. Pepper to Thunder: if each lawyer screens by his own virtue, what prevents "rule by an oligarchy of lawyers"?
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

You are writing an answer and need one sharp objection for each paragraph. Where does each line fit?

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Hart to Devlin fits the Cohabitation Law (7.4): if Ruritania's old moral code persecuted cohabiting couples, why is losing it bad?
  2. Fuller to Hart fits the secret Schedule (14.6): what fidelity does a judge owe a secret statute?
  3. TSH to Alexy fits the forty-years-on twist (8.5.3).
  4. Finnis to Rawls fits the Late-Limit Bill (6.5): doesn't bracketing the unborn's status leave it to numbers?
  5. Kennedy to Dworkin fits the Reasonable Rent clause (14.5): when both readings fit, is the choice more than politics?
  6. Pepper to Thunder fits Farah's tax scheme (14.24): if Farah screens by her virtue, who checks her?

Use each line once, as the critique in that paragraph, then give the reply from the relevant card.
