HYPO LESSON 15 · SECTION 15 · ABOUT 22 MIN · 15 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Frameworks

⚡ BIG IDEA

A framework is a test you run in order. Each hypo runs one framework, step by step, on made-up facts.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It is the sheet's wording, so it is what you will write in the exam.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 15 of the 7 Nov sheets. The Core version is the Theorist version minus 15.2, 15.8, 15.9, 15.12 and 15.14, which are marked [Theorist only] below.

Each framework is a test. So each hypo here gives one set of facts, and the application runs the steps in order, then applies the verdict rule. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: RF = Radbruch formula; BHC = broad historical consensus; TSH = Tan Seow Hon; † = from the slides.

115.1 Fuller: legality checklist

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: can people follow this rule as made and applied? Use: 3.1

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  • Desiderata: is the rule (1) general? (2) promulgated? (3) prospective? (4) clear? (5) consistent? (6) possible? (7) constant? (8) congruent with official action?
  • Verdict rule: total failure of one yields something "not properly called a legal system at all". Short of that, legality is a matter of degree, not substantive justice (15.13).
  • Rex, who failed in all eight ways and so made no law at all:
    1. case-by-case rulings;
    2. a secret code;
    3. rulings with hindsight;
    4. an obscure code;
    5. contradictions;
    6. impossible demands;
    7. constant amendment;
    8. rulings unrelated to the code.
  • TRAP:
    • (1) means rules at all, not breadth: palm-tree justice, attainder and unfettered discretion fail it;
    • (2) needs access, not universal knowledge;
    • (3) bars only abuse (Liu, W2).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Port Meridian Protest Law

Port Meridian's new Protest Act:

  • lets the Commissioner approve or refuse each protest "as he sees fit";
  • is published online, though few read it;
  • applies only to future protests;
  • bans protests "likely to cause unease";
  • contains a clause requiring 30 days' notice, and another allowing protests on 7 days' notice;
  • requires organisers to guarantee that "no participant feels distressed";
  • has been amended six times in two months;
  • is enforced only against opposition groups.
✔ APPLICATION · Step by stepDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. General? It largely fails: "as he sees fit" is unfettered discretion, closer to case-by-case rulings than to rules. (Generality means rules at all, not broad ones.)
  2. Promulgated? Yes. It is accessible, even if few read it; universal knowledge isn't required.
  3. Prospective? Yes. Only abuse of retroactivity is barred.
  4. Clear? No: "likely to cause unease".
  5. Consistent? No: 30 days' notice v 7 days' notice.
  6. Possible? No: no organiser can guarantee no one feels distressed.
  7. Constant? No: six amendments in two months.
  8. Congruent? No: it is enforced only against the opposition.

Verdict. No requirement fails totally across the whole system, so Port Meridian still has a legal system. But this Act is badly degraded as law, "less a law". And a fully compliant Act could still be unjust, which is a question for the RF and 15.13, not for Fuller.

215.2 Is–ought repair [Theorist only]

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: which unstated ought-premise yields this conclusion? Use: 4.4

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  1. Liu's method (W3): list the premises a neutral listener must accept; mark the moral ones, hidden ones too; and defend each. The dispute shrinks to a bedrock premise.
  2. Split the facts (is) from the conclusion (ought): no ought follows from an is alone (Hume).
  3. Supply the missing major premise. Once the parties agree on it, they "can go on to deduce ought-conclusions" (13).
  4. Test that premise: is it self-evident on reflection (Finnis), or mere preference?

Verdict rule: argue about the premise, not the inference.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Screen-Time Study

A study shows that teenagers who use social media more than 3 hours a day report more anxiety. A minister says: "Therefore the law should ban social media for under-16s."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. The premises a neutral listener must accept:
    • (a) the study is accurate (factual);
    • (b) social media causes the anxiety (factual);
    • (c) the state should protect children's mental health (moral);
    • (d) protection justifies a ban rather than lesser measures (moral, hidden);
    • (e) the costs to teenagers' freedom and friendships are outweighed (moral, hidden). The dispute shrinks to (d) and (e).
  2. Split is from ought. "Teens using it more are more anxious" is an is. "Ban it" is an ought. The first alone can't give the second.
  3. Supply the missing premise: "the state ought to prevent serious, avoidable harm to children's health by the least restrictive effective means". If both sides accept it, the facts can then decide whether a ban, or something lesser, follows.
  4. Test the premise. Is protecting children's health self-evidently good? On Finnis's view, life (including psychological health) is a basic good. But "by a ban" is not self-evident.

Verdict. Argue about premises (d) and (e), not about whether the study "proves" the ban.

315.3 Finnis: is this act permissible?

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: does it choose directly against a basic good? Use: 5.3

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  1. Which basic good is pursued?
  2. Is a basic good damaged as an end or a means? Then it is wrong: "Do not choose directly against a basic value".
  3. Side effects must pass the golden rule: "would I ... have thought the act reasonable had I been the person harmed?"

Verdict rule: intended damage, never; side effects, only if fair.

Liu's rulings (W5):

  • barred: the hostage (even a volunteer); the footbridge push; self-injury for insurance; the death penalty ("even if it's Hitler"); euthanasia; suicide;
  • permitted or arguable: the trolley switch; triage; a lung-damaging mining job; shooting to disarm, with death foreseen.

Requirement (6) weighs; requirement (7) vetoes.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Hospital Decisions
  • (a) A surgeon could save five patients by taking the organs of one healthy, unconsenting visitor.
  • (b) In a mass-casualty event, doctors leave the most hopeless patients untreated to save the most lives.
  • (c) A doctor gives a dying patient high-dose morphine to relieve pain, foreseeing it may hasten death.
  • (d) A doctor gives a lethal injection at a patient's request.
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • (a) Life is damaged as a means (the organs). Barred, whatever the numbers. Requirement (7) vetoes the efficient answer that (6) would weigh.
  • (b) The good pursued is life. Not treating is not killing, and death is a side effect. Is it fair? Would I accept it if I were the hopeless patient, knowing others could be saved? Arguably yes. Permitted, like triage.
  • (c) The good pursued is freedom from pain (life, in Finnis's broad sense). Death is a foreseen side effect, not the aim. If proportionate and fair, it is arguable, like shooting to disarm.
  • (d) Death is the means of ending suffering. Barred, as euthanasia.

415.4 Finnis: may the state legislate this?

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: does it serve the common good, intending no harm? Use: 5.5

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  1. Two uses (Liu, W5; W4 slide 11†):
    • judge laws directly: authorising an act against a good is wrong (for Finnis, the death penalty and abortion);
    • judge facilitation: coordination counts (one side of the road), and requirement (3) bars arbitrary distinctions between citizens.
  2. Aim: "peace and justice", not making people "integrally good".
  3. Means: never intend damage to a good; may prohibit acts that intend it (W4 slide 12†).
  4. Reasons must be "accessible to all people whatever their religious beliefs".
  5. Prudence: non-enforcement can be reasonable, to avoid "a war that one cannot win".

Verdict rule: prohibit intended harm, on accessible reasons, where prudent.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Online Falsehoods Bill (POFMA-style)

Port Meridian proposes a law letting a minister order corrections to deliberately false statements of fact online.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Two uses. Directly: the law doesn't itself authorise any act against a good. As facilitation: it protects the conditions for public knowledge, and coordinates a shared factual basis for public debate. It must not draw arbitrary lines, such as applying only to opposition parties.
  2. Aim: peace and justice, meaning an information environment that serves citizens' own pursuit of knowledge. It is not aimed at making citizens think correctly.
  3. Means: the state must not itself lie or suppress truth. It may prohibit deliberate falsehoods, since those intend to damage knowledge.
  4. Reasons: protecting public knowledge is a reason anyone can accept, religious or not.
  5. Prudence: a broad ministerial power risks chilling honest speech. Narrow scope and court review may be wiser, and in some settings, not enforcing it may be prudent.

Verdict. Permissible in principle, if confined to deliberate falsehoods, justified by accessible reasons, and prudently limited.

515.5 Rawls: is this law legitimate?

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: could every reasonable citizen endorse the reasons? Use: 6.1

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  1. Is it a constitutional essential, or basic justice?
  2. Is the speaker a public-forum actor, including citizens voting "as if they were legislators"?
  3. Are the reasons political values, or comprehensive reasons backed by public ones "in due course" (the proviso)?
  4. Reciprocity: are the reasons acceptable to others as free and equal citizens, "not as dominated or manipulated"? Denying basic liberties "normally" fails.

Verdict rule: legitimate if (3) and (4) hold.

Completeness: no argument may run "too immediate and fragmentary" from a doctrine to a policy. These are not political values: moral autonomy; moral desert; monogamy "as such".

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Casino Licence Debate

Port Meridian's Parliament debates licensing a second casino.

  • MP A argues: "Gambling is a sin."
  • MP B: "It will raise problem-gambling rates and harm families. Studies show it."
  • MP C: "Adults' moral autonomy requires that we allow it."
  • MP D: "Those who gamble deserve to lose their money."
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Essential or basic justice? Partly: it touches economic justice and family welfare, so public reason applies "so far as possible".
  2. Public-forum actors? All four are MPs, so yes.
  3. Political values?
    • A: comprehensive (religious), with no public reason following. Fails, unless A later adds public reasons.
    • B: political values (family welfare, public health). Passes.
    • C: moral autonomy (Mill's individuality) isn't a political value. Fails as stated, but could be reframed as political liberty.
    • D: moral desert isn't a political value. Fails.
  4. Reciprocity. B's reasons could be accepted by gamblers and non-gamblers as free and equal citizens. A's couldn't, by non-believers.
  • Completeness. No MP may jump straight from "my doctrine says X" to "so license / ban". Each must work through political values.

Verdict. A decision based on B-type reasons is legitimate, whichever way it goes.

615.6 Devlin: the interrogatories

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: is it beyond the limits of tolerance? Use: 7.3

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  1. May society judge morals?
  2. May the law enforce that judgement?
  3. Always, or on what principles (Devlin)?
  4. Not "the counting of heads": ask what twelve people chosen at random "might after discussion be expected to be unanimous" on (15).
  5. Elastic principles: "maximum individual freedom that is consistent with the integrity of society"; "a real feeling of reprobation" (16–17).
  6. A vice "so abominable that its mere presence is an offence" may be eradicated. One that is tolerable if confined calls for a balance (17). The law sets "the minimum and not ... the maximum".

Verdict rule: a majority's dislike is "not nearly enough" (17).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Private Cockfighting

A group in Ruritania holds private cockfights for betting, on a remote farm. A poll shows 60% "dislike" it.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Judge morals? Yes: cruelty to animals is a moral matter society may judge.
  2. Enforce by law? In principle, yes, since Devlin sets no theoretical limit.
  3. On what principles? Steps 4–6.
  4. The jury box. Would twelve random Ruritanians, after discussion, be unanimous that cockfighting is intolerable? Very likely, given the animals' suffering, unlike many contested sexual-morality questions.
  5. Elastic principles. Maximum freedom consistent with society's integrity. Is there a real feeling of reprobation, deeply felt and not manufactured? Likely yes.
  6. Eradicate or balance? Devlin treats cruelty to animals as beyond tolerance even in private, so it may be eradicated.

Verdict. The 60% "dislike" poll isn't enough. But the jury-box test, properly applied, supports a ban. (Hart reaches the same result by a different route: the animals' suffering.)

715.7 Hart: may the criminal law prohibit it? (and the coercion gradient)

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: what justifies this coercion, besides immorality as such? Use: 7.9

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework

Coercion is "prima facie objectionable".

  1. Harm to others? Distress at "the bare knowledge" of others' conduct does not count.
  2. Paternalism, if consent is defective: for example, punishing drug supply "except under medical prescription".
  3. Public decency: the offence must be "serious and likely", weighed against the freedom lost.
  4. Moralism alone: never.

Verdict rule (the sheet's own, on Liu's map; all law rests on force, criminal law most directly, W9): the more coercive the measure (punish, regulate, promote), the stronger the reason needed. Hart's own question is punishment only.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Recreational Veridine (7.0), Three Measures

Ruritania considers (a) jailing veridine users, (b) prescription-only sale, and (c) public-health campaigns.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Harm to others: private use harms mainly the user. Neighbours' distress at merely knowing it happens doesn't count.
  2. Paternalism: consent may be impaired (addiction, transitory desires), which supports (b), restricting supply, as Hart did for drugs.
  3. Public decency: public intoxication could be an offence. Private use isn't.
  4. Moralism alone: "using veridine is degrading" can't justify (a).

The gradient. (a) punishment needs the strongest reason, which is lacking. (b) regulation has a paternalist reason. (c) promotion needs the least. And Hart's own question concerns only (a).

815.8 Alexy: should a judge deny it legal character? [Theorist only]

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: is the injustice extreme, to a participant? Use: 8.3

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  1. Take the participant's view (say, a judge), not the observer's.
  2. Weak thesis: legal character is lost only at an "intolerable degree" of injustice (Alexy).

Concede: definitions "cannot, as such, change reality", and candour is "the strongest argument against" non-positivism, "but not its downfall".

Verdict rule: deny legal character only where the injustice was evident when done: no covert retroactivity.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Junta's Property Decree

A 2021 Valdorian judge must decide whether a 2010 Junta decree seizing the homes of the Kel minority was law, in a claim by the dispossessed owners against the current occupants.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Participant. The judge must decide what the law was, as a participant claiming correctness, not as a historian describing Junta practice.
  2. Intolerable? Seizing the homes of one ethnic group, without compensation, is extreme injustice. Legal character is lost.
  • Concede. Calling it "not law" doesn't change what happened to the owners in 2010. Candour remains the strongest objection.
  • Verdict rule. Was the injustice evident in 2010? Racial dispossession was obviously unjust at the time, so the occupants had notice. Denying the decree legal character isn't covert retroactivity. The owners succeed.

915.9 Dworkin: fit, then value [Theorist only]

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: which principle best fits and justifies the legal history? Use: 9.2

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  1. List the rival principles.
  2. Fit: "interpret the legal history he finds, not to invent a better history".
  3. Value: choose what "states a sounder principle of justice".

Verdict rule: concede that fit "will often fail to produce a unique interpretation", and state the political morality openly.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Rescue Volunteer (9.2)

Same facts as the hypo in 9.2; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Rival principles:
    • (A) liability for psychiatric harm extends to those foreseeably drawn into the danger, rescuers included;
    • (B) liability extends only to close relatives at the scene.
  2. Fit. Both fit some cases. (A) fits cases where rescuers recovered for physical injury. (B) fits the nervous-shock cases. Neither is invented.
  3. Value. (A) states a sounder principle of justice: people who answer the call to rescue shouldn't bear the cost of the defendant's negligence.
  • Verdict rule. Concede that fit didn't settle it. State openly that the choice rests on fairness to rescuers.

1015.10 Kennedy: the five courses

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: law and how-I-want-to-come-out conflict: what may the judge do? Use: 12.4, 8.7

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  1. go along, denouncing the law;
  2. withdraw, leaving "the dirty work" to another;
  3. decide openly on what the law should be;
  4. use an implausible legal argument;
  5. find facts known to be false, "obviously an extreme measure".

Verdict rule:

  • Kennedy endorses or excludes none of them "a priori".
  • The sheet's own rule: in a basically just system, choose (1) or (2); (3) only at the Radbruch threshold; (4) and (5) fail candour (12.4).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Deportation Order

In just Ruritania, a judge must order the deportation of a long-term resident whose visa lapsed by a clerical error. The statute leaves no discretion. The judge thinks deportation cruel.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Go along: order it, and write an opinion criticising the statute. That fits a basically just system.
  2. Withdraw: recuse, so another judge decides. Available, but it passes the dirty work on.
  3. Decide by what the law should be: refuse to order it. Only at the Radbruch threshold, and a deportation is harsh, but not intolerable injustice. So no.
  4. An implausible argument: for example, "the visa didn't truly lapse". This fails candour.
  5. A false finding: for example, "she proved residency rights". This fails candour, and is extreme.

Verdict. (1), perhaps with a call for ministerial discretion.

1115.11 Pepper: the limit and the remedies

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: lawful but wrong: what may the lawyer do? Use: 10.1

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  1. Law is the limit: conduct bad enough, it would seem, "ought to be made explicitly unlawful" (Pepper).
  2. Responses to legal realism:
    • societal: more enforcement ("daunting"), or rebuilt moral authority beyond law;
    • for lawyers: not policeman, judge or deceiver, but moral dialogue, which is costly and needs a receptive client.
  3. Conscientious objection, "rarely exercised".

Verdict rule: advise on the law, add moral dialogue, and object only in extreme cases.

Liu (S13):

  • leaving practice is "a pretty weak kind of answer";
  • choice of client is "more respectable", but assumes someone else will act. That fails if a view is widespread, or if only the lowest-scruple lawyers remain;
  • Pepper concedes "second-class citizenship".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Landlord's Lawful Eviction

A landlord asks lawyer Kai to evict an elderly tenant on the earliest lawful date, two weeks before the tenant's hip surgery. It is fully lawful.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. The limit is the law. If this were bad enough, Parliament should ban it. It hasn't.
  2. Kai shouldn't act as policeman, judge or deceiver. He mustn't refuse to tell the landlord his rights, or mislead him. He can raise moral dialogue: "Would a month's delay cost you much?" That costs time, and needs a receptive client.
  3. Objection is for extreme cases. This probably isn't one.
  • Verdict rule. Advise, discuss, and act.
  • Liu. If Kai simply quit practice, that would be a weak answer. If he declined the client, that's more respectable, but if every scrupulous lawyer declined, only the least scrupulous would remain, and the landlord gets served anyway. And Pepper admits that a client refused by every lawyer gets second-class citizenship.

1215.12 Liu's three lawyering scenarios† [Theorist only]

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: where is the injustice: system, rule or outcome? Use: 10.11

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  1. Is the system, by and large, just?
  2. If so, is this rule intolerably unjust?
  3. If the rule is just, is only this outcome unjust (a coerced confession excluded: W12 slide 9)?

Thunder (W12 slide 8†: the good life over the role; question roles; courage and moderation; personal and professional excellence are interdependent):

  • Does the work serve "justice, public order, and rule of law"?
  • Does it need courage against "pressure to conform", or moderation short of "avoidable injustice"?

Verdict rule (the sheet's own):

  • in (3), defend fully;
  • in (2), refuse, or argue the formula;
  • in (1), the role gives no shelter.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Teo's Three Files (10.11)

Same facts as the hypo in 10.11; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • File 3 (coerced confession excluded): the system and the rule are just; only the outcome is unjust. Defend fully. The work serves justice and the rule of law. It may take courage against pressure from colleagues who think the client should be convicted.
  • File 2 (racist eviction statute): the system is just, but the rule is intolerably unjust. Refuse, or argue in court that the formula denies the statute legal character. Moderation means not going further than avoiding the injustice.
  • File 1 (the Junta's sham courts): the system isn't just. The role gives Teo no shelter: "I was only a lawyer" won't excuse lending legitimacy to the sham.

1315.13 TSH: should a court strike it down? (RF plus BHC)

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: is it manifestly unjust by broad historical consensus? Use: 11.5, 12.4

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  1. Presume constitutionality "unless the threshold of injustice in Radbruch's formula is met" (TSH).
  2. Proof: a long-lasting consensus across many jurisdictions, for the same reason.
  3. Met (genocide, slavery): strike down, even an amendment. Not met (Roe): legislatures decide.

Her "catch": a world trend might carry the formula decades on, and consensus can go "dreadfully wrong".

Verdict rule: this test is for courts only. Legislators need no such consensus.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Child Labour Act

Ruritania amends its Constitution, by two-thirds, to permit children aged 10 and up to work 12-hour shifts in mines. Separately, a statute limits Sunday trading hours.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. Presume both constitutional.
  2. Proof. Is there long-lasting, multi-jurisdiction consensus, for the same reason, that forcing 10-year-olds into 12-hour mine shifts is intolerably unjust? Plausibly yes: it is a form of child servitude, condemned across the world for generations. For Sunday trading limits, there is no such consensus.
  3. Strike down the child-labour amendment, even though it is an amendment. Leave the Sunday trading law to Parliament.
  • The catch. Concede that consensus could someday go wrong.
  • Verdict rule. A legislator deciding whether to repeal the Sunday trading law needs no consensus, just good reasons.

1415.14 Who decides? [Theorist only]

▤ THE RULE · AS YOUR SHEET STATES IT

Key question: who rightfully decides: is anyone usurping or abdicating? Use: 12.1

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The framework
  1. Positive law allocates authority (a determinatio). In a basically just regime, "judicial usurpations ... even in what judges take to be good causes, are themselves unjust" (George).
  2. But "who rightfully decides" whether the allocation was prudent? An impasse.
  3. A whipped Parliament may not reflect consensus (6.8), and courts may be exhorted to uphold higher law "rather than playing politics".

Verdict rule: honour the allocation; depart only at the Radbruch threshold (15.13).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
The Euthanasia Case (12.1)

Same facts as the hypo in 12.1; reread them first.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  1. The allocation. Ruritania's Constitution gives Parliament the power to make criminal law. In a basically just regime, if the court invented a right to assisted death, that would be usurpation, even for a good cause (George).
  2. The impasse. But who decides whether giving Parliament that power was prudent? There is no clear answer.
  3. Caveats. If Parliament was whipped on euthanasia, its vote may not reflect consensus (6.8). And courts should uphold higher law, not play politics.
  • Verdict rule. Honour the allocation. Euthanasia law is not at the Radbruch threshold, so it is Parliament's call.

HYPO LESSON 16 · SECTION 16 · ABOUT 15 MIN · 8 QUESTIONS

Hypos: Singapore bank

⚡ BIG IDEA

Singapore material is evidence, not a trump card. Each hypo tests a claim about Singapore against what the sheet says actually happened.

How to work through a hypo
  1. 1Read the rule (teal box). It is the sheet's wording, so it is what you will write in the exam.
  2. 2Read the hypothetical (amber box). Before reading on, decide what the rule says about these facts.
  3. 3Tap Application (green box) and compare it with your answer.
  4. 4The exam cue (violet box) lists question words that should send you to this block. Each block ends with a quick check.
Applications:
ℹ NOTE
About these hypos

Built on 7 Nov from section 16 of the 7 Nov sheets (identical in the Core and Theorist versions). Same pattern: the item as the sheet states it, a made-up hypothetical in which you'd reach for it, then the application. The bills and fact patterns are invented; the Articles, cases and Hansard lines are the sheet's. The coverage table is the last section.

Abbreviations: LP = legal positivism; NLT = natural law theory; RF = Radbruch formula; TSH = Tan Seow Hon; YVK = Yong Vui Kong; LMS = Lim Meng Suang; PCR = professional conduct rules; † = from the slides.

116.1 Articles

16.1.1 Arts 4 and 162: supremacy

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The item

The Constitution is supreme law. A later inconsistent law is void; an earlier law is read to conform (W13 slide 8†). Use: LP is not thereby chosen (11.1).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A colonial-era ordinance from 1955 lets officials bar people "of bad character" from public parks. A 2020 Act lets the police detain protesters without any hearing. Both are challenged as inconsistent with Part 4.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The 1955 ordinance is pre-existing law, so under Art 162 it is read to conform with the Constitution. For example, "bad character" is read narrowly, to fit Art 12.
  • The 2020 Act is later law. To the extent it is inconsistent with the Constitution, Art 4 makes it void.
  • Neither result makes Singapore positivist. Art 4 is supreme because officials accept it, and reading "consistent with Part 4" still requires deciding what "liberty" and "equal" mean (11.1).

16.1.2 Art 5(2): amendment

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The item

Two-thirds of elected MPs can amend most provisions. Use: basic features were rejected (Teo Soh Lung), and left open in YVK 2015.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

Parliament, by two-thirds, amends Art 9 to allow detention without trial for "economic saboteurs".

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Formally, Art 5(2) allows it.
  • No basic-features shield. Singapore's High Court in Teo Soh Lung rejected the Indian doctrine of unamendable basic features, and the Court of Appeal in YVK 2015 left it open.
  • So the only legal check left is the narrow one TSH defends: an amendment that is intolerably unjust (genocide, slavery) falls to the RF (11.1.3). Economic detention probably doesn't reach that threshold, which shows how much power two-thirds holds (11.7).

16.1.3 Art 9(1): "in accordance with law"

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The item

"No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty save in accordance with law". Use: the four readings of "law"† (W13 slides 16–17).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The Littering (Caning) Bill (11.2).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Run the four readings:

  1. validly passed;
  2. natural justice;
  3. not absurd or arbitrary;
  4. consistent with international law.

The Bill survives each, and falls to the RF only if broad historical consensus condemns it. Choosing among the readings is a choice of theory (11.2).

16.1.4 Art 12: equality

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The item

"All persons are equal before the law and entitled to the equal protection of the law". Use: reasonable classification (11.3).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

The Left-Handed Drivers' Fee (11.3).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

The court asks whether "left-handed" is an intelligible line, rationally related to the regulation's object (road safety). If the link rests on junk science, the classification fails. And TSH adds that deciding which differences are morally significant needs a moral view of equality.

16.1.5 Art 156: marriage

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The item
  • (1) the law may "define, regulate, protect, safeguard, support, foster and promote" marriage;
  • (3)–(4) Part 4 cannot void laws or executive acts based on the man–woman definition, which stays in statute (Interpretation Act s 2(1); Women's Charter s 12(1)).

Use: TSH: a "pre-emptive strike against judicial activism". Liu: unentrenched, so a simple majority may change it (W9).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A couple challenges a Housing Board rule giving priority to married man–woman couples, citing Art 12.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Art 156 shields it. The rule is an executive act based on the man–woman definition of marriage (Women's Charter s 12(1)), so Part 4, including Art 12, can't void it.
  • TSH's view: this is exactly what Art 156 was for, pre-empting a court from redefining marriage through equality rights.
  • Liu's point: Art 156 itself isn't entrenched, so a future Parliament with a simple majority could change it. The shield is political, not permanent.

216.2 Cases

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Eleven Problems, Eleven Cases

For each fact pattern, identify the authority and the angle.

#Fact patternCaseHolding (from the sheet)Angle to argue
1An accused says Art 9's "law" requires a fair procedure, not just any statute.Ong Ah Chuan (PC)Art 9 "law" includes fundamental rules of natural justice.Substantive fairness was left open, and has since been narrowed (YVK 2015†).
2The State argues that any validly passed law binds, fair or not.Jabar (CA 1995)Dictum: law validly passed binds, whether or not "fair, just and reasonable".An LP line, but confined by YVK (2010)†: it isn't about a statute's constitutionality.
3The AG urges the court to ignore foreign rights jurisprudence.Colin Chan (HC 1994)The Constitution is read "within its own four walls"; unity is the "paramount mandate".The LP approach, per Liu† (W13 slide 6). Answer with Haw Tua Tau's universal fairness (11.4).
4A prisoner argues "life" meant 20 years when he was sentenced.Abdul Nasir (CA 1997)†Life imprisonment means natural life, prospectively only.A constancy problem (8.6), not "branded as criminals".
5A challenger says a moral law breaches Art 12, and Art 9 protects privacy.LMS (CA 2014)s 377A passes Art 12. Art 9 covers unlawful deprivation of life and detention, not privacy.Hart v Devlin is "quintessentially" for Parliament.
6A statute is so arbitrary that no framer could have meant it as "law".YVK (CA 2010)†Art 9 may exclude laws so absurd or arbitrary that the framers could not have meant them as law (W13 slide 17).A natural-law hook, short of the RF.
7A convict argues natural law forbids caning.YVK (CA 2015)No right may be made "out of whole cloth" as natural law, so there is no anti-caning right.There was no ruling on what natural law says of caning; and natural justice is procedural† (W13 slide 17).
8Activists seek a declaration that s 377A was unconstitutional.Tan Seng Kee (CA 2022)No standing. Obiter: Arts 9 and 14 likely not breached; Art 12 less definite.The Syed Suhail test might fail s 377A; the law was unenforceable until the AG gave notice†.
9A gay father seeks to adopt his surrogate-born son.UKM (HC 2018)He was allowed to adopt, despite s 377A.The "moral signpost" failed (11.6).
10A citizen convicted for corruption committed abroad claims Art 12 discrimination.Taw Cheng Kong (CA 1998)PCA s 37(1) reaches citizens' acts abroad, even without effects here. There is no Art 12 breach: all are "caught as a class".The presumption of constitutionality.
11A 2021 litigant asks what the last ruling on s 377A held.Ong Ming Johnson (HC 2020)s 377A upheld against Arts 9 and 12.The last ruling before Tan Seng Kee's doubt about Art 12.

How to use the table: in an essay, one case per point is enough. For example, in 11.2 use Ong Ah Chuan plus YVK 2015 for the natural-justice reading. In 3.2, use Tan Seng Kee for non-enforcement. In 7.6, use UKM for why the moral signpost "failed to do the work".

316.3 Hansard: who said what

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Ruritania's Cohabitation Debate

Ruritania's Parliament debates repealing its cohabitation law (7.4). You want a real Singapore speaker to quote for each argument.

Argument you're makingSpeaker and lineHow to use it
Public feeling is strong and divided; the law isn't actively enforcedHo Peng Kee, 22 Oct 2007: feedback was "emotional, divided", with the majority "calling for its retention"; police were not "proactively enforcing".Shows Devlin-style slowness, and the non-enforcement compromise (7.6, 7.7).
Repeal will spill over into public lifede Souza, 22 Oct 2007: "what is in private will not remain private".The principled slope (7.4).
The law breaches equality; harm must be concreteSiew Kum Hong, 22 Oct 2007: s 377A breaches Art 12(1); citing Hor, harm must be "recognisable and tangible".The harm principle, made demanding (7.1, 7.8).
Follow the majority, unless a minority needs protectionIndranee Rajah, 22 Oct 2007: in most cases "we would go with the majority view, unless there is a reason to protect the minority position".The STEELMAN for majority rule (7.11).
Harm can be intangibleThio Li-ann, 22 Oct 2007: harm "can be both physical and intangible".Widens "harm" (7.6).
Unenforced laws damage credibilityHri Kumar Nair, 22 Oct 2007: toothless laws "hurt our credibility".Against non-enforcement (7.7). He also noted that the 70% who "frowned on" it were never asked about criminalising (7.11).
Keep the status quo, and lag behind moral changePM Lee, 23 Oct 2007 (paraphrase): keep the status quo; stay a step behind on moral change.Devlin's slowness, and pragmatism (2.7, 7.6).
Crime needs a public-order reasonShanmugam, 28 Nov 2022: crime "generally" needs "a public order or public interest issue", "broadly similar" to Wolfenden.The FOR for repeal (7.5, 14.12).
Relying on non-enforcement is dangerousPerera, 28 Nov 2022: an unenforced law "based on the word of the government of the day, is unsatisfactory and dangerous".The STEELMAN against non-enforcement (3.2.2).
Sin is not crimePritam Singh, 28 Nov 2022: "In any secular society, sin and crime are separate categories."Against faith-based bans (7.10).
MPs must decide hard questionsMasagos, 29 Nov 2022: Art 156 is meant to prevent a "change in social norms following the repeal"; MPs have a "duty" to "come to a decision".The LEGISLATOR line (12.3).
Let the people decide by referendumPoa, 29 Nov 2022: a PSP referendum, since marriage "is a matter of social norm".The STEELMAN for a referendum (12.3).
Even an unenforced law stigmatisesHe Ting Ru, 29 Nov 2022: a law "plainly and obviously discriminatory" "sends a signal" that an "identity should be considered criminal, even if it is only on paper".Against keeping symbolic laws (3.2, 7.7).
✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

In the Ruritanian debate, pair each argument with its Singapore speaker. For example: "As Pritam Singh put it, in any secular society 'sin and crime are separate categories', so the faith-based case for keeping the law fails." Or: "As Perera warned, a law resting only on a promise not to enforce it is 'unsatisfactory and dangerous'." Quote one or two speakers per essay, not all thirteen.

416.4 Statutes and PCR

16.4.1 Penal Code s 377A

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The item

Criminalised "acts of gross indecency" between males, in public or private. The repeal (2022) came into force on 3 Jan 2023.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A student writes in 2026: "s 377A is still in force but not enforced."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Wrong. It was repealed, with effect from 3 Jan 2023. Use s 377A as history: the 2007 compromise (7.6), Tan Seng Kee (3.2.3), and the 2022 package (13.2).

16.4.2 Penal Code s 121A (before 2019)†

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The item

"imagining" the President's death, hurt or restraint was punishable by death or life imprisonment. It is Liu's example of congruence and discretion (W2 slide 11; 3.2, 3.4).

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A question asks how a law can fail Fuller's congruence requirement.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Old s 121A is the ideal example. "Imagining" can't be observed, so it could only be enforced arbitrarily: a guaranteed gap between rule and official action (congruence), and enforcement at prosecutors' discretion (3.4).

16.4.3 Termination of Pregnancy Act (as TSH described it, 2010–11)

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The item
  • abortion up to 24 weeks for any reason; from 16 weeks, only by a qualified practitioner;
  • later than that, only to save life or prevent grave permanent injury;
  • counselling, then 48 hours;
  • the 1969 Act passed 32–10 on a free vote;
  • the 1974 Act left the choice to the woman: "one of the most liberal in the world".
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

An essay on whether Parliament can stay neutral on abortion (6.5).

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • The 1974 Act leaving the choice to the woman is the "neutral" permissive model that TSH says actually settles the metaphysical question.
  • The 1969 free vote is the precedent for lifting the whip on conscience issues (6.8).
  • Caveat: TSH described the law as it stood in 2010–11, so state it as "as TSH described it".

16.4.4 Professional conduct (Liu, S13)

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The item

Pepper's limit includes the enforced conduct rules (fairness to unrepresented persons, not misleading the court, disclosing adverse authority). So the more robust they are, the less Pepper v Thunder changes what a lawyer does.

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

A Pepper lawyer and a Thunder lawyer both face an unrepresented opponent and an adverse precedent the opponent has missed.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.

Both must disclose the adverse authority, and both must treat the unrepresented person fairly, because the conduct rules require it. So here, Pepper and Thunder act alike. The gap between them is mindset, not outcome (10.10.4).

516.5 Applying the theorists: the 2022 package, and Liu's prompts

16.5.1 Liu's exercise on the 2022 package (W6, W9)

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The item
  • Mill: not enough: a safeguard (Art 156) was kept because the majority wasn't ready.
  • Finnis: likely approves (the common good; life, including procreation; Art 156 promotes). Whether it is "arbitrary" depends on your premises.
  • Rawls, on balance, approves:
    • consultation was the background culture;
    • the consensus reached was "not criminal", not full equality;
    • Art 156 stops courts outrunning that consensus;
    • sending a divisive question to Parliament, not unelected judges, is a public reason.
  • Against Rawls's approval: Rawls's exemplar of public reason is the Supreme Court (Liu, W9).
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL

"The 2022 package was a principled compromise. Assess it from the perspectives of Mill, Finnis and Rawls."

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
  • Mill: repeal is right, since private consensual conduct harms no one. But Art 156 goes further than Mill needs, preserving inequality because the majority wasn't ready.
  • Finnis: probably approves. The state promotes marriage (which serves the goods of life and sociability) without criminalising private conduct. Whether treating same-sex couples differently is "arbitrary" depends on whether you accept his premises about marriage.
  • Rawls, on balance, approves. The consultations were the background culture. The overlap reached was "it shouldn't be a crime", not full equality. Art 156 stops judges outrunning that consensus, and "let Parliament, not unelected judges, decide divisive questions" is itself a public reason.
  • The counterpoint: for Rawls, the paradigm of public reason is a supreme court. So keeping the question from the courts sits awkwardly with his own model.

16.5.2 Week 5b prompts†

▤ ON YOUR SHEET
The item

Apply Rawls and Finnis to surrogacy, casino gambling, POFMA and euthanasia (W5b slide 9). The pointers:

  • POFMA: 15.4, 5.5;
  • casinos: 15.5, 6.4, 5.7;
  • surrogacy: UKM (16.2);
  • euthanasia: Hart's "clouded" consent; for Finnis, intending death chooses against life.
🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Four Bills in One Session

Port Meridian's Parliament considers four bills, on these four issues.

✔ APPLICATIONDecide your answer first, then tap to compare.
IssueFinnisRawlsAlso use
POFMA-style falsehoods lawRun 15.4: protect knowledge; prohibit deliberate lies; prudence on chilling effects (5.5).Are the reasons public, such as an informed electorate?—
Casino licenceIs gambling "play"? Contested (5.7).Run 15.5: sort the four MPs' reasons (6.4).—
SurrogacyCommodifying gestation may treat life and family as means.Needs public reasons (child welfare, exploitation) (6.0).UKM shows the law adapting to surrogacy in practice (16.2).
EuthanasiaIntending death chooses directly against life: barred (15.3).—Hart: consent may be "clouded" (by depression, pressure, transitory despair), which supports strict safeguards (7.2).
